docs.title: Alwyn
docs.text:
Shipwright

Town Bain Harbour Where Shipyard Role Craftsman Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Cheerful, steady and good with his hands, he whistles while he works and never loses his temper. He finds his father's stubbornness exhausting and admires it anyway.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Alwyn is forty-one, and he has been working in the Bain Harbour shipyard since he was old enough to carry a bucket of pitch without spilling it. He is the son of Dunstan, the master shipwright, and everyone on the waterfront knows that the yard will be his one day. Most of them would say it already half is. These days Alwyn does the heavy work: he steams the planks, swings the adze, hauls the timbers into place and climbs the staging in the rain when his father's knees will no longer allow it. He whistles the whole time, and in all his years at the yard nobody has ever heard him lose his temper.

docs.title: The yard and the old man
docs.text:
Alwyn grew up in sawdust. His mother, Senara, painted the names on his father's hulls in curling gold letters, and when she died nine years ago Alwyn took over the brush, because nobody else in the yard had a steady enough hand. He still paints every name the way she taught him, and he has never told Dunstan that he practised for a month in secret before the first one.

He finds his father exhausting. Dunstan is gruff, stubborn and certain, and he talks to the ships as if they were old friends who might take offence. Alwyn has spent years trying to change the old man's mind about one thing in particular: the hulls. Since the deep water turned strange, the water past the headland has grown rougher, and the captains come home with stories of things that bump and scrape beneath them. Alwyn would like to build deeper keels, thicker planking and stronger ribs for the ships that work the deep water. Dunstan says the old designs were good enough for Old Bain, and that is usually the end of the conversation. Alwyn admires that stubbornness even as it drives him to distraction; he knows it is the same stubbornness that has kept every hull his father built afloat.

He gets on well with Peregrine, his father's apprentice, though he has learned to listen to Peregrine's ideas the way a fisherman sorts a catch, keeping one in ten. His oldest friend is Tegan the sailmaker, who has known him since they were both children underfoot in the yard. Tegan is making the sails for this summer's race boat in secret, and she will not tell even Alwyn what she is doing, which she clearly enjoys.

docs.title: Home
docs.text: Alwyn is married to Bryony, the baker of Merchant Street, and their house smells of bread and tar in equal measure. Bryony is up long before the sun and Alwyn is home long after it sets, so they meet in the middle of the day over salt rolls on the shipyard steps. They have two children. Poppy, who is eleven, delivers her mother's bread along Merchant Street and draws the ships in the bay; Alwyn keeps every drawing she gives him pinned up in the yard's tool shed. Kit, who is nine, is never anywhere but the shipyard if he can help it, and Alwyn has given up trying to get the sawdust out of his hair.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Alwyn wants to build a ship that can face whatever is down there and bring its crew home. He fears that one day a ship from his father's yard will not come back, and that he will have known how to make it stronger.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could help Alwyn gather the heavier timber he would need for a deep-water hull, without his father noticing. Or someone might find a way to show Dunstan, with proof he cannot argue with, what the deep water is doing to the old hulls.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Dunstan: father
  • Bryony: wife
  • Kit: son
  • Poppy: daughter
  • Tegan: friend

docs.title: Ambrose
docs.text:
Chartmaker

Town Bain Harbour Where Merchant Street Role Scholar Age Adult Sells Sea charts, tide tables and coastal maps

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Quiet, patient and fond of tiny handwriting. He apologises to his ink when he spills it.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Ambrose is fifty, quiet and patient, and fond of tiny handwriting. He is the chartmaker of Bain Harbour, and every captain in the harbour sails by charts he has drawn. His shop on Merchant Street is narrow, dim and full of paper, and it smells of ink and lamp oil. When he spills his ink, which is rarely, he apologises to it.

docs.title: The chartmaker's trade
docs.text:
Ambrose was born on Merchant Street, the son of a bookbinder long since dead, and he was apprenticed at fifteen to old Hedley, the harbour's chartmaker before him. Hedley was short-sighted, short-tempered and the finest draughtsman Ambrose has ever known. He taught Ambrose to listen to captains more carefully than they speak, because a captain who says "a bit north of the rock" may mean three different things. When Hedley died twenty-five years ago, Ambrose took the shop, the drawers, and the responsibility.

He draws sea charts, tide tables and coastal maps for every ship that leaves the harbour, and he updates them from the reports the captains bring him. He has never been a sailor himself. He gets seasick in a rowing boat on a calm day. But he knows the coast of Veligor better than most people who have sailed it, because every captain in Bain Harbour has described it to him, inch by inch, for twenty-five years.

docs.title: Quenna and Jowan
docs.text:
Ambrose met Quenna when she came into the shop as a young sailor, loudly demanding a chart of a stretch of coast that, he patiently explained, nobody had charted yet. She came back the next season with the soundings herself. They were married twenty-one years ago, and they are about as different as two people can be: she is brisk and loud and decides everything before the tide turns, and he takes a week over a single headland. He thinks she is the bravest person alive. She says he is the only person in the harbour she cannot rush.

Their son, Jowan, joined the Harbour Watch last spring. He has his mother's need to act and his father's handwriting, and Ambrose worries quietly that the first will one day carry him somewhere the second cannot follow.

docs.title: The locked drawer
docs.text:
Since the deep water turned strange, captains have been bringing Ambrose a new kind of mark: a place where something was seen in the water. A shape under the keel. A pale light far out. A net torn clean through. At first he added them to the ordinary charts, until he realised that frightened sailors were steering around them and missing the channels. So he started a separate chart, and he keeps it locked in a drawer in his workroom.

Very few people know about it. Quenna does, and each summer she takes the worst of its marks to the race and shares them with Goa Harbour's First Warden. Some of the captains know, because they bring the marks. Ambrose does not know what the marks mean, and he refuses to guess on paper. He has noticed only that there are more of them each year, and that they seem to be creeping closer to the headland.

docs.title: Poppy
docs.text: Poppy, the baker's daughter, has watched him through his shop window for years. One morning he invited her in, and now she comes every morning after her bread round. She has the steadiest hand and the sharpest eye he has seen since Hedley, and he has started teaching her properly. He has not shown her the locked drawer. He suspects she knows it is there.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could carry a sighting to Ambrose, check one of the marks on the locked chart in person, or help him chart a stretch of coast that changed after a storm.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Quenna: wife
  • Jowan: son
  • Poppy: admirer

docs.title: Barnaby
docs.text:
Bosun of the Bright Morrow

Town Bain Harbour Where Docks Role Worker Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Big, booming and soft-hearted, with a story for every scar. No one is sure how many of his stories are true.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Barnaby is the bosun of the Bright Morrow, and he is the biggest man on the Bain Harbour docks and very nearly the loudest. He is forty-six, big, booming and soft-hearted, with a laugh that rattles the rigging and a story for every scar. He has a great many scars. No one is sure how many of the stories are true, including, on some evenings, Barnaby.

docs.title: A story for every scar
docs.text:
Barnaby has been at sea since he was a boy, and he has been bosun of the Bright Morrow for nine years, since the day Captain Seraphine bought her. As bosun he looks after the ship's rigging, sails, anchors and boats, and the crew who work them, and he does it with enormous care and a great deal of noise. He can splice a line faster than anyone in the harbour and sings while he does it, badly. The crew love him. They also know that if they leave a rope uncoiled on his deck, the whole Waterfront will hear about it.

The scar across his left hand, he says, came from a swordfish that leapt over the bow and tried to steal his dinner. The one on his chin came from a fight with three smugglers in a sea cave, or from a gull, depending on who is listening. The long one on his forearm is from a parted line in a storm, and that one is true, because Seraphine was there; she says he caught the line before it took a sailor's head off, and Barnaby, for once, does not tell that story at all.

His most devoted listener is Finch, the dock errand runner, who sits on the bollards beside the Bright Morrow whenever she is in harbour and hears every story twice. Barnaby gives him the best ones. He has never had a son, and he would not say that is what Finch is to him, but he keeps a twist of barley sugar in his coat pocket for the boy on every voyage, and it has never once come home uneaten.

docs.title: The eyes
docs.text:
Last autumn, on a moonlit night far out in deep water, Barnaby was alone on deck with the watch asleep at the wheel, and he looked over the side. A pair of eyes as large as cartwheels looked back up at him from under the Bright Morrow's hull. They did not blink. Then they sank away into the dark, slowly, as if whatever owned them was in no hurry at all.

Barnaby told the story on the Waterfront the next day, and the Waterfront laughed, because it was Barnaby, and because the eyes were as large as cartwheels. He laughed along. He has told it many times since, and it is the only one of his stories that has never grown in the telling. Two people have never laughed at it. One is Finch, who believes every word. The other is Captain Seraphine, who listened to it once in silence and then went to her cabin and shut the door. Barnaby has thought about that a great deal.

He has not slept on deck since. He used to sling a hammock under the stars on every warm night of every voyage. Now he sleeps below, in the forecastle with the crew, and when the others tease him about it he tells them his back is getting old. It is not his back.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Barnaby wants someone to believe him who is not ten years old. He fears that if he ever looks over the side again on a moonlit night, the eyes will be closer.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could stand the night watch on the Bright Morrow and look over the side for him, sort the true stories from the tall ones, or find out what Seraphine knows that made her shut her cabin door.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Seraphine: captain
  • Finch: devoted listener

docs.title: Barnacle
docs.text:
Harbour Cat

Town Bain Harbour Where Fish Market Role Animal Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Lazy, greedy and dignified. She sleeps in the sun on the fish market steps and accepts tribute from all who pass.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Barnacle is the harbour cat of Bain Harbour. She is a large, well-fed tabby with a white chest, one torn ear and the bearing of a duchess, and she belongs to nobody and to everybody. She is lazy, greedy and dignified. She sleeps in the sun on the fish market steps and accepts tribute from all who pass, and she has never once said thank you.

docs.title: How she came
docs.text:
Nobody knows exactly where Barnacle came from. The most common story is that about seven years ago a scrawny striped kitten walked down the gangplank of a coasting ship that had just tied up, crossed the quay without looking left or right, climbed the fish market steps and lay down in the sun as if she had booked the place. The ship sailed on the next tide without her, and nobody aboard seemed to miss her.

Hesketh, the oyster seller, says he named her, on account of the way she stuck to the steps. Gwennol, the fishmonger at the next stall, says loudly that she named her and that Hesketh has never had an idea of his own in thirty years. The two of them have argued about it ever since, which is to say about as often as they argue about everything else. Barnacle answers to neither of them, and to anyone holding a fish.

docs.title: Her day
docs.text:
Barnacle's day runs on a strict schedule of her own design. At dawn she is at the Fish Market as the boats come in, sitting very straight and very still beside whichever stall is gutting first. Hesketh feeds her better than he feeds himself: the best of the scraps, an oyster now and then, and once, famously, half of his own dinner. She eats it with an air of doing him a favour. Bree, the fishmonger's daughter, slips her fish when nobody is looking, which Barnacle permits.

By mid-morning she has moved to the warmest step, beside Wenna the net-mender, who gives her fish heads and calls her the only creature in the market with any sense. Barnacle sleeps there through the middle of the day, belly to the sun, while the whole market steps around her. Jowan of the Harbour Watch salutes her when he passes. She does not return it.

In the evening she visits the back door of the Salt and Bread, where the kitchen sometimes has something for her and sometimes does not, and at night she goes to work. She hunts rats in the harbour warehouses, and old Hobart the warehouseman leaves a side door open a crack for her. He says she is the only member of staff who never miscounts.

docs.title: The water's edge
docs.text:
For most of her life Barnacle hunted along the tideline too. She would pick her way over the slipway at low tide after crabs and small fish left by the water, and sit at the very end of the quay watching the boats come in, with her tail hanging over the edge.

Then, a little over a year ago, she stopped. One morning on the slipway she froze, stared at the water, flattened her ears and went back up the steps at a run, and she has not been closer to the sea than the top step since. She will not walk the quay. She will not go down to the slipway even when the tide leaves fish flapping on it. If a bucket of seawater is set down near her, she moves.

The fishmongers have noticed. They say she has not gone near the water's edge since whatever she saw that morning, and that she is smarter than all of them. Bree finds it suspicious and has said so to everyone. Some of the older fishermen have quietly started to watch where Barnacle will and will not sit, the way their grandparents watched the gulls.

docs.title: What she wants
docs.text: Barnacle wants sun, fish and a lap at a time of her own choosing. She fears nothing on land, including dogs, dockworkers and Captain Seraphine. What she fears in the water, she cannot say.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could follow Barnacle on her night rounds through the warehouses, find out what she saw on the slipway the morning she stopped going down, or settle once and for all whether Hesketh or Gwennol gave her her name.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Hesketh: feeder

docs.title: Bree
docs.text:
Fishmonger's Daughter

Town Bain Harbour Where Fish Market Role Child Age Child

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Bossy, bright and absolutely fearless around anything with claws. She names every crab she catches.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Bree is ten years old and already runs a business. She is the daughter of Gwennol the fishmonger and Cobb the fisherman, the younger sister of Lowen and the granddaughter of Wenna the net-mender, and she helps at her mother's stall in the Fish Market most days. She is bossy, bright and absolutely fearless around anything with claws.

docs.title: The crab shell trade
docs.text:
Bree catches crabs in the rock pools under the harbour wall at low tide. She names every one of them, and she remembers the names. The big ones go to her mother's stall. The empty shells, scrubbed and dried in the sun, she sells to the other harbour children, who use them as boats, helmets, money and treasure. She charges a copper for a small shell and two for a large one, and she keeps her accounts on a slate under the stall. Ottilie, the clerk of the Harbour Hall, once saw the slate and said it was neater than half the ledgers she receives, and Bree has never forgotten it.

She has a long-running and entirely one-sided rivalry with Hesketh, the oyster seller at the next stall, who argues with her mother every single day. Bree has decided that if her mother is going to argue with him, she will too. Hesketh complains about her constantly and saves her the prettiest oyster shells.

She also feeds Barnacle, the harbour cat, scraps of fish when nobody is looking, which is how she learned that Barnacle will not go anywhere near the water's edge any more. Bree finds this suspicious and has said so to everyone.

docs.title: The family
docs.text:
Her mother has the loudest voice in the Fish Market and Bree intends to have the second loudest. Her father is quiet and lets her mother do the talking, and Bree loves him for being the one person who listens to every word she says. Lately he has been quieter than usual. She knows his nets came up torn twice this year, because her grandmother says so to anyone who will listen, and she knows that whatever did it was not, according to her grandmother, any fish Wenna ever knew.

Her brother Lowen has just signed on to his first trading voyage, and the house has been loud about it. Bree is on Lowen's side, mostly because she wants to go to sea herself and thinks it sets a good example.

docs.title: The race
docs.text: More than anything in the world, Bree wants to sail in the summer race around Veligor. She knows exactly how many times Bain Harbour has beaten Goa Harbour since the Harbour Master took the helm, and she can recite the winning margins. She has told Quenna, twice, to her face, that she is small enough to fit anywhere on a boat and light enough not to slow it down. Quenna laughed both times, which Bree has decided means "not yet" rather than "no".

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Bree wants to be the youngest sailor ever to crew the race boat. She is not afraid of the sea, but she is afraid of something happening to her father or brother out on it, and she would never say so.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could start in the rock pools, where Bree has found a crab that is not like any crab she has ever named, or with Bree stowing away aboard a boat on the morning of the race.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Gwennol: mother
  • Cobb: father
  • Lowen: brother
  • Wenna: grandmother

docs.title: Brisa
docs.text:
Harbour Watchwoman

Town Bain Harbour Where Waterfront Role Guard Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Sharp, fast and impatient, with a quick tongue and quicker feet. She can outrun anyone on the waterfront and likes to prove it.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Brisa is a watchwoman of the Harbour Watch, and she is the fastest runner on the Bain Harbour waterfront. She is nineteen, sharp, fast and impatient, with a quick tongue and quicker feet, and she likes to prove both. If a pickpocket runs on the docks, Brisa catches him. If someone says she cannot, she catches him faster.

docs.title: Why she joined
docs.text:
Brisa grew up on the Waterfront, the daughter of a fish-gutter and a carter, and spent her childhood running. She ran errands, ran races, ran away from the Fish Market whenever there was work to do there. Three years ago her parents moved inland to a cousin's farm near Kaldemor, where the work was steadier and the roads were said to be quieter. Brisa was sixteen. She refused to go, found a room above a sailmaker's loft, and stayed. Her parents write at harvest. She writes back at midwinter, briefly.

She joined the Harbour Watch last spring, not because she wanted to keep the peace, which she finds a little dull, but because it was the best way to see everything that happens in town. The Watch walks every pier and every alley, and it hears every story first, or at least second, after Finch the errand runner, who hears everything first and whom Brisa respects for it. Finch is also the only person on the waterfront who comes close to outrunning her. Twice since the night watch on the outer pier began, she has caught him trying to slip out along it in the dark, marched him back to the dock office, and threatened to tell Garrow the foreman. She has not told Garrow. She remembers what it was like to want to see everything.

docs.title: Jowan
docs.text:
Jowan joined the Watch at about the same time, and he is her friendly rival in all things. He is earnest, careful and far too proud of his coat; she is quick, careless and has never once worn hers buttoned properly. They compete over who reaches a disturbance first, who makes the catch, and whose report Halloran reads to the end. Brisa always arrives first. Jowan always writes more. She has never told him that his reports are better than hers, and she never will, but she has started reading them when he is not looking.

Halloran, their captain, settles most trouble with a hand on the shoulder and a mug of something hot, which Brisa thinks is far too slow and works far too well. She admires him and argues with him in roughly equal measure. Lately he has been standing a watch on the outer pier at night and will not say why, and it is driving her to distraction.

docs.title: The list
docs.text: Since she joined, Brisa has kept a list of the strange things the sailors report: a light under the water, a hull scraped in water too deep for rocks, a net cut clean through, a seal that would not come near the rocks. She writes them in a sewn notebook she keeps inside her coat, with the date and the name of whoever told her, and there are more than sixty entries now. She does not know what they mean. She thinks someone important ought to read it one day, and she would very much like to be standing there when they do. She has no idea that Delphine at the Salt and Bread has been keeping a ledger of her own, or that Halloran has never thought to ask for hers.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could take Brisa's list to someone who can make sense of it, race her along the waterfront for a wager, or help her find out, at last, what Halloran is watching for on the outer pier.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Halloran: commander
  • Jowan: friendly rival

docs.title: Bryony
docs.text:
Baker of Merchant Street

Town Bain Harbour Where Merchant Street Sells Bread, salt rolls and sailors' hard biscuits

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Alwyn: husband
  • Kit: son
  • Poppy: daughter
  • Delphine: customer

docs.title: Annis
docs.text:
Captain of the Saltlark

Town Bain Harbour Where Docks Role Council Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Weathered, blunt and superstitious, with a ritual for everything from casting off to tying her boots. She trusts the sea more than people, and people only a little.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Annis is seventy-six, the captain of the Saltlark, and the oldest captain on the harbour council. She is weathered, blunt and superstitious, and she has a ritual for everything, from tying her boots (left first, double knot, never on the deck) to casting off (a pinch of salt over the stern and a word to the water that nobody has ever been close enough to hear). She trusts the sea more than she trusts people, and people only a little.

docs.title: A long life on the water
docs.text:
Annis was born in a fisherman's cottage on the Waterfront and went to sea at ten, and she has commanded the Saltlark for forty-four years. The Saltlark is a small, deep, stubborn coasting ship, almost as old as her captain, and Annis will hear no word against her. Annis has never married and has no children. "The Saltlark is enough trouble," she says, and she means it fondly.

She remembers when the bay was as calm as a millpond. When she was young, she says, you could row out past the headland on a summer evening and hear nothing but the oars and the gulls, and the deep water was simply deep water. She does not say this as an old woman's complaint about the past. She says it as a captain giving a report.

docs.title: The water has changed
docs.text:
Since the Disturbance began, Annis has watched the sea change, slowly at first and then less slowly. The swells come wrong. The fish run in the wrong places. Birds she has known all her life no longer settle on the water past the headland. And on the Saltlark's last voyage, in deep water on a still night, something large brushed along her keel from bow to stern and was gone. The whole ship felt it. Annis took the Saltlark home at once, and the next morning she went to Ambrose the chartmaker and gave him the mark herself.

Her sailor Morwenna, who has crewed for her for twelve years and who is the closest thing Annis has to family, felt it too. Annis has noticed that Morwenna has not talked about it at home, and she has not pressed her.

Annis wants the harbour council to take the sea seriously before something goes wrong. She does not know what she wants it to do, exactly, and that is her trouble: every time she says so, Captain Corwin asks her what she would have them do and what it would cost. Corwin is her favourite rival on the council. They disagree on harbour dues, on loading order, on whether a ship should cast off under a new moon (it should not), and on almost everything else. She thinks he is a fine seaman and an infuriating man, and she would trust him with her ship, which she would not say about anyone else on the council.

docs.title: The old rival
docs.text: Her oldest rival is Thaddeus, who now spends his days on a bench by the water. When they were young, the two of them raced each other across the bay at every chance and quarrelled over who ought to skipper the harbour's boat in the summer race around Veligor. More than thirty years ago the helm went to Thaddeus, and he lost to Goa Harbour by a boat's length. Annis has told him ever since that she would have won. Thaddeus says she would have lost by two. They have had this argument several hundred times and both of them would be lost without it.

docs.title: What she fears
docs.text: Annis is not afraid of storms, or of wrecks, or of dying at sea, which she has always expected to do. She is afraid that the harbour will wait for proof until the proof is a ship that does not come home.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could sail on the Saltlark to the place where her keel was brushed, help Annis put a case to the council that even Corwin cannot dismiss, or perform one of her rituals for her when, for the first time in forty-four years, she cannot.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Corwin: council rival
  • Morwenna: sailor
  • Thaddeus: old racing rival

docs.title: Corwin
docs.text:
Captain of the Heron

Town Bain Harbour Where Docks Role Council Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Calm, dry and slow to speak, the kind of captain who never raises his voice because he never needs to. He hates waste and loves a good argument.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Corwin is fifty-two and has been captain of the Heron for twenty years, running cargo up and down the coast of Veligor without losing a single crate. He is calm, dry and slow to speak, and he never raises his voice, because he has never needed to. Crews who have sailed with him say that a quiet word from Corwin is worse than a shouting from any other captain in the harbour, and that he has never once given an order twice.

docs.title: Twenty years without a crate
docs.text:
Corwin went to sea as a cabin boy and worked his way aft over many years, as a deckhand, then a bosun, then a first mate on other men's ships. He bought a share in the Heron at thirty-two, and the rest of her a few years later with money he had saved by never wasting any. The Heron is not the fastest ship in the harbour, a fact Captain Seraphine likes to mention, but she is the most reliable. Merchants who want their goods to arrive on time, dry and complete send them on the Heron, and they pay a little more for it without complaining.

That record is Corwin's pride. He keeps every cargo list he has ever signed in a sea chest in his cabin, and he can tell you what the Heron carried on any voyage in the last twenty years if you give him a minute.

docs.title: The council
docs.text:
Corwin sits on the harbour council, and Quenna, the Harbour Master, counts him among the people she relies on most. He is not her friend in the way Mabyn is, but she trusts his judgement because he hates waste of every kind: wasted money, wasted time, wasted words. He also loves a good argument, and the council gives him one most weeks.

His favourite opponent is Captain Annis of the Saltlark. They disagree on almost everything: harbour dues, the order ships should load in, whether a captain ought to cast off under a new moon. Since the deep water turned strange, their arguments have turned to it. Annis wants the council to act on what the sailors are seeing. Corwin wants to know what, exactly, she would have them do, and what it would cost. In truth he takes the sea as seriously as she does, and he has more than once carried his own marks to Ambrose the chartmaker after a bad night. He simply will not agree with Annis in public, because neither of them would know what to do if he did.

docs.title: The cost of safety
docs.text: Corwin now pays adventurers to sail with every voyage, and he grumbles about the cost at every council meeting. His regular hire is Tristram, a harpooner who used to hunt big fish and now stands at the Heron's bow in deep water, still as a post, for hours at a time. Corwin thinks Tristram is worth every coin, and complains about every coin anyway.

docs.title: Family
docs.text: Corwin has no wife or children. His nephew Caspian is the Heron's navigator, the youngest in the harbour, and Corwin is quietly very proud of him, though he would sooner lose a crate than say so. He knows Caspian hopes to navigate the race boat this summer. He has also noticed that the boy goes pale when a storm builds, and he has said nothing about that either. This summer he has taken on Lowen, the fisherman's son and Caspian's friend, as a deckhand, on Caspian's word.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could sail with the Heron as a hired guard, find out why one of her regular cargoes has started arriving short, or settle, once and for all, one of Corwin's arguments with Annis.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Quenna: council chair
  • Annis: council rival
  • Caspian: nephew
  • Tristram: hired harpooner

docs.title: Seraphine
docs.text:
Captain of the Bright Morrow

Town Bain Harbour Where Docks Role Worker Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Bold, restless and fond of a grand gesture. She never turns down a dare and rarely turns down a contract.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Seraphine is the captain of the Bright Morrow, the fastest trading ship in Bain Harbour, and she would like you to know it. She is thirty-six, bold, restless and fond of a grand gesture. She never turns down a dare and rarely turns down a contract, and she brings the Bright Morrow into harbour under more sail than anyone thinks wise, swinging up to the pier with a flourish that makes the dockworkers duck and Garrow the foreman swear.

docs.title: The fastest ship in the harbour
docs.text:
Seraphine went to sea at fourteen as a ship's girl on a coasting trader, and she spent the next thirteen years climbing from the rigging to the quarterdeck on other people's ships, impatient at every step. At twenty-seven she bought the Bright Morrow from a merchant who was giving up the sea. She was old and slow then, and everyone on the Waterfront told Seraphine she had paid too much. Seraphine rebuilt her rig with taller masts and more canvas, scraped her hull clean, and within a year the Bright Morrow was beating every ship in the harbour from the headland to the pier. That was nine years ago. She has not been beaten since, and she has never let anyone forget it.

She carries spices, cloth and anything that needs to arrive quickly, and merchants pay her a premium for speed the way they pay Captain Corwin of the Heron a premium for care. Seraphine and Corwin are opposites and both enjoy it. She likes to remind him, loudly and at the council's door, that the Heron is the second fastest ship in the harbour at best. He likes to remind her, quietly, that he has never lost a crate. Ysolde, the Keeper of the Light, tells her every chance she gets that she comes in far too fast and will one day meet the harbour wall. Seraphine blows her a kiss from the deck.

docs.title: What she saw
docs.text:
Seraphine has sailed more deep-water voyages than any other captain in the harbour, because the fastest routes run furthest out, and she has seen more of the new creatures in the deep water than anyone. She will not describe what she saw. Asked about it at the Salt and Bread, she laughs and changes the subject, and if pressed she buys the whole table a drink, which is a grand gesture and also a very effective way of ending a conversation.

What she does instead is pay. Since that voyage she has sailed with hired adventurers on every trip, more of them than any other captain, and she pays them better than anyone on the waterfront. Her current favourite is Keziah, a sword for hire from inland who counts the exits in every room and has a dry wit Seraphine enjoys. Seraphine has asked Keziah to sign on for the whole summer, and she does not understand why such a cool head always looks so grey at sea.

Her bosun, Barnaby, has sailed with her since the day she bought the ship. He is big, loud and soft-hearted, and his stories are famous for being exaggerated. When he came back from the night watch last autumn and told the Waterfront about a pair of eyes as large as cartwheels looking up at him from under the hull, everyone laughed. Seraphine did not. She listened to the end, went to her cabin, and shut the door. She has never told him why.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Seraphine wants to be the first ship to sail somewhere no Bain Harbour ship has been, and she keeps a blank sheet of chart paper rolled in her cabin, for waters past the edge of anything Ambrose the chartmaker has drawn, on which she means to draw the first line herself. She fears nothing she will name. But she has stopped taking dares that involve the deep water at night.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could sign on as one of Seraphine's hired adventurers, take her up on a dare she cannot refuse, or find out what she saw from her deck, which she has told no one at all.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Barnaby: bosun
  • Keziah: hired sword

docs.title: Caspian
docs.text:
Navigator of the Heron

Town Bain Harbour Where Docks Role Worker Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Confident, clever and a bit vain about his star-reckoning. He is secretly afraid of storms.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Caspian is the navigator of the Heron, and at twenty he is the youngest navigator in Bain Harbour. He is confident, clever and a little vain about his star-reckoning: he can put the Heron's position on a chart within a mile on a clear night, and he will tell you so before you ask. He is Captain Corwin's nephew, and he is secretly, badly afraid of storms.

docs.title: The night of the storm
docs.text:
Caspian's father, Petroc, was a sailor on a coasting trader, and his mother, Kerra, is Corwin's younger sister. When Caspian was seven, a winter storm came up the coast in a single afternoon, and Petroc's ship did not come home. Caspian remembers standing on the harbour wall with his mother in the rain, watching the lighthouse beam swing out over water so rough it looked white, and waiting for a sail that never came. He has never told anyone that he remembers it so clearly.

His uncle looked after them both from then on, in the quiet way Corwin does everything: money left on the table without comment, a word with a merchant here and there, and a seat at his own table every time the Heron was in. When Caspian was thirteen, Corwin took him aboard as cabin boy. Five years ago his mother married again, a lamp-oil merchant from Selsior, and moved there with him. Caspian chose to stay with the Heron. She writes to him every midwinter, and he writes back at length about stars.

docs.title: Reading the sky
docs.text:
Caspian learned the names of the stars in Maren's front room on Merchant Street, sitting on an upturned crate, and outgrew her lessons in about a year. After that he learned from the Heron's old navigator, Jago, who taught him to take a star's height with a quadrant, to keep a dead-reckoning log in a hand neat enough for Ambrose to read, and never to trust a coastline in fog. When Jago died two years ago, Corwin made Caspian navigator in his place. Some of the older captains muttered that it was family favour. Caspian answered them by bringing the Heron home on time, every time, and he still enjoys mentioning it.

He is proud of his skill, and a bit vain about it, and he knows it. He keeps his quadrant polished like a sword and has opinions about every chart in Ambrose's shop. Corwin says nothing about any of this, which Caspian takes, correctly, as approval.

docs.title: Storms
docs.text: The fear is the part nobody sees. On a clear night Caspian is the most confident sailor aboard. When the sky thickens and the swell begins to come wrong, his hands go cold and he cannot stop thinking of the harbour wall in the rain. He does his work anyway, perfectly, and believes no one has noticed. In fact his uncle has noticed him go pale more than once, and has said nothing about it, which is exactly how Corwin shows he cares.

docs.title: Lowen
docs.text: Caspian's closest friend is Lowen, the fisherman's son, three years younger and far less sure of himself. They met on the harbour wall when Lowen was a boy gutting fish for his mother's stall and Caspian was a cabin boy showing off the stars, and Lowen was the only one who actually wanted to learn them. This summer, when Lowen wanted to go to sea against his father's wishes, Caspian put in a word with his uncle, and Corwin took Lowen on as a deckhand for the Heron's next coastal run. Caspian feels responsible for him, and a little frightened by how much.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Caspian wants to be chosen as navigator for this summer's race around Veligor. The Harbour Master picks her own crew, and he means to make the choice obvious. He fears that the race, or some voyage after it, will run into a storm, and that the whole harbour will finally see his hands shake.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could sail with the Heron through a bad night and help Caspian hold his nerve without letting anyone see, find the star sights Jago swore by in a notebook nobody has opened since his death, or help Caspian prove to Quenna that he is the navigator her race boat needs.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Corwin: uncle
  • Lowen: friend

docs.title: Clemence
docs.text:
Harbour Healer

Town Bain Harbour Where Waterfront Role Healer Age Adult Sells Salves, bandages and seasickness tonic

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Calm, practical and gently teasing. She has seen every kind of injury a ship can cause and is unimpressed by most of them.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Clemence is the harbour healer, and her door on the Waterfront is the one people knock on when a rope has taken the skin off their palms, a hook has gone where a hook should not go, or a crate has landed on a foot. She is fifty-two, calm, practical and gently teasing, and she has seen every kind of injury a ship can cause. Most of them do not impress her. Sailors who come in white-faced and groaning are told, kindly, that they will live, and that they should have worn gloves.

docs.title: The healer's house
docs.text:
Clemence was born in the narrow house where she still works, a few doors from the Salt and Bread, with bunches of herbs hanging from every beam and a smell of camphor that clings to the curtains. Her mother, Tressa, was the harbour healer before her, and Clemence grew up rolling bandages, grinding salves and holding the lamp while her mother stitched. When Tressa died twenty-two years ago, Clemence was thirty and had been doing half the work already. Nobody asked who the new healer was. They simply kept knocking.

She never married. She says she has enough people relying on her as it is. Her house has a front door for ordinary trouble and a back door onto the alley for people who would rather not be seen coming in, and she keeps both doors' secrets equally.

She sells salves, bandages and seasickness tonic. The tonic is her mother's recipe, made with ginger and peppermint, and she buys the ginger from Marisol on Merchant Street. Lately Marisol's ginger has come in late, and twice this spring Clemence has had to make the tonic weaker than she likes.

docs.title: Ysolde
docs.text:
Her closest friend is Ysolde, the Keeper of the Light. The friendship began sixteen years ago, on the day Ysolde's husband Kenver died suddenly while mending his nets on the fish market steps. Wenna, who was mending beside him, sent a boy running for Clemence, and there was nothing to be done. Clemence was the one who climbed the lighthouse stairs to tell Ysolde. Ysolde listened, nodded, and then went up and lit the lamp, because ships were out. Clemence stayed with her at the top of the tower until the morning, and has been climbing those hundred and seventeen stairs ever since.

These days she goes up once a week with a salve for Ysolde's knees, and the two of them drink tea at the top of the tower and agree about almost everyone in Bain Harbour. Clemence is the only visitor Ysolde invites, and she knows it. She does not know about the pale lights her friend has seen under the water. Ysolde has never mentioned them, and Clemence, who notices most things, has noticed only that Ysolde looks out past the headland a little longer than she used to.

docs.title: The back door
docs.text: Her most regular back-door patient is Keziah, the young sword for hire who sails with Captain Seraphine. Before every voyage of the Bright Morrow, Keziah knocks at dawn for a bottle of seasickness tonic, and Clemence hands it over with a remark about sailors who cannot keep their breakfast down. She has never told anyone, and she never will. She teases Keziah only gently, because she thinks the girl is braver than half the captains in the harbour for going to sea at all.

docs.title: The notes
docs.text:
Lately Clemence has been treating injuries she cannot explain. A deckhand came in with a row of round welts across his forearm, each the size of a coin, from something he never saw. A dockworker had a long, shallow scrape down his calf, too straight for a rock and too clean for a hook. Twice there have been stings that matched no jellyfish she knows, and she knows them all. Clemence writes each one down in a casebook: the date, the patient, the ship, the wound, and what the patient said happened, which is rarely the same as what she thinks happened.

She has not shown the casebook to anyone. She suspects others in the harbour are keeping notes of their own, and she has begun to wonder what would happen if they were laid side by side.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Clemence wants to understand what she is treating, because she cannot treat properly what she cannot name. She fears the day someone is carried to her door with a wound she cannot close.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could bring Clemence ginger from a cargo that never arrived, find the creature that left a row of coin-sized welts on a deckhand's arm, or carry her casebook to someone else who has been writing things down.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Ysolde: friend
  • Keziah: secret patient

docs.title: Cobb
docs.text:
Fisherman

Town Bain Harbour Where Fish Market Role Worker Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Quiet, steady and soft-spoken, he lets his wife do the talking and seems happy about it. He knows every rock in the bay.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Cobb is forty-four, a fisherman of the bay, and the quietest member of the loudest family in the Fish Market. He is married to Gwennol, whose voice carries across the whole market, and he is perfectly happy to let her do the talking. He is the son of Wenna the net-mender and the father of Lowen and Bree. He is steady and soft-spoken, and he knows every rock in the bay.

docs.title: The little boat
docs.text:
Cobb fishes from a small open boat called the Puffin, which his grandfather built more than sixty years ago from timber he hauled down from the hills himself. She has been patched, re-planked and re-caulked so many times that there may not be a single original board left in her, but Cobb says she is still his grandfather's boat, and nobody argues with him. He takes her out before dawn every day the weather allows and is back by mid-morning, so that Gwennol has fish to sell while it is still fresh.

His father, Davey, fished the bay from the same boat until he died of a winter fever twelve years ago. Cobb learned the water from him the old way: by rowing it, by watching it, and by losing nets to every rock until he remembered where they were. He can tell you the depth over any rock in the bay from the colour of the water above it, and he has never lost a net to one since he was twenty.

docs.title: Torn nets
docs.text:
Twice this year Cobb's nets have come up torn clean through. Not snagged or frayed, as a rock or a dogfish might leave them, but opened in a long straight rent, as if something had simply gone through them. Both times it was in the deeper water just inside the headland, where he has fished all his life. His mother mended both nets on the fish market steps and announced to the whole market that no fish she ever knew made tears like that. Cobb did not disagree.

He has said nothing about it to the council, because he is not the kind of man who speaks at councils, but he has stopped going out past the middle of the bay. He always meant to take his son out deeper with him, once Lowen was old enough. Now he wants to know what tore his nets before he takes anyone out there.

docs.title: His son
docs.text:
Lowen did not wait. He signed on as a deckhand aboard Captain Corwin's Heron for a trading voyage along the coast, against his father's wishes. Cobb has not shouted about it; Gwennol did enough shouting for both of them. He knows the Heron is the most careful ship in the harbour and that Corwin has not lost a crate in twenty years. He also knows that crates are not sons. He is proud of the boy and frightened for him, and he has not yet found the words for either.

His daughter Bree is the opposite of him in every way, and he adores her. She tells him everything, at length, and he listens to every word.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Cobb wants a quiet bay and his family around the table in the evening. He fears whatever is out past the middle of the bay, and he fears it more because he cannot name it.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could go out with Cobb in the Puffin to see what tears his nets, or bring him proof of what it was so that he can finally sleep.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Gwennol: wife
  • Bree: daughter
  • Lowen: son
  • Wenna: mother

docs.text:
Cloth Merchant

Town Bain Harbour Where Merchant Street Sells Woollens, oilskins and bright cloth

docs.text: • Marisol: business partner

docs.title: Delphine
docs.text:
Innkeeper of the Salt and Bread

Town Bain Harbour Where Waterfront Role Service Age Adult Sells Hot meals, ale and rooms by the night

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Generous, sharp and unflappable, she can quiet a room of sailors with one look. She never forgets a debt or a kindness.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Delphine is forty-three and keeps the Salt and Bread, the busiest inn on the Bain Harbour waterfront. She is generous, sharp and unflappable, and she can quiet a room full of sailors with a single look. She never forgets a debt or a kindness, and she keeps both in the same book behind the bar, in two columns.

docs.title: The Salt and Bread
docs.text:
The Salt and Bread has stood on the waterfront for three generations. Delphine's grandmother opened it in a former net loft, her mother kept it after, and Delphine grew up between the kitchen and the taproom, carrying mugs before she could see over the bar. Her mother, Ysella, died eight years ago and left the inn to her. Delphine has changed almost nothing, except to put in more tables, because there are always more sailors.

It is a warm, loud place with low beams, a great fire and a long table near the hearth where the ships' crews sit. The bread comes fresh every morning from Bryony's bakery on Merchant Street, and Delphine says without embarrassment that half her custom comes for Bryony's salt rolls. The hot meals come from Delphine's own kitchen. Rooms are let by the night, mostly to sailors between ships and, more and more these days, to the adventurers who come to the harbour looking for work on the captains' voyages.

Most nights Lorcan sings. He is dramatic, charming and hopeless with money, and he owes Delphine more than he would like to calculate. She keeps him on because he can make the whole inn sing by the second verse, and because a full room drinks more. Lorcan is writing a new shanty about the summer race and needs Bain Harbour to win so that he can finish it. Delphine has told him to write two endings.

docs.title: Her brother
docs.text: Delphine's brother is Halloran, captain of the Harbour Watch. He drinks at the Salt and Bread most evenings after his rounds and settles most of the waterfront's trouble before it reaches her door. They have looked after each other since their mother died, and they are as alike as two people can be who have chosen opposite sides of a bar. Lately Halloran has been posting a watch on the outer pier at night. He tells her it is a precaution. She knows her brother, and she knows it is more than that.

docs.title: The book of tales
docs.text:
The sailors gather at the Salt and Bread to swap tales of what they saw at sea, and since the deep water turned strange the tales have changed. Once they were about storms, mermaids and the one that got away. Now they are about shapes under the keel, lights in the deep water and nets torn clean through, and the people telling them are not drunk and not laughing.

So Delphine has started writing the strangest ones down. She keeps them in a ledger of their own, separate from her accounts, with the teller's name, the ship, the date and, as near as she can get it, the place. She thinks someone ought to. She does not know who should read it. She has thought of showing it to Ambrose the chartmaker, whose charts every captain trusts, and of taking it to the council. So far she has done neither, because once she shows it to someone, it stops being stories.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Delphine wants the Salt and Bread full and loud and warm for another three generations. She fears the night when one of the regular crews does not come in, and she has to cross a name out of her book of debts.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could bring Delphine a tale for her ledger, carry the ledger to someone who should read it, or settle one of the debts she has never forgotten.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Halloran: brother
  • Lorcan: singer at her inn
  • Bryony: baker

docs.title: Dunstan
docs.text:
Master Shipwright

Town Bain Harbour Where Shipyard Role Council Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Gruff, stubborn and secretly sentimental. He talks to the ships he builds and claims they answer.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Dunstan is seventy-four and has built more hulls than anyone alive in Bain Harbour. He is the master shipwright, he speaks for the shipwrights on the harbour council, and he has been the master of the shipyard for forty years. He is gruff, stubborn and secretly sentimental. He talks to the ships he builds, and he claims they answer, and after an hour in his yard you may start to believe him.

docs.title: Sixty years of hulls
docs.text:
Dunstan came to the shipyard at fourteen as an apprentice to old Master Garth, who had been building ships there since before anyone could remember, and who taught him that a hull is shaped by the sea before it is shaped by the shipwright. When Garth died, Dunstan took the yard. He has built fishing boats, coasting traders, ferries, the Harbour Watch's launch and a good share of the ships that trade from the harbour today. He can tell you which of them is sound, which is vain, and which sulks in a following sea, and he will.

He married Senara, a fisherman's daughter with a gift for lettering, and for over thirty years she painted the names on his hulls in curling gold. She died nine years ago. Dunstan has not talked about it since, except to the ships. Their son, Alwyn, paints the names now, in his mother's hand, and Dunstan checks every letter and never finds fault.

docs.title: The old designs
docs.text:
Dunstan believes the old designs were good enough for Old Bain, and he says so whenever his son raises the matter of the deep water. Alwyn wants thicker planking and deeper keels for the ships that work past the headland. Dunstan wants to know what was wrong with the hulls that have carried this harbour for a hundred years. The truth, which he would not admit under torture, is that he has been out to look at the scrapes on the hulls that come back from the deep water, and he did not like what he saw. He is not ready to say that the sea has changed. Saying it would mean that he can no longer promise the crews that his ships will bring them home.

His apprentice, Peregrine, is in his second year and full of ideas, about one in ten of them good. Dunstan has a plan for Peregrine's ideas: he lets the boy talk until he runs out of breath, then puts him to work planing. He has not looked at Peregrine's faster hull. He knows that if he looks at it, he might have to admit it is good.

docs.title: The race boat
docs.text:
Dunstan has built Bain Harbour's race boat for as long as anyone on the council can remember, and Quenna has skippered his boats for fourteen summers. This summer he is building a new one, the eighth race boat of his life, and he will not let anyone see the plans, not even Quenna, who will sail her. He keeps the drawings rolled in an oilcloth under his bed. Tegan is sewing the sails in secret to measurements he gave her on a scrap of paper, and he will not tell even her what the hull looks like.

He still has not forgiven the mast that broke in the squall twenty-two years ago, when Bain Harbour's boat had to be towed clear by Goa Harbour's and the race was declared void. He built that mast. He has built every race mast since with a little more timber in it than he strictly needs.

docs.title: Family
docs.text: His grandson Kit is his shadow, and Dunstan pretends this is a nuisance. His granddaughter Poppy draws his ships, and he has every drawing. He has no idea that Kit has carved his name inside the new hull, but if he found out he would be prouder than he could stand.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might fetch a particular timber Dunstan insists on for the new keel, or find out who has been seen trying to peek into the shipyard after dark, wanting a look at the plans.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Quenna: race skipper
  • Alwyn: son
  • Kit: grandson
  • Peregrine: apprentice

docs.title: Finch
docs.text:
Errand Runner

Town Bain Harbour Where Docks Role Child Age Child

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Cheeky, quick and always knows the latest news first. He would rather run than walk anywhere.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Finch is ten years old and runs messages up and down the docks of Bain Harbour for a copper a time. He is cheeky, quick and never still, and he would rather run than walk anywhere, including across a room. If something happens on the waterfront, Finch knows about it first, and if it has not happened yet, he has usually heard a rumour that it is about to.

docs.title: A boy of the docks
docs.text:
Finch was born on the docks, more or less. His mother, Liddy, sold hot pies from a tray to the dockworkers and sailors, and Finch spent his first years under her tray, learning the name of every ship and every crew by the smell of their pipes. Liddy died of a fever when he was five. His father was a sailor who shipped out before Finch was born and never came back, and Finch has never wasted a minute wondering about him.

After his mother died, the docks simply kept him. Garrow, the dock foreman, let him sleep in the warm loft above the dock office at the head of the pier, where the tally books are kept, and started paying him a copper to carry a message to a ship or a warehouse. Five years later Finch is Garrow's errand runner in everything but title, and he carries messages for half the waterfront besides. He knows which captain is waiting on which cargo, which warehouse door sticks, and which sailor will give him an extra copper for running fast. Garrow shouts at him for dawdling, which he never does, and has never once forgotten to leave him supper.

docs.title: Lessons
docs.text: Most mornings, when the docks are quiet, Finch goes to Maren's lessons on Merchant Street, where he sits next to Kit the shipwright's boy and tries to look as if he is not enjoying himself. Maren is strict about spelling and Finch is not, but he is the fastest at sums in the room, because he has been counting coppers since he could walk. He likes the stars best. Maren has noticed that he learns anything at all if it is about the sea, and she has started making most of his lessons about the sea.

docs.title: Barnaby's stories
docs.text: Finch's favourite person in Bain Harbour is Barnaby, the bosun of the Bright Morrow, who has a story for every scar and tells them all to Finch on the bollards by the ship. The waterfront laughs at Barnaby's tale of the eyes as big as cartwheels that looked up at him from under the hull one moonlit night. Finch does not laugh. He believes every word, and he has noticed something nobody else seems to: Barnaby has not slept on deck since.

docs.title: What he wants
docs.text:
Finch has heard every sailors' story about the deep water, and he wants to see a sea creature with his own eyes more than he has ever wanted anything. He has tried twice to slip out along the outer pier at night, where Halloran of the Harbour Watch now keeps a watch he calls a precaution. Both times he was caught by Brisa, the one watchwoman on the waterfront who can run faster than he can. She marched him back to the dock office and told him she would tell Garrow. She has not told Garrow yet. Finch thinks this means she likes him.

He is afraid of almost nothing, except of being sent away from the docks to live somewhere quiet.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could pay Finch to carry a message no one else should read, follow him the night he finally gets past the watch on the outer pier, or ask him what he has overheard, because he always has.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Garrow: employer
  • Maren: teacher
  • Barnaby: storyteller

docs.title: Garrow
docs.text:
Dock Foreman

Town Bain Harbour Where Docks Role Worker Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Loud, fair and always in a hurry. He knows exactly how long it takes to unload any ship and gets cross when it takes longer.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Garrow is the dock foreman of Bain Harbour, and you can hear him from the far end of the pier. He is forty-nine, loud, fair and always in a hurry, and he knows exactly how long it takes to unload any ship in the harbour, down to the last barrel. When it takes longer, he wants to know why, and he wants to know now.

docs.title: Up from the crates
docs.text:
Garrow came to the docks at fourteen as a porter, carrying sacks of salt on his back for a copper a sack. He was not the strongest boy on the docks, but he was the one who noticed that the crews wasted half their day waiting for each other, and by the time he was twenty he was telling grown men where to stand. He has been foreman for sixteen years. He runs the dock crews, sets the order ships unload in, and keeps the cargo moving from ship to warehouse before the next tide brings in the next ship. He has never married. He lives in a narrow house on the Waterfront that he mostly uses for sleeping, because the rest of his life happens on the docks.

His best dockworker is Tully, who has carried crates since he was a boy, can lift more than any two other men and thinks every problem looks smaller after lunch. Garrow shouts at Tully for eating on the job and saves him the last of his own bread. He knows Tully is saving every coin for a boat of his own, and he gives him the extra shifts first.

docs.title: Hobart
docs.text: Garrow's oldest friend is Hobart, who has kept the harbour warehouses since before Garrow was born. When Garrow was a boy porter, it was Hobart who taught him to count a cargo properly, crate by crate, and never to trust a ship's manifest until he had counted it himself. They have argued about the counts every week for thirty-five years. Hobart is slightly deaf in one ear and always seems to hear Garrow's side of the argument with that one. Garrow pretends to find this maddening. He visits the warehouses every evening anyway.

docs.title: The second pier
docs.text:
Garrow has one cause, and everyone in the harbour has heard it. Bain Harbour needs a second pier. On a busy day there are ships riding at anchor in the bay waiting for a berth, and every hour they wait is an hour of wages, spoiling fish and angry captains. Garrow is not on the harbour council, which is for captains, shipwrights and merchants, but he raises the second pier with any councillor who walks along the docks, and he once stood outside the Harbour Hall for a whole council meeting holding a drawing of it. Quenna, the Harbour Master, likes him and says the council will think about it. He has heard that before.

This spring his case got stronger. Halloran, the captain of the Harbour Watch, asked him to stop unloading at the far end of the outer pier after dark, and would not say why. Garrow grumbled, agreed, and now tells every councillor that a harbour that cannot use the end of its own pier at night had better build another one.

docs.title: The boy in the loft
docs.text:
Garrow's errand runner is Finch, who sleeps in the loft above the dock office and carries messages for a copper a time. Garrow took him in when the boy's mother died five years ago, and he has never called it anything but business. He shouts at Finch for dawdling, though Finch has never dawdled in his life. He is afraid that one day Finch will run off down the pier after one of the sailors' sea stories and not come back.

Garrow also teaches Sea Legs, the dockworker's knack of keeping your footing on anything that moves and getting straight back up when something knocks you down, to anyone who will work a full tide unloading the barges beside his crew.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could help Garrow make the case for the second pier, find out why Halloran closed the end of the outer pier at night, or settle a count that Garrow and Hobart cannot agree on.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Tully: dockworker
  • Hobart: old friend
  • Finch: errand runner

docs.title: Gwennol
docs.text:
Fishmonger

Town Bain Harbour Where Fish Market Sells Fresh fish, smoked fish and crab

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Cobb: husband
  • Bree: daughter
  • Lowen: son
  • Hesketh: rival stallholder

docs.title: Halloran
docs.text:
Captain of the Harbour Watch

Town Bain Harbour Where Waterfront Role Guard Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Steady, warm and hard to surprise. He settles most trouble with a hand on the shoulder and a mug of something hot.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Halloran is the captain of the Harbour Watch, and he keeps the peace on the Bain Harbour waterfront mostly by being impossible to rattle. He is forty-seven, steady, warm and hard to surprise. He settles most trouble with a hand on the shoulder and a mug of something hot, and sailors who were shouting a moment earlier find themselves sitting down and explaining their side of it to him instead.

docs.title: The Salt and Bread
docs.text:
Halloran grew up at the Salt and Bread, the waterfront inn his grandmother opened in an old net loft and his mother, Ysella, kept after her. His father, Edwy, was a sailor who was lost at sea in a winter storm when Halloran was twelve, long before anyone talked about creatures in the deep water. After that Halloran was the one who carried the drunks home and sorted out the fights in the taproom, while his younger sister Delphine grew up carrying mugs behind the bar. He learned there everything he knows about keeping the peace: that most trouble is tiredness, that most tired people want to be listened to, and that a warm drink settles more arguments than a raised voice.

Ysella died eight years ago and left the inn to Delphine. Halloran still drinks there most evenings after his rounds, at the end of the bar nearest the door, and he and his sister have looked after each other ever since. They are very much alike. She keeps the peace from behind the bar, he keeps it in front of it, and between them very little trouble on the waterfront gets as far as a broken chair.

docs.title: The Watch
docs.text:
Halloran joined the Harbour Watch at twenty-two and has been its captain for eleven years. The Watch is small: a handful of watchmen and watchwomen who walk the docks and the Waterfront, check moorings, keep an eye on the warehouses and break up arguments between sailors and tired dockworkers. It also keeps a launch, built by Dunstan the shipwright, for fetching people out of the water.

He treats every watchman exactly the same, and that includes Jowan, the Harbour Master's son, who joined last spring and salutes everybody. Halloran is fond of the boy and has quietly noticed that his reports, though far too long, are the most careful in the Watch. He is fond too of Brisa, who joined at the same time, is the fastest runner on the waterfront and never lets Jowan forget it. Their rivalry makes both of them better, and Halloran sees no reason to stop it.

docs.title: The outer pier
docs.text:
This spring Halloran began posting a watch on the outer pier at night, and he will only say it is a precaution. The truth is something he has told only the Harbour Master. Early one morning this spring he walked to the end of the outer pier at low tide and found the Watch's own launch hanging from a mooring line pulled taut straight down into the water, and long fresh grooves scored into the pilings below the waterline, deeper than any boat could have made. By the time he had fetched help, the line had gone slack and the water was still.

Since then he has kept men on the pier every night and stood most of those watches himself. He has asked Garrow to stop unloading at the end of the pier after dark. Jowan has asked three times for the outer pier watch, and Halloran has said no three times, not because the boy is not good enough, but because Quenna is the one person he has told about what he found under that water, and he will not stand her son over it. Delphine knows it is more than a precaution. He has not told her, and she has not asked, which is how he knows she knows.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Halloran wants the waterfront to stay the kind of place where the worst trouble is a sailor who has had too much to drink. He fears that one night the watch on the outer pier will see what made those grooves, and that a hand on the shoulder will not settle it.

He has not yet asked Brisa for the list of strange things she has been keeping. He should.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could stand a night on the outer pier with Halloran, dive under the pier at low tide to look at the pilings, or bring together the people in the harbour who have each been quietly writing down what the sea is doing.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Delphine: sister
  • Brisa: watchwoman
  • Jowan: watchman

docs.title: Quenna
docs.text:
Harbour Master

Town Bain Harbour Where Harbour Hall Role Ruler Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Brisk, loud and quick to laugh, with a sailor's habit of deciding things before the tide turns. She listens to everyone at the council table and then says exactly what she thinks.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Quenna has been Harbour Master of Bain Harbour for eight years, and in that time she has never once let a council meeting run past the turn of the tide. She is forty-six, brisk, loud and quick to laugh, with a sailor's habit of deciding things before the water changes its mind. She listens to everyone at the council table, captains, shipwrights and merchants alike, and then says exactly what she thinks. The council chose her from among themselves, and most of them say it was the easiest choice they ever made and the noisiest one they have lived with since.

docs.title: A captain first
docs.text:
Quenna grew up on the Waterfront and went to sea as a deck girl at twelve. By twenty-seven she was master of her own trading ship, the Kittiwake, and tired of watching middlemen in Selsior take a cut of every barrel she carried. So she walked inland to Kaldemor to buy direct, arrived in the town square with salt on her boots, and argued with its mayor, Tobin, about the price of cider for an entire afternoon. That was nineteen years ago. Every autumn since, Kaldemor's harvest carts have come down to Bain Harbour with cider, flour, pottery and woodwork, and gone home with salt, dried fish, rope and spices. Quenna still goes up to Kaldemor for the harvest fair each autumn to settle the year's prices with Tobin over fresh bread. She thinks he is the shrewdest bargainer on Veligor pretending to be a sweet old man, and she has never once got the better of him. He says the same of her.

Last autumn one of Kaldemor's carts never reached the harbour. Quenna has not stopped thinking about it.

docs.title: The race and the rival
docs.text:
Quenna sails her own boat in the summer race around Veligor, built by Dunstan, the master shipwright, who will not let even her see the plans for this year's hull. She has skippered Bain Harbour's boat for fourteen summers, and she has never once admitted that the other side might win.

The other side, for the last twelve of those summers, has been Iska of Goa Harbour. They met twenty-two years ago, when both were young crew. That year a squall dismasted Bain Harbour's boat off a rocky headland, and Goa Harbour's boat turned back to tow them clear. It was Iska, then nineteen, who threw the line, and Quenna, then twenty-four, who caught it. Neither boat finished; the race was declared void, the only time that has ever happened, and the two crews spent the night drinking together in the nearest cove. Quenna and Iska have been friends ever since.

Since they became skippers against each other, Bain Harbour has won nine races to Goa Harbour's three, four of those nine by a single length. Goa's last win came six summers ago. By old custom the losing skipper buys the first round at the finish feast, and Quenna has bought it only three times in twelve years and complained bitterly every time. She thinks Iska is the finest pilot alive, and she would rather swim around Veligor than say it to her face. Lately, at the finish feast, the two of them talk less about the race and more about the sea: what each harbour's sailors have seen in the deep water, and where.

docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Quenna is married to Ambrose, who draws the charts every captain sails by. Since the deep water turned strange, the captains have brought him marks for places where something was seen in the water, and Quenna is one of very few people who knows about the separate chart he keeps locked in a drawer; she shares its worst marks with Iska each summer. Their son Jowan joined the Harbour Watch last spring and wants desperately to prove he did not get the post because of her. She knows he would rather be crewing in the race, and she has not yet decided whether to let him. She is also the one person Halloran, the captain of the Watch, has told why a watch now stands on the outer pier at night, and she has kept it to herself.

At the council she relies on Captain Corwin, Marisol the spice merchant and Ottilie, her clerk, and she trusts Mabyn, who keeps the hall door, with anything at all.

docs.title: What she fears
docs.text: Quenna fears the sea she grew up on is changing faster than her harbour can. A quest could find the missing Kaldemor cart, check a mark on Ambrose's locked chart, or crew for her in the race.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Ambrose: husband
  • Jowan: son
  • Corwin: trusted council captain
  • Ottilie: clerk
  • Mabyn: friend
  • Dunstan: race boatbuilder
  • Marisol: council ally
  • Iska: rival racer and friend
  • Tobin: trading partner

docs.title: Hesketh
docs.text:
Oyster Seller

Town Bain Harbour Where Fish Market Sells Oysters, cockles and mussels

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:

  • Barnacle: favourite cat

docs.title: Hobart
docs.text:
Warehouseman

Town Bain Harbour Where Docks Role Worker Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Methodical, dry and slightly deaf in one ear, which he uses to his advantage. He trusts his own counting over anyone's ledger.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Hobart keeps the harbour warehouses of Bain Harbour, the long stone sheds behind the docks where every cargo goes between ship and buyer. He is seventy-eight, methodical and dry, and slightly deaf in his left ear, which he uses to his advantage: he hears what he wants to hear and nothing else, and he always seems to hear the other side of an argument with that ear. He trusts his own counting over anyone's ledger, including his own.

docs.title: Fifty years of crates
docs.text:
Hobart came to the warehouses at twenty as a porter, when they were kept by an old warehouseman whose name he will tell you only if you have a long afternoon. He was slow and he was careful, and the old man noticed that the slow, careful porter never once lost a crate. At twenty-eight Hobart took the keys, and he has kept them for fifty years, longer than Garrow, the dock foreman, has been alive.

He lost the hearing in his left ear in his thirties, when a block came loose in a gale and swung past his head close enough to ring it like a bell. He says the ear has been very useful ever since. He never married. He lives in two rooms above the oldest of the warehouses, with a window that looks out over the roofs to the bay, and he says he sleeps better with the smell of tar and rope below him than he would anywhere else.

docs.title: The count
docs.text:
Hobart's rule is simple: never trust a manifest until you have counted it yourself. Captains write what they loaded, merchants write what they paid for, and clerks write what they were told, and none of it is the same as what is actually in the shed. So Hobart counts every cargo that comes in, crate by crate, sack by sack, cask by cask, with a stub of chalk and a tally on the door post, and only then does he write it in his book. Ottilie, the clerk of the Harbour Hall, has been known to come down to the warehouses with her ledger to compare numbers. She is the only person whose figures he respects, and he has never told her so.

He taught Garrow to count like that when Garrow was a boy porter of fourteen, thirty-five years ago, and they have argued about the counts every week since. Garrow comes by every evening on his way home, shouting before he is through the door, and Hobart lets him shout and then tells him the right number. Garrow pretends to find him maddening. Hobart pretends not to have heard. They are each other's oldest friend, and neither has ever said that aloud either.

He has strong views on cargo. He likes salt, which stacks; he dislikes fish, which does not keep; and he complains every time he has to count Marisol's lead-lined tea chests, which weigh twice what they ought to. At night he leaves a side door open a crack for Barnacle, the harbour cat, who hunts the rats among the sacks. He says she is the only member of staff who never miscounts.

docs.title: The oldest crates
docs.text: At the very back of the oldest warehouse, behind three generations of forgotten barrels, stand four crates of dark, heavy wood, bound with iron gone almost black, stamped with a mark nobody in the harbour recognises. Hobart claims they have been there since Old Bain's day. They appear on the first page of the oldest ledger in his office, in a hand so faded nobody can read the entry, and no one has ever come to claim them. He has never opened them. He says that is not a warehouseman's business. Mabyn, the keeper of the hall door, says they are full of Old Bain's spare boat-hooks. Hobart says Mabyn has a story for everything.

docs.title: What he notices
docs.text: Lately the warehouses are emptier than they should be at this time of year. Fewer cargoes come in, and the ones that do come late. Hobart has noticed, because he counts everything, and he has started keeping a second tally on the door post: not of crates, but of ships expected and ships arrived. The gap is getting wider.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could settle a count that Hobart and Garrow cannot agree on, find out what is in the four oldest crates and who left them, or help Hobart read the faded first page of the oldest ledger.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Garrow: old friend
  • Kenwyn: old trading partner

docs.title: Jowan
docs.text:
Harbour Watchman

Town Bain Harbour Where Docks Role Guard Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Eager, earnest and a little too proud of his new coat. He salutes people who do not expect it.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Jowan is eighteen and a watchman of the Harbour Watch, and he is a little too proud of his new coat. He joined the Watch last spring, a few months after his seventeenth birthday, and he still salutes people who do not expect it: merchants, fishwives, the harbour cat. He is eager, earnest and terribly anxious to do everything right, because he is the son of Quenna, the Harbour Master, and Ambrose the chartmaker, and he wants very badly to prove he did not get his post because of his mother.

docs.title: Growing up in the Harbour Hall
docs.text:
Jowan was born the year after his mother took command of her ship, the Kittiwake, and spent his first summers in a basket on her deck.
