He has about two thirds of what a small, plain boat from Dunstan's yard would cost, if Dunstan had time to build one, which this summer he does not. Tully wants to fish the bay in the mornings and carry small cargoes along the coast in the afternoons, and never again to carry anything for anyone but himself. He has walked down to the beach below the Waterfront more than once to look at the old boat that lies there under a sailcloth, and he has never quite worked up the nerve to ask whose it is.

He has heard the stories from the deep water like everyone else, and he has heard that Cobb no longer takes his boat past the middle of the bay. Tully says that he only wants a little boat for the bay anyway, and that the bay is a friendly place. He says it a little more often than he used to.

docs.title: What he fears
docs.text: Tully fears very little that can be carried, and is not afraid of hard work or of anybody's temper. What he does fear, privately, is that by the time he has saved enough, there will be nothing left out on the water worth having a boat for.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might find Tully a boat sooner than he hoped, help him carry something too heavy even for him, or have Hobart ask him at last to move the four old iron-bound crates at the back of the oldest warehouse, which nobody has shifted in living memory.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Garrow: foreman

docs.title: Wenna
docs.text:
Net-Mender

Town Bain Harbour Where Fish Market Role Resident Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Sharp-tongued, proud and quick with her fingers. She knows everyone's business and approves of very little of it.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Wenna mends nets on the fish market steps, as she has done all her life, and from her step she sees everyone who comes into the Fish Market and knows the business of most of them. She is seventy-one, sharp-tongued, proud and quick with her fingers, and she approves of very little of what she sees. Her netting needle moves so fast it blurs. Her opinions move faster.

docs.title: The steps
docs.text:
Wenna's mother mended nets on the same steps before her, and Wenna sat beside her from the age of five, filling needles with twine and learning every knot a fishing net can hold. By the time she was twelve she could mend a hole faster than her mother, and she has never let anyone forget it. Every fishing family in the bay brings her their nets, and she can tell, by looking at a tear, what made it: rocks fray, dogfish chew, seals bite round holes, and careless fishermen leave knots she describes to their faces at length.

She married Davey, a fisherman of the bay, who fished from the Puffin, the little open boat his own father had built. Davey was the quietest man in the harbour and the only one who could make Wenna laugh without trying. He died of a winter fever twelve years ago. She mended his last net the week after and gave it to their son.

That son is Cobb, who fishes from the Puffin now and is as quiet as his father was. Wenna thinks this is a great mercy, since the rest of the family is not. Cobb married Gwennol, the fishmonger, whose voice carries across the whole market, and Wenna has argued with her daughter-in-law about the price of fish, the gutting of fish and the raising of children for twenty years. Gwennol is the only person in the Fish Market who argues back properly, and Wenna respects her more than she will ever admit.

docs.title: The grandchildren
docs.text: Her grandson Lowen has just signed on as a deckhand aboard Captain Corwin's Heron, against his father's wishes. Wenna told the whole market that the boy was a fool, and then sewed him a new canvas kit bag with a double seam, because a fool should at least have a bag that does not split. Her granddaughter Bree is bossy, fearless and runs a business in crab shells from the rock pools; Wenna says she gets it from her mother and is privately sure she gets it from her grandmother.

docs.title: The day Kenver died
docs.text: Wenna was mending beside Kenver, the lighthouse keeper's husband, sixteen years ago on the morning he died. One moment he was singing over his nets, the next he was gone. She sent a boy running for Clemence, the healer, and held Kenver's hand until she came, though there was nothing anyone could do. She has never said much about that morning. She still keeps his place on the step clear, and she still finishes mending on the side of the steps where he sat.

docs.title: The torn nets
docs.text:
Twice this year Cobb's nets have come up torn clean through, both times in the deeper water just inside the headland. Wenna mended both. They were not frayed or chewed or bitten. They were opened in long straight rents, longer than her arm, as clean as if a blade had been drawn through them, and yet the edges were not cut but pulled. She announced to the whole market that no fish she ever knew made tears like that, and she has repeated it to everyone since. She has also kept a strip of the torn net, which she has shown nobody, rolled up in her basket under the spare twine.

What frightens her is not the tears. It is that Cobb has stopped going out past the middle of the bay, and that her son, who has never been afraid of the water in his life, has not said why.

docs.title: The steps' company
docs.text: Barnacle, the harbour cat, sleeps in the sun on the steps beside her and accepts fish heads from Wenna with great dignity. Wenna says Barnacle is the only creature in the market with any sense. Lately Nerissa, the pearl diver, has taken to sitting on the step below hers on days she would once have spent diving. Wenna has asked her nothing, which for Wenna is a kindness of enormous size.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could take Wenna's strip of torn net to someone who might know what made it, go out with Cobb to the place where the nets were torn, or win Wenna's approval, which nobody in living memory has managed on the first try.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Cobb: son
  • Bree: granddaughter

docs.title: Wilmot
docs.text:
Ropemaker

Town Bain Harbour Where Waterfront Role Craftsman Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Slow, kind and endlessly patient, he believes any problem can be solved with the right knot. He hums sea songs older than anyone else remembers.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Wilmot is the ropemaker of Bain Harbour, and he has walked his rope walk on the Waterfront for fifty years. He is seventy-two, slow, kind and endlessly patient, and he believes that almost any problem in the world can be solved with the right knot, and that the rest can be made a good deal better by one. He hums while he works, always, and the songs he hums are sea songs older than anyone else in the harbour remembers. Ask him where he learned them and he will tell you: from the man who taught him rope, who learned them from the woman who taught him.

docs.title: Fifty years of rope
docs.text:
Wilmot came to the rope walk at twenty-two, a fisherman's son who had found he was better with lines than with fish. The rope walk then belonged to old Penrose, a ropemaker so particular that he made Wilmot spin yarn for a whole year before he would let him lay a single rope. Wilmot did not mind. He has never minded waiting for anything. When Penrose died, Wilmot took over the rope walk, and he has kept it ever since: a long, low shed that runs along the back of the Waterfront, so long that the boys of the harbour race from one end of it to the other and arrive out of breath.

His wife, Hedra, worked beside him for most of those years, spinning yarn at the far end of the walk while he laid rope at the near one, and they used to sing to each other down the whole length of the shed. She died eighteen years ago. They had no children. Wilmot still hums her half of the songs as well as his own.

docs.title: His day
docs.text:
Every morning Wilmot walks backwards down the rope walk, paying out hemp from the bundle at his waist and twisting it into yarn, while a child turns the great wheel at the far end. He pays whichever child he can find a copper for it, and he finds fewer every year. Then the yarns are twisted into strands, and the strands laid into rope, slowly, the whole length of the shed, until he has a coil that will hold a ship to a quay in a gale.

His rope goes everywhere. Merriwether the chandler buys most of it and sells it to every ship that leaves the harbour, along with a great many lists. Tegan the sailmaker buys her bolt rope from him directly, and says nobody else's rope sits as true along a seam, which Wilmot considers the finest thing anyone has said about him in years. More of it goes up to Kaldemor every autumn in the harvest carts. Lately Merriwether has been asking him for heavier and heavier lines, thick cables and hawsers for captains who want to be sure of their anchors, and Wilmot makes them, though they are hard work for old hands. He has not asked what the captains want them for. He thinks a man can guess.

docs.title: The last apprentice
docs.text:
Wilmot worries that no young person in Bain Harbour wants to learn his trade. He has had only one real apprentice in fifty years: Tamar, who came to the rope walk as a boy of fourteen and turned out to have the best hands Wilmot had ever seen. Tamar married Morwenna of the Saltlark, and he died of a lung fever the winter after their son Ossie was born, seven years ago. Wilmot has not had an apprentice since. He has never met a young person who wanted to walk backwards down a shed for a living, and he does not blame them, but he does not know what will become of the rope walk when his legs give out.

The nearest thing he has to a pupil is Kit, Dunstan's grandson, who came to him knowing a great many knots already and went away knowing a few more. Wilmot taught them slowly and kindly, humming between each one. Kit wants to be a shipwright, and Wilmot knows it. He teaches him anyway, because a knot taught is never wasted.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: Wilmot has never seen the piece of rope that Ossie keeps under his pillow, tied in a knot nobody can name, though he would know Tamar's work anywhere. A quest might bring the boy and the old ropemaker together, find Wilmot a young person willing to turn the wheel for longer than an afternoon, or help him lay a cable heavier than any he has made before. Lorcan once asked him for the words to one of his oldest songs, and Wilmot found, to his surprise, that he knew the tune but had forgotten the last verse. Someone in the harbour may still remember it.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Merriwether: customer

docs.title: Ysolde
docs.text:
Keeper of the Light

Town Bain Harbour Where Lighthouse Role Service Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Solitary, wry and clear-sighted, she counts ships the way other people count sheep. She has opinions about every captain in the harbour and shares them freely.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Ysolde is the Keeper of the Light, and she has kept the lighthouse on the headland lit for forty years without missing a single night. She is seventy, solitary, wry and clear-sighted, and she counts ships the way other people count sheep. She has an opinion about every captain in Bain Harbour, formed from the top of her tower over decades of watching them come in, and she shares it with anyone who climbs high enough to hear it.

docs.title: Forty years of nights
docs.text:
Ysolde was the lighthouse keeper's daughter. Her father, old Peder, kept the light before her, and she grew up on its stairs, learning to trim a wick before she learned to tie her shoes. When Peder died forty years ago, the harbour council asked who would keep the light, and Ysolde, then thirty, said she already was. Nobody has asked since.

She married Kenver, a fisherman with a fine voice and no sense of time, who used the lighthouse as his clock and said he could find home in any fog by the sound of his wife being cross with him. Their daughter Morwenna was born in the lighthouse two years after Ysolde took the light. Kenver died sixteen years ago, quite suddenly, mending his nets on the fish market steps. Ysolde lit the lamp that night as usual, because ships were out, and nobody in the harbour has ever forgotten it.

docs.title: The tower and the harbour
docs.text:
Every afternoon Ysolde trims the wicks and polishes the great lamp, and every dusk she climbs the hundred and seventeen stairs to light it, more slowly than she used to. Her knees complain. Her friend Clemence, the harbour healer, climbs up once a week with a salve for them, and the two of them sit at the top of the tower drinking tea and agreeing about most people in Bain Harbour. Clemence is the only visitor Ysolde actually invites.

From the gallery she sees everything. She thinks Captain Annis is the only captain left who sails as if the sea were listening. She thinks Captain Corwin is a clock with a hull on it, which she means as a compliment. She thinks Captain Seraphine comes into the harbour far too fast and will one day meet the harbour wall, and she tells her so whenever she can. She watched Quenna learn to sail as a deck girl, and she says the Harbour Master has been deciding things too quickly ever since, and has usually been right.

Morwenna has sailed with Annis for twelve years, and while she is at sea, Ysolde's grandson Ossie lives at the lighthouse. He is eight, solemn and full of questions, and he has decided to be a lighthouse keeper too. Ysolde pretends this is a bad idea and has started teaching him everything she knows.

docs.title: The lights
docs.text:
Three summers ago, on a still night, Ysolde saw pale lights moving under the water far out past the headland, where there should have been nothing at all. They moved slowly, together, like a shoal of lanterns, and then they were gone. She has seen them again since, on perhaps a dozen nights, always far out, always in deep water, and, she thinks, a little closer each summer.

She has told no one. Not Clemence, not the council, not her daughter, who has troubles of her own at sea, and certainly not Ossie. She has not even written them in the lighthouse log, which Peder kept honestly before her and she has kept honestly since. She marks them instead in the margin, in a little sign of her own, and tells herself that is honest enough. She does not know what the lights are. She has her guesses, and she does not like any of them.

docs.title: What she fears
docs.text: Ysolde is not afraid of the dark, or of storms, or of growing old in a tower. She is afraid that the lights will come close enough for everyone to see them, and that she will have to explain why she did not say so sooner.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could climb the tower to keep the light on a night Ysolde's knees will not let her, decipher the marks in the margin of her log, or carry what she has seen to someone who can do something about it.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Morwenna: daughter
  • Ossie: grandson
  • Clemence: friend

docs.title: People of Cavelor
docs.text:
The 15 people of Cavelor in the game's first release.

Name Role Marrun Keeper of the Oath Brask Captain of the Deep Watch Thera Warden of the Seal Oswin Master of the Ledgers Kell Apprentice Archivist Halvara Head of the Root Gardens Ysra Healer of the Halls Gorran Smith of Cavelor Doran Warden Back from the Surface Varn Scout of the Outer Tunnels Annick Singer of the Oath Grisel Retired Warden Ottel Child of the Root Gardens Rhenna Child of the Oath Hall Corvan Keeper of the Stores

docs.title: Annick
docs.text:
Singer of the Oath

Town Cavelor Where Oath Hall Role Performer Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Lively, teasing and generous with her voice. She can turn the gloomiest Warden's shift change into a sing-along.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Annick is thirty-one, the Singer of the Oath, and the keeper of the old songs that the first guardians brought down into the roots. She is lively, teasing and generous with her voice, and she can turn the gloomiest shift change on the Deep Watch into a sing-along before the outgoing Wardens have finished handing over their lanterns. Cavelor is a serious city with a serious duty. Annick is one of the main reasons it has never been a gloomy one.

docs.title: The keeper of the songs
docs.text:
The songs Annick keeps are older than the city. Some came down with the Savage warriors who stayed below, some with the Magicians who helped make the seal, some with the Commons diggers and the Aristocrat officers, and over the centuries they have been sung together so often that they have braided into one tradition. There are walking songs for the passages, counting songs for the roster, lullabies, mourning songs and the long chant of the Oath Below itself. Very few are written down. They live in Annick's head and in the heads of the people she has taught.

She learned them from old Singer Aldra, who chose her at nine because she could not stop humming, and who sang with her every day until Aldra died eleven years ago. At sixteen, still Aldra's pupil, Annick sang the Oath songs in the Oath Hall on the day Queen Aveline and Keeper Marrun swore their alliance, and she has never been so frightened or so proud in her life.

Now she teaches the songs to every child in Cavelor. Her favourite pupil, though she tries not to have one, is Rhenna, Ysra the healer's daughter, who is shy and serious and already knows the whole Oath by heart. Annick is trying to teach her to sing it loudly. It is going slowly.

docs.title: Corvan
docs.text:
Annick's sweetheart is Corvan, Keeper of the Stores at the top of the Upper Stair. He is cheerful, chatty and an incurable haggler, and the two of them can keep a conversation going through an entire meal without either drawing breath. She teases him about his hidden jar of surface honey, which she is not supposed to know about and which she has found three times. Neither of them is in any hurry to settle anything. They are happy as they are, and Cavelor is small enough that everyone already treats them as a pair.

She takes her own turns on the Deep Watch like every adult in the city, and she is a better Warden than people expect. Even on the lowest passages she sings under her breath, very quietly, because she says the silence down there is too heavy to carry alone.

docs.title: The song about the sun
docs.text:
Since Doran came back from the surface last autumn, Annick has been trying to write a new song: a song about the sun. No one in the long tradition ever wrote one, because for centuries no one in Cavelor saw it, and none of those who have climbed the Stair since the expedition was a singer. Doran gives her more stories than she can use, and every verse she writes from them feels wrong: too bright, or too borrowed, or like a song about a lantern with grand ideas. She has started to suspect that she cannot write it properly without seeing the sun herself, and she has not decided what to do about that.

She worries, too, about the old songs. The Wardens are tired. The children ask harder questions than they used to. Annick believes a song can hold a city together in a bad hour, and she is quietly afraid that one day she will need to find the right one.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might help Annick finish her sun song, perhaps by bringing back something from the surface that Doran's stories cannot. Or someone might help her recover a lost verse of an old guardian song, half-remembered and tucked into the Archive's margins.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Corvan: sweetheart
  • Rhenna: pupil
  • Doran: source of sun stories

docs.title: Corvan
docs.text:
Keeper of the Stores

Town Cavelor Where Upper Stair Sells Dried mushrooms, root-fruit, lamp oil and lantern glass

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Halvara: supplier
  • Annick: sweetheart

docs.title: Doran
docs.text:
Warden Back from the Surface

Town Cavelor Where Upper Stair Role Adventurer Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Bright, restless and impossible to keep quiet about the sky. He squints at every lantern now and calls it "almost as good as noon".

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Doran is nineteen, the younger child of Gorran the smith and the younger brother of Thera, and since last autumn he has been the most talked-about young Warden in Cavelor. He went up the Upper Stair last summer with one of Keeper Marrun's messengers, and he came home a different person. People started calling him "Sunward" within a week of his return, half as a joke and half because there was no better word for him. He did not mind. He thought it was the best name anyone had ever been given.

docs.title: Growing up below
docs.text:
Doran grew up in the noise and heat of his father's forge by the Upper Stair, where the old vents carry the smoke up through the rock. His mother, Maelis, died in the damp fever sixteen years ago, when he was three, and he remembers her only as a voice singing in the next room. Gorran raised both children alone, loudly and lovingly, and Thera, three years older, decided early that someone in the family had to be sensible. Doran decided just as early that it would not be him.

He learned the Oath Below before he could read, like every child in Cavelor, and took his first turn on the Deep Watch at sixteen. He was a good Warden, quick and sharp-eared, but even then Brask had to remind him more than once that a lantern is for watching the passage, not for making shadow puppets on the wall. His best friend has always been Kell, Oswin's grandson, and the two of them spent their childhood arguing about the Balrog stories in the Archive's margins and daring each other to climb a little higher up the Stair than they were allowed.

docs.title: The surface
docs.text:
Marrun chose Doran to go up because he was quick on his feet, cheerful on long roads and, Marrun said, "the only one of you who will actually look at everything." Doran was gone nearly two months. He climbed out of the roots into daylight and had to sit down on the grass for an hour because his eyes would not stop watering. He walked across a sea of grass that went on further than any cavern, saw rain for the first time, and stood in the streets of Selsior while the messenger handed Marrun's letters to the crown. He came back with sunburnt ears, a pocket full of seeds that will not grow below, and more stories than anyone could stand to hear twice.

He tells them anyway. He squints at every lantern now and calls it "almost as good as noon". Annick has been pestering him for details for her song about the sun, and he gives her far too many. Little Ottel, Brask's son, refuses to believe the sun is really as big as Doran says, which Doran considers a personal challenge.

docs.title: What he carries
docs.text:
Under the brightness, Doran is ashamed of himself. He wants to go back. He wants it badly, every day, while his sister stands the deepest watch she is allowed and the ledgers fill faster than ever. He feels that wanting the sky is a kind of desertion, and he has told no one except Kell. His father would laugh and tell him to go; Thera would not laugh at all. He is not sure which would be worse.

He has an odd rivalry with Varn, the scout of the outer tunnels, who thinks a map is worth more than any number of stories and says so in as few words as possible. Doran thinks Varn is jealous that Marrun did not send him up instead. Varn has never said whether that is true.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: Doran would leap at any task that takes him up the Upper Stair again, and a quest might give him one, or make him choose between the surface and a duty below. He also knows the route the messengers take better than any other young Warden, which could matter if a message ever has to travel fast.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Marrun: keeper who sent him to the surface
  • Gorran: father
  • Thera: sister
  • Kell: best friend
  • Annick: songwriter
  • Ottel: doubter
  • Varn: rival

docs.title: Gorran
docs.text:
Smith of Cavelor

Town Cavelor Where Upper Stair Role Craftsman Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Gruff, loud and soft-hearted, with a laugh like a hammer on stone. Believes any problem can be fixed if you heat it enough.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Gorran is sixty-six, the Smith of Cavelor, and the loudest man under the World Tree. He is gruff, soft-hearted and fond of shouting across his forge whether or not anyone is listening, and his laugh sounds like a hammer coming down on stone. He believes any problem can be fixed if you heat it enough. He is aware that this is not always true. He prefers not to dwell on it.

docs.title: The forge by the Upper Stair
docs.text:
Gorran's forge stands by the Upper Stair, where old vents carved by the first guardians carry the smoke up through the rock and out somewhere far above. He took it over from his own father, who took it over from his, and there has been a smith of their line at that anvil for longer than anyone has bothered to count. Every blade a Warden carries, every lantern frame on the Deep Watch, every piece of armour in the guardroom has been made or mended there. Gorran knows each one by its marks. He can tell you which Warden is hard on their lantern, which one never oils a blade, and which one has been quietly sharpening theirs every night this spring.

He still takes his own turn on the Deep Watch once a week, on the upper passages, because every adult in Cavelor does and he sees no reason to stop just because his knees complain. Brask, who draws up the roster and is his oldest friend, has offered more than once to let him off. Gorran tells him to count something else.

docs.title: His children
docs.text:
Gorran married Maelis, a gardener with a voice like a bell, when he was already past forty, and he still says it was the luckiest day of his life. She died in the damp fever sixteen years ago, leaving him with two small children and a forge that would not wait. He raised Thera and Doran loudly, badly in places, and with enormous love.

Thera, twenty-two, is the most dependable Warden on the Deep Watch, and he is so proud of her he can hardly speak about it, which for Gorran is saying something. He also worries that she has carried too much since she was six, and that it is his fault. Doran, nineteen, came back from the surface last autumn talking about nothing but the sky, and Gorran laughs at every story and quietly saves them up. He knows Doran wants to go back. He would tell the boy to go, if the boy ever asked. He suspects Doran will not ask.

docs.title: More blades every year
docs.text:
Eleven years ago, the first monsters reached Cavelor's outer tunnels. Since then, Brask has asked Gorran for more weapons every year: more blades, more spear-heads, heavier armour for the scouts. Gorran makes them, and makes them well, and does not like what it means. For all of Cavelor's history, the Wardens' blades were mostly for show and ceremony; the guardians watched the seal, and nothing came to test them. Now Varn the scout brings back his armour scored with claw marks, and Gorran mends it without a joke, which is how people know he is worried.

He is afraid of a day when there is not enough metal, or not enough hands, or not enough time. He is more afraid that one day he will be asked to make something that cannot be fixed by heating it.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might gather ore or rare metal from the dangerous outer tunnels for Gorran's forge, or help him forge something special for the Wardens. Someone might also, gently, help him and Doran finally have the conversation each of them is waiting for the other to start.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Brask: friend
  • Thera: daughter
  • Doran: son

docs.title: Grisel
docs.text:
Retired Warden

Town Cavelor Where Upper Stair Role Resident Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Sharp-tongued, nosy and wickedly funny, with a memory for every scandal in Cavelor. Still sits facing the deep passages out of habit.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text:
Grisel is eighty-four, and she walked the Deep Watch for sixty years. She took her first turn at sixteen and her last at seventy-six, eight years ago, when her knees finally won an argument she had been losing for a decade. She lives now in a small room by the Upper Stair, with a chair by the door that faces down toward the deep passages. She has turned it to face the Stair more than once. It always ends up facing the deep again, and nobody, least of all Grisel, can say how.

She is sharp-tongued, nosy and wickedly funny, and she has a memory for every scandal in Cavelor going back seventy years: who courted whom, who fell asleep on watch (once, in their youth, and never again), who lost a lantern down a crack in the floor and claimed a draught blew it out. She will tell any of it to anyone, with relish, and she has never once been wrong about a name or a date.

docs.title: Marrun's partner
docs.text:
For nearly thirty years, Grisel's watch partner was Marrun, now Keeper of the Oath. She was three years older and, she says, "a great deal more sensible, which isn't saying much." They walked the lowest passages together so often that they could tell each other's footsteps from the far end of a tunnel. She still can. When Marrun comes up the Stair to visit, she knows it is him before he is in sight, and she has the kettle on before he knocks. Their partnership ended thirty-three years ago, when Grisel broke her leg in a fall on the lower stair. By the time she was walking again, the roster had paired them both elsewhere, and neither wanted to ask for the other back in case it looked like favouritism. She still thinks that was the stupidest decision either of them ever made.

Grisel never married. She says she had no time for it and too much sense. Cavelor has been her family, and she treats every Warden in it like a slightly disappointing niece or nephew.

docs.title: The night of the expedition
docs.text:
Fifty years ago, Grisel was on shift the night the Great World Tree Expedition first came down the stair. She had swapped turns with a sick Warden, and Marrun was asleep after a long watch. She heard footsteps in the upper passages that belonged to no one she knew, raised her lantern, and saw strangers from the surface, astonished and dusty, staring at her as if she were a ghost out of a song. It was Grisel who sent for Marrun.

She tells the story to anyone who will listen: the explorers' faces, the questions, the songs that night in the Oath Hall, the way the whole city crowded in to stare and be stared at. It is a wonderful story, and she tells it wonderfully. And every time, she stops before the part where the seal changed. She stops in a different place each time, sometimes with a joke, sometimes with a complaint about her knees, sometimes by simply getting up to put the kettle on.

docs.title: Kell
docs.text:
Her most faithful listener is Kell, Oswin's grandson, the apprentice archivist, who will sit for hours with ink on his fingers and his mouth slightly open. Grisel adores him and teases him without mercy. She has noticed that he has started counting the places where she stops. She has not decided what she will say when he finally asks.

What she will not tell anyone is that she has never forgiven herself for being the one on shift that night: for raising her lantern and smiling, and sending for Marrun, and letting the explorers in with nothing but joy. She knows it was not her fault. She knows Marrun thinks so too. It has not helped in fifty years.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might finally get Grisel to tell the end of her story, and with it some small detail of those days that nobody else remembers. Or she might send an adventurer to settle some old Cavelor mystery that only she still recalls.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Marrun: former watch partner
  • Kell: listener

docs.title: Halvara
docs.text:
Head of the Root Gardens

Town Cavelor Where Root Gardens Role Worker Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Warm, practical and always a little muddy. She talks to her mushrooms and feeds anyone who looks tired.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Halvara is forty-one, Head of the Root Gardens, and the person who keeps all of Cavelor fed. She is warm, practical and always a little muddy, she talks to her mushrooms as if they were slow but well-meaning children, and she feeds anyone who looks tired, which in Cavelor this spring is nearly everyone. Wardens coming off a long shift have learned that the quickest way home often runs past her beds, where a bowl of something hot tends to appear in their hands without their asking.

docs.title: The Gardens
docs.text:
The Root Gardens fill a chain of caverns between the great roots of the World Tree, where the faint glow of the Tree's magic and the deep springs make it possible to grow food without the sun. There are long beds of pale mushrooms in a dozen kinds, some for eating, some for drying and some for lamp-wicks, and vines of root-fruit that climb the roots themselves and hang their small, sweet, knobbly fruit from the ceiling. Halvara knows every bed. She can tell from the smell of the soil whether a crop will come in early, and from the colour of a cap whether it needs more water or less.

She learned the work as a girl under the gardeners of her day, and one of them was Maelis, Gorran's wife, who taught her to sing to the seedlings and died in the damp fever sixteen years ago. Halvara has been head of the Gardens for ten years. She still sings to the seedlings. She will tell you it helps, and she will not tell you whether she means the seedlings or herself.

What the Gardens grow beyond the city's needs she sends up to Corvan, Keeper of the Stores at the top of the Upper Stair, who dries and trades it and argues with her cheerfully about weights. She lets him win about half the time, because it makes him happy, and because she knows exactly which half.

docs.title: Her family
docs.text:
Halvara is married to Brask, Captain of the Deep Watch, and they have one son, Ottel, who is eight. Brask is stern and careful and counts everything twice; Halvara is the only person who can make him put the roster down for an evening. Ottel spends his days in the Gardens with her, supposedly helping, mostly collecting stones. She checks his pockets before every wash.

She has noticed that Brask comes home later and quieter since he doubled the Wardens on the lowest passages this spring. She has not asked him what he hears down there. She knows he would tell her if she asked, and she knows it would cost him, so she feeds him instead and waits.

docs.title: The deepest beds
docs.text:
For the last three years, the deepest mushroom beds, the ones closest to the lower passages, have been growing strangely. Some crops come in too fast and too large. Some caps have turned a colour she has never seen in thirty years of gardening, and the soil there is warm in a way it should not be. She does not know what it means. It may mean nothing at all. But she has asked the Archive to write it down, just in case it matters, and every month she takes Oswin a careful note of what she has seen.

She worries that it does matter. She worries more that, one day, the Gardens will not be able to feed everyone, and that she will be the first to know.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might gather rare spores or soil from the outer tunnels for Halvara, or help her test whether the strange deep beds are safe to eat. Someone might also carry a sample from those beds up to the scholars of the surface, to see whether anyone there can explain it.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Brask: husband
  • Ottel: son
  • Corvan: buyer

docs.title: Marrun
docs.text:
Keeper of the Oath

Town Cavelor Where Oath Hall Role Ruler Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Grave, patient and slow to speak, but his rare laughs fill the whole hall. He listens to everyone, from the oldest Warden to the smallest child, before he decides anything.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Marrun is eighty-one, and he has walked the Deep Watch since he was sixteen: sixty-five years of passages, lanterns and listening, longer than most of Cavelor's people have been alive. He has been Keeper of the Oath for twenty-two years, since old Keeper Ardith died, and he leads Cavelor and the Wardens of the Seal from the Oath Hall. He is grave, patient and slow to speak, but his rare laughs fill the whole hall, and the children of Cavelor sometimes try to make him laugh on purpose, just to hear the echo.

docs.title: The watch and the night it changed
docs.text:
Marrun learned the Oath Below before he learned to read, like every child in Cavelor, and he took his first turn on the Deep Watch with a lantern almost too heavy to hold. For nearly thirty years his watch partner was Grisel, and the two of them walked the lowest passages together so often that they could tell each other's footsteps from the far end of a tunnel.

Fifty years ago, when Marrun was thirty-one, Grisel was on shift the night the Great World Tree Expedition first came down the stair. Marrun was asleep after a long watch, and it was Grisel who sent for him. He remembers the explorers' astonished faces and the joy of that first meeting better than almost anything in his life. He remembers, too, the days that followed, when the explorers pushed deeper than the guardians advised, and the morning the ledgers recorded the change in the seal. His oldest friend, Oswin, who keeps the ledgers now, knows that page by heart. So does Marrun. Neither of them has ever needed to look at it again.

For fifty years since, he has watched the seal weaken in the ledgers, entry by entry. Grisel stops her stories before that part. Marrun does not have that choice.

docs.title: The Keeper's work
docs.text:
Marrun listens to everyone, from the oldest Warden to the smallest child, before he decides anything. Brask, captain of the Deep Watch, draws up the turns so that no passage is ever left unwalked, and Marrun trusts him completely; lately Brask has doubled the Wardens on the lowest passages, and Marrun approved it without a word, because he hears the same things Brask does. Marrun has never married. He likes to say the Watch was his marriage and Cavelor his children, and nobody in the city has ever thought he was joking.

More and more of his days go to writing to the surface. He sends messengers up the Upper Stair with letters for the crown and for anyone else who will read them, trying to make the kingdom understand how worried Cavelor is. Last year he sent young Doran up with one of those messengers, and Doran came home in love with the sun. Marrun understands that better than Doran thinks.

docs.title: The queen's oath
docs.text:
For most of fifty years, the surface listened kindly and did little. The old king who sent the expedition received Cavelor's messengers with real grief, but the warnings were filed more often than answered. Then, fifteen years ago, in the first year of her reign, Queen Aveline came down the Upper Stair herself, the first reigning monarch ever to do so. She walked a full shift of the Deep Watch beside Marrun without complaint, asked more questions than any Warden-in-training, and in the Oath Hall the two of them swore an alliance: the crown would answer every message from below, and Cavelor would send word of every change in the seal.

She has kept that promise. Their letters have passed each month since, she has come down twice more, and four years ago Marrun went up to Selsior for the first and only time, stood under the Great Bell and found the sky far too large. He says she is the first person on the surface who listened to him to the end. He worries that she carries too much, and that he is the one who keeps handing it to her.

The alliance brought something else down the Upper Stair. Since that first year, every warrior of the Royal Guard who passes the Swordmaster's trial comes down to the Oath Hall to swear the Swordmaster's oath before the Keeper: to stand with the guardians if the seal ever fails, and to carry Cavelor's warnings to the surface. Marrun hears every one of those oaths himself. He watches each young Swordmaster's face when they first see the Deep Watch, and he keeps a page in his own hand of every name that has sworn.

docs.title: What he fears
docs.text:
Marrun fears the day he has to send word that a letter cannot answer. He does not know how long the seal will hold, or what might mend it, and he will not pretend otherwise.

A quest might carry an urgent message up the Upper Stair, or help Brask learn what the Wardens hear on the lowest passages at night.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Brask: captain of the watch
  • Oswin: oldest friend
  • Grisel: former watch partner
  • Doran: trusted young messenger
  • Aveline: sworn ally

docs.title: Kell
docs.text:
Apprentice Archivist

Town Cavelor Where Archive Role Scholar Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Eager, talkative and full of questions, with ink on every finger. He thinks out loud and apologises for it constantly.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Kell is nineteen, Apprentice Archivist, and the grandson of Oswin, Master of the Ledgers. He is eager, talkative and full of questions, he has ink on every finger and usually a smudge on his nose, and he thinks out loud and apologises for it constantly. "Sorry, sorry, I'm just thinking," is said so often in the Archive that the older scholars have started finishing it for him.

docs.title: Raised among the ledgers
docs.text:
Kell's parents, Ilse and Tamm, both died in the damp fever sixteen years ago, when he was three. Ilse was Oswin's only daughter. Kell's grandmother had died years before he was born, so Oswin, already old, dry and precise, took a small, loud boy into his rooms beside the Archive and raised him among the ledgers. Kell learned to read from tremor records and to count from the numbered shelves. He thinks it was a perfectly normal childhood. Everyone else in Cavelor thinks it explains a great deal.

He loves his grandfather enormously, and he spends a fair part of each day finding Oswin's spectacles. He knows that Oswin is secretly sentimental, because Oswin keeps every drawing Kell ever made in a drawer labelled "Miscellaneous Tremors", and Kell has never let on that he knows.

docs.title: Copying the records
docs.text:
Kell's work is copying. The great ledgers of the Archive go back to the founding, and the oldest volumes are crumbling at the edges, spotted with damp and brittle with age. If one were lost to damp or fire, a piece of Cavelor's memory would be gone forever. So Kell copies them, page by page, into fresh books that are stored in a different hall from the originals. It is slow work, and he has years of it ahead of him, and he loves it.

What he loves most are the margins. Over the centuries, the guardians who kept the ledgers wrote all sorts of things beside the tremor counts: notes, prayers, jokes, recipes, complaints about the cold, and above all the stories their families brought down from the surface about the Balrog. A Savage-born Warden wrote that it came out of the deep earth, woken by the noise of war. A Magician hand wrote that it came through a tear in the world. A Commons scribe called it "the Burning" and said it had always been there. An Aristocrat clerk recorded only numbers. Kell has copied every one of them into a book of his own.

docs.title: The question nobody answers
docs.text:
Kell wishes, more than anything, that someone would finally tell him which of the stories is true. He has asked his grandfather, who said "each might hold a piece of it" and went back to his ledger. He has asked Keeper Marrun, who listened to the whole question and then said he did not know. He is beginning to suspect that nobody knows, and he cannot decide whether that is terrifying or the most exciting thing he has ever heard.

He also listens, for hours, to old Grisel's stories of her sixty years on the Deep Watch, and he has noticed that she always stops before the part where the seal changed. He has started counting the places where she stops. He has not decided whether to ask her why.

His best friend is Doran, who came back from the surface in love with the sky. Kell is the only person Doran has told that he wants to go back, and Kell has kept that secret faithfully, while privately wishing he could go too, just to see whether the surface libraries hold any of the margins' missing pieces.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might help Kell find a lost or damaged ledger, or carry a question up to the scholars of Selsior or Fairy Forest about the Balrog stories. Someone might also help him get Grisel to tell the end of her story, if she ever will.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Oswin: grandfather
  • Doran: best friend
  • Grisel: storyteller

docs.title: Oswin
docs.text:
Master of the Ledgers

Town Cavelor Where Archive Role Scholar Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Precise, dry and secretly sentimental. He can find any tremor in centuries of ledgers, but never his own spectacles.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Oswin is eighty-three, Master of the Ledgers, and the keeper of Cavelor's memory. He is precise, dry and secretly sentimental. He can find any tremor in centuries of ledgers within a minute of being asked, and he cannot find his own spectacles at all, which are usually on his head, or in the soup, or in his grandson's pocket.

docs.title: Two boys in the Oath Hall
docs.text:
Oswin and Marrun, now Keeper of the Oath, have been friends since they were small boys learning the Oath Below side by side in the Oath Hall, Oswin two years older and already correcting everyone's pronunciation. They took their first turns on the Deep Watch within two years of each other. Marrun was born to walk the passages. Oswin was born to write things down, and the old Master of the Ledgers, Edrith, took him into the Archive at eighteen. He still took his Warden turns, and still does, though these days Brask quietly gives him the shortest passages and Oswin quietly pretends not to notice.

Oswin has been Master of the Ledgers for thirty-eight years, since Edrith died. Marrun is the only person in Cavelor who calls him by a childhood nickname, and Oswin is the only one who can tell Marrun he is being stubborn and be thanked for it.

docs.title: The page
docs.text:
Fifty years ago, Oswin was thirty-three and Edrith's under-archivist. The Great World Tree Expedition had come down the stair only days before, and Cavelor was full of astonished explorers and joyful noise. On the morning the ledgers recorded the change in the seal, it was Oswin's turn at the desk, and it was his hand that wrote the entry.

He knows that page by heart. So does Marrun. Neither of them has ever needed to look at it again. Before that page, the ledgers recorded centuries of small, steady entries: a tremor here, a flicker there, the seal's glow holding. Since that page, Oswin has filled more ledgers than in all the years before, and every year's are thicker than the last.

docs.title: His family
docs.text: Oswin's wife died twenty-four years ago, and his only daughter, Ilse, and her husband Tamm died in the damp fever sixteen years ago, leaving behind their three-year-old son. Oswin raised Kell himself, among the shelves, and the boy grew up eager, talkative and inky, with far too many questions. Kell is now Oswin's apprentice, copying the oldest ledgers so that nothing can be lost to damp or fire. Oswin tells him every day that he is too slow and too chatty. He keeps every drawing Kell ever made in a drawer labelled "Miscellaneous Tremors", and he believes Kell does not know.

docs.title: The reports
docs.text:
Every Warden reports what they see, and Oswin reads all of it. The reports of Thera, Gorran's daughter, are his favourites: careful, complete and never exaggerated, the only ones he never has to ask questions about. He suspects she is holding something back, because she has begun to look at him as if deciding something. He is waiting for her to decide.

Halvara of the Root Gardens brings him a monthly note about her strange deepest beds, and he enters each one in the ledgers, just in case it matters. He no longer knows which small things matter and which do not. That frightens him more than any single entry.

docs.title: What he wants
docs.text: Oswin wants the record to be complete when someone finally needs it. He does not know how to mend the seal, and the ledgers do not say. But he believes that if an answer is ever found, it will be found by someone reading carefully, and he means to leave them everything they need.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might help Oswin search the oldest ledgers for a forgotten entry, or carry a copy of the records up to the surface for safekeeping. Someone might also help him find his spectacles, which is a quest in itself.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Marrun: oldest friend
  • Kell: grandson
  • Thera: Warden who reports to him

docs.title: Ottel
docs.text:
Child of the Root Gardens

Town Cavelor Where Root Gardens Role Child Age Child

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Curious, stubborn and fearless in the way of children who have never been told no for long. Collects interesting stones.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Ottel is eight years old, the only child of Brask, Captain of the Deep Watch, and Halvara, head of the Root Gardens. He has his father's stubborn jaw and his mother's habit of being slightly muddy at all times, and he has never in his life seen the sun. He is not convinced that he is missing much.

docs.title: A child of the Gardens
docs.text:
Ottel spends most of his days in the Root Gardens, where his mother tends the pale mushroom beds and the root-fruit vines that feed the whole city. He is supposed to be helping. Sometimes he is. More often he is lying on his stomach between the beds, watching the little white crawlers that live in the soil, or digging in the loose rock at the edge of the caverns for stones. Halvara lets him, as long as he waters the seedlings first, and she has learned to check his pockets before washing anything.

He collects interesting stones. He has dozens, sorted into boxes his father counted for him (twice), and he can tell you where every one was found and why it is better than the others. There are banded ones from the old water channels, glittering ones from near the forge, a black one so smooth it looks wet, and one he will not show anyone. That one is his best stone, and he is saving it to give to the sun.

docs.title: The trouble with the sun
docs.text:
The trouble began when Doran came back from the surface last autumn and told everyone that the sun was bigger than the whole of Cavelor and brighter than every lantern in the city lit at once. Ottel thought about this very carefully and decided it was not possible. Nothing could be that big and still hang in the air. Nothing could be that bright without burning everyone up. He told Doran so, in front of Annick and three Wardens, and he has not changed his mind since, not even when the Swordmasters who come down to swear their oath in the Oath Hall agree with Doran.

Doran, unfortunately, will not give up. Every time they meet, he has a new piece of evidence: the sunburn on his ears, the way surface people squint, the size of the shadows. Ottel answers every one of them. He has decided, privately, that if the sun is real he will give it his best stone, because something that big should have a present, and if it is not real he will keep the stone. Either way he wins.

His closest friend is Rhenna, Ysra the healer's daughter, who is a year older and much more serious. She already knows the whole Oath by heart and practises standing very straight, and Ottel thinks this is very funny and also a little impressive. They play at Wardens in the empty corners of the Gardens, and Rhenna always insists on doing it properly.

docs.title: What he does not know
docs.text: Ottel is fearless in the way of children who have never been told no for long. He does not understand yet why his father has been coming home later and quieter this spring, or why his mother sometimes stands for a long time by the deepest mushroom beds and frowns. He has noticed, though. He notices most things, and he is beginning to collect worries the way he collects stones, sorting them carefully and showing them to no one.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: Ottel might wander somewhere he should not while hunting for a new stone, and need to be found. One day, when he is old enough, someone might take him up the Upper Stair so he can see the sun for himself and decide whether to hand over his stone.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Brask: father
  • Halvara: mother
  • Rhenna: playmate
  • Doran: storyteller

docs.title: Rhenna
docs.text:
Child of the Oath Hall

Town Cavelor Where Oath Hall Role Child Age Child

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Shy, thoughtful and serious beyond her years. She already knows the whole Oath by heart.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Rhenna is nine years old, the daughter of Ysra, Healer of the Halls, and she has grown up in the Oath Hall, among the healer's cots and the long benches where the Wardens gather between shifts. She is shy, thoughtful and serious beyond her years. She already knows the whole Oath Below by heart, every line of it, and she can recite it faster than most adults and more correctly than some.

docs.title: A child of the Oath Hall
docs.text:
The Oath Hall is the heart of Cavelor, where Keeper Marrun listens and decides, where the Oath is sworn and sung, and where Ysra tends to the Wardens who come up from the Deep Watch with scrapes, burns and the bone-weariness of long shifts. Rhenna has spent her whole life watching tired Wardens come in and rested ones go out. She fetches water and clean cloths for her mother, sits very still while Ysra hums the old Oath songs over a burn, and listens to everything the Wardens say when they think no child is paying attention.

She knows more than she lets on. She knows which Wardens are limping and pretending not to. She knows that more of them come to her mother than used to, because she has counted, the way Captain Brask counts things. She has not told anyone that she counts. She is not sure whether it is allowed.

docs.title: Learning the Oath
docs.text:
Rhenna learned the Oath from Annick, the Singer of the Oath, who teaches the old songs to every child in Cavelor. Annick says Rhenna is the best pupil she has had in years, and is trying very hard to teach her to sing loudly. Rhenna knows every word and every note and sings all of them in a voice like a moth's wings. Annick says it will come. Rhenna is not convinced, but she practises anyway, alone, in the empty corners of the Archive stairs where the echo is kind.

She is also practising standing very straight. She stands straight while she waits for her mother, straight at the back of the Oath Hall when Marrun speaks, straight while she eats her supper. When she is grown she will take her first turn as a Warden, like every adult in Cavelor, and she wants to be ready. She has decided that a Warden who stands straight will not be afraid, and so she has been standing straight for years, just in case.

docs.title: Ottel
docs.text: Her best friend is Ottel, Brask and Halvara's son, a year younger and her opposite in every way: loud where she is quiet, stubborn where she is careful, fearless about everything. They play at Wardens in the Root Gardens, and Rhenna always insists on doing it properly, with real roster turns and the full Oath at the start of each shift. Ottel complains, and then does it anyway. She privately thinks he will make a very good Warden one day, if he ever stops arguing.

docs.title: The sky
docs.text:
Rhenna has never been to the surface, and she is a little afraid of it. When Doran came back last autumn talking about the sky, she listened to every word and lay awake afterwards. A sky, he said, has no roof. It goes up forever. Rhenna cannot imagine standing under something that goes up forever and not falling into it. Ottel says the whole thing is made up. Rhenna knows it is not, which is worse.

She has never said this to her mother. She thinks a girl who knows the whole Oath ought not to be afraid of the sky.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might need someone who knows the Oath word for word, and find a nine-year-old who does. One day, someone might take Rhenna up the Upper Stair and stand beside her while she looks at the sky for the first time.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Ysra: mother
  • Annick: teacher
  • Ottel: playmate

docs.title: Varn
docs.text:
Scout of the Outer Tunnels

Town Cavelor Where Deep Watch Role Adventurer Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Wiry, wry and hard to rattle, with a scout's habit of standing with his back to the wall. Speaks in short sentences.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Varn is thirty-seven, Scout of the Outer Tunnels, and the person in Cavelor who knows best what lies between the city and the surface. He is wiry, wry and hard to rattle. He stands with his back to the wall in every room, even the Oath Hall, even at supper. He speaks in short sentences. People who ask him long questions get short answers, and people who ask him short questions sometimes get no answer at all, only a look that suggests the question was obvious.

docs.title: The outer tunnels
docs.text:
Cavelor lies deep beneath the World Tree, and the way up to the surface runs through the Upper Stair and then a long maze of outer tunnels, root-passages and old caverns. For most of Cavelor's history those tunnels were quiet: damp, dark, occasionally dangerous from falling rock, but empty. The guardians mapped them once, centuries ago, and then mostly forgot about them, because nobody had any reason to go that way.

That changed with the expedition, and changed again eleven years ago, when the first monsters reached the outer tunnels. Varn had been mapping them for four years by then, mostly because he liked being alone in the dark with a lantern and a stick of charcoal. Since then, mapping them has become one of the most important jobs in Cavelor. Varn walks them alone or in pairs, marks which passages are safe, which have collapsed, and which have been claimed by something with claws. His maps hang in the guardroom at the head of the Deep Watch, and Marrun's messengers will not climb without checking them first.

He reports to Brask, Captain of the Deep Watch, and the two of them understand each other perfectly. Brask counts everything twice. Varn walks everything twice. Neither of them talks more than he must. Gorran the smith mends Varn's armour when he comes back with it scored, and lately he comes back with it scored more often than not.

docs.title: The tracks
docs.text:
Wild creatures have grown bold and vicious in the outer tunnels since the seal weakened. That much Varn expected. What he did not expect, this spring, was tracks. He found them in passages that, by the oldest maps in the Archive, have been empty for centuries: side tunnels that lead nowhere, dead ends sealed by old rockfalls, places where no one has walked since the founding. Something has been walking there now. More than one something. He does not know where the tracks come from or where they lead, and he will not guess aloud.

He wants to follow them. He cannot do it alone, and Brask cannot spare Wardens from the doubled watch on the lowest passages. So Varn is looking for someone brave enough to come with him, and steady enough not to talk the whole way.

docs.title: Doran
docs.text:
Varn's rival, by common agreement, is Doran, Gorran's son, who came back from the surface last autumn talking about the sky. Doran thinks Varn is jealous that Marrun sent Doran up instead of him. Varn has never said whether that is true. What he does say, often, is that a map is worth more than a story, and that Doran tells too many stories. Doran says a map is just a story with lines. They race each other up the Upper Stair whenever they both happen to be at the bottom of it. Varn usually wins. He never mentions it. That annoys Doran far more than gloating would.

Varn has no family left in Cavelor; his parents, both Wardens, died some years ago. He says the tunnels are company enough. Nobody quite believes him.

Varn also teaches Lantern Sight, the scout's way of carrying a light that shows the hidden footholds of the dark passages, to anyone who has come down the Upper Stair and can walk the outer tunnels behind him without losing their nerve.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might follow Varn's tracks into the forgotten passages and find out what made them. Or it might help him clear a collapsed tunnel on the messengers' route before the next letter has to go up to the crown.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Brask: commander
  • Doran: rival

docs.title: Brask
docs.text:
Captain of the Deep Watch

Town Cavelor Where Deep Watch Role Guard Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Blunt, steady and tireless, with no patience for excuses and endless patience for a frightened recruit. Counts everything twice.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Brask is forty-four, and for twelve years he has been Captain of the Deep Watch. It is his job to draw up the turns, so that every adult in Cavelor takes a shift and no passage around the seal is ever left unwalked, not for one hour, not on feast days, not when half the city is down with a cough. He has never once let a gap open in the watch, and he means to hand it on to whoever comes after him in the same condition. He is blunt, steady and tireless, has no patience at all for excuses, and has endless patience for a frightened recruit. He counts everything twice: lanterns, Wardens, footsteps, the days until the next turn of the roster.

docs.title: How he came to the watch
docs.text:
Brask was born in the Oath Hall quarter to a family of Wardens, and both his parents walked the Deep Watch until the end of their lives. He took his first turn at sixteen and was, by every account, a dull Warden in the best sense: always early, never distracted, never once caught leaning on a wall. Old Captain Dunmar noticed and began giving him the roster to check. When Dunmar died twelve years ago, Keeper Marrun asked the Wardens who should take the roster on, and nearly every one of them said Brask's name before Marrun had finished the question.

He keeps the roster in a thick book in the guardroom at the head of the Deep Watch, written in a square, careful hand. He knows every Warden's strengths, every family's sicknesses and birthdays, and exactly who will swap a shift and who must be ordered to. Marrun trusts him completely, and Brask would walk into the dark for Marrun without asking why.

docs.title: His family and friends
docs.text:
Brask married Halvara, head of the Root Gardens, fourteen years ago, and their son Ottel is eight. Halvara is warm where he is stern, and she is the only person in Cavelor who can make him stop counting for an evening. Ottel collects stones and argues with everyone, and Brask secretly loves that the boy never backs down. His oldest friend is Gorran the smith, who makes the Wardens' blades and lanterns and who laughs at Brask's silences until Brask laughs too.

On the watch, Thera, Gorran's daughter, is the Warden he relies on most: he can give her the hardest stretch of the lowest passages and never think about it again. Varn, the scout of the outer tunnels, reports to him, and Brask values his maps above any amount of talk. Ysra the healer scolds him for walking extra shifts on top of the ones he assigns himself, and he ignores her with great politeness.

docs.title: What he hears
docs.text:
This spring Brask doubled the Wardens on the lowest passages. He told the Wardens it was a precaution, and Marrun approved it without a word. What he does not say, to anyone, is what he hears down there on quiet nights. He has written it in the margins of his roster in a private shorthand, and then crossed it out, and then written it again. He will not say it aloud because he is not certain of it, and Brask does not report anything he has not counted twice.

He is afraid, though he would never use the word, that one day the roster will not be enough: that there will not be enough adults in Cavelor to walk every passage the seal needs walked. He has done the sums. He does them again every week.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might help Brask learn what the Wardens hear on the lowest passages at night, or fill a gap in the roster when too many Wardens are hurt or exhausted at once. A brave surface-dweller who can stand a shift without complaint would earn his respect quickly, though he would never say so.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Marrun: keeper
  • Halvara: wife
  • Ottel: son
  • Thera: most dependable Warden
  • Gorran: friend
  • Varn: scout
  • Ysra: healer who scolds him

docs.title: Thera
docs.text:
Warden of the Seal

Town Cavelor Where Deep Watch Role Guard Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Quiet, sharp-eyed and fiercely proud of her duty. She takes the Oath more seriously than anyone her age, and hates to be told to rest.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Thera is twenty-two, a Warden of the Seal, the elder child of Gorran the smith and the older sister of Doran. She is quiet, sharp-eyed and fiercely proud of her duty, and she takes the Oath Below more seriously than anyone her age in Cavelor, possibly more seriously than some who are three times her age. She hates to be told to rest. People have stopped trying.

docs.title: The sensible one
docs.text:
Thera's mother, Maelis, died in the damp fever sixteen years ago, when Thera was six. Her father grieved loudly and kept the forge running, and her little brother cried for weeks, and Thera, as she remembers it, simply decided that someone in the house had to keep things in order. She learned to cook before she was eight, kept the forge accounts by ten, and made sure Doran went to his lessons even when he had other plans. She loves her father's noise and her brother's brightness, but she has never quite believed that either of them would remember to eat without her.

She took her first turn on the Deep Watch at sixteen, the day after her birthday, and has never missed one since. In six years she has become, by Captain Brask's own word, the most dependable Warden he has. Only Wardens with ten years' service walk the very lowest stretch of passages beside the prison, so Thera stands the deepest watch she is allowed, as close to that line as the roster will put her, and she knows exactly how many turns remain before she may cross it.

docs.title: Reports to the Archive
docs.text: Every Warden reports what they see, but Thera reports everything. Every flicker in the seal's glow, every tremor in the stone, every lantern that gutters for no reason goes to Oswin, Master of the Ledgers, written out in her small, careful hand. Many of them turn out to be nothing, and she knows it, and she reports them anyway. Oswin, who has read more Warden reports than anyone alive, says hers are the only ones he never has to ask questions about. She has never told him how much that means to her.

docs.title: The notebook
docs.text:
This spring, Thera began keeping a private notebook. In it she writes down small changes that no one else seems to have noticed: things too slight or too strange to put in an official report, or that only make sense when you lay many nights side by side. She has not shown it to anyone. She is not yet sure whom to show it to. Brask would take it seriously but might pull her off the deep passages to protect her. Oswin would add it to the ledgers, and then it would be real. Her father would worry, and Doran would tell everyone.

She is also, though she would deny it, a little hurt that Doran went to the surface and came back so in love with it. She does not want to go up. She does not understand why anyone would want to leave while the seal needs watching. Part of her suspects that is not entirely fair to him.

docs.title: What she fears
docs.text: Thera fears being wrong in either direction: raising an alarm over nothing and wasting everyone's trust, or keeping silent about something that mattered. She does not know what is happening to the seal, and nobody else does either, but she is determined that if there is something to see, she will be the one who saw it first.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might earn Thera's trust enough that she shows someone her notebook, or help her check one of its observations against the ledgers. Someone might also, very carefully, have to make her rest.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Brask: captain
  • Gorran: father
  • Doran: brother
  • Oswin: archivist who reads her reports

docs.title: Ysra
docs.text:
Healer of the Halls

Town Cavelor Where Oath Hall Role Healer Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Calm, gentle and immovable once she has made up her mind. She hums old Oath songs while she works.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Ysra is thirty-eight, and for sixteen years she has been the Healer of the Halls. Her room is a warm alcove off the Oath Hall, lined with cots, shelves of dried roots and jars, and a basin of spring water that she changes more often than anyone thinks necessary. The Wardens come to her off the Deep Watch with scrapes from the narrow passages, burns from lanterns and torches, sprained ankles from the lower stair, and above all the deep, grey bone-weariness of shifts walked too long and too often. She is calm and gentle with all of them, and she hums the old Oath songs under her breath while she works, so that most Wardens in Cavelor associate those tunes with the smell of salve. Once Ysra has made up her mind, though, she does not move, and the Wardens have learned that arguing with her is like arguing with the rock.

docs.title: The fever year
docs.text:
Ysra was chosen at fourteen by old Healer Maudry, who had kept the healer's alcove for longer than anyone could remember and wanted someone patient to follow her. Ysra took her first turn on the Deep Watch at sixteen, like every Warden, and spent the hours between turns learning to set bones, clean wounds and tell a tired Warden from a sick one.

Then, sixteen years ago, when Ysra was twenty-two, the damp fever came through the halls. It was the worst season the alcove had known in living memory. Ysra and Maudry nursed the sick for weeks on end, sleeping in turns on the floor between the cots, and Maudry caught the fever herself near the end and died of it. Ysra fought for every patient she had, and she lost some she will never stop thinking about: Maelis, Gorran's wife, who sang to her even while she burned; and Ilse and Tamm, who left a three-year-old son, Kell, for Oswin to raise. When the fever finally passed, Ysra was twenty-two and the only healer Cavelor had. Nobody asked whether she was ready. She simply kept the alcove open the next morning, and has kept it open every morning since.

She does not talk about that year. But she scrubs the cots with boiled water every week, she checks the drains of the lower halls for standing damp, and when anyone in Cavelor coughs in a certain way, she is at their door before they have finished.

docs.title: Rhenna
docs.text:
Her daughter Rhenna is nine and has grown up in the alcove, fetching water and clean cloths and sitting very still while her mother tends a burn. Ysra loves her quietly and completely. She knows her daughter is shy and serious, that Annick thinks her the best pupil in years, and that she already knows the whole Oath by heart. She has noticed that Rhenna has taken to standing very straight, and she has not asked why, because she remembers being nine. What she does not know is that Rhenna counts the Wardens who come in, just as her mother does, or that the girl has lain awake since last autumn afraid of the sky. Ysra would be gentle about both, if Rhenna ever told her.

In seven years Rhenna will take her first turn on the Deep Watch. Ysra tries not to count those years either.

docs.title: What she sees
docs.text:
Ysra keeps a patient book, as Maudry did before her, with a line for every Warden she treats. She has kept it for sixteen years, and the numbers tell a story she does not like. They began to climb eleven years ago, when the monsters reached the outer tunnels, and they have climbed every year since. This spring, when Brask doubled the Wardens on the lowest passages, they climbed faster. The injuries are not the worst of it. It is the tiredness: Wardens falling asleep on her cots before she has finished with them, young ones with old men's hands, people insisting they are fine while they lean on the doorframe.

She takes the book to Brask every month. He reads every page, thanks her, and changes nothing, because there is no one else to put on the roster, and they both know it. Brask himself is her worst patient: he walks extra shifts on top of the ones he assigns himself, and when she scolds him he listens with great politeness and ignores every word. She has started scolding him in front of Halvara, which works slightly better.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Ysra wants an apprentice, someone to learn the work before she needs to hand it on, but every pair of hands in Cavelor already belongs to the watch. She wants remedies the Root Gardens cannot grow, and she has started asking Corvan for jars of surface honey, which is the best thing she has found for burns; he gives them to her with visible pain. Most of all she wants her people to rest, and she fears that the watch is wearing them down faster than they will admit. She fears, too, that another fever could come, and that this time there would be no Maudry beside her at all.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might carry Ysra's request for surface herbs and salves up the Upper Stair, perhaps to the healers and herb-growers of Fairy Forest, and bring them back down. Another might help her convince Brask, just once, to sleep through a night when he is not on the roster.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Rhenna: daughter
  • Brask: patient who ignores her

docs.title: Ailo
docs.text:
Garden Helper

Town Fairy Forest Where Herb Gardens Role Worker Kind Child of the Tree

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Calm, unhurried and deeply content, Ailo can work for hours without a word and seems to enjoy every minute.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Ailo helps in the Herb Gardens, the terraced beds and glasshouse-hollows below the Heart Tree where Fairy Forest grows its healing plants. Ailo is one of the Children of the Tree, and a Garden Helper by title, though anyone who has watched Ailo at work would say the title undersells it. Ailo is calm, unhurried and deeply content, can work for hours without a word, and seems to enjoy every one of those hours. Weeding, watering, staking beans, carrying compost up the terraces: Ailo does all of it at the same steady pace, and somehow it is always finished by the time it needs to be.

docs.title: The gardens
docs.text:
Ailo came to the Herb Gardens to help, and stayed. Hesper, the Mistress of the Herb Gardens, who is blunt and kind and smells faintly of mint, took Ailo on the way she takes on anyone willing to be at work in the beds before breakfast, and has never once had cause to regret it. Hesper says the gardens have never grown so well. The seedlings come up stronger, the slow herbs come up sooner, and plants she had given up on in the glasshouse-hollows have started to flower.

Hesper has asked Ailo why, more than once. Ailo only smiles. Hesper, who is used to being answered rather than smiled at, has decided for now to be grateful instead of curious. Others in the forest have asked too, and they have all received the same smile, and gone away no wiser. Whether there is any secret at all, or whether Ailo simply works carefully and well and takes pleasure in it, nobody can say, and Ailo has never said.

docs.title: Merrow
docs.text:
Ailo's closest friend is Merrow, the gardener, who does the digging, weeding and watering that keeps the gardens alive. Merrow is big-hearted and slow-talking, and fiercely protective of his seedling beds, and he found in Ailo the first companion he had ever worked beside without wishing they would talk less. The two of them can spend a whole morning on one terrace and part at noon having said ten words between them, both perfectly content. Merrow has never asked Ailo why the gardens grow so well. He thinks it would be rude. Ailo appreciates that more than Merrow knows.

Ailo knows that Merrow is afraid of the Forest Edge, and that his wife Celandine, the herbalist at the remedy stall, keeps wanting to go there for a plant that grows nowhere else. Ailo has heard Merrow beg her not to go and has heard her answer, and has stayed out of it, as a friend should. But Ailo has started, quietly, to learn everything the gardens' old books say about plants that grow near the Edge.

docs.title: The seedling beds
docs.text: Lately something has been digging up Merrow's seedling beds at night. Nobody knows what. Merrow comes in at dawn to find holes in the rows and seedlings scattered, and his big face goes very still. Ailo has said nothing about it either, but most mornings now Ailo is in the gardens before Merrow, working along the disturbed beds and setting the seedlings back one by one, so that by the time Merrow arrives the damage is half mended. Merrow has noticed. Neither of them has mentioned it.

docs.title: What Ailo wants and fears
docs.text:
Ailo wants the gardens to go on growing, and wants Merrow, Celandine and Hesper to go on being exactly who they are. If Ailo fears anything, it is hard to tell, because Ailo is not one for complaining; but those who know Ailo best have seen Ailo pause, now and then, at the gate of the gardens in the evening, and look out toward the outer paths for a long moment before going home.

A quest might ask a traveller to sit up one night with Ailo and see what comes to Merrow's seedling beds, to fetch a plant from near the Forest Edge so that Celandine need not go, or to try, once more, to get Ailo to say why the gardens grow so well, which will almost certainly fail.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Merrow: friend

docs.title: Alder
docs.text:
Grove School Student

Town Fairy Forest Where Grove School Role Resident Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Easygoing and funny, he hides his homesickness behind jokes about the forest having no sea.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Alder is a student at the Grove School, a long way from home, and he would like it known that the forest has a serious shortage of sea. He is sixteen, easygoing and funny, and he hides his homesickness behind jokes about it: that the trees are only waves that forgot to come down, that the Lantern Paths would be much improved by a tide, that he has not seen a proper horizon since autumn and is beginning to forget which way is flat. The other students laugh. Alder laughs too. He means every word.

docs.title: From the harbour
docs.text:
Alder grew up in Goa Harbour, among the cliffs and forests of its wild coast, in a family of fishers who still work the boats there and write to him whenever a carter is heading inland. He grew up on the quays and the cliff stairs, mending nets and watching the pilots take ships through the inlet, and he assumed he would do the same.
