Her mother Fennel, Aspen's only child, had a fine voice too, and sang her to sleep with the old lullabies; Lyra's father, a travelling fiddler, died before she was old enough to remember him, and she has only a story or two about him and the tunes her mother said were his. When Lyra was ten, twenty-two years ago, Fennel died of a fever in a hard winter. Lyra went to live with Aspen and her grandmother Elda, and when Elda died four years later, it was Aspen alone who raised her.

Those were long evenings, and often neither of them could sleep. So Aspen sang. He knew the songs his own grandparents had sung, the songs the treewrights sang while they worked, the songs about the first Magicians and the Listening Woods, and the old war songs nobody sang at parties. He sang them all, badly and with great feeling, and Lyra learned every one. She says he saved her life with them, and Aspen, who is talkative about everything else, goes quiet when she says it.

He still comes to hear her nearly every evening and sits as close to the front as he can. He also corrects her when she changes a word, and she changes one now and then just to watch him do it.

docs.title: The bridge by the tea house
docs.text: On fine evenings Lyra sings on the branch-bridge outside the Dewdrop Tea House, so that the guests inside can hear her through the open windows. Tansy, who keeps the tea house, is one of her oldest friends. When Lyra first came to live on the Lantern Paths, a grieving ten-year-old, Tansy's mother Hollyn fed her honey cakes in the kitchen, and Tansy, then fourteen, let her stand on a chair in the tea room and sing to the guests. Lyra has been singing for the Dewdrop's guests ever since, and Tansy has never once let her pay for a cake. Lyra pays her back with songs, and with Liri, whom she has been teaching rhymes since the girl could talk.

docs.title: The war songs
docs.text: Among the songs Lyra sings are the ones about the Balrog War: the First Burning, the truce, the long days at the foot of the World Tree, the Savage front line that held, and the Magicians who worked the seal. They are not cheerful songs. Lyra sings them anyway, every few evenings, because she thinks people ought to know them, and because lately she has noticed that people are listening to them differently. Travellers who have come in off the roads go very still during the war songs, and do not clap afterwards.

docs.title: The verses nobody remembers
docs.text:
Lyra is collecting the verses nobody else remembers. She asks every old person in the forest to sing her what they know, and writes down every verse that differs from Aspen's. She has found lullabies with extra lines, work songs with whole verses missing from the common versions, and a war song that three different old singers each knew a different ending to. Each spring, when the highland visitors come from Midbarium to see the Eldest, she trades songs with them, and has learned that some of the old war songs are sung in Midbarium too, with the same tunes and different words.

One fragment troubles her. It belongs to one of the oldest songs about the Magicians at the Tree, and it does not fit: a few lines about what the Magicians did, in an order that seems to matter, with words in them that nobody she has asked can explain. Aspen knew only half of it. An old woman on the lower paths knew a little more, and died last winter before Lyra could ask her again. Lyra does not know what it means, or whether it means anything at all. It has never occurred to her that the scholars at the Heart Tree might want to hear it. She thinks of songs as songs.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Lyra wants every old song in the forest written down and sung, so that none of them ends with her. She fears that the old singers are going faster than she can find them, and that the verse that mattered most was lost with someone she did not reach in time.

A quest might ask a traveller to find an old singer in a distant village who might know the rest of a verse, to carry Lyra's book of songs to the Heart Tree, or simply to sit on the bridge outside the Dewdrop one evening and request a song nobody has asked for in years.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Tansy: friend
  • Aspen: grandfather

docs.title: Merrow
docs.text:
Gardener

Town Fairy Forest Where Herb Gardens Role Worker Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Big-hearted, slow-talking and fiercely protective of his beds of seedlings.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Merrow is the gardener of the Herb Gardens, which means that every bed, terrace and seedling tray in them has passed through his big, careful hands at least once. He does the digging, weeding and watering that keeps the gardens alive, and he does it without hurry and without complaint. He is forty-one, big-hearted and slow-talking, and fiercely protective of his beds of seedlings. Students who cut across them on the way to the school learn very quickly not to do it twice.

docs.title: The gardener
docs.text:
Merrow grew up on the forest's lower paths, the son of a deadfall gatherer who collected fallen wood for the forest's hearths and never took a living branch. Both his parents are gone now. He was a slow scholar and a slower talker, and the Grove School found that his gift was small; but Hesper, Mistress of the Herb Gardens, watched him carry a bird's nest out of a bed he was meant to be clearing and set it carefully in a hedge, and offered him work the same afternoon. He has been in the gardens ever since, more than twenty years now.

Hesper is his employer and, though neither of them would use the word, something close to a second mother. She is blunt with him and he is patient with her, and between them they keep the gardens in better order than any herbalist can remember.

docs.title: Celandine
docs.text: Merrow's wife is Celandine, the herbalist who runs the remedy stall by the garden gate. They have been married twelve years. She is gentle, orderly and a little anxious, and labels everything twice; he grows half of what she brews, and is quietly, enormously proud of her remedies. He will tell any customer at the stall that his wife's salve is the best in the kingdom, and then go red and return to his digging. They have no children, and the seedlings, Celandine says, get all the fussing a child would.

docs.title: Ailo
docs.text: Ailo, one of the Children of the Tree, came to help in the gardens and has become Merrow's close friend. Ailo is calm and unhurried and can work for hours without a word, and Merrow, who is the same, found that he had never worked so happily beside anyone. The two of them can spend a whole morning on one terrace and part at noon without having said ten words, both perfectly content. Hesper says the gardens have never grown so well. Merrow has never asked Ailo why. He thinks it would be rude, and besides, he is not sure he would understand the answer.

docs.title: The Forest Edge
docs.text:
Merrow is quietly afraid of the Forest Edge. Years ago, carrying compost to a garden plot near the outer paths, he saw the edge watch bring in a guard who had been badly hurt by something from the woods beyond, and he has not forgotten the guard's face or the sound of the stretcher. He goes nowhere near the Edge if he can help it.

Celandine, though, wants to go there. There is a plant that grows only near the Forest Edge, and she is sure it would make a better remedy than anything in the gardens. She keeps asking. Merrow keeps begging her not to go. He knows she is right about the plant, and he knows he cannot stop her forever, and he cannot think what he will do on the day she decides to go anyway.

docs.title: What he wants
docs.text: Merrow wants his wife safe, his seedlings undisturbed, and a quiet life in the gardens until he is too old to dig. A quest might ask a traveller to go to the Edge in Celandine's place, or with her; to help Merrow find the courage to go himself; or to track down whatever has been digging up his seedling beds at night.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Hesper: employer
  • Celandine: wife
  • Ailo: friend

docs.title: Niv
docs.text:
Glade Dweller

Town Fairy Forest Where Children's Glade Role Resident Kind Child of the Tree

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Shy, gentle and easily overwhelmed by crowds, Niv is fiercely loyal to the few people Niv trusts.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Niv is a Glade Dweller from the Children's Glade, one of the Children of the Tree, and one of the quietest people in Fairy Forest. Niv is shy, gentle and easily overwhelmed by crowds, and a market day on the Lantern Paths, with its noise and press and everyone talking at once, can send Niv home before noon. But the few people Niv trusts have learned that Niv's quiet is not weakness. Niv is fiercely loyal to them, and will stand between any one of them and trouble without a moment's thought.

docs.title: Coming down
docs.text: Niv is one of the newer Children to settle in the forest, and like most newer Children, Niv was met by Halcy. Halcy, who was among the first to come down and has made a habit of helping those who came after, found Niv somewhere quiet to sleep, explained the forest's customs one at a time instead of all at once, and stayed close until Niv was ready to manage alone. Niv still finds that the hardest part of the forest is how many people there are in it, and how much they all want to say. Halcy has never once asked Niv to say more than Niv wanted to, and Niv has never forgotten that. Halcy still looks in on Niv often, usually on the way to somewhere else, and never staying longer than Niv can manage.

docs.title: Oriel
docs.text:
Not long after Niv came down from the Tree, Halcy brought Niv to Oriel, the Master Treewright, who tends the oldest living-tree homes around the Heart Tree. It seemed an unlikely match. Oriel is gruff and seventy-six and slow to trust anything that grew in less than a century, and he distrusts most new things on principle. He found, to his own surprise, that he did not distrust Niv at all.

What suits Niv about Oriel is his silence. He does not ask how Niv is feeling. He does not fill the quiet. He walks the old homes, lays a hand on the bark and listens to the wood, and Niv walks beside him and listens too. Niv now lives in a tree home that Oriel tended, a small, sheltered one with a single round window, and visits him almost every day. Some days they say a dozen words between them. Some days they say none, and both count it a good day.

Niv knows that Oriel has been worried lately, though Oriel has not said about what. He has been spending longer in a few of the oldest homes, standing very still with his hand on the bark, and coming out with his mouth set. Niv has not asked. Niv thinks a person is entitled to their own silence, which is the same thing Oriel thinks about Niv.

docs.title: Looking toward the Tree
docs.text: Niv often stands at the edge of the glade, at the place where the trees thin, looking toward the World Tree. Sometimes it is a moment; sometimes it is an hour. Niv has never told anyone why. Halcy has noticed and has decided not to ask until Niv is ready to say. Oriel has noticed and has never asked at all. Other people in the glade have asked, kindly or curiously, and Niv has only smiled and gone home. Whether it is homesickness, or habit, or something else entirely, nobody in the forest knows, and Niv is not saying.

docs.title: What Niv wants and fears
docs.text:
Niv wants a quiet life among a few good people, and wants those people safe. Niv fears crowds, loud voices and sudden changes, and fears, though Niv has said this to nobody, anything happening to Oriel, who is old and works alone.

A quest might ask a traveller to help Niv carry something through a crowded market day, to find out what has been troubling Oriel so that Niv can help, or simply to stand beside Niv at the edge of the glade for a while, saying nothing, which is a great compliment if Niv allows it.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Oriel: friend
  • Halcy: guide

docs.title: Ondine
docs.text:
Keeper of the Lanterns

Town Fairy Forest Where Lantern Paths Role Craftsman Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Exacting, proud and secretly sentimental. She can tell which of her lanterns is dimming from across the forest.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Ondine is Keeper of the Lanterns, and every light on every path, bridge and stair in Fairy Forest is, one way or another, her responsibility. She leads the lantern-makers who make, hang and tend them, and she can tell which of her lanterns is dimming from across the forest. Nobody quite knows how. She says she simply looks, and that anyone else could if they bothered. She is sixty-eight, exacting and proud, and secretly sentimental, a secret she keeps very badly from everyone except herself.

docs.title: The workshop
docs.text:
Ondine grew up on the Lantern Paths and came to the lantern workshop at fourteen, as a sweeper of glass dust for old Keeper Lisbet, who made the lanterns before her. Lisbet taught her to cut glass, to mix glow-oil, to seal a lantern against rain and to hang it so it would not swing in a storm, and above all to look at a stretch of dark path and ask what the person walking it would need to see. When Lisbet died thirty-one years ago, the workshop and the title passed to Ondine. She has made the forest's lanterns ever since, and she still sweeps her own glass dust at the end of every day, because she does not trust anyone else to find every splinter.

She was eighteen when the Great World Tree Expedition came home, and she remembers the outer paths as they were then: a few soft lanterns for mushroom-pickers and courting couples, lit late and left to gutter. That is the forest she was taught to light.

docs.title: The outer paths
docs.text: For the last nineteen years, Ondine has made the lanterns along the outer paths a little brighter every autumn. She began quietly, after an edge guard told her that something had come right up to the last lantern and stopped. Now the outer lights are the strongest in the forest, and the edge watch walks among them at night with spears. Ondine keeps a book in her workshop recording every increase, year by year and lantern by lantern. She has never shown it to the Heart Tree. She does not like what the numbers say, and she does not like that nobody has asked her for them.

docs.title: Faelan
docs.text:
Her apprentice is Faelan, who has broken more lantern glass than any apprentice she has ever taken, and she has told him so, often. Five years ago, at sixteen, he talked his way into her workshop by describing a lantern he wanted to make one day. She told him the idea was impossible and took him on the same afternoon. She has never told him why: it was the first time in years that anyone had described a light by how it would make a person feel.

He is clumsy and he hums, but he has the best eye for colour the workshop has known, and lately she has started asking his opinion about the glass for the outer paths. She knows he is saving for a lantern of his own design, and suspects it is for Linnet, the young treewright he walks out with. She has said nothing. She has simply started leaving the off-cuts of good green glass on his bench. She also keeps, in a box under her own bench, the prettiest of the coloured panes he has broken, because the colours were right even when his hands were not.

docs.title: Vesper
docs.text: Her daughter Vesper sells the workshop's lanterns, and her own travelling lights, from the shop at the front. Vesper has none of her mother's patience and all of her skill, and the two of them argue about the shop's prices every single day. Ondine thinks Vesper charges too much for travelling lights to people who have no choice but to use the roads after dark. Vesper thinks her mother charges too little for everything else, and that sentiment does not pay for glass. Each is right about half of it, which is why the argument never ends. Ondine is prouder of Vesper's travelling lights than she has ever said aloud.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Ondine wants every path in the forest lit well enough that nobody walking it is afraid. She fears that one autumn she will make the outer lanterns brighter and it will not be enough, and she fears, too, the day she has nothing left to make them brighter with.

A quest might ask a traveller to replace a dimming lantern on a path too far out for the workshop to reach safely, to fetch a rare mineral for a stronger glow-oil, or to carry Ondine's book of lantern brightnesses to someone at the Heart Tree who ought to read it.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Faelan: apprentice
  • Vesper: daughter

docs.title: Oriel
docs.text:
Master Treewright

Town Fairy Forest Where Heart Tree Role Craftsman Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Gruff, gentle-handed and slow to trust anything that grew in less than a century.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Oriel is the Master Treewright of Fairy Forest, and he tends the oldest living-tree homes around the Heart Tree: the rooms and stairways and sleeping-hollows that the first Magicians coaxed from the trunks long before the Age of Division ended, and that families still live in today. He is seventy-six, gruff, gentle-handed and slow to trust anything that grew in less than a century. That includes most people. It does not include trees.

docs.title: Hands and bark
docs.text:
Oriel was apprenticed young to old Master Brannoc, who held the forest's oldest homes before him and who died many years ago. Aspen came to Brannoc four years later, a talkative boy who could not keep still, and Oriel decided on the first day that he did not like him. They have been friends for more than half a century. Aspen talks; Oriel grunts; neither of them has ever found anyone else who understood the work so well. Aspen retired six years ago when his hands grew stiff, and Oriel has not forgiven him for it, because he now has nobody his own age to complain to about the young.

Oriel's work is slow and almost silent. He spends his days walking the old homes, laying a hand on the bark, listening to the wood, coaxing a split to close or a new room to open over a season or a year. He has never cut a living branch in his life and says he never will. He never married. The trees, he says, are company enough, and they do not ask him how he is feeling.

docs.title: Linnet
docs.text:
When Aspen retired, the living homes along the Lantern Paths needed a keeper, and Oriel took on Linnet as his apprentice to keep them. She is patient, practical and a little too serious for her age, and she talks to the trees she tends as if they were old neighbours, which Oriel pretends to find foolish and privately thinks is exactly right. She hopes one day to grow a home from a seedling herself. Oriel has told her she is not ready. He has not told her that he thinks she will be, sooner than he would like.

He knows about Faelan, the clumsy lantern apprentice who hums while he works and comes calling for Linnet far too often. Oriel disapproves of him on principle and has caught himself liking the boy anyway.

docs.title: Niv
docs.text: Niv, one of the Children of the Tree, lives in a tree home Oriel tended, and visits him almost every day. Halcy brought Niv to him not long after Niv came down from the Tree, and Oriel, who distrusts most new things, found that he did not distrust Niv at all. Niv is shy and gentle and easily overwhelmed, and Oriel's silence suits Niv better than anyone's conversation. They sit together in the old homes while he works, and Niv sometimes stays beside him for a whole morning, listening to the wood as he does. Oriel has seen Niv standing at the edge of the glade looking toward the World Tree, and has never asked why. He thinks a person is entitled to their own silence.

docs.title: The homes that will not wake
docs.text:
Lately a few of the oldest homes around the Heart Tree have been slow to wake in spring. Their buds come late, their sap runs thin, and the rooms feel colder than they should. It is only a handful, and only the very oldest, the ones the first Magicians shaped. Nobody else has noticed yet. Oriel wants to know why before anyone does.

He has thought of disease, of drought, of old age. None of them fits. He has thought, late at night, of the forest's roots, which are said to reach all the way to the World Tree's, and of what else lies under the World Tree. He has put that thought away each time, and each time it comes back.

A quest might ask a traveller to fetch soil or water from a distant root, to help Oriel quietly examine a sleeping home without alarming the family inside, or to keep Aspen from noticing, since Aspen would tell everyone by supper.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Aspen: old friend
  • Linnet: apprentice
  • Niv: friend

docs.title: Orla
docs.text:
Glade Dweller

Town Fairy Forest Where Children's Glade Role Resident Kind Child of the Tree

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Mischievous, quick-witted and never cruel, Orla thinks the forest takes itself far too seriously.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Orla is a Glade Dweller from the Children's Glade, one of the Children of the Tree, and the forest's most dedicated and least suspected trickster. Orla is mischievous, quick-witted and never cruel, and has come to the firm conclusion that Fairy Forest takes itself far too seriously. The Magicians frown over their old records, the Council frowns over its promises, the edge watch frowns into the dark, and Orla thinks that a forest with this much magic in it ought to laugh a great deal more than it does.

docs.title: The rules
docs.text:
Orla has rules, and keeps them strictly. A trick must never take anything. A trick must never break anything. A trick must never frighten anyone, or hurt them, or make them look foolish in front of other people. A good trick, in Orla's view, is one that makes its target stop, stare, and then, if all goes well, laugh, and afterwards feel slightly better about the day. Orla thinks of it less as mischief than as a kind of gift, and is a little offended that nobody has ever thanked Orla for one, though Orla admits this would require being caught.

Orla has never been caught.

docs.title: Thorne
docs.text:
For some months now, Orla's whole attention has been on Thorne, the youngest and loudest of the edge guards. Thorne is twenty-one, brash, brave and much too eager for a fight, and Orla, watching him march out to the last lanterns night after night with his jaw set and his spear gripped too hard, decided that he needed to laugh more than anyone in the forest. Orla has also decided not to stop until he does.

So, at night, Thorne's things move. Never far, never anything taken: his spear leaning on the other side of the door, his boots set side by side a little further down the bench, his cup a hand's width from where he left it. Mostly, everything ends up a little to the left. Once Orla shifted every single item in his kit, neatly, by exactly the same small distance, and watched from somewhere nearby as he stood over it for a very long time. Thorne swears that on another night his spear moved a little to the left of his hand while he was holding it. Orla will not say how, or whether it happened that way at all.

Thorne has not laughed yet. He has suspected Kestrel, the wandering Magician, who truthfully denied it and enjoyed his not believing her. He has suspected two other guards, a student, a squirrel, and for one bad night himself. He now checks his kit twice before every watch, which Orla considers progress of a sort, and which his captain, Seren, privately thinks no bad thing. Seren has noticed the tricks are harmless, and has let them be. Orla has noticed Seren noticing, and is grateful.

He came close to laughing, once, the night of the spear. Orla saw the corner of his mouth go, and then he set it again. Orla counts that as the best night so far.

docs.title: Under the joke
docs.text: Orla is not as light-hearted about Thorne as the tricks suggest. Orla has watched him come back from the outer lanterns with his face pale and his hands shaking, and has watched the edge watch carry in hurt travellers past him. Orla thinks that a young man who cannot laugh at a moved boot will not know how to step back from something in the dark, and that the forest is growing frightened and too proud to say so. Making Thorne laugh is a joke. It is also the only way Orla knows to help.

docs.title: What Orla wants and fears
docs.text:
Orla wants to hear Thorne laugh, just once, properly. After that Orla has a list, and the Grove Council is on it. Orla fears being caught before the job is done, and fears more that one night Thorne will go out past the last lantern and Orla will not get the chance.

A quest might ask a traveller to help Orla plan the trick that finally works, to keep Thorne from catching Orla in the act, or, if Thorne asks for help setting a trap, to choose which of them to help.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Thorne: target

docs.title: Sefa
docs.text:
Glade Storyteller

Town Fairy Forest Where Children's Glade Role Performer Kind Child of the Tree

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Warm, playful and a natural entertainer, Sefa loves an audience and loves listening even more.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Sefa is the Glade Storyteller, one of the Children of the Tree, and every afternoon in the Children's Glade there is a ring of the forest's children sitting in the grass in front of Sefa, waiting to hear what happens next. Sefa is warm, playful and a natural entertainer, with a voice for every character and a pause in exactly the right place. Sefa loves an audience. But anyone who has watched Sefa for long knows that Sefa loves listening even more.

docs.title: Trading stories
docs.text:
Sefa does not simply tell stories; Sefa trades them. A child who wants a story must bring one, and almost anything counts: a dream, a rumour from school, what a grandmother said about the winter the river froze, the reason a particular bridge on the Lantern Paths creaks. Sefa listens to every one of them with complete attention, asks questions nobody else would think to ask, and then pays for it with a story of Sefa's own, which is usually better and sometimes, mysteriously, about the very thing the child just described.

Lumi, one of the Children and a student at the Grove School, comes to the glade most days with the news from school, and always asks afterwards whether Sefa's story was true. Sefa never says. Lumi has decided this is the best game in the forest and is keeping score. Sefa is keeping score too, and has not told Lumi what of.

Not long ago Lumi asked, without saying why, what a friend should do when a friend has a dangerous secret. Sefa answered with a story about two foxes and a frozen pond. Lumi went away to think about it and has been thinking about it ever since. Sefa knows exactly what the story meant, and has decided that Lumi will understand it best by working it out alone.

docs.title: Aspen
docs.text: Most afternoons, once the glade has emptied, Sefa walks to the Dewdrop Tea House and meets Aspen, the retired treewright, by the window. The two of them trade stories over a pot of Tansy's tea for as long as the light lasts. Aspen tells about the day news of the expedition came, the bridge he nearly fell off, the forest gathered under the Heart Tree arguing all night, and he improves a different part every time. Sefa notices every improvement and loves them all. Aspen suspects that Sefa is collecting his stories. He is right, and he is flattered, and he would very much like someone to write them down properly before he forgets which parts he made better.

docs.title: The great collection
docs.text:
Sefa is gathering the forest's tales into one great collection: the children's stories, the old people's memories, the songs and sayings and half-remembered rhymes, the stories travellers bring in off the roads, and Sefa's own. It is kept on bundles of bark-paper in Sefa's home in the glade, and there are a great many bundles now. Sefa says it is the forest's memory, and that a forest which forgets its stories forgets itself.

Sefa refuses to say which of the stories in it are Sefa's own. Asked directly, Sefa only smiles and offers to tell another one. Some people in the forest find this maddening. Most have decided it does not matter, because the stories are good. A few have tried to catch Sefa out by bringing in a story of their own invention, to see whether it turns up in the collection, and found it there a week later, much improved, with no sign of whose it had been.

docs.title: What Sefa wants and fears
docs.text:
Sefa wants every story in the forest gathered before it is lost, and wants an audience for each one. Sefa fears, though the glade would never guess it, that some stories are being forgotten faster than they can be found, as the old people who knew them grow fewer.

A quest might ask a traveller to bring Sefa a story from a far town, to find an old person on the forest's lower paths who knows a tale nobody else remembers, or to work out which of Sefa's stories are true, though Sefa will never say whether the answer is right.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Aspen: friend
  • Lumi: friend

docs.title: Seren
docs.text:
Warden of the Forest Edge

Town Fairy Forest Where Forest Edge Role Guard Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Steady, watchful and few-worded, she would rather turn a visitor back politely than draw a weapon.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Seren is Warden of the Forest Edge, and she commands the small watch that stands where the lantern-lit paths give way to the wild woods beyond. She is forty-one, steady, watchful and few-worded, and she would much rather turn a visitor back politely than draw a weapon. Most visitors, meeting her calm grey stare at the last lantern, find that they did not really want to go any further after all.

docs.title: The old watch and the new
docs.text:
The edge watch is older than anyone can remember, and for almost all of that time its work was gentle. Its guards stood at the forest's borders and stopped visitors from taking more than the forest could spare: too much firewood, too many mushrooms, a sapling dug up for some garden in Selsior. They turned people back with a smile and a lecture, and that was the whole of the job.

Seren joined the watch at nineteen, when it was already beginning to change, and learned the work from old Warden Ebba, who had held the post for many years and who died ten years ago. Seren has been Warden ever since. In her time the watch's work has doubled. It still stops visitors from taking too much; but now it also keeps monsters from the paths, carries hurt travellers to the Herb Gardens, and walks the outer lanterns at night with spears in hand. The watch is fewer than a dozen strong, and it was never meant for this.

She has asked the Grove Council more than once for more hands. The Council has listened, and agreed, and found her one or two, and each time the woods beyond have grown worse faster than the watch has grown. She does not blame the Council. She keeps asking.

docs.title: Her guards
docs.text: Thorne is the youngest and loudest of her guards. He joined to see some action and has seen plenty, and he is brash, brave and much too eager for a fight: a better guard than he looks, and a worse one than he thinks. Seren is patient with him, which he mistakes for approval, and strict with him, which he mistakes for dislike. Lately he swears someone has been playing tricks on him at night, moving his things about. Seren has noticed that whatever it is never takes anything, never harms anything, and never goes near the other guards, and she has decided, for now, that a guard who checks his kit twice is no bad thing.

docs.title: Her friends
docs.text:
Kestrel, the wandering Magician, stops at the Edge between journeys, and Seren keeps a bed for her in the watch hut. Kestrel is cocky and restless and as loyal as anyone Seren knows, and she brings the best reports from the roads of anyone in the kingdom. Seren tells her which of her plans are foolish, and Kestrel occasionally listens. Seren also knows Kestrel and Thorne are rivals, and quietly makes sure Thorne is on the other end of the line whenever Kestrel goes out after something.

Juniper, the wilds naturalist, is her other friend at the Edge: curious, fearless and careless of her own safety. Seren has twice gone out past the last lanterns to bring Juniper back from somewhere she should not have been, sketchbook still in hand. She likes Juniper enormously and worries about her more than she worries about anyone.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Seren wants enough guards to do the work properly, and she wants the forest's people to go on believing the Edge is quiet. She fears the night when the watch is not enough, and something comes up the outer paths past the lanterns toward the homes and the school.

A quest might ask a traveller to stand a night watch at the Edge, to bring Juniper back from the wilds before dark, or to find out who has been slipping past the lanterns after the watch changes.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Thorne: guard
  • Kestrel: friend
  • Juniper: friend

docs.title: Siora
docs.text:
Grove School Student

Town Fairy Forest Where Grove School Role Child Age Child

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Shy, thoughtful and hard on herself, she practises long after everyone else has gone home.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Siora is a student at the Grove School, and she is usually the last one there. Long after the other students have gone home to supper, she can be found in the grove of young trees beside the school, alone or nearly so, trying the same small spell for the fortieth time. She is twelve, shy, thoughtful and hard on herself, and her gift is real but slow to wake. Her spells fizzle more often than they work. She is afraid of being sent home before it wakes.

docs.title: Far from home
docs.text:
Siora comes from Selsior, where her parents keep a small dyer's shop on a crowded lane and expected her to keep it after them. Her gift showed itself at ten, in a way so quiet that only she noticed at first: the candles in the shop leaned towards her when she was concentrating, and the dye in the vats sometimes turned a shade brighter than it should have. When her mother finally saw a candle do it, the family sent her to the Grove School, which teaches anyone with the gift, from any town in the kingdom. She came to the forest at eleven and is in her second year. She lodges with the other students from far away in the school's lodging-hollows, and she writes home every month, and says in every letter that she is doing well.

She is not sure that is true. Most of the students who came when she did can now make a light hang in the air, or coax a twig to bend, or hear what Sorrel means when he tells them to listen. Siora can do all of those things sometimes, and none of them reliably. Somebody told her, in her first winter, that students whose gifts never wake are sent home. She does not know if it is true and is too frightened to ask.

docs.title: Amaryl
docs.text: Her hardest lessons are in Growing, with Amaryl, who is brisk, warm and demanding and praises almost nobody. Siora has never heard Amaryl praise her, and takes that as a sign. She does not know that Amaryl watches her more closely than any other student this year, and thinks slow gifts are like slow-growing trees, whose wood is strongest. Amaryl has no intention of letting Siora go anywhere. She has simply not said so, because she has not yet seen the praise earned, and Siora has not yet seen that she is waiting for it.

docs.title: Alder
docs.text:
Her closest friend is Alder, an older student from Goa Harbour, who is easygoing and funny and misses the sea. He has fallen into the habit of staying with her while she practises late, sitting on a root and making jokes about the forest's shortage of tides until she laughs. Her spells come out a little better when she is laughing. She has noticed this and has not told him, partly because it would embarrass them both and partly because she is afraid it will stop working if she says it out loud.

She thinks Alder is the only person at the school who never makes her feel slow. She has also noticed that he goes quiet whenever anyone mentions the end of term and the road home, and that his jokes about the road are not quite like his other jokes. She worries about him more than he knows.

docs.title: The night it worked
docs.text: One evening this spring, practising alone after Alder had gone, Siora tried the simplest coaxing spell Amaryl teaches, on a young hazel, and it worked perfectly: the whole branch turned to meet her hand, as easily as if it had been waiting to be asked. She has not been able to do it since, and she has told no one, because she is not sure she did not dream it.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Siora wants her gift to wake properly, and to stay at the school long enough to find out what it can do. She fears being sent home with nothing to show for it, and she fears, almost as much, being praised before she has earned it.

A quest might ask a traveller to help Siora practise somewhere nobody else will see, to find the hazel that answered her and learn why, or to carry one of her cheerful monthly letters home to Selsior along with a truer message she has not dared to write.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Amaryl: teacher
  • Alder: friend

docs.title: Sorrel
docs.text:
Teacher of Listening

Town Fairy Forest Where Grove School Role Scholar Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Soft-spoken and unhurried, he believes most mistakes come from talking too much. His lessons are mostly silence, and his students love him anyway.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Sorrel teaches Listening at the Grove School: the first and oldest Magician lesson, in which a student learns to hear the trees, the wind and the creatures of the forest before trying any magic at all. He is forty-five, soft-spoken and unhurried, and he believes most mistakes come from talking too much. His lessons are mostly silence. His students complain about this loudly and constantly, and they love him anyway, which he finds mildly puzzling and does not try to explain.

docs.title: Calyra's pupil
docs.text:
Sorrel grew up in the forest and came to the Grove School at eight, a small, quiet boy who was already better at hearing things than at saying them. His first teacher was Calyra, who taught listening to the youngest students for forty years before the forest chose her as Eldest. She was the first grown-up he had met who did not mind a silence, and he followed her lessons for years after he was meant to have finished them.

At twenty-eight he came back to the school to help her, sitting at the side of her lessons, walking the youngest students out to their trees and fetching the ones who wandered off. When Calyra became Eldest nine years ago, the lesson passed to him. He still teaches it almost exactly as she did, except that he says even less. Calyra, who visits the school more often than an Eldest strictly needs to, once sat at the back of his class for a whole morning and afterwards told him only, "Good." He has kept that word ever since.

He never married. He lives alone in a small tree home a short walk from the school, and he spends his evenings walking the paths with his hands in his pockets, listening.

docs.title: The lessons
docs.text:
A listening lesson with Sorrel begins with a walk and ends with a question. In between, the students sit with their backs to a tree and are quiet for as long as they can bear. Then he asks what they heard, and he accepts no answer that sounds like something they were told. The best students take a year to understand what he wants. Some never do, and he teaches them just as patiently.

Liri, Tansy's daughter, is in his youngest class this year. She is bright, bold and wants the exciting spells first and the listening never, and she can now sit still in his lessons for almost a quarter of an hour, which Sorrel calls progress and Liri calls torture. He likes her very much. He thinks the children who fight the silence hardest often hear the most once they stop.

Aurel, the junior teacher, is his student in a different sense. Aurel finished his own schooling three years ago and now teaches the youngest, and he writes every lesson out word for word and then forgets the notes. Sorrel thinks this is the best thing that could happen to him and has never once suggested he stop writing them. When Aurel comes to him in a panic after a lesson has gone wrong, Sorrel listens to the whole story, says one sentence, and sends him home to sleep.

Amaryl, who teaches Growing, has worked beside him for many years. She thinks his lessons are too quiet; he thinks hers are too loud. Each of them sends their best students to the other.

docs.title: The uneasy edges
docs.text:
Lately Sorrel has been saying that the forest sounds uneasy at its edges, and he cannot explain what he means. It is not a noise, exactly. On his dawn walks to the outer lanterns the birds seem to start their singing a little later than they used to, and stop a little sooner. The wind in the outer trees has a note in it he does not recognise. Twice he has stood at the last lantern and had the feeling, which he would never put in a lesson, that the woods beyond were listening back.

The edge watch knows him by sight now, the quiet teacher who stands at the outer lanterns at dawn with his eyes closed. He has tried to describe what he hears to the Council and given up halfway through a sentence. He is not the sort of man who likes to frighten people, and he does not know whether he should be frightened himself.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Sorrel wants every child who passes through the Grove School to leave knowing how to be quiet long enough to hear something. He fears that what he is hearing at the edges is real, that it is growing, and that the forest's oldest lesson may turn out to be the only warning it gets.

Sorrel also teaches Blink, the short step forward through the air that the Grove School teaches anyone with patience, magician or not, to any traveller who can sit through one of his listening lessons without fidgeting.

A quest might ask a traveller to walk with Sorrel to the outer lanterns at dawn and tell him honestly what they hear, to help Aurel through a lesson Sorrel has quietly arranged to miss, or to follow a sound in the outer woods that Sorrel cannot name.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Aurel: student
  • Liri: student
  • Amaryl: colleague

docs.title: Tansy
docs.text:
Keeper of the Dewdrop Tea House

Town Fairy Forest Where Lantern Paths Role Service Age Adult Sells Dew tea, honey cakes and a bed for the night

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Warm, busy and impossible to surprise, she remembers every guest's favourite cake.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Sooner or later, everyone in Fairy Forest ends up at the Dewdrop Tea House. Students come after lessons with coins they should be saving, travellers come in off the roads still shaking the dust from their cloaks, and scholars from the Heart Tree come late at night because they have forgotten, again, to eat. Tansy, who keeps it, is ready for all of them. She is warm, busy and impossible to surprise, and she remembers every guest's favourite cake, sometimes years after their last visit.

docs.title: The house on the Lantern Paths
docs.text:
The tea house sits on the Lantern Paths, in the hollow of a broad old tree with a branch-bridge running past its door and a ring of lanterns hung along its eaves. Downstairs is the tea room, all mismatched cups and low tables; upstairs are a handful of small rooms where a traveller can have a bed for the night. Tansy sells dew tea, gathered at dawn from the broad leaves around the house, honey cakes, and that bed, and she does a brisk trade in all three.

The house was her mother's before it was hers. Hollyn ran the Dewdrop for most of Tansy's childhood, and Tansy grew up carrying trays and learning which scholar took three spoons of honey. Hollyn died eleven years ago, and Tansy has run the house alone ever since. She has changed almost nothing, except the cakes, which she insists are better.

docs.title: Liri
docs.text:
Tansy is thirty-six, and she is raising her daughter Liri alone. Liri's father, Edrin, kept the bees whose honey still goes into the Dewdrop's cakes. He died of a winter fever when Liri was one, and Liri does not remember him. Tansy kept his hives, and on quiet mornings she tends them herself, though she is not fond of bees and says so to them every time.

Liri is nine and has been at the Grove School for a year. She is bright, bold and impatient, and Tansy knows exactly whom she takes after. Lately the girl has been too quiet at supper, too interested in the travellers' stories about the roads, and too friendly with her best friend Lumi in a whispering, pointed sort of way. Tansy suspects Liri is planning something. She does not yet know what, and it is the only thing in the forest she would hate to be surprised by.

docs.title: Friends and suppliers
docs.text:
Vesper, who sells lanterns further along the path, is one of Tansy's oldest friends; the two of them can argue about prices for an hour and part laughing. Lyra, the singer, is another, and on fine evenings she sings on the bridge outside the tea house so that Tansy's guests can hear her through the open windows. The garlands that hang over every table, and the baskets the honey cakes are carried in, come from Halcy in the Children's Glade. Tansy buys from Halcy every week and would not change supplier for any price.

Old Aspen sits by the window most afternoons and tells the story of the expedition's return to whoever will listen. His friend Sefa often joins him, and Tansy keeps the pot full.

docs.title: What she hears
docs.text:
A tea house hears everything. Tansy knows which roads have grown worse this season, because the travellers tell her; she knows which seal scholars have stopped sleeping, because they come in at midnight; she knows the edge watch is stretched thin, because its guards eat standing up. She keeps all of it to herself unless someone needs to know.

A quest might ask a traveller to help Tansy find out what Liri is planning before Liri does it, to fetch dew from a far grove when the near leaves run dry, or to carry a basket of cakes to a scholar who has not left the Heart Tree in three days.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Liri: daughter
  • Vesper: friend
  • Lyra: friend
  • Halcy: supplier

docs.title: Thessaly
docs.text:
Grove Councillor

Town Fairy Forest Where Heart Tree Role Council Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Proud, precise and quick to object, but the first to admit when she has been out-argued. She keeps a ledger of every promise the Council makes.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Thessaly is a councillor of the Grove, and the one whose objection everyone in the Council chamber is waiting for. She is seventy-one, proud, precise and quick to object, and she keeps a ledger of every promise the Council makes. She is also, and this surprises visitors more than anything else about her, the first person in the room to admit it when she has been out-argued. She says a mind that cannot change is only a stone that talks, and she has no wish to be a stone.

docs.title: The older sister
docs.text:
Thessaly grew up in the forest with her younger sister Briony, three years behind her and as different from her as a bramble from a ruler. Thessaly was the child who corrected the grown-ups' sums; Briony was the child who made the grown-ups laugh while Thessaly did it. Their parents, who are long dead, used to say that between the two of them they made one perfectly reasonable person. Thessaly never married. Briony is her family, and she would not say so in front of her for anything.

Thessaly's gift was for exactness. At the Grove School she taught the forms of spellwork for many years: the precise shapes, words and order of a working, the part of magic where a small mistake becomes a large one. Her students called her the hardest teacher in the school and, a few years later, the most useful. Twenty-two years ago she took a seat on the Grove Council, and on her first day there she bought a plain ledger and wrote down every promise the Council made that afternoon. She has never missed a meeting since.

docs.title: The ledger
docs.text:
The ledger is now fourteen volumes long, kept on a shelf in her tree home. Every promise goes in: to mend a bridge, to answer a letter, to consider a request. When a promise is kept, she draws a single neat line through it. When it is not, the entry stays, and she reads it out at the next meeting, and the one after that. After every meeting she checks her ledger against Ilwen's minutes. About once a season she finds a difference between them, and the two of them settle it with great politeness and some private enjoyment.

Thessaly counts "we will consider it" as a promise, which the rest of the Council finds tiresome. Several of the longest unlined entries are the Council's promises to consider the Warden's requests for more guards at the Forest Edge. Thessaly reads them out every time. She has not yet persuaded the Council to do more than add one or two guards at a time, and she has begun to wonder whether reading them out is enough.

docs.title: The choosing
docs.text:
Nine years ago, when Eldest Ferris died, the forest's teachers and elders gathered to choose a new Eldest from among themselves. Two names were spoken most often, Calyra's and Thessaly's, and Calyra won by a handful of voices. Thessaly congratulated her in front of everyone, took her own seat, and opened her ledger. Only Briony knew what it had cost her, and only Briony was allowed to see it.

Since then she has been Calyra's sharpest critic and her most reliable ally. She tells Calyra, in Council, exactly where she thinks the Eldest is wrong, and when the Council has decided, she defends the decision as if it had been her own idea. Calyra says a council without Thessaly would agree itself off a cliff. Thessaly says a council with only Thessaly would never get to the cliff at all, and that this would be an improvement.

In meetings Briony sits across from her and, when a debate turns sour, says something too quietly for anyone else to hear. Thessaly then has to hide her face behind her ledger until she has stopped laughing. She has asked Briony to stop. She has never meant it.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Thessaly wants every line in her ledger drawn through before she is too old to draw them. She fears, more each year, that the forest is making promises faster than it can keep them, and that one day the unlined entries will be the only true history of how the troubles came.

A quest might ask a traveller to help the Council keep one of its oldest unkept promises, to find the reason behind a difference between Thessaly's ledger and Ilwen's minutes, or to carry a sharp, careful letter from Thessaly to someone who has not answered the Council in a long time.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Calyra: old rival and friend
  • Briony: sister

docs.title: Thorne
docs.text:
Edge Guard

Town Fairy Forest Where Forest Edge Role Guard Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Brash, brave and much too eager for a fight. He is a better guard than he looks and a worse one than he thinks.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Thorne is the youngest and loudest of the edge guards, and he would like everyone to know that he is also the bravest. He is twenty-one, brash, brave and much too eager for a fight. He is a better guard than he looks, because he never sleeps on watch, never turns his back on the dark and has never once run from anything. He is a worse guard than he thinks, because he has never once stopped to wonder whether running might have been wiser.

docs.title: Looking for action
docs.text:
Thorne grew up on the Lantern Paths, where the most exciting thing that happened most weeks was a lantern going out. He had a little of the gift and spent a few restless years at the Grove School, where he was by his own account the worst student of listening the forest had ever produced. He left as soon as he was allowed. When he was sixteen his parents moved to Selsior to keep a stall there, and he refused to go with them. They write to him; he writes back when he remembers.

At eighteen he joined the edge watch to see some action. Three years later he has seen plenty. He has walked the outer lanterns at night with a spear, helped carry hurt travellers to the Herb Gardens, and stood his ground at the last lantern while something large and angry made up its mind about him in the dark. He tells these stories at the Dewdrop Tea House with only modest improvements.

docs.title: The Warden
docs.text: Seren, Warden of the Forest Edge, is his captain. She is patient with him, which he mistakes for approval, and strict with him, which he mistakes for dislike. In truth she thinks he could be a fine guard if he lives long enough to learn caution, and she sets him tasks with that in mind. Thorne thinks she is the best fighter at the Edge, though he has never seen her fight, because she always seems to settle things before it comes to that. He has not yet worked out that this is the point.

docs.title: Kestrel
docs.text: Kestrel, the wandering Magician, is his rival. She stops at the Edge between journeys to trade news with the watch and to tease him, and she does both thoroughly. The two of them argue about who has seen the worst monsters, who reacted fastest, and whose way of dealing with them is less reckless, which is an argument neither of them should be allowed to win. Thorne will never say so, but when Kestrel comes in off the roads with her sleeves singed and a new story, he listens to every word.

docs.title: The trickster
docs.text:
For some months now, someone has been playing tricks on Thorne at night. His things move. Never far, and never anything taken: his spear leaning against the other side of the door, his boots set side by side a little further down the bench, his cup on the shelf a hand's width from where he left it. Mostly, he has noticed, everything ends up a little to the left. Once he came off watch and found every item in his kit shifted, neatly, by exactly the same small distance.

Thorne is convinced someone in the forest is doing it, and he is right. He half suspects Kestrel, who has truthfully denied it and enjoys very much that he does not believe her. He has also suspected two other guards, a student, a squirrel and, for one bad night, himself. He has started checking his kit twice before every watch, which Seren privately thinks is no bad thing. He has not caught anyone. He does not know that it is Orla, one of the Children of the Tree, who has decided that he needs to laugh more and will not stop until he does.

He has not laughed yet. He has come close, once, when he found his own spear moved a little to the left of his hand while he was holding it, and he is still not sure how that was done.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Thorne wants to prove he is the best guard at the Edge, and he wants to catch whoever is moving his things. He fears, though he would deny it, that the night he finally meets something he cannot stand against, he will not have the sense to step back, and that Seren will be the one who has to carry him in.

A quest might ask a traveller to stand a night watch beside Thorne and keep him from charging into the dark, to help him set a trap for the trickster, or, if they work out who it is, to help the trickster finally make him laugh.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Seren: captain
  • Kestrel: rival
  • Orla: secret prankster

docs.text:
Lantern Seller

Town Fairy Forest Where Lantern Paths Sells Lanterns, glow-oil and travelling lights

docs.title: Wynne
docs.text:
Copyist of the Old Records

Town Fairy Forest Where Heart Tree Role Scholar Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Quiet, observant and stubborn. She notices what others skip and says so only when she is sure.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Wynne is the Copyist of the Old Records at the Heart Tree. Her work is to copy the forest's crumbling Magician records, letter by letter, onto fresh paper, so that the originals can be closed and laid to rest in the dark of the record rooms. It is slow, careful, silent work, and Wynne is very good at it. She is nineteen, quiet, observant and stubborn. She notices what other people skip, and she says so only when she is sure.

docs.title: The bookbinder's daughter
docs.text:
Wynne was born in Selsior, where her mother Mirren, Isaura's daughter, keeps a bookbinder's shop with Wynne's father. She grew up among stacks of paper, pots of glue and the smell of leather, and before she could read properly she could tell, by touching a book's spine, how it had been sewn and whether anyone had mended it since. Her mother taught her to fold a sheet, stitch a quire and see a repair from across a room. It never occurred to Wynne that this was an unusual thing for a child to know.

At fourteen, five years ago, she came to Fairy Forest to live with her grandmother. She had a little of the gift, enough to sit the Grove School's lessons, but she spent every free hour in the Heart Tree's record rooms, and by sixteen Isaura had given up pretending not to notice and set her to copying. Her mother writes every month. Wynne writes back every month, and her letters are mostly about paper.

docs.title: Her grandmother
docs.text: Isaura, Keeper of the Old Records, is stern, careful and secretive by duty, and with Wynne she is gentler than with anyone else alive. The house had been very quiet since Isaura's husband Corvin died, and Wynne knows she filled it. They eat supper together most nights and talk about anything except the seal. Wynne is the only person who can make her grandmother put down her pen in the middle of a page, and she does it on purpose, about once a week, to make her eat.

docs.title: Caelum
docs.text: Caelum, the brilliant and sleepless seal scholar who has been Isaura's student for twenty years, is her rival. It embarrasses him, she knows, because she is nineteen and a copyist and he is supposed to be the scholar. Twice now she has pointed out, very politely, a date he copied wrong. Both times she was right, and both times he went red to the ears and thanked her through his teeth. Wynne does not dislike him. She thinks he reads too fast, and that a man who reads too fast is bound to miss things. She would rather be right in front of him than anywhere else.

docs.title: Ilwen
docs.text: Her friend is Ilwen, the Steward of the Heart Tree, who greeted her on the stair the day she arrived and showed her where everything was, down to the page and shelf. He is calm and tidy and polite, and he is the only person in the Heart Tree who never asks her what she is working on. They eat lunch on the landing of the great stair on fine days and talk about handwriting.

docs.title: The gap
docs.text:
This spring, copying one of the old seal records, Wynne found a gap in its numbering. The leaves run in order, and then several are simply not there. Anyone else might think they had rotted away. Wynne, who grew up in a bindery, looked at the stitching and saw that the pages had not fallen out. They had been taken out, long ago, cleanly, by someone who knew how to remove leaves from a book without leaving much trace, and the thread had been drawn tight again afterwards.

She has not told anyone. She has not decided whom to tell. Her grandmother would want to know, but Wynne is afraid of what it would do to her: Isaura has spent fifty years reading those records, and Wynne has seen how tired she is. Caelum would want to know, and would run with it before the ink was dry. Ilwen would listen and keep the secret, but it is not his burden to carry. So far Wynne has only asked Ilwen, very sideways, whether the Heart Tree has any list of its oldest shelves older than the one in use. He told her the exact page and shelf where such a list might be, and did not ask why.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Wynne wants to be sure before she speaks; it is the rule she lives by. She fears that by the time she is sure, it will be too late for it to matter.

A quest might ask a traveller to help Wynne search the Heart Tree's oldest shelf lists for some sign of where the missing pages went, to carry a letter between her and her mother in Selsior about bindings, or to help her decide, at last, whom to tell.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Ilwen: friend
  • Isaura: grandmother
  • Caelum: rival
