docs.title: Agna
docs.text:
Net-Mender

Town Goa Harbour Where Fishers' Coves Role Craftsman Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Blunt, wry and tireless; she has an opinion about everyone's knots.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Agna is seventy-two and the net-mender of the Fishers' Coves, and she has kept the coves' nets whole for fifty years. Every boat in the coves has fished with her mending, and every fisher in the coves has heard what she thinks of their knots. She is blunt, wry and tireless. She sits on an upturned crate at the top of the shingle with a net across her knees and a wooden needle in her fist, and she does not stop working to talk, or to laugh, or to tell you that the knot you tied this morning would shame a seal.

docs.title: A cove girl
docs.text:
Agna was born in the coves, the daughter of a cove fisher named Niall and a net-mender named Kirsty, and she learned to fill a needle before she could read. Her mother taught her to mend in the evenings by the fire, holding up each knot to the light and pulling it until it either held or gave. When Kirsty's eyes began to fail, Agna, at twenty-two, took her place on the crate. She has not given it up since.

When Agna was ten there came a spring tide higher than anyone in the coves remembered. Her father lifted her onto the rocks at the top of the flood and let her cut a notch with his gutting knife to mark where the water stood. She still tells the story, usually to grandchildren who have heard it before, and the notch is still there on the cove rocks. Agna has not walked out to look at it in years. Her knees prefer the crate.

docs.title: The calm years
docs.text: Agna remembers when the sea was calm enough to fish at night. When she was young the cove boats went out on still summer nights with a lantern in every bow, and the girls on the shore could count them strung out across the water like a second line of stars. She went out herself, more than once, with her friend Maili, who later married Varro the warden. The night fishing thinned through the years when Sorcha was growing up, and nobody in the coves has fished at night for more than twenty years. Agna tells the young ones about it as if it were a fairy tale. Some of them think it is.

docs.title: Family
docs.text:
Agna married Donal, a cove fisher, a big slow man with large careful hands who never once tied a knot she could fault, which she says is the only reason she married him. He died of a winter fever fifteen years ago. Their daughter Sorcha has his boat, the Sea Thrift, and has patched it so often that Agna says there is more mending in it than boat. Sorcha is as loud and stubborn as her mother, which is why they argue every day, and why neither could do without it.

Agna approves of Calder, her son-in-law, mostly because he mends things without being asked. She taught her granddaughter Eilidh knots before letters, and has never yet told her a knot was better than "not bad", because the girl would stop trying. Her grandson Ronan she calls "the magpie", and she saves him the bright things that come up snagged in the nets: sea-glass, a brass button, once a little bell. She also has an opinion about the bridge knots of Kestra, whose mother Shona was a cove net-maker. Agna says they are "Shona's knots, near enough", which from Agna is a medal.

docs.title: The torn nets
docs.text:
These last few years Agna has begun to find nets torn by something with teeth far bigger than any fish she knows. Not the ragged holes a seal leaves, or the clean cuts of a rock, but long bites through a dozen meshes at once, always from the boats that went out past the point. Calder has measured some of the tears with his hands. Sorcha has stopped taking the children past the point. Agna mends every one and says nothing in front of Eilidh, who notices.

Last month a broken point of something hard and pale, curved, about as long as her finger, came up caught in the mesh of one of those nets. It is not bone she knows, or shell. She keeps it wrapped in a rag at the bottom of her mending basket and has shown it to no one, not even Calder.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Agna wants the coves' nets to come back whole. She wants to live long enough to tell Eilidh her knots are good. She fears she is mending nets for a sea that is no longer the one she learned on, and that one day the thing that bites them will not let go of the boat.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might carry Agna's finger-long fragment to someone who could say what it came from, or go out past the point with a net of her mending to see what tears it. Another might begin with Agna asking, gruffly, for someone to walk out to her old notch on the cove rocks and tell her where the water is.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Sorcha: daughter

docs.title: Ailsa
docs.text:
Keeper of the Tide Book

Town Goa Harbour Where Wardens' House Role Scholar Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Precise, dry and quietly delighted by patterns; she can recite a tide from forty years ago.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Ailsa is seventy-three and the Keeper of the Tide Book, the great ledger in the Wardens' House where the sea wardens of Goa Harbour have written down every tide since the first camp on the shore. She is precise, dry and quietly delighted by patterns. Ask her about the spring tide of a certain storm forty years ago and she will tell you the hour of the turn, the height on the quay steps, the wind, and which warden wrote it down, and then she will tell you he spelled the wind wrong.

docs.title: The book and its keeper
docs.text:
The Tide Book is not really one book any more. Its oldest pages, from the first camp, are a mixture of Savage tally marks and a careful Magician hand, and they have been rebound so many times that the spine is newer than the wardens who use it. Later volumes stand beside it on a long shelf in a dry room at the back of the Wardens' House, and the current one lies open on a slanted desk under the window. Every day the wardens bring Ailsa their tides: the hour of high and low water, the strength of the run through the gap, the eddies, the weather. She writes them in, checks them against the same moon in every year before, and asks sharp questions when something does not fit.

Ailsa came to the Wardens' House at seventeen, as copyist to old Keeper Innes, in the same spring that Varro became a warden. She has been keeper herself since she was twenty-seven, forty-six years now, and she and Varro are the last two left from those early days. He trusts her memory more than his own. She trusts his eyes more than her own. Between them, they used to say, they made one very good warden.

Her closest friend is Halvard, the clerk of the Wardens' House, who records the ships while she records the water. They eat their midday bread together at her desk most days. He cannot bear the crooked stack of loose notes she keeps at her elbow and straightens it every time he passes, and she puts it crooked again as soon as he is gone, because watching him try not to notice is one of the small pleasures of her day.

docs.title: The pages that do not match
docs.text:
For the past few years the new pages have not matched the old ones as well as they should. It is nothing a passing reader would see. The spring highs run a hand's breadth higher than the same moons did in the past. The slack water at the turn comes a few minutes late, then a few more. The strongest run through the gap has drifted, very slightly, toward the cliff on the forest side. Any one of these could be a careless warden or a strange year. All of them together, year on year, are a pattern, and patterns are what Ailsa understands best.

She has not said so out loud. She is trying to work out why before she does, because a keeper who cries out without a reason is no use to anyone. Iska, the First Warden, has seen the pages herself and asked her once what they meant. Ailsa told her, "Not yet." She has noticed that Varro, who always asks about anything odd in the water, has not asked her about this at all, and she suspects that means he has felt it too and is afraid of the answer. She is a little afraid of it herself.

docs.title: What she fears
docs.text: Ailsa fears that the water she has spent her life writing down is turning into water she does not know. She fears, more privately, that the answer is already somewhere in the oldest pages, in a hand she can only half read.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might carry tide marks to Ailsa from somewhere along the coast that the wardens do not reach, help her compare the oldest pages with what the coves and the cliffs remember, or find someone who can read the Magician hand of the first camp.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Varro: old colleague
  • Halvard: friend

docs.title: Arlo
docs.text:
Son of the First Warden

Town Goa Harbour Where Inlet Quay Role Child Age Child

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Serious, curious and stubborn; he asks why until the grown-ups give up.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Arlo is nine years old, the only child of Iska, the First Warden, and Dunmor, the lamplighter of the quays. He was born in the cliff house above the Inlet Quay, and the first sound he can remember is the water running hard through the gap at the turn of the tide. He is serious, curious and stubborn, and he asks "why" until the grown-ups give up. Most of them give up quite early. His grandmother Ysmay never does, which is one of the reasons he likes her best.

docs.title: A warden's son
docs.text:
Arlo has never wanted to be anything but a sea warden. His grandmother was one for forty years, his mother is the most respected pilot in Goa Harbour, and he does not see why he should have to wait until he is grown to start. The trouble is that his mother is almost never home at the hour he wants to learn, and when she is, his father has usually just persuaded her to sit down and eat, and Arlo has learned not to spoil that.

So he goes to Varro instead. Most mornings, before the lanterns are out, Arlo slips out of the house, down the cliff stairs and onto the quay, where the eldest of the sea wardens stands watching the water before anyone else is up. The first few times, Varro pretended not to see him. Then one grey morning he said, without turning round, "If you are going to stand there, stand where you can see the eddy," and since then Arlo has been his shadow. Varro does not praise him. He asks him what the water is doing, waits, and says "no" or "closer" or, very rarely, "aye." Arlo would rather have one "aye" from Varro than a basket of sweets.

Arlo believes that nobody knows about these mornings. His mother knows perfectly well and has decided to pretend she does not. His father knows too, because his father lights the lanterns and puts them out, and very little happens on the quay at dawn without him seeing it.

docs.title: Friends and family
docs.text:
Arlo's best friend is Eilidh, the fisher's daughter from the coves, who also wants to be a sea warden. They read the tide together from the cove rocks in the evenings and argue about it. Eilidh is quicker and Arlo is more careful, and each secretly thinks the other will make the better pilot. Her little brother Ronan tags along when he is not wandering off after something shiny, and Arlo puts up with him because Eilidh would not forgive him otherwise.

His grandmother lets him sit at her window above the Cliff Stairs and tells him exactly what every pilot passing through the gap is doing wrong. Arlo writes the best of her complaints down and checks them against what Varro says. Usually they agree, which delights them both when he tells them.

docs.title: What he wants and what he fears
docs.text: Arlo wants to take a ship through the gap with his own hands before he is twelve, which nobody has done in living memory, and he wants to crew the Gap Runner in the summer race on the day it finally beats Bain Harbour. He fears that the sea will keep getting rougher until there are no young pilots left to train, because he has heard Nessa say so at the Wardens' table when the grown-ups thought he was asleep on the bench. He also fears, though he would never admit it, that his mother will one day go out through the gap on a bad tide and not come back.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: Arlo has noticed something on the quay at dawn that Varro has not mentioned: the water in the lowest steps sometimes looks disturbed, as if something had just climbed out of it. He has not told anyone yet, because he wants to be sure first. A quest might find him following the clue too far, or need his sharp eyes and his habit of being where he is not supposed to be.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Iska: mother
  • Dunmor: father
  • Ysmay: grandmother
  • Varro: patient teacher
  • Eilidh: best friend

docs.title: Bethoc
docs.text:
Keeper of the Gap Inn

Town Goa Harbour Where Lantern Market Role Service Age Adult Sells Hot stew, ale and rooms for the night

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Warm, quick-witted and unshockable; she has heard every sailor's story twice.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Bethoc is forty-five and keeps the Gap Inn on the Lantern Market, where sailors, hunters, drovers and travellers all end up sooner or later. She is warm, quick-witted and unshockable. She has heard every sailor's story twice, and the second time she usually corrects the details. Her stew is the best on the quay, her ale is honest, and her rooms are small, clean and nearly always full.

docs.title: The inn
docs.text:
The Gap Inn is a long, low timber house with a stone hearth at one end and a view of the inlet from the other, and Bethoc was born in the room above the kitchen. Her father, Malcolm, kept the inn for thirty-five years before her, and her mother died when she was a baby, so Bethoc grew up behind the bar, carrying bowls before she could see over it. Malcolm died eleven years ago, and the inn has been hers since. Some of the old regulars still call it "Malcolm's," and she lets them.

Her day starts before dawn with the stew pot and ends long after dark with the last singer. In between she pours, cooks, mends quarrels, sends drunk sailors back to their ships, and listens. People tell Bethoc things. She has never been sure why, but she knows more about Goa Harbour than anyone except perhaps Hamish at the rope lift, and unlike Hamish she keeps most of it to herself.

docs.title: The board
docs.text:
Five years ago Bethoc grew tired of hunters arguing at her tables about where a creature had been seen, and on what night, and by whom. She nailed a broad plank to the wall by the door and chalked the sightings on it herself: what, where, when and who said so. It has been there ever since. Now the hunters check it every morning before they go out. Torva reads it in silence and leaves; Kenna reads it and complains that nothing on it is big enough. Fishers, drovers and timber cutters add to it, and Bethoc wipes off old sightings once a month and keeps a tally of how many there were in a little book under the bar.

The tally is the part nobody else sees, and it is the part that worries her. Each year the book needs more pages. She has begun to show it, quietly, to the people who might do something with it.

docs.title: The people of the inn
docs.text:
Cormac, the old shanty singer, has had the same seat by the fire for longer than Bethoc has kept the inn. He sings the songs of the shared camp, weeps at his own verses, and flatters her shamelessly in the hope of a free cup, which he usually gets. Mhairi, his old pupil, plays the fiddle for Bethoc most nights and at the summer race send-off, and plays faster whenever people try to stop dancing. Bethoc pays her in coin, stew, and the right to play whatever she likes.

And then there is Brodie, the fishmonger, Bethoc's sweetheart for the past three years. He is loud where she is dry, and he names every fish he sells, which she pretends to find ridiculous. He comes in every evening after the market closes and sits at the end of the bar until she has time for him, however long it takes. Neither of them has said anything about marrying, and the whole Lantern Market has opinions about that.

docs.title: What she wants
docs.text: Bethoc wants her inn full, her people fed and her board empty, and she suspects she will only ever get two of the three. She fears the night when one of the hunters who reads her board in the morning does not come back to the inn in the evening.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: The sighting board is a natural place for a quest to begin: a strange entry chalked by someone nobody saw come in, or a creature that turns up on it three nights running in the same spot. Bethoc might also ask someone to carry her tally book to the Wardens' House, if she could be sure they would not read it on the way.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Cormac: regular
  • Mhairi: fiddler
  • Brodie: sweetheart

docs.title: Brigid
docs.text:
Herb Gatherer

Town Goa Harbour Where Forest Shore Role Healer Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Shy, gentle and observant; she notices everything and says very little.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Brigid is seventeen and the herb gatherer of the Forest Shore, the apprentice of Elspeth the healer. Twice a day, whenever the tide goes out, she is down on the rocks with a flat basket and a short knife, picking the sea-herbs that Elspeth turns into salves and tonics. She is shy, gentle and observant. She notices everything and says very little, and people who talk to her often walk away realising that they have told her a great deal and learned almost nothing about her.

docs.title: The girl on the rocks
docs.text:
Brigid does not remember her parents. When she was two, the log raft they were working broke up rounding the point on a bad tide, and neither came ashore. She was raised by her grandmother, Oonagh, who gathered dulse and sea-herbs on the Forest Shore rocks and sold them to the healer and the smokehouses. Oonagh took the little girl out on the rocks from the time she could walk on weed without falling, and taught her the beds one by one: which grew on the sunny side of which rock, which wanted the full tide over them, which could only be cut every third spring.

Oonagh died when Brigid was eleven. Elspeth, who had been buying Oonagh's herbs for thirty years, came to the funeral, looked at the thin, silent girl holding a basket she would not put down, and took her home. Brigid has slept in the loft of the low stone house ever since, among the bunches of drying herbs that hang from every beam, and has been Elspeth's apprentice for six years.

docs.title: The craft
docs.text:
Elspeth says there is no magic in the sea-herb craft, only knowing which herb, which tide and which hour, and that the knowing is the magic. Brigid has the knowing already, for the gathering at least. She can tell a bed's health from the colour of its edges at twenty paces, and she knows the hour a herb is strongest by the smell of it on her fingers. The brewing she is still learning, slowly, because Elspeth teaches by doing and Brigid learns by watching, and neither of them says much while they work.

She has seen what the brewing is for. The hunters bring their wounded to Elspeth's door several times a week now, and Brigid holds the bowls and the lamps. She has watched Elspeth stitch Torva more than once, and she has seen Osric, Elspeth's son, sit silent by the fire on his bad nights. Brigid never asks him anything. She thinks that is perhaps why he does not mind her being there.

docs.title: The withering beds
docs.text:
Last autumn the oldest beds on the low rocks at the forest end of the shore began to fail. The leaves came up pale, then went soft and dark at the root, and the beds shrank from the bottom edge upward. By this spring five of the eleven beds she has picked all her life were withering, and two of them were nearly gone. She has not found a cause. She has wondered whether she cut them too hard, whether some sickness is in them, whether something grazes them at night. She has also noticed, without knowing what to make of it, that the wrack line on those rocks sits a little higher than it used to.

She has not told Elspeth. Elspeth's great fear is running out of herbs while the wounds keep coming, and Brigid cannot bring herself to be the one who tells her it has begun. Instead she has been walking further along the wild coast at low tide to fill her basket from beds she barely knows, and still coming home with it a little lighter. Elspeth has noticed the lighter baskets and been gentler with her, which makes it much worse.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Brigid wants to be a healer as good as Elspeth, though she would never say so, and has no idea Elspeth thinks she will be better. She wants the old beds to come back. She fears that Elspeth will think she has failed her, and she fears, more quietly, the stretches of wild coast she now walks alone, where the forest comes right down to the rocks.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might walk the far rocks with Brigid at low tide to guard her while she gathers, or find out what is killing the old beds. Another might help her find the words, and the courage, to tell Elspeth.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Elspeth: teacher

docs.title: Brodie
docs.text:
Fishmonger

Town Goa Harbour Where Lantern Market Sells Fresh fish, smoked fish and salted fish for the road

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Sorcha: supplier
  • Bethoc: sweetheart

docs.title: Caddoc
docs.text:
Trapper

Town Goa Harbour Where Forest Shore Role Adventurer Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Grumbling, cautious and clever with his hands; he complains constantly and never quits.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Caddoc is forty-two and a trapper of the Forest Shore. He sets his traps along the strip of rock and scrub between the forest and the sea, where the creatures come out of the trees at night, and he complains about every single part of the work: the weather, the bait, the price of wire, the price of pelts, his knees, the gulls, and the general unfairness of a world that makes a man get up before dawn to look at holes in the ground. He has been doing it for twenty-six years. He has never once quit.

docs.title: From the hills
docs.text:
Caddoc was born in the highlands, in a trapping family that worked the hills above the hill road where Goa Harbour's wool and pelts come down to the coast. His father taught him to set a snare before he could read, and to make every part of a trap himself, because a trap you bought was a trap you did not understand. When Caddoc was sixteen his father went up into the high pasture to check a line in a snowstorm and did not come back. His mother had died years before. Caddoc packed his father's tools, walked down the hill road with a drover's flock, and never went back up.

He has lived on the Forest Shore ever since, in a hut full of springs, cords, wire and half-built cages, which he will tell you is a mess and will not let anyone tidy. He is clever with his hands in a grumbling, absent way; he will mend your latch while explaining why it was badly made in the first place, and refuse payment, and complain about that too.

docs.title: Partners and buyers
docs.text:
Caddoc's hunting partner is Torva, who leads the hunters of the wild coast. They have worked side by side for seven years. She hunts what comes out of the forest by day; he catches what comes out by night. They trust each other completely and have never said so, and if either of them ever did, the other would be deeply embarrassed. Lately Torva has started coming out with him at dawn to look at his traps, and that, more than anything in the traps, is what is keeping Caddoc awake. Torva does not waste her mornings on nothing.

His pelts go to Greer, the fur trader of the Lantern Market, who ships them all over the island. Fewer trappers come down from the highlands every year, which means Greer needs Caddoc more than she used to and pays him more than she used to, and he still grumbles that it is not enough. Greer pretends to be wounded by this. They both enjoy it.

docs.title: The traps that are sprung
docs.text:
For most of a season now, something has been springing Caddoc's biggest traps, the heavy cage traps he builds for the worst of the night creatures, without being caught. The bait is gone. The doors have dropped. The cages are empty. There is no hair on the wire, no blood, and the ground around them has been swept smooth, as if by a tail or by something that did not want to leave tracks. Caddoc has rebuilt the triggers three times, each more cunning than the last. Each time, within a week, they are sprung again.

He tells everyone it is a nuisance. It is beginning to frighten him, and he is not easily frightened. Whatever it is, it is clever enough to learn his traps, and Caddoc has spent his life believing that cleverness was the one thing the creatures did not have.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might sit up through the night with Caddoc beside his biggest trap, help him build a trigger that even the clever thing cannot learn, or carry his pelts to Greer on a morning he will not leave the shore.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Torva: hunting partner
  • Greer: buyer

docs.title: Calder
docs.text:
Cove Fisher

Town Goa Harbour Where Fishers' Coves Role Worker Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Quiet, patient and endlessly mending something; he hums old camp songs while he works.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Calder is forty, a cove fisher, and the calm half of the best boat in the Fishers' Coves. He is quiet, patient and endlessly mending something: a net, a rowlock, a child's sandal, a neighbour's gate. While he works he hums the old camp songs, the ones from the days when Savage hunters and Magicians first fished the inlet together, and he hums them so constantly that people in the coves only notice when he stops.

docs.title: The songs and the boy
docs.text:
Calder's parents both died in the same hard fever winter when he was five, and he was raised by his grandmother, Morven, in a stone cottage above the far end of the coves. Morven knew every camp song there was and sang them at the fire, at the nets and at the gutting table, and Calder learned them the way other children learn to walk. She died when he was twenty. He still sings her verses, a few of which nobody else in Goa Harbour seems to know, though Cormac at the Lantern Market has tried more than once to coax them out of him over a cup at the Gap Inn.

As a boy Calder spent more time on the Inlet Quay than in the coves, because that was where the boats were built, and that was where he met Tamsin. She was a fierce, skinny girl who wanted to know how everything fitted together; he was the boy who would hold the other end of the plank for as long as she needed. They have been friends ever since. These days she builds and rebuilds Goa Harbour's race boat, the Gap Runner, and Calder is the friend she complains to when the winter rebuild is going badly, which is every winter.

docs.title: Sorcha and the children
docs.text:
Calder married Sorcha thirteen years ago. She is loud and he is quiet, she finds the fish and he mends whatever broke in the finding, and between them they bring in the best catch of any boat in the town. People who do not know them wonder how he puts up with the shouting. People who do know them have seen him make her laugh until she has to sit down.

Their daughter Eilidh is ten and bossy and already reads the tide from the cove rocks every evening; their son Ronan is seven and dreamy and always somewhere he is not supposed to be. Calder is the parent Ronan shows his treasures to, because Calder listens. He has seen the smooth stone Ronan keeps hidden in his pocket, once, and promised not to tell. He has kept the promise, though it worries him that the stone is always faintly warm.

docs.title: The bigger boat
docs.text: Calder wants to build a bigger boat one day, a proper deep-water boat with room for a crew, and race it around Veligor himself. He has drawn it a hundred times on the backs of tally sheets. Tamsin has looked at the drawings and told him exactly what is wrong with each, which from Tamsin is high praise, and she has promised to help him build it once the Gap Runner finally beats Bain Harbour. He knows Sorcha has been setting aside a little of every good catch toward it. He has not told her he knows.

docs.title: What he fears
docs.text: Calder is not a worrier by nature, but the sea has turned rougher, and he has started to hum less on the water. His mother-in-law Agna finds the nets torn by something with teeth far bigger than any fish, and he has mended those tears himself and measured them with his hands. He does not say what he thinks they mean.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might help Calder gather timber for his boat, track down someone who remembers the rest of one of Morven's half-forgotten verses, or quietly find out what Ronan's warm stone is without breaking a promise.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Sorcha: wife
  • Eilidh: daughter
  • Ronan: son
  • Tamsin: friend

docs.title: Cormac
docs.text:
Shanty Singer

Town Goa Harbour Where Lantern Market Role Performer Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Theatrical, sentimental and a shameless flatterer; he cries at his own songs.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Cormac is seventy-nine and the oldest shanty singer in Goa Harbour. He sings the songs of the shared camp, from the days when Savage hunters and Magicians first fished the inlet together, and he sings them at the Gap Inn most nights from the same seat by the fire that he has had since Bethoc's father kept the inn. He is theatrical, sentimental and a shameless flatterer. He tells every landlady she has the finest ale on Veligor, every fisher that his catch is the stuff of songs, and every child that they have a singer's ear. Then he sings, and weeps at his own verses, and the remarkable thing is that by the end of the song most of the room is weeping with him.

docs.title: A life of songs
docs.text:
Cormac grew up on the Lantern Market, the son of a sailmaker who sang at his work, and he learned the camp songs the way children in Goa Harbour used to, from everyone at once: the net-menders in the coves, the old pilots on the quay, the drovers coming down from the hills. He tried being a sailmaker himself and was dreadful at it. He tried crewing a trading ship and spent the whole voyage singing to the crew instead of working. By twenty he had given up pretending, and he has sung for his supper ever since.

The finest voice he ever heard belonged to Morven of the coves, who knew more of the old verses than anyone alive. They sang together for forty years and argued for most of them about which of their versions was right. When she died, twenty years ago, Cormac sang at the shore for her and could not finish. He still thinks she knew things he does not. Her grandson Calder, the quiet fisher, hums some of her verses while he mends his nets, and Cormac has tried more than once to coax them out of him over a cup at the Gap Inn. Calder only smiles.

docs.title: The inn and the pupil
docs.text: The Gap Inn is Cormac's home in every way but the bed. Bethoc, who keeps it now, has known him all her life. She lets him flatter her into a free cup most evenings and pretends she does not know exactly what he is doing. Mhairi, the fiddler, was his pupil: he taught her the old tunes when she was a girl who could barely hold the bow, and now she plays them faster than he can sing them, on purpose, to make him laugh. He calls her the best thing he has ever done. She is writing a song about the summer race, and he is quietly hurt that she has not asked him for a single verse of it.

docs.title: The verse about the gap
docs.text:
Cormac swears that he knows a verse about the gap that nobody else remembers. He learned it as a boy from an old pilot on the quay who made him repeat it until he had it perfectly, and told him to keep it. He has sung the first line of it at the Gap Inn a few times, something about the hour the water forgets, and then stopped, and refused to go on, and wept. People think it is one of his performances. It is not. He has never been sure he has the end of it right, and he believes Morven had another version, and that Calder may have heard it.

He swears the verse is important. He cannot say why, only that the old pilot was frightened when he taught it, and Cormac has never forgotten the look on his face. Lately, with the sea growing rougher and the talk in the inn turning to strange things in the water, he has started to feel that he is running out of time to find out.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might coax Morven's verses out of Calder for Cormac, carry the gap verse to Ailsa at the Wardens' House to see if it matches anything in the Tide Book, or simply persuade Cormac to sing the whole verse through once to the right listener.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Bethoc: landlady
  • Mhairi: pupil

docs.title: Corrie
docs.text:
Apprentice Pilot

Town Goa Harbour Where Inlet Quay Role Worker Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Careful, earnest and anxious to get everything right; she writes notes on the back of her hand.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Corrie is nineteen and an apprentice pilot of the sea wardens, learning to take ships through the gap under Kor, the newest and boldest of the full wardens. She is careful, earnest and anxious to get everything right. She writes notes on the back of her hand in ink, tide times and warnings and things Kor has said, and by evening her left hand is usually blue to the wrist. Every night she copies the day's notes into a little oilcloth-covered book before she washes them off. She has filled four of these books. She has never lost one.

docs.title: The quay girl
docs.text:
Corrie grew up on the Inlet Quay with her mother, Rhona, who gutted fish for the smokehouses and raised her alone. Her father was a deckhand on a trading ship who sailed out before she was born and never came back to Goa Harbour; she has no wish to find him. Rhona died of a fever when Corrie was twelve, and after that the quay raised her. She ran errands for captains, carried messages to the Wardens' House, fetched rope and pies and lost cats, and learned the name of every boat and the temper of every skipper.

Four years ago, on a wet night, a stranger came down the gangplank of a coastal trader with one sea-chest and asked where she might find a bed. Corrie found her a loft above a net store, and that stranger was Esk, the sellsword. They have been friends ever since. Esk is the only person Corrie has ever met who is more careful than she is.

docs.title: Learning the gap
docs.text: At seventeen Corrie talked her way onto the oars of the wardens' pilot boats, and she rowed for two years before anyone let her take a tiller. Last spring Kor became a full warden, and she was made his apprentice. Kor is cheerful and a little reckless; he whistles while he pilots and swears the tide likes him. Corrie learns more from his mistakes than from his advice, and keeps a separate page in her book for each kind. She admires him enormously and thinks he will drown one day if someone does not keep an eye on him, so she does.

docs.title: What she saw
docs.text:
Last month Corrie was in the pilot boat ahead of a timber ship, bringing it through the gap at slack water, when something large and dark passed beneath the ship. It was longer than the hull and moved against the tide, slowly, and then it was gone. Kor was looking the other way. When she told him, he laughed and said it was a cloud shadow. When she told the wardens, they were kind about it, which was worse. Only Halvard, the clerk, wrote it down, without a word, and Corrie does not know why.

Esk believed her at once, and then told her quietly that it was not the first: Esk has seen things of her own, far out beyond the gap, and describes them to no one but Corrie. Corrie writes those down too, on the back of her hand, and copies them into the back of her oilcloth book, on pages she has numbered and dated with great care. She thinks that if she can only make the record complete enough, the wardens will have to listen.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Corrie wants to be a full sea warden, and to be the kind of warden people trust without question. She fears that she never will be now, that she will always be the apprentice who saw a monster in the gap. She fears much more that she was right, and that the next time it passes under a ship, the ship will not come out the other side.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might keep watch with Corrie in the pilot boat at slack water to see the shadow again, help her lay her notes in front of the wardens, or bring Corrie and Halvard together to compare what each has written down.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Kor: mentor
  • Esk: friend

docs.title: Dougal
docs.text:
Night Watchman of the Quay

Town Goa Harbour Where Inlet Quay Role Guard Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Sleepy-looking but sharp-eared; he tells terrible jokes to keep himself awake.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Dougal is sixty-six and the night watchman of the Inlet Quay, and he has walked it from dusk to first light for thirty years. He counts the lanterns, he counts the boats, he checks the mooring lines and the warehouse doors, and then he starts again from the other end. He looks permanently half asleep, with heavy eyelids and a slow, rolling walk, and he is not. He can hear a rope creak against the wrong bollard from the far end of the quay. To keep himself awake he tells jokes, terrible ones, to the gulls, the boats, the lanterns and anyone foolish enough to stop and talk.

docs.title: Before the watch
docs.text:
Dougal grew up on the Inlet Quay and went to sea young as a deckhand on the timber ships, hauling cargo out through the gap behind the wardens' pilot boats. He liked the work and hated the seasickness, which never left him in twenty years of sailing. In his early thirties he came ashore for good and worked as a quay porter, and at thirty-six, when old Ewart, the night watchman, decided his legs had walked enough nights, Dougal asked for the lantern and the stick. Ewart handed them over with a single piece of advice: count everything, every night, because one night the count will be wrong. Dougal has counted ever since.

He never married. He lives in a little stone watch-hut at the end of the quay, near the foot of the Long Stair, and sleeps there through the day with a blanket over the window. He says the quay is the only family that never asks him where he has been.

docs.title: The night quay
docs.text:
Dougal's evening begins when Dunmor the lamplighter lights the last lantern and ends when Dunmor comes back at first light to put them out. In between, Dougal knows every sound the quay makes. He knows which boats knock in a swell and which grind, which warehouse door rattles in a north wind, and which of the lanterns burns a shade lower than its neighbours. He has seen a great many things on the quay at night that were nobody's business, and he has told none of them. He has, for instance, seen the First Warden's son Arlo slipping down to the quay at dawn as he goes off duty, and has said nothing about it, which in Goa Harbour seems to be the custom.

At the change of the night watch he walks to the bottom of the stairs and shares a pot of tea with Ruan, the captain of the Cliff Watch. They have done it for years. Ruan was a new recruit once, falling asleep on his feet at his post, and Dougal kept him awake with jokes until his watch was over. Ruan says the jokes were so bad he stayed awake out of fury. Dougal says that is the whole point.

His favourite, which he tells at least once a week: why did the gull sit on the lantern? Because it wanted to be a light-house bird. Nobody has ever laughed. Dougal laughs every time.

docs.title: The tracks
docs.text:
Early this spring, on his last round before first light, Dougal found wet tracks on the lowest steps of the quay, where the stone runs down into the water. They were wide and splayed, with the marks of claws at the ends of long toes, and they came up out of the sea onto the bottom steps and went back down again. They were wider than his boot. Since then he has found them on about a dozen mornings, never much higher than the bottom few steps, always drying fast. He measures them against his boot, and then he sluices them away with a bucket of seawater before the quay wakes, so that nobody takes fright.

He has told only Ruan. He trusts Ruan to know what to do with it, and he does not trust himself to tell it without making it a joke. Once or twice this spring, on a still night, he has also seen the lanterns on the lowest landing dip all together and come back. He assumed Dunmor knew. Neither of them has mentioned it to the other.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Dougal wants to walk the quay until his legs go, as Ewart did, and hand the lantern to someone who will count. He fears the night his count will be wrong, and he has begun, for the first time in thirty years, to keep his back to the wall when he passes the lowest steps.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might sit up with Dougal on the lowest steps of the quay through a night to see what leaves the tracks, or help him carry his measurements up to the Wardens' House when Ruan finally decides to speak. Another might begin on the morning his count of boats comes up one short.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Ruan: friend

docs.title: Dunmor
docs.text:
Lamplighter of the Quays

Town Goa Harbour Where Inlet Quay Role Service Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Gentle, unhurried and content; he knows every lantern on the quay by its flicker.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Dunmor is forty-four, the lamplighter of the quays, and the husband of Iska, the First Warden. Every evening at dusk he walks the Inlet Quay with his long pole and his tinder box and lights the forest-crafted lanterns one by one, and every morning at first light he walks it again to put them out. He is gentle, unhurried and content, which in Goa Harbour, a town of quick tides and quicker tempers, makes him something of a curiosity. He knows every lantern on the quay by its flicker, and he will tell you which one is sulking.

docs.title: The lamplighter's son
docs.text:
Dunmor's father, Tormod, was lamplighter before him, and Dunmor walked the quay at his side from the time he could carry the tinder box. His mother died when he was a boy, and the lanterns became the thing he and his father shared instead of talk. Tormod died twenty-two years ago, and Dunmor, at twenty-two, simply picked up the pole the next evening and went on. Nobody appointed him. Nobody needed to.

The lanterns themselves are made by Gunna, the master lantern-maker of the Lantern Market, by a craft handed down from the Magicians of the first camp. Dunmor does not know how they are made, and he has never asked; he thinks some things are better kept by the people who keep them. He does know what each one needs. He brings Gunna the ones that are failing before anyone else can see that they are, and she has said, in her teasing way, that he understands her lanterns better than her apprentice does. Dunmor has had the kindness never to repeat that to Tarran.

docs.title: Iska
docs.text:
Dunmor met Iska on the quay steps, as most people in Goa Harbour meet the First Warden. She was a young warden coming in late from a night pilotage, soaked and furious at a captain who had nearly put his ship on the rocks, and he held up a lantern for her on the slippery bottom step. He held it up for her most nights after that, for a year, before she noticed that he was waiting for her and not the ships. They married twelve years ago.

Iska is quick, sure and hard to rattle; Dunmor is slow and patient and impossible to hurry. He is the one person in the town who can make the First Warden sit down and eat, and he does it every evening, after the lanterns are lit, with a bowl of something hot and no argument at all. He worries about her more than he lets her see. When she takes a ship through the gap on a bad tide, he lights the lanterns on the end of the quay first, and stays by them.

docs.title: Arlo and Ysmay
docs.text: Their son Arlo is nine, and he sneaks down to the quay at dawn to watch old Varro read the water. Dunmor, who is on the quay at dawn every day of his life putting out the lanterns, saw him the very first morning. He has never said a word to the boy, only made sure the lantern on the lowest step is the last one he puts out. Ysmay, his mother-in-law, thinks Dunmor is far too soft. She also says he is the best thing that ever happened to her daughter, though never where Iska can hear.

docs.title: What he has noticed
docs.text: Some nights this spring, the lanterns on the lowest landing of the quay have guttered all at once, though there was no wind, and steadied again a few moments later. Dunmor has not told anyone. He is not sure there is anything to tell. But he has begun to light those lanterns last, and to stand by them a while.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might help Dunmor fetch a failing lantern back to Gunna through a dark night, or watch the lowest landing with him to learn what makes the lanterns gutter.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Iska: wife
  • Arlo: son
  • Gunna: lantern-maker

docs.title: Eilidh
docs.text:
Fisher's Daughter

Town Goa Harbour Where Fishers' Coves Role Child Age Child

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Bossy, clever and impossible to fool; she keeps her little brother in line.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Eilidh is ten, the elder child of Sorcha and Calder, and by general agreement the person in the Fishers' Coves it is hardest to fool. She is bossy, clever and quick, and she keeps her little brother Ronan in line with a firmness that makes grown fishers step out of her way. She can already gut a fish faster than most adults in the coves, which she will demonstrate to anyone who doubts it, and to several people who do not.

docs.title: Cove-born
docs.text:
Eilidh was born in the coves and has spent her whole life between the boats, the nets and the rocks. Her mother is the loudest fisher in Goa Harbour and her father the quietest, and Eilidh has inherited her mother's voice and her father's patience, though she only uses the patience on fish. Her grandmother Agna, the net-mender, taught her knots before letters, and is the only person whose opinion of her work Eilidh truly fears. When Agna says a knot of hers is "not bad", Eilidh walks on air for a day.

Until a few years ago she went out on the Sea Thrift whenever she liked, and she was proud of it. Then the sea turned rougher, and her mother stopped taking the children past the point. Eilidh has asked why at least forty times and has never had a proper answer. She suspects it has something to do with the torn nets her grandmother brings back and does not talk about, and she is right, but nobody will tell her so.

docs.title: The tide reader
docs.text:
Eilidh means to be a sea warden. Not a fisher, not a pilot's helper: a warden, one of the people who guide every ship through the gap. Every evening, after the catch is in and the fish are gutted, she climbs out onto the cove rocks and watches the tide come and go, and writes what it does on a slate she keeps in a crack in the rock. Her best friend Arlo, the First Warden's son, often comes too, and they argue about the water until it is too dark to see it. Eilidh is quicker; Arlo is more careful. She knows he gets lessons from old Varro on the quay at dawn, and she is jealous of it, though she would rather eat a raw crab than say so.

Ronan comes along when he can be found. Eilidh complains about him constantly and has never once gone home without him.

docs.title: What she has noticed
docs.text: There is an old mark on the cove rocks, a notch her grandmother cut as a girl to show where the highest spring tide reached. Eilidh has watched it all spring, and the water has gone over it twice. She has written this on her slate and underlined it. She is waiting until she is sure before she shows anyone, because she does not want to be laughed at by the wardens, and she does not want to be told she is only a child.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Eilidh wants to stand at the Wardens' table one day and be taken seriously. She wants to go back out past the point. Most of all she wants nothing bad to happen to Ronan, who wanders off after anything that glows and has, she is fairly sure, a secret in his pocket she has not yet managed to get out of him. She fears that the grown-ups are hiding something about the sea, and that they are hiding it because they are frightened.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might help Eilidh prove what her slate shows by carrying it to someone at the Wardens' House who will listen, or help her find Ronan on an evening he has wandered somewhere he should not have.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Sorcha: mother
  • Calder: father
  • Ronan: brother
  • Arlo: best friend

docs.title: Elspeth
docs.text:
Healer

Town Goa Harbour Where Forest Shore Role Healer Age Elder Sells Sea-herb salves, poultices and tonics

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Serene, firm and quietly funny; she scolds her patients and then tucks them in.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Elspeth is seventy-one and the healer of Goa Harbour. She lives and works in a low stone house on the Forest Shore, where the trees meet the rocks, with bunches of drying sea-herbs hanging from every beam and a kettle that has not been cold in living memory. She is serene, firm and quietly funny. She scolds her patients and then tucks them in, and most of the town has been both scolded and tucked in by her at least once.

docs.title: The sea-herb craft
docs.text:
The remedies Elspeth keeps are older than the kingdom. When the Magicians came to the inlet in the Age of Division, they came partly for the sea-herbs that grow on the tide rocks, and they learned to make salves, poultices and tonics from them that no forest herb could match. They taught the craft to the shared camp on the shore, and it has passed from healer to apprentice ever since. Elspeth learned it from old Fenella, who kept this same house before her, and she has kept it for forty-five years.

She will tell you there is no magic in it, only knowing which herb, which tide and which hour. Then she will tell you that the knowing is the magic, and go back to grinding.

docs.title: Family
docs.text: Elspeth married Aonghas, a woodsman of the Forest Shore, when she was young. He died thirty years ago, when the forest was still a quieter place, of a chill he caught clearing a windfall in the rain. Their son Osric followed his father into the woods and is a woodsman too. He is an uneasy, watchful man, superstitious in a way his father never was, and he will not work past sunset for any wage. Last autumn something happened to him deep in the forest, the day every bird went silent at once. He has never told his mother what he saw, and Elspeth, who can get the truth out of anyone else in Goa Harbour, has not been able to get it out of him. She has stopped asking. She leaves a lamp in her window every night instead, and he has noticed.

docs.title: Brigid
docs.text: Her apprentice is Brigid, a shy, gentle girl who gathers the sea-herbs on the rocks at low tide. Brigid notices everything and says very little, and Elspeth thinks she will be a better healer than Elspeth ever was, which she has not told her, because it would only make the girl blush for a week. Lately Brigid has been quieter even than usual, and her baskets have been a little lighter. Elspeth has put it down to the extra work and resolved to be gentler. She has not guessed the reason.

docs.title: Too many wounds
docs.text: For most of her life, Elspeth's work was fevers, births, broken fingers and fishhooks. Now it is claws and teeth. The hunters of the wild coast bring their wounded to her door several times a week, and she can barely gather and brew fast enough to keep up. Torva, who leads them, is her most frequent patient and her favourite, because Torva is the only person in the town who does exactly what Elspeth tells her. Elspeth has stitched most of her scars, including the long one along her jaw, and she scolds her for every one.

docs.title: What she fears
docs.text: Elspeth fears running out. Not of courage, which she has plenty of, but of herbs: the old beds can only give so much each tide, and the wounds keep coming. She fears, too, that whatever Osric saw is still out there, and that he will not be the last to see it.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might gather sea-herbs from the far rocks at low tide when Brigid cannot go, or find new beds further along the wild coast. Another might go into the deep forest to the place where the birds went silent, and come back with something Elspeth can tell her son.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Osric: son
  • Brigid: apprentice
  • Torva: patient

docs.title: Esk
docs.text:
Sellsword of the Wild Coast

Town Goa Harbour Where Inlet Quay Role Adventurer Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Quiet, wary and courteous; she pays her debts and keeps her past to herself.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Esk is a sellsword of the wild coast, a woman of about thirty-four who came to Goa Harbour on a trading ship four years ago and never left. She is quiet, wary and courteous. She pays her debts to the copper, keeps her blades clean and her past to herself, and hunts monsters for whoever will pay her to. In a town that loves to talk, Esk listens, and people have learned that when she does say something, it is worth hearing.

docs.title: The stranger who stayed
docs.text:
Nobody in Goa Harbour knows where Esk came from. The ship that brought her had worked its way round the coast from port to port, and she came down its gangplank with one sea-chest, a short sword, a long knife and the look of someone who had been travelling for a long time. She paid her passage, asked where she could find a bed and work, and has been here since. Asked about her life before, she smiles politely and changes the subject, and she is so good at it that most people only realise afterward that she has told them nothing at all. There is an old burn scar across the back of her left hand that she keeps covered when she can, and a name she sometimes says in her sleep, according to the woman who rents her the loft above the net store on the Inlet Quay. Nobody has worked out whose.

The first person she met in Goa Harbour was Corrie, who was then not yet an apprentice pilot, only a careful, earnest girl running errands on the quay, and who found Esk that loft on the night she landed. They have been friends ever since.

docs.title: The work
docs.text:
Esk takes whatever hunting work comes: clearing a creature out of a cove, guarding a timber party, walking a drover's flock down from the hills. More and more, though, she sails with the fishing boats that go far out beyond the gap, as a guard against whatever comes up out of the water. That work pays well, because few people will do it. Esk does it because she wants to see.

Gwenna, the outfitter, is her friend, and her most honest critic. Gwenna was an adventurer herself until a bad fall in the sea caves, and she tells Esk exactly how each plan will get her killed. Esk listens, adjusts the plan, and buys her rope from no one else. Gwenna keeps a list of everyone who has gone into the sea caves and not come back. Esk has asked, once, never to be on it, and Gwenna said that was up to Esk.

Teague, the highland drover, wants her to guard his next trip down the hill road, after monsters cost him half a flock last spring. She has not said yes yet. She has not said no. She is, as usual, thinking about it.

docs.title: What she has seen
docs.text: Far out, in the deep water beyond the gap, Esk has seen things she does not have names for: a long shadow keeping pace with a boat for half a morning, a patch of sea that went flat and dark in a fresh wind, lights below the surface on a moonless night. She will not describe them at the Gap Inn, or to the wardens, or to anyone except Corrie. When Corrie saw something large and dark pass beneath a ship in the gap last month and nobody believed her, Esk did, and told her it was not the first. Corrie writes down everything Esk tells her on the back of her hand and copies it out at night.

docs.title: What she wants
docs.text: Esk wants to understand what is in the deep water before it comes into the gap. She wants to stay in Goa Harbour, which surprises her. She fears that her past will follow her here, and she fears, more lately, that it will not have to, because something else is coming first.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might sail out with Esk to find the long shadow again, help Corrie make the wardens listen, or guard Teague's flock beside her on the hill road.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Gwenna: friend
  • Teague: hopeful employer
  • Corrie: friend

docs.title: Fionn
docs.text:
Stair Runner

Town Goa Harbour Where Cliff Stairs Role Child Age Child

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Quick, cheeky and fearless; he knows every shortcut on the cliffs.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Fionn is ten years old and the fastest stair runner on the cliffs of Goa Harbour. For a copper a trip he will carry a message, a parcel or a forgotten lunch from the Inlet Quay to the highest house in the clifftop quarter and back, and he will usually be back before you have finished counting out the copper. He is quick, cheeky and fearless. He knows every shortcut on the cliffs: the gap behind the smokehouse where you can drop two landings at once, the ledge under the third rope bridge, the goat path that cuts the Long Stair in half if you do not mind holding on with your fingers. Gorm, the Master of the Stairs, pretends to be furious about every one of these. Fionn knows perfectly well that he is not.

docs.title: The boy by the windlass
docs.text:
Fionn's father, Duncan, was a cove fisher who drowned in a storm when Fionn was barely one. His mother, Ishbel, died of a wasting cough two winters later. He does not remember either of them clearly, only a blue shawl and a song about a gull. Since he was three he has lived with his uncle Hamish in the little house beside the windlass of the rope lift, at the top of the cliffs, and he has grown up to the creak of the rope and the sound of Hamish talking to whoever is in the basket.

Hamish is chatty, jolly and nosy, and knows everyone's business in Goa Harbour. Fionn adores him and has learned, in self-defence, to keep a secret better than anyone else in town. He brings Hamish all the news he picks up on the stairs, which Hamish loves, and keeps back the one thing Hamish would hate.

docs.title: Following the hunters
docs.text:
That one thing is the forest. Whenever he can, Fionn slips away after Torva's hunters as they set out from the Forest Shore, and creeps after them to the edge of the trees. He is sure nobody has noticed. In fact Torva noticed the very first time. She lets him come as far as the last stump and no farther, and she makes sure one of her hunters is always between him and the trees, and none of them has ever said a word to him about it, or to Hamish. Fionn thinks he is the best tracker in the town. He is, in fact, very good, and the hunters have begun to say so to each other when he is out of earshot.

He is saving his coppers in a tin under the floorboards for a bow of his own. He thinks that if he can shoot, Torva will have to take him into the trees. Torva has other ideas, but she has not told him those either.

docs.title: The high bridge
docs.text: Fionn knows Kestra's rope bridges better than anyone but Kestra, and he has crossed the highest of them more times than he is allowed. One evening this spring, coming home late across it after sunset, he saw something pale moving on the cliff face below the bridge: low and flat against the rock, quicker than a cat. It was gone before he could look properly. A few days later, Kestra found the ropes on that bridge chewed. Fionn has not told her what he saw, because he would have to explain why he was on the bridge after dark, and Hamish would find out.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Fionn wants to be a hunter like Torva, and to go into the deep forest and come back with a story big enough to tell at the Gap Inn. He fears very little, which is what worries the grown-ups. The one thing that does frighten him is the thought of Hamish alone at the windlass with nobody to bring him the news.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might need a guide to every shortcut on the cliffs, or someone to persuade Fionn to tell Kestra what he saw on the high bridge. It might also find him one day past the last stump, in trouble, with nobody between him and the trees.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Hamish: uncle
  • Torva: unfooled watcher

docs.title: Iska
docs.text:
First Warden

Town Goa Harbour Where Wardens' House Role Ruler Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Quick, sure and hard to rattle; she reads people the way she reads the tide and rarely wastes a word.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Iska was born to the tide. Her mother, Ysmay, was a sea warden for forty years, and Iska spent her childhood on the Inlet Quay watching the water race through the gap. Varro, now the eldest of the sea wardens, taught her to pilot when she was barely tall enough to see over a gunwale, and by the time she was grown, no one could remember a pilot who read the inlet better. Seven years ago the other wardens chose her as First Warden, and she has led Goa Harbour from the Wardens' House ever since. She is forty-one, quick, sure and hard to rattle, and she reads people the way she reads the tide. She rarely wastes a word.

docs.title: The First Warden's day
docs.text:
Iska still takes ships through the gap herself, though not as often as she would like. Most mornings begin in the Wardens' House with Halvard, her clerk, and the list of every ship due through the inlet; most evenings end on the quay. Nessa, who was the other name spoken when the wardens chose their First Warden and backed Iska herself in the end, is her friend and fellow warden, and the one who keeps telling her the wardens need more young pilots. Iska agrees and has not yet found the time. Kor, the newest full warden, already takes more ships through than anyone, and she has noticed how hard he works whenever she is watching. Ruan, captain of the Cliff Watch, is not a sea warden, but she trusts him with the cliffs as she trusts her wardens with the water, and his reports of creatures climbing at night worry her more than she shows.

Iska is married to Dunmor, who lights the quay lanterns every evening and is the one person who can make the First Warden sit down and eat. Their son Arlo wants to be a sea warden like his mother and grandmother, and sneaks onto the quay at dawn to watch Varro read the water. Iska pretends not to know. Ysmay never wanted to be First Warden herself and is fiercely proud that her daughter is, which Iska finds both touching and slightly alarming.

docs.title: The race and the rival
docs.text:
Every summer Iska skippers Goa Harbour's boat in the race around Veligor against Bain Harbour, and has for the last twelve summers. These days that boat is the Gap Runner, which Tamsin built after Goa's last win and keeps in perfect trim; it has never yet beaten Bain Harbour, and Tamsin has sworn this is the summer it finally will. Jory crewed it for the first time last summer and talks of nothing else.

Her rival across the island is Quenna, Harbour Master of Bain Harbour, and they have known each other for twenty-two years. They met when both were young crew. A squall dismasted Bain Harbour's boat off a rocky headland, and Goa Harbour's boat turned back to tow them clear. Iska, nineteen, threw the line; Quenna, twenty-four, caught it. Neither boat finished, the race was declared void for the only time in its history, and the two crews spent the night together in the nearest cove. They have been friends ever since.

In twelve races as rival skippers, Bain Harbour has won nine and Goa Harbour three, and four of Bain's wins came by a single length, which is more often than Iska likes to admit. Goa's last win was six summers ago. The losing skipper buys the first round at the finish feast, and Iska has bought it far too often. She thinks Quenna is the loudest, bravest and luckiest sailor on Veligor, and the best friend she has outside her own harbour. Lately the two of them spend the finish feast comparing what their sailors have seen in the deep water, and Iska brings home marks from Bain Harbour's charts that she adds, quietly, to the wardens' own.

docs.title: What she fears
docs.text:
Iska fears the inlet is changing. Ailsa's new pages in the Tide Book no longer match the old ones as they should, and the seas have grown rougher every year. Iska has piloted the gap for most of her life, and she does not like the feeling that the water is starting to keep secrets from her.

A quest might help Iska test a new line through the gap, carry word of a sea sighting to Bain Harbour, or crew the Gap Runner in the race.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Dunmor: husband
  • Arlo: son
  • Ysmay: mother
  • Varro: mentor
  • Nessa: friendly rival
  • Halvard: clerk
  • Kor: hopeful crewman
  • Ruan: trusted captain
  • Tamsin: boatwright
  • Jory: crewman
  • Quenna: rival racer and friend

docs.title: Gorm
docs.text:
Master of the Stairs

Town Goa Harbour Where Cliff Stairs Role Craftsman Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Stubborn, proud and secretly sentimental; he talks about stone the way others talk about family.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Gorm is forty-six and the Master of the Stairs, the head of the builders who carve and mend the stairways and rope bridges that climb Goa Harbour's cliffs. He is stubborn, proud and secretly sentimental. He talks about stone the way other people talk about family: this step is sulking, that landing has never forgiven the winter, the old stair above the quay is getting tired and wants looking after. Strangers laugh. People who have lived on the cliffs for a few years stop laughing, because Gorm is usually right.

docs.title: Learning the stone
docs.text:
Gorm was born in a cliff house halfway up the Long Stair, the oldest stairway in the town, which climbs from the Inlet Quay to the top of the cliffs. His father was a quarryman who cut stone for the quay walls and died of a fall when Gorm was thirteen. The boy spent the next winter sitting on the steps outside the house, refusing to go anywhere, until Ulric the stonecarver sat down beside him one morning, put a chisel in his hand, and told him that if he was going to sit on a step all day he might as well learn how it was made.

Ulric taught him everything: how to read the grain in a cliff face, where a stair wants to go and where it will fight you, how to cut a step that drains in the rain and holds in the frost. Gorm became Master of the Stairs eleven years ago, when Ulric decided his own hands were better spent on the hardest steps than on arguing with crews. Gorm still goes to Ulric with every difficult piece of rock, and still pretends he is only asking for a second opinion. He has walked past Ulric's little carved animals on a thousand steps and loves every one of them. It has never occurred to him to read them in order.

docs.title: The crews and the rival
docs.text:
Gorm's builders are a small, loud crew of stone-cutters and riggers. The best of them is Kestra, who strings the rope bridges on the cliff paths above the harbour and crosses them blindfold. Gorm is proud of her and shouts at her constantly, mostly because she will not wear a safety line. Lately something has been chewing the ropes on the highest bridge, and Kestra means to catch it. Gorm means to make sure she does not get killed trying, and has not yet worked out how.

His friendly rival is Hamish, who works the rope lift from the quay to the top of the cliffs. Gorm calls lifts lazy. He says a town that stops climbing its own stairs will forget how they were made. Hamish says Gorm just cannot bear anything that goes up the cliff without a step under it. They have had this argument at the Gap Inn for years, and both enjoy it far too much to settle it. Gorm is very fond of Hamish's nephew Fionn, who runs messages on the stairs and knows shortcuts that Gorm himself never cut, and he pretends to be furious about every one of them.

docs.title: The far cove stair
docs.text: Last autumn Gorm promised Iska, the First Warden, a new stair down to the far cove before the summer race, so that the town could stand on the rocks there and watch the boats go out. It was a proud promise, and it is going badly. The rock on the lower part of the cliff is harder and more broken than it looked; a whole flight cracked in the spring frost and had to be cut again; and his crews will no longer work the lowest landings after dark, because of what has started climbing the cliffs at night. The race is weeks away. Gorm is behind, and he would rather cut every step himself than admit it.

docs.title: What he fears
docs.text: Gorm fears that the stairs are being climbed by things they were never built for. He has found fresh scratches on the stone of the high landings, deep and in sets of four, and he has quietly begun cutting the edges of new steps sharper and steeper on the seaward side. He has told Ruan of the Cliff Watch, and no one else.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might guard Gorm's crew on the far cove stair through a night's work, carry a cracked stone up to Ulric for judgement, or finally make Gorm read Ulric's carvings from the top step to the bottom.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Ulric: mentor
  • Kestra: builder
  • Hamish: friendly rival

docs.title: Greer
docs.text:
Fur Trader

Town Goa Harbour Where Lantern Market Sells Furs, pelts, fur-lined cloaks and hoods

docs.title: Ysmay
docs.text:
Retired Sea Warden

Town Goa Harbour Where Cliff Stairs Role Resident Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Sharp as a hook and twice as stubborn; she watches the inlet from her window and criticises every pilot.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Ysmay is seventy, a retired sea warden, and the mother of Iska, the First Warden of Goa Harbour. She is sharp as a hook and twice as stubborn. She lives in a narrow stone house near the top of the Cliff Stairs, and from its one good window she can see the whole length of the inlet down to the gap. She spends most of the day at that window, and she has an opinion about every pilot who takes a ship through. The opinion is usually unkind and nearly always correct.

docs.title: Forty years on the water
docs.text:
Ysmay grew up on the Inlet Quay and went out with the pilots as soon as anyone would let her into a boat. She became a sea warden at twenty and stayed one for forty years, until her eyes and her back told her, ten years ago, that a warden who cannot see the far eddy in the rain has no business in the gap. For all forty of those years Varro worked beside her. They have shouted at each other across a deck in a gale more times than either can count, and they are the oldest friends either of them has. These days she criticises the pilots from her window and he criticises them from the end of the quay, and they compare notes.

She never wanted to be First Warden. She was asked to stand more than once, and each time she said the same thing: that a First Warden spends her days at a table, and Ysmay wanted the water. Nobody who knows her believes that is the whole reason, and nobody has ever got the rest of it out of her.

docs.title: Iska
docs.text:
Ysmay married Lorn, a deckhand on the coastal trading ships, when she was young. He was lost overboard in a winter gale when Iska was five, and Ysmay, a warden with a small child and no one at home to mind her, simply took the girl down to the quay with her every day. That was how Iska came to be on the water so young, and how Varro came to start teaching her when she was seven. Ysmay let him. She says it was because she was busy. The truth is that she knew she would have been too hard on her own daughter, and Varro would be exactly hard enough.

When the wardens chose Iska as First Warden seven years ago, Ysmay was not in the room, because retired wardens are not. She was at her window. She saw Varro come out of the Wardens' House and look up at the cliff, and she knew. She is fiercely proud of her daughter and tells everyone in Goa Harbour so, except Iska, to whom she mostly gives advice. Iska finds this both touching and slightly alarming, which suits Ysmay perfectly.

docs.title: Family at the window
docs.text: Ysmay thinks Dunmor, her son-in-law, is far too soft. She also says he is the best thing that ever happened to her daughter, though never where Iska can hear. Her grandson Arlo is her favourite person in the world. He comes up the stairs to sit at her window, and she tells him exactly what every pilot below is doing wrong while he writes the best of it down. He checks her complaints against what Varro says on the quay. Usually they agree, and both old wardens are delighted every time he tells them so.

docs.title: What she sees
docs.text: Lately the pilots have been taking the gap on lines Ysmay would never have chosen, swinging wide where the old eddy used to be and then correcting late. She has been blaming them for it loudly, because that is easier than the other possibility: that they are not wrong, and the water has moved. Varro has not argued with her about it, which worries her more than anything he could have said.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might carry one of Ysmay's sharp notes down to a pilot who has earned it, help Arlo check her complaints against the tide, or sit at her window through a night watch to see what she has seen moving in the gap after dark.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Iska: daughter
  • Arlo: grandson
  • Varro: old friend

docs.title: Gunna
docs.text:
Master Lantern-Maker

Town Goa Harbour Where Lantern Market Role Craftsman Age Elder Sells Quay lanterns, hand lanterns and storm lanterns

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Calm, mysterious and gently teasing; she answers questions with questions.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Gunna is seventy-seven and the Master Lantern-Maker of Goa Harbour. Her workshop stands at the back of the Lantern Market, low and dim and smelling of beeswax, cut green wood and something sharper that nobody has ever managed to name, and from it come the forest-crafted lanterns that light the town's quays at night. They burn steady in any wind and never seem to need much oil, and they give a light that is warmer and softer than any flame has a right to be. She is calm, mysterious and gently teasing. Ask her a question and she will usually answer with another one, and by the time you have worked out the answer to hers, you will often find you have answered your own.

docs.title: An old craft
docs.text:
The craft Gunna practises was handed down from the Magicians of the first camp, who brought it to the shore along with the sea-herbs and the habit of reading the tides. It has passed from one lantern-maker to the next ever since, always to a single pupil at a time, and never written down. Gunna learned it from her great-aunt Seona, who kept the same workshop before her and took the girl in at ten, when her hands were small enough for the finest work. Seona died forty-four years ago, and Gunna has been the master since she was thirty-three.

She makes three kinds of lantern: the great quay lanterns that hang on the landings of the Inlet Quay, the hand lanterns that every fisher and warden carries, and the storm lanterns that go out on ships and come back, sometimes, with the ships. A hand lantern takes her a few days. A quay lantern takes her the best part of a month, and she will not be hurried, not by sea wardens, not by captains, and not by Ruan of the Cliff Watch, who wants one on every high landing and asks her each week how many are ready. She always asks him in return how many nights he thinks a hurried lantern would last. He has never answered.

docs.title: The lamplighter and the apprentice
docs.text:
Dunmor, the lamplighter of the quays, brings her his failing lanterns, usually before anyone else could tell they were failing. He does not know how they are made and has never asked, and Gunna likes him all the better for it. She once told him, teasing, that he understood her lanterns better than her apprentice did. She is fairly sure he has had the kindness never to repeat it.

Her apprentice is Tarran: eager, clumsy and full of ideas. Half of his lanterns are brilliant and half of them do not light, and Gunna has never had an apprentice whose good half was so good. He is sure she is keeping the best part of the craft from him. He is right. Gunna has not yet decided whether Tarran is the one to receive her oldest secrets, and it is not a question of skill. He wants to make a lantern bright enough to drive the monsters off the cliff landings. Gunna wants to know, before she teaches him anything more, whether he understands why the Magicians of the first camp never made one.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Gunna is looking for an apprentice worthy of her oldest secrets, and she is aware, as she has been every winter for some years now, that she is not getting any younger. She fears that the craft will end with her, as other crafts of the first camp have ended. She fears, almost as much, that it will be passed on to the wrong hands.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might fetch Gunna the rare forest materials her lanterns need from places the timber crews no longer go, carry a new lantern up to the high landings for Ruan, or face one of her questions and try to answer it well enough to earn a secret of the craft.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Tarran: apprentice
  • Dunmor: lamplighter

docs.title: Gwenna
docs.text:
Outfitter

Town Goa Harbour Where Lantern Market Sells Rope, grappling hooks, torches, waxed cloaks and travel food

docs.text:

  • Esk: friend

docs.title: Haldor
docs.text:
Head of the Timber Crews

Town Goa Harbour Where Forest Shore Role Worker Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Big, careful and soft-spoken; he thanks every tree before it falls.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Haldor is forty-eight and the head of the timber crews of Goa Harbour, the cutters who fell trees where the forest runs down to the shore and float the logs round to the Inlet Quay. He is big, careful and soft-spoken, the kind of man who lowers his voice when everyone else raises theirs. Before every tree comes down, he lays a hand on the bark and thanks it. Some of the young cutters grin at this. None of them has ever seen him skip it.

docs.title: The day the tree fell
docs.text:
Haldor was born on the Forest Shore and went to work with the crews at fifteen, carrying water and sharpening axes. At twenty-three he was cutting on the crew of Una, the best feller on the shore, when a tree she had judged a hundred times came down the wrong way and killed her.
