Haldor was close enough to hear the trunk crack and too far away to do anything. Una left a daughter of eleven, Torva, who grew up to lead the hunters of the wild coast. Haldor has never spoken to Torva about that day, and she has never asked him. They work side by side now, his crews cutting and her hunters watching the trees around them, and the silence between them is not unfriendly.

He took two lessons from it. The first was that a tree is never just timber, and should be thanked. The second was that no load of wood is worth a cutter. He has been head of the crews for twelve years, and in all that time he has never lost one. He means to keep it that way.

docs.title: The crews
docs.text: Haldor's crews work in pairs and threes along the Forest Shore, felling, trimming and rolling the logs down to the water, where they are lashed into rafts and towed round the point to the quay at slack tide. The youngest of his cutters is Merrin, who keeps a running tally of who has felled the most and wants a crew of her own. Haldor thinks she will get one and that she is not ready yet, and he has told her both, which she only heard half of. Osric, the woodsman, is the son of Elspeth the healer and the best man in the forest Haldor ever had. Last autumn Osric came out of the deep woods white and shaking and has not gone back since, and he will not work past sunset for any wage. Haldor has never pushed him to say what he saw. He suspects he would rather not know.

docs.title: Pulling back
docs.text:
Twice this year Haldor has pulled his crews out of the deeper woods. The first time was at the end of winter, when a cutting party came back to find their camp torn apart and every axe-handle bitten through. The second was this spring, when something large followed a crew through the trees for an afternoon without ever showing itself, and Haldor called them all out before dark and did not send them back. Now the crews cut only along the edge of the forest, within shouting distance of the shore, with Torva's hunters close by.

That has made Tamsin, the boatwright, very unhappy. She wants deep-forest timber for the Gap Runner, the tall, close-grained, slow-grown wood that only grows far in, and she is sure it is the difference between losing to Bain Harbour and winning. They have had the same argument so often that the quay hands can recite both sides. Haldor respects her more than she knows. He still will not send a crew in for a keel.

docs.title: What he fears
docs.text: Haldor fears the forest itself is changing. The edge-wood his crews cut now is poorer every month, and he can feel the cutters getting restless. One day soon one of them will go into the deep woods without asking him, and he will not be there.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might guard a single cutting party into the deep forest for the tree Tamsin wants, find out what bit through the axe-handles, or go after a cutter who has gone in alone.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Merrin: cutter
  • Osric: woodsman
  • Tamsin: demanding customer

docs.title: Halvard
docs.text:
Clerk of the Wardens' House

Town Goa Harbour Where Wardens' House Role Official Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Fussy, orderly and kind underneath; he cannot leave a crooked ledger alone.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Halvard is forty-six and the Clerk of the Wardens' House, the man who writes down every ship that comes through the gap and every pilot who brings it in. He is fussy, orderly and kind underneath. He cannot leave a crooked ledger alone, or a crooked chair, or a crooked picture on somebody else's wall, and he will straighten all three while apologising for it. He also gets seasick standing on the quay, which in a town of sailors has made him the subject of a great many affectionate jokes. He takes them well. He has heard them all.

docs.title: From the valley to the sea
docs.text:
Halvard grew up on a farm in Linmoor, a green farming valley far inland, where the nearest water was a slow brown river and the most dangerous thing in a year was a late frost. His parents are long dead, and the farm is worked now by his older sister, who writes to him once a year to ask when he is coming home. The answer, every year, is not yet.

He came to Goa Harbour at twenty-four, because he had never seen the sea and wanted to before he settled down. He took passage on a timber ship out of the inlet for the sake of the view, was sick for three days straight, and came back down the gangplank grey-faced and certain of only one thing: he would never sail again. He has kept that promise. He found work copying cargo lists for a trader on the Lantern Market, did it so well that the wardens noticed, and has been their clerk for fifteen years.

docs.title: The ledgers
docs.text:
Halvard's day begins early in the Wardens' House with Iska, the First Warden, and the list of every ship due through the inlet. He tells her which captains are late, which are early, which owe the pilots' fee from last season, and which have asked for a particular warden. Then he spends the rest of the day writing down what actually happened: ship, captain, cargo, pilot, tide, time through the gap. His ledgers go back fifteen years in his own neat hand and many more in the hands of the clerks before him. Varro once said he had taken more ships through the gap than anyone could count, Halvard's ledgers included. Halvard went and counted. He has not told Varro the number, because Varro did not really want to know.

His best friend is Ailsa, the Keeper of the Tide Book. She records the water and he records the ships, and they eat their midday bread together at her desk most days. She keeps a crooked stack of notes at her elbow, and he straightens it every time he passes. He suspects she crooks it again on purpose. He straightens it anyway.

docs.title: What the ledgers say
docs.text: Lately Halvard has started a new column. It began as a note in the margin when a captain complained that his hull had been scraped in the gap by "something soft, and then something hard." Then another said the same. Then Corrie, Kor's apprentice, swore she saw something large and dark pass beneath a ship, and nobody believed her. Halvard did not say he believed her. He simply wrote it down, with the date and the tide, in the new column, and he has kept writing everything like it since. There are nine entries now. He has not shown them to anyone, because he is a clerk and not a warden, and he is afraid of being laughed at for the seasick man's fears.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might carry Halvard's new column to Ailsa so the two of them can lay it beside the Tide Book, take a letter to his sister in Linmoor, or ask the captains on the quay what scraped their hulls.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Iska: employer
  • Ailsa: friend

docs.title: Hamish
docs.text:
Rope-Lift Keeper

Town Goa Harbour Where Cliff Stairs Role Service Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Chatty, jolly and nosy; he knows everyone's business because everyone rides his lift.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Hamish is thirty-nine and the keeper of the rope lift on the Cliff Stairs, the great creaking basket that hauls goods and tired legs from the Inlet Quay to the top of the cliffs. He is chatty, jolly and nosy, and he knows everyone's business, because sooner or later everyone rides his lift. A fisher with a sore back, a merchant with a crate of lanterns, a warden too tired to face the Long Stair: they all step into the basket, and for the long slow minutes it takes to rise up the cliff, there is nothing to do but talk to Hamish. Most people tell him more than they meant to. Bethoc at the Gap Inn says he knows as much about Goa Harbour as she does, and unlike her, he does not keep it to himself.

docs.title: The lift
docs.text: The lift is a timber frame bolted into the clifftop, with a great windlass, a counterweight of stone-filled baskets running in a channel of its own, and a heavy rope that Hamish oils by hand every week. It was built long before he was born. Old Murdo worked it for thirty years, and Hamish, who had spent his boyhood riding it whenever Murdo would let him, took it over fifteen years ago when the old man's arms gave out. He has kept it running every day since, in wind, rain and fog, and he has never dropped a crate. He is enormously proud of that, and will tell you so, on the way up.

docs.title: Fionn
docs.text:
Hamish's younger sister, Ishbel, married a cove fisher called Duncan, and they had one son, Fionn. Duncan was drowned in a storm when the boy was barely one, and two winters later Ishbel died of a wasting cough. Hamish was thirty-two, unmarried, and had never looked after anything more delicate than a rope. He took Fionn home to the little house beside the windlass, and has raised him there ever since.

Fionn is ten now: quick, cheeky and fearless, and he runs messages up and down the cliff stairs for a copper a trip. Hamish lets him, because a boy who knows every step and shortcut on the cliffs is a boy who will not fall off them. He is fiercely proud of him and worries about him constantly, which he hides by telling everyone in the basket stories about Fionn's latest mischief. The one thing Hamish does not know, for all his nosiness, is that Fionn follows the hunters to the edge of the forest whenever he can. Torva knows, and so do half the hunters. Nobody has told Hamish. It is the only secret on the cliffs that has ever got past him.

docs.title: The friendly rival
docs.text:
Hamish's rival is Gorm, the Master of the Stairs. Gorm calls lifts lazy and says a town that stops climbing will forget how its stairs were made. Hamish says Gorm simply cannot bear anything going up a cliff without a step under it. They have argued about it at the Gap Inn for years, and neither would give the argument up for anything.

Hamish dreams of building a second lift, down the cliff to the far cove. He has drawn it a dozen times on the back of cargo lists. Now Gorm has promised the First Warden a new stair to that very cove before the summer race, and is behind, and Hamish has been heard to say, loudly and often, that a lift would have been finished by now. Gorm has not yet thrown anything at him. It is a matter of time.

docs.title: What he fears
docs.text: Hamish fears that something will happen to Fionn while he is stuck at the windlass with a basket halfway up the cliff and cannot let go. Lately, too, he has felt the lift rope shudder on still nights, as if something had brushed against it on the cliff face in the dark.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might ride the lift and listen to everything Hamish knows, help him check the rope after one of those shuddering nights, or carry his drawings of the second lift to Gorm and survive the reply.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Gorm: friendly rival
  • Fionn: nephew

docs.title: Jory
docs.text:
Race Crew

Town Goa Harbour Where Inlet Quay Role Worker Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Loud, loyal and tireless; he would row around Veligor alone if Iska asked him to.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Jory is twenty and works the Inlet Quay, hauling timber, wool and anything else that needs carrying from the landings into the holds of the ships. He is loud, loyal and tireless. He can be heard from one end of the quay to the other, usually talking about the race, and he can carry a bale of highland wool on each shoulder while he does it. Last summer he crewed the Gap Runner for the first time, and nobody on the quay has heard the end of it since.

docs.title: A quay boy
docs.text:
Jory was born on the Inlet Quay, the son of a porter who carried cargo there for thirty years until her back gave out. She has gone to live with her sister on a farm far inland, and writes to him in a big, careful hand that he reads aloud to anyone nearby. Jory took over her work at fourteen and found that he was good at it. He knows which captains pay on time, which mates count every bale twice, and how to swing a log off a timber raft and onto a deck without anyone noticing it was ever heavy.

When he is not hauling cargo he works in Tamsin's boatyard, and she works him harder than any captain. He scrapes, sands, carries planks and holds the other end of whatever she is fitting, for as long as she needs, without a word of complaint. Tamsin once told him, by accident, that he was the best thing to happen to the boat in years. He pretended not to hear, so that she would not take it back, and he has thought about it every day since.

docs.title: The Gap Runner
docs.text:
Iska picked Jory for the race crew last summer because he had turned up at the yard every evening for two winters, and because, she said, he was the only person on the quay who could row all day and still be cheerful at the end of it. The Gap Runner lost to Bain Harbour, as she had every summer since Tamsin built her. Jory does not care. He talks about the race as though it were the greatest day in the history of Goa Harbour: the send-off, with Mhairi fiddling on the quay; the gap at dawn; the long haul around Veligor; the moment he saw Bain Harbour's sail ahead and knew they could catch it, if only the course had been a little longer. Every time he tells it, the course gets a little shorter and Bain Harbour's lead a little smaller.

Iska is his hero in a way she is nobody else's. He would row around Veligor alone if she asked him to, and he has said so in her hearing, which she pretended not to enjoy. He would never question one of her calls. When Tamsin starts on the subject of a certain tack two summers ago, before Jory's time, he finds something urgent to carry.

docs.title: Friends and hopes
docs.text:
Kor, the youngest of the full sea wardens, is Jory's friend from boyhood on the quay. Jory knows Kor wants a place in the race crew more than anything, because Kor asks him about every stroke of last summer's race and then goes very quiet. Jory has decided, privately, that if Iska ever has to choose between them, he will give up his own seat. He has told no one this, least of all Kor.

He wants the Gap Runner to win more than he wants anything for himself. He wants to see Tamsin's face when she does, and to be at the oars when it happens. He fears being left out of this summer's crew, and he fears, much more quietly, the way the cargo ships have started to come in from the gap with their crews pale and silent, and the way the captains now drink their first cup at the Gap Inn without saying a word.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might help Jory haul a heavy timber cargo onto a ship before the tide turns, or take his place on the quay for a week so he can train on the Gap Runner. Another might row with him in a practice run around the headlands, on a day when the water does not behave.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Iska: skipper
  • Tamsin: boss

docs.title: Kenna
docs.text:
Young Hunter

Town Goa Harbour Where Forest Shore Role Adventurer Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Restless, proud and quick to anger, but fiercely loyal to her friends.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Kenna is nineteen and the newest of the hunters of the wild coast, the small band led by Torva that keeps the monsters of the forest and the shore away from Goa Harbour's paths. She is restless, proud and quick to anger, and she is fiercely loyal to her friends; she will fight anyone who says a word against them, and quite often does. She wants, more than anything, to bring down a creature big enough to be talked about at the Gap Inn, and so far she has not.

docs.title: The Forest Shore
docs.text:
Kenna grew up on the Forest Shore among the timber crew families, in a house so close to the trees that the branches scraped the roof in a high wind. Her parents towed the log rafts round the point to the Inlet Quay, and when she was sixteen they went along the coast for steadier work at a timber camp far from Goa Harbour. Kenna refused to go. She lodged with a crew family, mended nets for her keep, and spent every spare hour watching Torva's hunters go out and come back. She was at the edge of the trees so often that the hunters stopped noticing her, which is exactly what she wanted.

Last autumn Torva finally took her on. Kenna had expected to be tested with a monster. Instead Torva had her sit at the forest edge for three days straight and tell her afterward everything that had moved. Kenna still has not decided whether this was a lesson or a punishment.

docs.title: Torva
docs.text:
Kenna would follow Torva anywhere, and she says so often, which Torva ignores. What Kenna does not see is how much of herself Torva sees in her: the same temper, the same hunger to be talked about, the same stubborn refusal to be told. Torva keeps her on the safest paths and the dullest watches, and Kenna resents every one of them. Each morning Kenna reads Bethoc's sighting board at the Gap Inn after Torva has read it, and complains loudly that nothing on it is big enough. Bethoc tells her to be careful what she wishes for. Kenna is not.

She is fond of Fionn, the stair runner, though she would never admit it. She grumbles to the other hunters every time he creeps after them to the last stump, and she has quietly started pressing clear prints into the mud there and naming them aloud when she knows he is listening, so that he learns to read them without ever knowing he has been seen.

docs.title: Merrin and the race
docs.text:
Kenna's rival is Merrin, the youngest of Haldor's timber cutters, and it has been that way since they were nine. That summer, ten years ago, the two girls raced at low tide along the Forest Shore, from the raft landing out to the end of the point and back. Kenna was ahead at the turn. Merrin came back over the weed-covered rocks instead of the sand, and won by a stride, while Kenna slipped trying to follow her and skinned both knees. Kenna has said ever since that going over the rocks was cheating. Merrin has said ever since that nobody told her she could not. Nobody had agreed any rules at all, which only makes it worse.

They have been competing ever since, at everything: who can climb the tallest stump, who gets more work, who is talked about more at the Gap Inn. Kenna knows Merrin keeps a tally of who has felled the most trees. She suspects, correctly, that the race is the first line in it.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Kenna wants a kill big enough to be chalked on Bethoc's board with her name beside it, and she wants Merrin to see it. She fears being ordinary, and she fears, though she would never say it, that she will freeze the first time she meets something truly big. Torva has told her that everyone does. Kenna did not believe her.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might find Kenna gone into the deep forest alone, after whatever has been springing Caddoc's traps, and need to bring her back before Torva notices. Another might force Kenna and Merrin to work together on a cutting party, and see which of them breaks first.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Merrin: rival
  • Torva: mentor

docs.title: Kestra
docs.text:
Rope-Bridge Builder

Town Goa Harbour Where Cliff Stairs Role Craftsman Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Fearless, light-footed and impatient with anyone who looks down.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Kestra is twenty-three and strings the rope bridges that carry Goa Harbour's cliff paths across the clefts above the harbour, from the low spans over the quay to the highest bridge just below the clifftop quarter. She is fearless, light-footed and impatient with anyone who looks down. She can cross any bridge in the town blindfold, and has, more than once, to win a bet. She will not wear a safety line, and she does not intend to start.

docs.title: Rope and stone
docs.text:
Kestra grew up in a cliff house above the Inlet Quay. Her mother, Shona, made nets in the coves and taught her every knot she knew before Kestra could write her name. Shona died of a fever when Kestra was fifteen, and the girl, who had already been spending every day clinging to the bridges, simply stayed up there. Gorm, the Master of the Stairs, had taken her onto his crew the year before as a rope-carrier, mostly to stop her climbing things without permission. Within two years she was rigging bridges of her own, and within five she was the best rigger the crew had.

Gorm is proud of her and shouts at her constantly, mostly about the safety line. Kestra shouts back. She thinks a line is something to trip on, and that the way to be safe on a rope bridge is to know the bridge, every plank and every knot, so well that your feet never need to ask. Ruan, the Captain of the Cliff Watch, tests every rope on the cliffs once a month by hanging his weight off it, and he tests hers twice. Kestra finds this insulting and has told him so. He has thanked her and gone on doing it.

docs.title: Her day
docs.text:
Most mornings Kestra walks every bridge in the town, end to end, running her hands along the ropes and listening to the planks. She replaces what is worn before it frays and what is frayed before anyone notices. In the afternoons she splices new rope at the top of the Cliff Stairs, and in the evenings she is often to be found at the Lantern Market, at the back of Gunna's workshop, where Tarran is.

Tarran, the lantern-maker's apprentice, is her sweetheart. He is clumsy and full of ideas, and she is neither, and they suit each other better than anyone expected. She is the only person who has never laughed at one of his lanterns that did not light. He is the only person she lets watch her cross a bridge blindfold, because he is too busy worrying to look down.

docs.title: The chewed ropes
docs.text:
This spring, on a morning walk, Kestra found the ropes of the highest bridge chewed. Not frayed, not cut: chewed, from below, with the strands bitten through one by one on the seaward side, where nothing should be able to reach. She spliced them that day. Since then she has found fresh damage again and again, always on the highest bridge, always from below, and never once has she seen what does it.

Kestra means to catch it. She has sat out on the highest bridge after dark, which Gorm has forbidden and Ruan does not know about, waiting with a coil of rope and a long knife. Nothing came while she watched. Tarran has promised to make her a lantern bright enough to see the whole cliff face beneath the bridge, and she is waiting for it with more patience than she has ever shown for anything.

She does not know that Fionn, the stair runner, crossed that bridge one evening a few days before she found the first damage, and saw something pale moving fast on the rock below it. If she did, she would want to know exactly what he saw, and she would want to know it now.

docs.title: What she fears
docs.text:
Kestra fears very little on a bridge. What frightens her is the idea that someone else, someone who does not know the ropes as she does, will step onto the highest bridge on the night it finally gives.

Kestra also teaches Rope Slide, the bridge-builder's quick way down a rope or ladder and safely off its end, to anyone who will help her check every lashing on one of her bridges first.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might sit out on the highest bridge with Kestra after dark, persuade Fionn to tell her what he saw, or carry Tarran's new lantern up to her before he can change his mind about it.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Gorm: master builder
  • Tarran: sweetheart

docs.title: Lachlan
docs.text:
Adventurer

Town Goa Harbour Where Lantern Market Role Adventurer Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Bright, boastful and generous; he makes friends in minutes and plans in seconds.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Lachlan is twenty-two and an adventurer of the wild coast, one of the young men and women who hunt monsters and explore the cliffs and coves around Goa Harbour for pay, for glory, or simply because they cannot sit still. He is bright, boastful and generous. He makes friends in minutes and plans in seconds, and most of his plans work, which only encourages him. He buys the first round at the Gap Inn far more often than he can afford, and he tells stories there that are nearly all true.

docs.title: The coves
docs.text: Lachlan grew up in the Fishers' Coves. His parents went off to crew the trading ships that sail round the far side of the island when he was small, and they rarely come back to Goa Harbour; he was raised by his grandfather Alasdair, a cove fisher who had been everywhere along the wild coast in a small boat and had a story about every rock. The best stories were about the sea caves, the dark mouths that open at the foot of the cliffs at low tide, where the water booms in and out and nobody sensible goes. Alasdair had been a little way in, once, as a young man, and came out faster than he went. He would never say why, and he laughed about it, and Lachlan never quite believed the laugh. Alasdair died three winters ago. Lachlan still has his old oilskin and his tide-reckoner, and uses both.

docs.title: The caves
docs.text:
Lachlan wants to be the first person to map the sea caves under the cliffs. He has started. He has a sheet of oilcloth on which he has marked every cave mouth along the cliff foot between the Inlet Quay and the far cove, with the tide at which each one can be entered and how far in he has been. The answer, so far, is not very far: a few dozen yards in most of them, a little further in two, before the light goes and the water starts to come back. Every expedition goes a little deeper. He brings back shells, odd stones and stories, and he gives most of the shells away.

Gwenna, the outfitter of the Lantern Market, was an adventurer herself until a bad fall in the sea caves, and Lachlan is certain she still has maps from those days. He asks for them every time he buys rope from her, which is often. She says no every time. She tells him exactly how his plans will get him killed, and he listens, adjusts them, and comes back the next week to ask again. He knows she keeps a list of everyone who has gone into the caves and not come back. He has never asked to see it. He tells himself this is out of respect.

docs.title: The boy who follows him
docs.text: Ronan, the dreamy younger son of Sorcha and Calder, thinks Lachlan is the greatest hero in Goa Harbour, and Lachlan, who also grew up in the coves wanting to be somewhere else, is kinder to him than he lets anyone see. He once let Ronan carry his coil of rope down to the quay, and the boy has never forgotten it. Every time Ronan asks to come to the caves, Lachlan laughs and says "when you are bigger." He has begun to worry that Ronan will not wait.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Lachlan wants his name on the first true map of the sea caves, and he wants it soon, before someone else has the same idea. He fears very little in daylight. What he does not say at the Gap Inn is that in the deepest cave he has reached, at the very end of the light, he heard the water moving where the tide should have been still, and he turned back without knowing why. It was the first time he has ever turned back from anything, and he understands his grandfather's laugh a little better now.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might go with Lachlan into the sea caves at the lowest tide of the month, help him wear down Gwenna for her old maps, or find Ronan at a cave mouth with Lachlan's rope before Lachlan does.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Ronan: admirer
  • Gwenna: reluctant advisor

docs.title: Merrin
docs.text:
Timber Cutter

Town Goa Harbour Where Forest Shore Role Worker Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Fast, proud and competitive; she keeps a running tally of who has felled the most.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Merrin is nineteen and the youngest timber cutter on Haldor's crews, the cutters who fell the trees where the forest runs down to the Forest Shore and float the logs round to the Inlet Quay. She is fast, proud and competitive. She keeps a running tally of who on the crews has felled the most trees, notched with a knife on the handle of her axe and copied, when the handle fills, onto the inside of her door. She is not at the top of it yet. She is closer every month.

docs.title: The raft-woman's daughter
docs.text: Merrin was born on the Forest Shore. Her mother, Catriona, steered the log rafts round the point to the quay at slack tide, and Merrin rode on the logs with her as soon as she could hold on. Catriona died of a winter chill when Merrin was twelve. Merrin went to the crews the next spring, carrying water and sharpening axes as Haldor himself had once done, and swung her first axe at fifteen. She lives in a small timber house among the crew houses, alone, and likes it that way.

docs.title: The tally
docs.text: Merrin's tally began long before her axe. The first line in it, she would tell you, is a race she ran against Kenna when they were both nine, at low tide along the Forest Shore, from the raft landing out to the end of the point and back. Kenna was ahead at the turn. Merrin came back over the weed-covered rocks instead of the sand, because it was shorter, and won by a stride. Kenna, who slipped on the rocks trying to follow, has called it cheating for ten years. Merrin has pointed out for ten years that nobody made any rules. They have been rivals ever since, at everything, and now Kenna is one of Torva's hunters, which means she is often standing at the edge of the trees, watching Merrin's crew work, and that is the best and worst arrangement either of them could have imagined.

docs.title: Haldor and the crew
docs.text:
Merrin admires Haldor more than anyone on the shore, though she teases him about the way he lays a hand on every tree and thanks it before it comes down. She does it herself now, quickly, when she thinks nobody is looking. She wants a crew of her own to lead, and she has asked Haldor for one more than once. He told her that she will get one, and that she is not ready yet. She only heard the first half.

The second half is the reason she is restless. Since Haldor pulled the crews back to the forest edge this year, the wood there has been poorer every month, and the tally has slowed for everyone. Merrin can see the tall, slow-grown trees in the deep forest from the edge, and she knows that Tamsin, the boatwright, would give almost anything for one of them for the Gap Runner. She has started to think that the cutter who brings that tree out of the forest would get a crew of her own the next day.

She works alongside Osric, the woodsman, who knows the forest better than anyone and will not go into the deep woods for any reason. Merrin used to think him only superstitious. Lately she has caught herself watching him watch the trees, and she has not liked it.

docs.title: What she fears
docs.text: Merrin fears being the youngest forever: always promising, never trusted. She fears, too, the silence in the deep forest that Osric will not talk about, though she tells herself she does not.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might guard Merrin into the deep forest after the tree Tamsin wants, stop her from going in alone, or set her and Kenna a contest that settles the race at last.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Haldor: crew head
  • Kenna: rival

docs.title: Mhairi
docs.text:
Fiddler

Town Goa Harbour Where Lantern Market Role Performer Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Mischievous, bright and tireless; she plays faster when people try to stop dancing.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Mhairi is twenty-one and the fiddler of the Gap Inn, where she plays most nights for Bethoc's customers, and of the summer race send-off, where she plays on the quay as the Gap Runner goes out through the gap. She is mischievous, bright and tireless. She plays faster when people try to stop dancing, and slower when they are sure the tune is over, and she has never yet played a set without someone falling over on purpose to make her laugh.

docs.title: A fiddle from an offcut
docs.text:
Mhairi grew up on the Lantern Market, above a ship's chandler's. Her father was a ship's carpenter who made her first fiddle out of an offcut of mast timber when she was seven, badly, so that it squeaked on every note. He sailed on the coastal traders and was lost with his ship in a winter storm when she was eleven. She still has the squeaking fiddle, and keeps it on the wall above her bed. The one she plays now she bought herself, with three years of coppers from playing at the market.

She learned the old tunes from Cormac, the shanty singer, who heard her squeaking away on the Lantern Market when she was eight and could barely hold the bow, and decided on the spot that she had a singer's ear. He tells every child that, but in her case he kept coming back. He taught her the songs of the shared camp, the ones the Savage hunters and Magicians sang when they first fished the inlet together, and he taught her that a tune is a story you can dance to. Now she plays them faster than he can sing them, on purpose, to make him laugh, and he calls her the best thing he has ever done.

docs.title: The inn
docs.text: Bethoc took her on at fifteen, after Mhairi had played for a whole evening outside the door of the Gap Inn until the customers inside complained they could not hear her properly. Bethoc pays her in coin, in stew, and in the right to play whatever she likes, and Mhairi values the last most of all. She knows every regular, every hunter who reads the sighting board, and every sailor's favourite tune. When a hunter comes back late and wounded, she plays something soft until Elspeth arrives. When the sailors start a fight, she plays louder until they forget what it was about.

docs.title: The race song
docs.text:
Mhairi is writing a song about the summer race. It has a verse for the gap at dawn, a verse for Iska at the tiller, a verse for Tamsin hammering on the slip through the winter, and a rowdy verse for Jory that he has asked her to make longer. It has no last verse, because the last verse is the finish, and she will not write the Gap Runner losing. Goa Harbour has to win so she can finish it. She has told the whole Gap Inn this, loudly, and the crew have begun to feel it as a kind of pressure.

She has not asked Cormac for a single verse. It is not because she does not want his help. She wants to give him the whole song finished, as a gift, to prove that she has learned everything he taught her. She does not know that he is quietly hurt, and if she did, she would be horrified.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Mhairi wants to play the finished race song at the finish feast, with Goa Harbour winning. She wants Cormac to hear it and cry for the right reasons. She fears the song will never be finished, and she fears, a little, the old gap verse that Cormac starts and never ends, because she has seen his face when he stops.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might help Mhairi gather the stories she needs for her verses from the race crew, carry her unfinished song to Cormac and find a way to make them both talk, or keep the Gap Inn dancing on a night when something is chalked on Bethoc's board that frightens everyone.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Bethoc: employer
  • Cormac: old mentor

docs.title: Moira
docs.text:
Cliff Watch Guard

Town Goa Harbour Where Cliff Stairs Role Guard Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Bold, restless and always the first to volunteer; she climbs the stairs two at a time for fun.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Moira is twenty-one and a guard of the Cliff Watch, the band that keeps the cliff stairs of Goa Harbour and the paths that come down to them from the forest. She is bold, restless and always the first to volunteer, and she climbs the stairs two at a time for fun, from the Inlet Quay to the clifftop, and then goes back down to do it again. The other guards have stopped trying to keep up with her. Ruan, her captain, has stopped trying to make her walk.

docs.title: Why she joined
docs.text:
Moira grew up in a cliff house above the Inlet Quay and spent her childhood listening to the hunters at the Gap Inn talk about the things they had seen on the wild coast. She joined the Cliff Watch at seventeen, four years ago, for one reason only: she wanted to see a monster up close. In those days the watch still spent most nights walking the stairs with lanterns and seeing nothing at all, and for her first year she was bitterly disappointed.

Then, three winters ago, a creature came up the cliff face itself, not down the forest paths, and reached the high landing before anyone could stop it. Moira was on watch. She was the one who ran to the head of the Long Stair and rang the iron bar, and she was close enough afterward to see Torva and two of her hunters drive the thing back over the edge, and to see what it had done to Torva's jaw. She had wanted to see a monster up close. Since then she has seen far more of them than she wanted, and she has never once said so out loud.

docs.title: Torva and the stairs
docs.text:
Moira admires Torva more than anyone in Goa Harbour, and says so to anyone who will listen. Torva counts her a friend, which Moira still finds hard to believe. Moira would much rather be out on the wild coast with Torva's hunters than climbing the stairs every night, and she has asked Torva, more than once, to take her. Each time Torva tells her that the stairs need her more. Moira thinks Torva is being kind. Ruan knows Torva is telling the truth, and he keeps Moira on the watch and says nothing about it.

She works hard for Ruan, even when she is sulking about the hunters. She volunteers for the high landings, the darkest stretches of the cliff and the late watches nobody else wants, because that is where the climbers come. She has helped carry Ruan's demands for more lanterns to Gunna's workshop, and she has made friends with Tarran, the apprentice, because he is the only person who has promised her a lantern sooner. She knows Kestra from the bridges, and they race each other up the stairs some evenings. Kestra usually wins, and Moira usually claims she let her.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Moira wants to go out with the hunters, just once, into the forest and back. She wants to prove she is as good as any of them. What she fears she keeps to herself: that one of these nights she will be the one at the bar again, and that this time there will be nobody like Torva near enough to come.

She has noticed that the climbers are coming more often, always on the darkest nights, and that they seem to be getting better at finding the parts of the cliff the lanterns do not reach. She has said this to Ruan. He nodded and wrote it down, and his face told her he already knew.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might stand a night watch on the high landings with Moira, persuade Torva to let her go out with the hunters for a single day, or race her up the Long Stair for a wager she has no intention of losing.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Ruan: captain
  • Torva: friend

docs.title: Morag
docs.text:
Wool Trader

Town Goa Harbour Where Lantern Market Sells Highland wool, knitted jumpers, blankets and sea-mittens

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Greer: friendly competitor
  • Teague: drover

docs.title: Osric
docs.text:
Woodsman

Town Goa Harbour Where Forest Shore Role Worker Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Uneasy, watchful and superstitious; he will not work past sunset for any wage.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Osric is forty-four and a woodsman of the Forest Shore, the only son of Elspeth the healer. He is uneasy, watchful and superstitious. He hangs a twist of rowan over his door, knocks twice on a stump before he sits on it, and will not work past sunset for any wage, however much is offered and however near the job. Haldor, the head of the timber crews, calls him the best man in the forest he ever had. Osric no longer goes into the forest at all, except to its very edge.

docs.title: His father's trade
docs.text:
Osric's father, Aonghas, was a woodsman too, and the boy followed him into the trees as soon as he could walk the paths. Aonghas taught him to choose which trees should be cut and which left, to read the way a trunk would fall before the first stroke, and to find his way home in any weather by the moss and the light. When Osric was fourteen, Aonghas caught a chill clearing a windfall in the rain, and died of it. Osric took his father's axe and went on doing his father's work, and he has been doing it ever since.

He was always a careful man, more careful than his father, who laughed at the old woodsmen's sayings. Osric never laughed at them. He kept the sayings because they kept him alive: never whistle under the big trees, never sleep with your back to the deep wood, be out of the forest before the sun is. For thirty years he walked the deep forest ahead of the crews and marked the trees they would cut, and since Haldor took over the crews twelve years ago he has been the woodsman Haldor sent in first. He went alone, and he always came back.

docs.title: Last autumn
docs.text:
Last autumn, Osric was cutting alone deep in the forest when every bird went silent at once. He came out of the woods that evening white and shaking, without his father's axe, and he has not been back there since. He will not say what he saw. Not to Haldor, who has never pushed him. Not to the crews, who have asked. Not to his mother, who can get the truth out of anyone else in Goa Harbour and has not been able to get it out of him.

Elspeth has stopped asking. Instead she leaves a lamp in her window every night, and Osric has noticed. He lives in a small hut a short walk from her house, and on the worst nights he walks over and sits by her fire without saying anything, and she lets him.

docs.title: The work now
docs.text: Osric still works for Haldor, along the edge of the forest where the crews cut now, with Torva's hunters close by. He marks the trees, warns the cutters when the wind is wrong, and watches the deep woods all day long. The young cutters think him frightened of shadows, and say so. Merrin, the youngest, used to laugh at him. She has stopped. Osric has seen her looking into the deep forest at the tall trees there, and he knows that look, because he wore it himself for thirty years. He has not yet found a way to warn her that does not mean telling her what he saw.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Osric wants the forest to go back to being only a forest. He fears that it never will. He fears, too, that one day someone he cares for will walk into the deep woods to the place where the birds went silent, and he will have to decide whether to follow.

Whatever he saw there, it is still there. Of that much, at least, he is sure.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might go to the place where the birds went silent to bring back his father's axe, and with it something Osric can finally tell his mother. Another might follow Osric on the one night he breaks his own rule and goes into the forest after sunset.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Haldor: crew head
  • Elspeth: mother

docs.title: Ronan
docs.text:
Fisher's Son

Town Goa Harbour Where Fishers' Coves Role Child Age Child

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Dreamy, curious and always wandering off; he collects shells, feathers and anything that glows.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Ronan is seven, the younger child of Sorcha and Calder, and the boy the Fishers' Coves are most often out looking for. He is dreamy, curious and always wandering off, not because he means to disobey but because there is always something a little further along the shore that needs looking at. He collects shells, feathers, sea-glass, gull bones and anything at all that glows, and he keeps the best of them in a driftwood box under his bed that nobody else is allowed to open.

docs.title: A wandering boy
docs.text:
Ronan was born in the coves and has never known anything but the sound of the sea. His mother shouts his name along the shore most evenings, and he usually answers from somewhere surprising: up a rope on the drying racks, inside an upturned boat, waist-deep in a tide pool with his sleeves soaked. His sister Eilidh, three years older, keeps him in line as well as anyone can, which is to say not very. He complains about her bossing and follows her everywhere. When she goes out onto the cove rocks in the evening to read the tide with her best friend Arlo, Ronan comes too and looks for crabs while they argue.

His father is the one he tells things to. Calder listens to every story about every shell as if it were the most important news in Goa Harbour, and Ronan loves him for it. His grandmother Agna calls him "the magpie" and saves him the odd bright thing she finds snagged in the nets.

docs.title: The stone
docs.text:
Last autumn, at the bottom of the deepest tide pool beyond the far cove, Ronan found a stone unlike any other. It is smooth as an egg, dark grey with a paler band around it, and it fits exactly in his closed hand. It is always faintly warm, even in the cold, and on very dark nights Ronan is almost certain it glows, just a little, if he holds it near the water.

He keeps it hidden in his pocket and tells nobody. He showed it once to his father, who looked at it for a long time and then promised not to tell anyone, which Ronan thought was the right answer. He has not shown it to Eilidh, because she would make him give it to a grown-up, and he is not ready to give it to anyone. He does not know what it is. Nobody does. Sometimes, when he holds it, he has the feeling it wants to go back into the sea, and sometimes he has the feeling it is very glad not to be there.

docs.title: Lachlan and the caves
docs.text:
Ronan's hero is Lachlan, the adventurer, who grew up in the coves too and who means to be the first to map the sea caves under the cliffs. Lachlan once let Ronan carry his coil of rope down to the quay, and Ronan has not stopped talking about it since. Ronan wants to go with the adventurers to the sea caves more than he has ever wanted anything, and nobody will allow it. His mother says no. His father says no, more gently. Eilidh says no and tells their mother he asked. Even Lachlan, laughing, says "when you are bigger."

Ronan has heard that Gwenna the outfitter keeps a list of people who went into the sea caves and did not come back. He thinks about that list at night. It frightens him, and it does not stop him wanting to go.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might begin with Ronan missing from the coves at dusk, and a trail of shells leading toward the cliff caves. Another might start the night his stone glows brightly enough for someone else to see.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Sorcha: mother
  • Calder: father
  • Eilidh: sister
  • Lachlan: hero

docs.title: Ruan
docs.text:
Captain of the Cliff Watch

Town Goa Harbour Where Cliff Stairs Role Guard Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Steady, broad-shouldered and few-worded; he trusts a good rope more than a good speech.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Ruan is forty-three and the Captain of the Cliff Watch, the small band of guards who keep the cliff stairs of Goa Harbour and the paths that come down to them from the forest. He is steady, broad-shouldered and few-worded. He trusts a good rope more than a good speech, and he tests every rope on the cliffs himself, once a month, by hanging his whole weight off it. The rope-makers find this flattering. Kestra, who strings the bridges, finds it insulting, and Ruan tests hers twice.

docs.title: The watch
docs.text:
Ruan grew up in a cliff house above the Long Stair and joined the watch at eighteen, when it was a sleepy post for men too old to fish and boys too young to sail. He has been its captain for ten years. In that time the Age of Disturbance has turned the post into real work, and the watch has grown from a handful of guards to a dozen, which is still not enough. They stand on the high landings where the forest paths reach the top of the cliffs, walk the stairs at night with lanterns, and ring the iron bar at the head of the Long Stair when something comes.

Moira is the boldest of his guards, always the first to volunteer and the first up the stairs, two at a time. Ruan knows she would rather be out on the wild coast with Torva's hunters, and he knows that the stairs need her more than the hunters do, so he keeps her and says nothing about it. Dougal, the old night watchman of the quay, has been his friend since Ruan was a new recruit falling asleep at his post and Dougal kept him awake with terrible jokes. They still share a pot of tea at the bottom of the stairs at the change of the night watch.

Iska, the First Warden, trusts Ruan with the cliffs the way she trusts her wardens with the water, and he reports to her every week at the Wardens' House. He keeps the reports short. She has never once asked him to make them longer.

docs.title: The climbing things
docs.text:
Three winters ago, Ruan's watch saw the first creature come up the cliff face itself rather than down the forest paths. It reached the high landing before anyone could stop it, and it took Torva and two of her hunters to drive it back over the edge. Ruan held the lantern while Elspeth stitched Torva's jaw that night, and he has not forgotten it. Since then the climbers have come more often, always at night, always on the darkest stretches of the cliff.

Ruan's answer is light. He wants lanterns on every high landing, the forest-crafted kind that Gunna makes, which burn steady in any wind. Gunna has told him a good lantern cannot be hurried, and he believes her, which does not make the nights shorter. Her apprentice Tarran has promised him something brighter, sooner. Ruan has not said no.

docs.title: What he is carrying
docs.text: Two people have brought Ruan things they have told no one else. Dougal has found wet, clawed tracks on the lowest steps of the quay some mornings, coming up out of the water. Gorm, the Master of the Stairs, has found deep scratches in sets of four on the stone of the high landings. Ruan has not yet put the two together in front of Iska, because he wants to be sure what he is telling her. He is beginning to fear that by the time he is sure, it will be too late to matter. Things coming down from the forest he understands. Things coming up from the sea are something else.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might help Ruan carry lanterns up to the high landings before dark, keep watch on the lowest quay steps with Dougal to see what leaves the tracks, or stand with the Cliff Watch on a night when the iron bar rings.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Moira: guard
  • Dougal: friend
  • Iska: First Warden

docs.title: Sorcha
docs.text:
Cove Fisher

Town Goa Harbour Where Fishers' Coves Role Worker Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Loud, warm and practical; she runs her boat and her family the same way, with a lot of shouting and a lot of love.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Sorcha is thirty-eight, the loudest voice in the Fishers' Coves and the owner of the best catch of any boat in Goa Harbour. She runs her boat and her family the same way, with a lot of shouting and a lot of love, and most people in the coves have been on the receiving end of both. She is warm, practical and impossible to ignore. When Sorcha laughs on the water, they say, the gulls go quiet to listen.

docs.title: Born in the coves
docs.text:
Sorcha is the daughter of Agna, the net-mender, who has kept the coves' nets whole for fifty years. Her father, Donal, was a cove fisher, a big, slow-spoken man who taught her to handle a boat before she could swim properly. He died of a winter fever fifteen years ago, and his boat, the Sea Thrift, came to Sorcha. She has fished from it ever since, and she will not hear a word about replacing it, though it has been patched so often that her mother says there is more mending in it than boat.

Agna and Sorcha are very alike, which is why they argue. Agna has an opinion about everyone's knots, Sorcha's included, and Sorcha has an opinion about everything else. They see each other every day and would be lost without it.

docs.title: Calder and the children
docs.text:
Sorcha married Calder thirteen years ago. She says she chose him because he was the only man in the coves who could be shouted at without shouting back; he says he simply waited until she noticed him. He is the calm half of the best boat in the coves: she finds the fish, he mends whatever broke finding them, and between them they bring in more than anyone. She teases him endlessly about his dream of building a bigger boat and racing it around Veligor, and quietly puts aside a little of every good catch toward it.

They have two children. Eilidh, ten, is bossy, clever and already guts a fish faster than most grown-ups, and Sorcha sees so much of herself in her that it sometimes frightens her. Ronan, seven, is dreamy and forever wandering off after shells and feathers, and Sorcha spends half her evenings shouting his name along the shore.

docs.title: The rougher sea
docs.text: For most of Sorcha's life, the children came out on the Sea Thrift as soon as they could sit still, and went wherever the fish were. These last few years the sea has turned rougher, and the weather beyond the point has become hard to trust. Her mother finds nets torn by something with teeth far bigger than any fish she knows. Sorcha has stopped taking Eilidh and Ronan out past the point at all. Eilidh is furious about it. Sorcha has not explained, because she is not sure what she would say.

docs.title: The market and the favour
docs.text: Sorcha sells most of her catch to Brodie, the fishmonger at the Lantern Market, whose smoked fish goes out on ships all over Veligor. Two winters ago she let him have a whole season's catch on credit when his smokehouse roof fell in, and he swore he would repay the favour. He keeps forgetting. She keeps reminding him, loudly, in front of customers, and secretly enjoys it more than any repayment.

docs.title: What she wants
docs.text: Sorcha wants her children to inherit a sea they can fish safely, and she wants Calder to have his boat. She fears the day the coves cannot feed themselves from the water, and the night one of her own does not come home.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might help Sorcha find out what is tearing her mother's nets beyond the point, or finally collect Brodie's favour. She would also pay well, in fish, for anyone who could keep Ronan in sight for a whole afternoon.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Calder: husband
  • Eilidh: daughter
  • Ronan: son
  • Agna: mother
  • Brodie: buyer

docs.title: Tamsin
docs.text:
Boatwright

Town Goa Harbour Where Inlet Quay Role Craftsman Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Fierce, inventive and never satisfied; she rebuilds the race boat every winter whether it needs it or not.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Tamsin is forty, the boatwright of the Inlet Quay, and the builder and keeper of Goa Harbour's race boat, the Gap Runner. She is fierce, inventive and never satisfied. Every winter she hauls the Gap Runner up onto the slip and rebuilds some part of her, whether she needs it or not, and every spring she launches a boat she swears is faster than the last. She has sworn that this is the summer it finally beats Bain Harbour. She has sworn it before.

docs.title: The yard and the old master
docs.text:
Tamsin grew up on the Inlet Quay, the daughter of a rope-maker who died when she was small, and she spent her childhood under the hulls in the boatyard, asking how everything fitted together. Her best friend in those years was Calder, a quiet boy from the coves who would hold the other end of a plank for as long as she needed, and he is her best friend still.

The yard then belonged to old Fergus, the boatwright who built Goa Harbour's previous race boat, the Grey Heron. He took Tamsin on at twelve because she would not go away, and taught her everything he knew in the gruff, sideways way of a man who did not like to be thanked. The Grey Heron carried Iska to every one of Goa Harbour's three wins as skipper. In the last of them, six summers ago, the old boat crossed the line first with her keel sprung, and she never sailed again. Fergus died that winter. Before he went, he told Tamsin the next boat was hers to build and that she was to make it better than his.

docs.title: The Gap Runner
docs.text:
Tamsin built the Gap Runner the winter after Goa's last win, and in the five summers since, she has never beaten Bain Harbour. Twice she has lost by a single length, and Tamsin can describe every one of those lost feet of water in detail, at length, to anyone who sits still. She has changed the mast, the keel, the hull's line and the set of the sails, and she does not believe the fault lies with Iska, the skipper, or with the crew. She believes it lies with the timber.

The best boat timber on this coast grows in the deep forest, tall, close-grained and slow. That is exactly where Haldor, the head of the timber crews, will no longer send his cutters, because the monsters have twice driven them back this year. Tamsin and Haldor have had the same argument so many times that the quay hands can recite both sides. She thinks he is overcautious; he thinks she would trade a cutter's life for a length of keel. Neither is entirely wrong, and both know it, which makes the argument worse.

docs.title: The crew and the friend
docs.text:
Jory, who crewed the Gap Runner for the first time last summer, works in her yard whenever he is not hauling cargo, and she works him hard. He never complains. She thinks he is the best thing to happen to the boat in years and has told him so exactly once, by accident. Iska she trusts completely, as a skipper and as a friend, though she has never forgiven her for one tack in the race two summers ago.

Calder brings her his drawings of the deep-water boat he wants to build one day. Tamsin tells him precisely what is wrong with each of them, and has promised to help him build it once the Gap Runner wins. She means it. She also suspects she is using the promise to make herself win.

docs.title: What she fears
docs.text: Tamsin fears that the race will not wait for her: that the seas will grow too rough to run it, or that she will grow too old to rebuild the boat one more winter, before the Gap Runner ever crosses the line first. She fears, too, that Fergus would be disappointed.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might escort a timber party into the deep forest for the one tree Tamsin wants, help her test the rebuilt Gap Runner in rough water, or carry a peace offering between her and Haldor.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Calder: friend
  • Haldor: stubborn supplier
  • Iska: skipper
  • Jory: helper

docs.title: Tarran
docs.text:
Lantern-Maker's Apprentice

Town Goa Harbour Where Lantern Market Role Craftsman Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Eager, clumsy and full of ideas; half of his lanterns are brilliant and half of them do not light.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Tarran is twenty and the apprentice of Gunna, the Master Lantern-Maker of Goa Harbour, in her low, dim workshop at the back of the Lantern Market. He is eager, clumsy and full of ideas. Half of his lanterns are brilliant and half of them do not light, and he cannot always tell beforehand which half a new one will fall into. His fingers are scarred from hot wax and cut glass, his eyebrows have been singed off twice, and he is the happiest person in the workshop by a long way.

docs.title: The apprentice
docs.text:
Tarran grew up on the Lantern Market, under the stalls and between the carts, and spent most of his childhood standing at Gunna's door, staring at whatever was on her bench until she sent him away. At fourteen he stood there for a whole week without being sent away, and on the eighth day she handed him a broom. He has been her apprentice for six years. The craft passes from one lantern-maker to a single pupil at a time, and it is never written down, so Tarran carries all of it in his head, along with a great many ideas of his own that Gunna has not asked for.

Gunna is calm, mysterious and gently teasing, and she answers almost every question with another question. Tarran has learned an enormous amount from her, and he is sure she is keeping the best part of the craft from him. He is right. He can make a hand lantern now that burns steady in a gale, and a quay lantern that Dunmor the lamplighter will hang without a second look. But there are steps Gunna still does alone, with the door shut, and there is a sharp smell in the workshop that he has never been able to name or find the source of.

docs.title: The bright lantern
docs.text:
Tarran wants to make a lantern bright enough to drive the monsters off the cliff landings. He has heard the iron bar ring at the head of the Long Stair in the night, and seen the hunters coming back to Elspeth's door, and he cannot understand why a craft that can light a quay in any weather has never been turned against the dark things that come up the cliffs. Once, when he asked Gunna, she asked him why he thought nobody had made one before. He said it was because nobody had tried hard enough. She smiled and said nothing more, and he has had the uncomfortable feeling ever since that he gave the wrong answer.

He has tried anyway. His brightest lantern so far lit the whole of the Lantern Market for half a night and then cracked its own glass. Another burned blue, for no reason he could find, and has never been repeated. He has promised Ruan, the Captain of the Cliff Watch, something brighter and sooner than Gunna will give him, and Ruan, who is desperate, has not said no. Gunna knows about the promise. She has not mentioned it, which worries Tarran more than a scolding would.

docs.title: Kestra
docs.text: Kestra, who strings the rope bridges on the cliffs, is Tarran's sweetheart. She is fearless and precise and impatient, and she is the only person who has never laughed at one of his lanterns that did not light. Something has been chewing the ropes on her highest bridge, and she means to catch it, and Tarran has promised to make her a lantern bright enough to see the whole cliff face beneath the bridge. It is the most important lantern he has ever tried to make. He is terrified it will be one of the ones that do not light.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Tarran wants Gunna to trust him with her oldest secrets, and he wants to keep his promises to Ruan and Kestra. He fears that he will have to choose between them. He fears, too, that Gunna has a reason for keeping the bright lantern from him, and that he will find it out the hard way.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might fetch Tarran the materials for his bright lantern without Gunna knowing, carry a finished one up to the high landings to see what happens when it is lit, or try to answer Gunna's question for him before he answers it wrong again.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Gunna: master
  • Kestra: sweetheart

docs.title: Teague
docs.text:
Highland Drover

Town Goa Harbour Where Lantern Market Role Worker Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Easygoing, weathered and full of stories that grow with each telling.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Teague is fifty and a highland drover, the man who brings Morag's wool and the highland trappers' pelts down from the hills to Goa Harbour by the hill road. He is easygoing, weathered and full of stories that grow with each telling. Ask him about the hill road and he will tell you about the time he was snowed into a shepherd's bothy for nine days with a goat that could count. Ask him again next year and it will be twelve days, and the goat will have learned to play dice.

docs.title: The hill road
docs.text:
Teague was born in a herding hamlet high in the hills, where the grass gives out into rock and the wind never quite stops. He has walked the hill road down to the coast since he was a boy driving sheep behind his uncle, long dead now, and he has driven his own flocks on it for thirty years. He knows every bend, every ford, every spring and every bothy along it, and the narrow stretch near the top where the road crosses between two crags and the shepherds call it the Saddle, because it is the one place where a flock has to go single file.

For the last twenty-two of those years he has driven for Morag, the wool trader of the Lantern Market. He brings down her wool and fleeces after the shearing, takes back salt, tools and news, and spends a week or two in Goa Harbour between trips, mostly at the Gap Inn, telling stories to anyone who will buy him a cup. Morag feeds him every time he comes to her stall, scolds him for being thin, and worries about him every time he takes the road. He pretends not to notice. He would be lost without her, and she knows it.

docs.title: Last spring
docs.text:
The hill road was always rough, but it was never deadly. Last spring it was. Teague was bringing a flock down with two herd-dogs and a hired boy when something came out of the rocks at the Saddle at dusk and went through the sheep in the narrow place where they could not scatter. By morning he had lost half the flock. Nobody was killed, though one of the dogs has never been the same, and the hired boy went back up into the hills and did not come down again.

When Teague tells this at the Gap Inn, the creature is twice the size of a cart, has too many legs and breathes smoke. When he tells it to Morag, it is shorter, and he does not tell her the part where he lay behind a rock until dawn listening to it. When he tells it to nobody, late at night, he admits that he never really saw it at all.

docs.title: Looking for company
docs.text: The next trip is due after the summer shearing, and Teague will not take the road again without brave company. He has asked Esk, the sellsword from the Inlet Quay, to guard the flock. She has not said yes, and she has not said no, and Teague has decided this is the most encouraging answer he has ever had. He has also asked half the adventurers at the Gap Inn, and most of them have laughed and said they would come if he paid them in stories. He is not sure they were joking. He would pay them anyway.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Teague wants the hill road to be the road he grew up on again: long and cold and dull and safe. He fears it never will be, and that the highland trappers and herders, who already come down less every year, will one day stop coming at all. He fears, too, that Morag will be the one waiting at the stall the day he does not come back, and that is the story he never tells.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might guard Teague's flock on the hill road through the Saddle, go up ahead of him to find out what is waiting in the rocks there, or persuade Esk to give him an answer at last.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Morag: employer
  • Esk: possible guard

docs.title: Torva
docs.text:
Hunter of the Wild Coast

Town Goa Harbour Where Forest Shore Role Adventurer Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Cool, scarred and dryly funny; she never boasts and never misses.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Torva is thirty-six and leads the hunters of the wild coast, the small band who keep the monsters of the forest and the shore away from Goa Harbour's paths and timber crews. She is cool, scarred and dryly funny. She never boasts and never misses, and in a town that loves a story as much as Goa Harbour does, the fact that she will not tell hers has only made people tell it for her.

docs.title: Where she comes from
docs.text:
Torva grew up on the Forest Shore, where the trees come down to the rocks and the timber crews float their logs round to the quay. Her mother, Una, was a timber cutter, and Torva spent her childhood running between the stumps with a sling. Una was killed by a falling tree when Torva was eleven, and the girl went to live with whichever crew family had room. She learned to track from the old hunters who came through, to shoot from anyone who would lend her a bow, and to keep her feelings somewhere nobody could reach them.

She has led the hunters for nine years. Nobody exactly chose her. The others simply started waiting for her before they went out, and after a while it became true.

docs.title: The work
docs.text:
Torva's days begin at the Gap Inn, where Bethoc keeps a board of monster sightings on the wall. Torva reads it every morning, says nothing, and then sends her hunters where the board says the trouble is worst. She walks the forest paths, checks the edges of the timber crews' cutting, and goes down onto the wild coast where things come out of the trees at night.

Her hunting partner is Caddoc, the trapper, who complains about everything and has never once quit. They have worked side by side for years and trust each other completely, which neither of them would say aloud. Lately something has been springing Caddoc's biggest traps without being caught, and Torva has started going out with him to watch them, which worries him more than the traps do.

Her apprentice is Kenna, the newest of her hunters: proud, quick to anger, and desperate to bring down something big enough to be talked about at the Gap Inn. Torva sees a great deal of herself in Kenna and is working hard to make sure Kenna does not learn the same lessons the same way.

docs.title: Scars and friends
docs.text:
Torva carries a long scar along her jaw from a creature that came up the cliffs three winters ago, and several smaller ones she will not discuss. Elspeth, the healer, has stitched most of them. Elspeth scolds Torva every time and tucks her in anyway, and Torva is the only person in Goa Harbour who does exactly what Elspeth says, because Elspeth is the only person who has ever frightened her.

Moira, of the Cliff Watch, admires Torva openly and would rather be out on the wild coast with her than guarding the stairs. Torva counts Moira a friend and has told her, more than once, that the stairs need her more. And then there is Fionn, the stair runner, who follows the hunters to the edge of the forest whenever he can and thinks nobody has noticed. Torva noticed the first time. She lets him come as far as the last stump and no farther, and makes sure one of her hunters is always between him and the trees.

docs.title: What she wants to know
docs.text: Every year there are more monsters on the wild coast, and every year they come closer to the town. Torva wants to know why. She has heard the old stories about the Balrog, and the talk that drifts in from across the island about its deep places, but she trusts what she can track, not what she is told. What she has tracked is this: the creatures are not just more numerous, they are coming from deeper in the forest, as if something there were pushing them out.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might go with Torva into the deep forest to find where the monsters are coming from, help Caddoc catch whatever is springing his traps, or keep an eye on Fionn on a day Torva cannot.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Moira: admirer
  • Caddoc: hunting partner
  • Kenna: apprentice
  • Elspeth: healer
  • Fionn: secret follower

docs.title: Ulric
docs.text:
Stonecarver

Town Goa Harbour Where Cliff Stairs Role Craftsman Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Slow, thoughtful and kind; he carves a little animal into every step he cuts.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Ulric is seventy-nine and the stonecarver of the Cliff Stairs, the man who taught Gorm everything he knows about stone and who still cuts the hardest steps in Goa Harbour himself. He is slow, thoughtful and kind. He speaks as he works, a word at a time, with long pauses in which you can hear the sea, and he has never been known to hurry anything, a step or a sentence. Into every step he cuts he carves a little animal, no bigger than a palm: a crab, a hare, a gull, a seal. Most of the town has walked over hundreds of them without a second look.

docs.title: Learning the stone
docs.text:
Ulric was born on the clifftop, the son of a goatherd, and spent his boyhood scrambling the cliffs he would one day cut. At fourteen he was taken on by old Struan, then Master of the Stairs, a short-tempered, soft-hearted man who made him sweep stone dust for a year before he let him hold a chisel. Struan taught him that a step must be cut for the hundredth foot, not the first, and that a stair belongs to the cliff and only borrows the town. Struan also carved small things into his steps now and then, a shell or a knot, and it was from him that Ulric took the habit, and made it his own.

Ulric became Master of the Stairs at forty-one, when Struan's hands gave out, and held the post for twenty-seven years. Thirty-three years ago he found a thirteen-year-old boy sitting on the step outside his dead father's house halfway up the Long Stair, refusing to go anywhere, and sat down beside him with a chisel. That boy was Gorm. Eleven years ago, at sixty-eight, Ulric decided his hands were better spent on the hardest steps than on arguing with crews, and handed the Master's post to Gorm. He has never regretted it, though he still corrects Gorm's mallet grip when he thinks no one is looking.

Ulric never married. He lives alone in a narrow cliff house on one of the upper landings of the Long Stair, with a bench outside the door where he sharpens his chisels in the evening light.

docs.title: The story in the stair
docs.text:
The Long Stair is the oldest stairway in the town, and over fifty years Ulric has recut its worn steps one at a time, in his own order and at his own pace. Every step he cut there he carved with care, and the animals on the Long Stair are not chosen at random. Read from the top step down to the quay, they tell the story of the first camp. A wild goat stands on the top step, for the Savage hunters who came down from the hills. A few steps lower an owl watches from a branch, for the Magicians who came through the forest. Then the goat and the owl together; a cormorant diving, for the first fishing; a crab among weed, for the sea-herbs; an otter floating on its back watching the water, for the first wardens learning the tides; a moth at a lantern; a gull over two cliffs, for the gap.

He learned the story from the camp songs, from Struan's tales, and from long evenings at the Gap Inn listening to Cormac and to Morven, Calder's grandmother, when she still sang there. The very last step, at the bottom where the stair meets the quay, he has left blank. The songs end in different ways, and Ulric does not know which ending is true. He will not carve a guess.

Nobody has ever read it. Gorm loves every animal on every step and has never once thought to read them in order. Fionn, who runs the stairs by his own shortcuts, skips half of them, and Ulric tells him he is reading the story with the pages torn out. Ulric has never told anyone what the carvings say. He wants someone to notice. He thinks that if a story has to be explained, it was carved badly.

docs.title: The hardest steps
docs.text: These days Ulric is cutting the flight on Gorm's new far cove stair that cracked in the spring frost, through rock so hard and broken that the crews call it the Anvil. He works by daylight only, slowly, and he has noticed without being told that Gorm has started cutting the seaward edges of new steps sharper and steeper. He has not asked why. He is waiting for Gorm to tell him, as Gorm always does in the end.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Ulric wants someone to read the Long Stair from top to bottom and understand it before his hands give out. He wants to know how the story ends, so he can carve the last step. He fears dying with it unread, and he fears, a little, that the ending he cannot find is one the town will need.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might read Ulric's carvings down the Long Stair and bring the story back to him, or hunt for an old verse that tells him what belongs on the last step. Another might guard him through a long day on the Anvil, where the far cove stair runs closest to the water.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Gorm: pupil

docs.title: Kor
docs.text:
Sea Warden

Town Goa Harbour Where Inlet Quay Role Worker Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Cheerful and a little reckless; he whistles while he pilots and swears the tide likes him.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Kor is twenty-four and the newest of Goa Harbour's full sea wardens, the pilots who guide every ship through the fast and treacherous waters of the inlet. He is cheerful and a little reckless. He whistles while he pilots, the same three tunes over and over, and he swears the tide likes him. He became a full warden only last spring, and already he takes more ships through the gap than anyone else in the Wardens' House.

docs.title: The quay boy who would not wait
docs.text:
Kor grew up on the Inlet Quay, and he spent his boyhood on the steps there with the other quay children, Jory among them, watching the pilot boats go out to meet the ships. At fifteen he began rowing the pilot boats, and Nessa, the sharpest-tongued of the wardens, took him on as her apprentice. She argued with him about every tide for eight years, made him repeat every lesson until he could do it asleep, and told him, when he finally took his first ship through the gap alone, that he had been lucky. He said the tide liked him. She said the tide liked nobody, and bought him the first round at the Gap Inn anyway.

He is good, and he knows it. He reads the water quickly and acts on it faster, and he takes the gap at moments when older wardens would wait for slack. So far it has always worked. The captains love him because he is quick and cheerful and never keeps them waiting. Varro, the eldest of the wardens, watches him from the end of the quay and says nothing, which Kor has decided to take as praise.

docs.title: Corrie
docs.text:
Since last spring Kor has had an apprentice of his own: Corrie, a careful, earnest girl from the quay who writes everything on the back of her hand. Kor is fond of her and a little baffled by her. She learns more from his mistakes than from his advice, and keeps a separate page for each kind, and he suspects, correctly, that she is keeping an eye on him.

Last month, bringing a timber ship through the gap at slack water, Corrie told him she had seen something large and dark pass beneath the hull. Kor was looking the other way. He laughed and said it was a cloud shadow, and he still thinks so. He did not mean to be unkind, and he has been surprised by how quiet she has been since. He has not taken it back, and he has caught himself, once or twice, looking down into the water on that stretch of the gap a little longer than he used to.

docs.title: The race crew
docs.text: Kor's great secret, which is not much of a secret to anyone who watches him, is that he hopes Iska will pick him for the race crew this summer. He wants to sail the Gap Runner around Veligor more than he has ever wanted anything. Iska has noticed how hard he works whenever she is watching. He has not asked her outright. He asks Jory instead, about every stroke and every tack of last summer's race, and goes very quiet at the answers.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
