docs.text: Kor wants the race, and after that he wants to be the warden every captain on the coast asks for by name. He fears very little on the water, which is what worries Nessa. What he does fear, a little, is being found out as lucky rather than good. He has started to wonder whether the tide really likes him, or whether it has simply not yet made up its mind.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might ride in Kor's pilot boat on a day he decides not to wait for slack water, or put in a word for him with Iska before she chooses the crew. Another might take Corrie's notes out into the gap with him, and see whether he can still call it a cloud shadow.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Corrie: apprentice
  • Iska: First Warden

docs.title: Nessa
docs.text:
Sea Warden

Town Goa Harbour Where Wardens' House Role Council Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Sharp-tongued, funny and fiercely competitive; she argues every point at the Wardens' table and then buys the first round.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Nessa is forty-two and a sea warden of Goa Harbour, one of the pilots who guide every ship through the inlet and who sit together at the long table in the Wardens' House to decide the town's business. She is sharp-tongued, funny and fiercely competitive. She argues every point at the Wardens' table, whether she agrees with it or not, to make sure it can survive an argument, and then she goes down to the Gap Inn and buys the first round for everyone she argued with.

docs.title: Varro's other pupil
docs.text:
Nessa grew up in the Fishers' Coves and was rowing a boat before she could swim. She came to the Inlet Quay at ten, determined to be a pilot, and Varro, the eldest of the wardens, took her on. She argued with every lesson he gave her, and then did exactly what he said. He was the only teacher she ever had who did not mind, and she has never forgotten it. She became a full warden at twenty-two, twenty years ago, and has piloted the gap ever since.

Iska, a year younger, had already been learning from Varro for two years when Nessa arrived, and from the start the two girls were rivals: for Varro's attention, for the hardest ships, for the fastest crossings. They are friends now, and have been for most of their lives, but the rivalry never quite went away, and neither of them wants it to.

docs.title: The choosing
docs.text:
Seven years ago, when the wardens met to choose a new First Warden, two names were spoken: Iska's and Nessa's. Nessa wanted it. She knew she would be good at it, and she knew her friends were counting the voices around the table and finding them close. Then, before it came to a count, Nessa stood up and spoke for Iska herself. She has never fully explained why, and she makes a joke of it whenever anyone asks: that she wanted to keep her evenings free, or that she could not bear to stop arguing at the table and start chairing it. Varro made sure she knew afterward that he had thought it a near thing. She has told no one that this mattered to her more than the post would have.

She is Iska's friendliest rival and her most honest critic. She argues with the First Warden at the table more fiercely than anyone, and defends her outside it more fiercely still.

docs.title: Young pilots
docs.text:
Nessa's great cause is the young pilots. The seas around Goa Harbour have grown rougher in recent years, the old wardens are retiring, and there are not enough apprentices on the pilot boats to replace them. She says so at nearly every meeting of the wardens, loudly enough that the children who sleep on the benches by the wall have heard her. She trained Kor herself, from his first year on the pilot boats until he took his first ship through alone, and she is proud of him and worried for him in equal measure, because he is the best young pilot she has seen in years and the most reckless. She wants a dozen more like him, only more careful.

Iska agrees with her and has not yet found the time to act. Nessa has decided to stop waiting. She has begun taking quay children out in the pilot boats at slack water, one at a time, without asking the table first.

docs.title: What she fears
docs.text: Nessa fears that the gap is getting harder to read, and that one rough season the wardens will be one pilot short on the wrong day. She does not fear losing an argument. She fears winning one too late.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might help Nessa find and test new young pilots on the quay, carry her case to Iska in a way the First Warden cannot put off, or row with her through the gap on a rough day to prove a point she has been arguing for a year.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Iska: friend and fellow warden
  • Varro: old teacher

docs.title: Varro
docs.text:
Eldest of the Sea Wardens

Town Goa Harbour Where Wardens' House Role Council Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Gruff, patient and slow to praise; he still walks the quay at dawn to watch the water before anyone else is up.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Varro is seventy-six, the eldest of the sea wardens of Goa Harbour, and the man most of its pilots learned the gap from. He is gruff, patient and slow to praise. Every morning, before the lanterns go out and before anyone else is up, he walks the length of the Inlet Quay and stands at the end of it to watch the water. He has done this for longer than most of the town has been alive.

docs.title: A life on the inlet
docs.text:
Varro was born to a cove family and went out with the pilots as a boy, holding lines and keeping quiet. He became a sea warden at twenty and has been one for fifty-six years. In that time he has taken more ships through the gap than anyone can count, Halvard's ledgers included, and he has never lost one. He says that is luck. The other wardens say it is because Varro never trusts the tide, not even the ones he knows.

He married Maili, a fisher from the coves, when he was young, and they had no children. She died of a fever fourteen years ago. Varro does not speak of her often, but he still keeps her oilskin hanging by his door, and on the anniversary of her death he walks the quay a second time, at dusk.

docs.title: The teacher
docs.text:
If Varro has children, the wardens say, they are the pilots. He taught Iska when she was barely tall enough to see over a gunwale, a fierce little girl of seven who asked the same question until the water answered it. He taught Nessa too, who argued with every lesson and then did exactly what he said. He is proud of both of them and has told neither, though he did speak for Iska when the wardens chose their First Warden, and he made sure Nessa knew he thought it a near thing.

Ysmay, Iska's mother, served beside him for forty years, and they are old friends in the way of people who have shouted at each other across a deck in a gale. These days she criticises the pilots from her window above the Cliff Stairs and he criticises them from the end of the quay, and they compare notes. Ailsa, the keeper of the Tide Book, is the other old colleague left from his early years. He trusts her memory more than his own.

docs.title: The knees and the hard questions
docs.text:
Five years ago Varro's knees stopped letting him take ships through the gap; a pilot who cannot brace himself in a cross-sea is no use to anyone, and he was the first to say so. He did not stop being a warden. The others still bring him every hard question about the tides, and he still answers most of them before they have finished asking.

He has a new pupil now, though nobody has made it official. Arlo, Iska's son, started creeping onto the quay at dawn to watch him, and after a few mornings Varro told him where to stand. Now the boy is there most days, and Varro asks him what the water is doing and waits for an answer. He is harder on Arlo than he ever was on Iska, because Arlo is better at nine than she was.

docs.title: What troubles him
docs.text: The water is not behaving. Nothing Varro can point to, nothing he could write in the Tide Book: just a slackness where there should be pull, a pull where there should be slack, eddies a few yards out of their old places. He has begun to wonder whether he is simply getting old. He has not asked Ailsa, because he is afraid she will tell him he is not.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: Varro would trust someone capable to row him out to the mouth of the gap at slack water, so he can look at the eddies close to for the first time in five years. A quest might also carry his questions to Ailsa, or test a line through the gap that only he remembers.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Iska: pupil
  • Nessa: former pupil
  • Arlo: eager shadow
  • Ysmay: old friend
  • Ailsa: old colleague

docs.title: Alfie
docs.text:
Head of the Carpenters' Guild

Town Kaldemor Where Workshops Role Craftsman Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Careful, patient and proud of a square joint, he measures three times and cuts once. He hums when the work is going well and goes silent when it is not.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: You can tell how Alfie's day is going from the far end of the Workshops lane. When the work is going well, he hums, a low, tuneless, contented sound that keeps time with his plane. When it is not, he goes silent, and the whole lane goes a little quieter with him. He is fifty-two, careful, patient and proud of a square joint, with a carpenter's pencil behind one ear and a folding rule in his apron that is older than his apprentice. He measures three times and cuts once. He has never in his life cut twice.

docs.title: The guild
docs.text:
Alfie leads the Carpenters' Guild of Kaldemor, which is to say that when something wooden in town needs mending, building or arguing about, it ends up on his bench. He was born in Kaldemor, the son of a joiner (dead these twenty years), and was apprenticed at thirteen to old Fennick, who led the guild before him. Fennick died fifteen years ago, and the carpenters chose Alfie to lead them in his place, mostly, they said, because nobody else would ever be as fussy about a joint.

The guild's great charge is the great treehouse behind the town square, the oldest building in Kaldemor, and Alfie keeps it in repair: its stairs, its rails, its rooms and Lottie's schoolroom at the top, and the old beams that tie the rooms into the living tree. He also keeps the stairs of the clock tower in the Park, which is how he and Ewan became friends. Ewan cannot bear dust or anyone touching things that swing; Alfie cannot bear a loose tread or a joint that has been rushed. They understood each other at once. They still meet most evenings at the foot of the tower and say very little about clocks and stairs for an hour.

Ten years ago, when Quill came to Kaldemor, it was Alfie's carpenters who built the Gauntlet in the Park to Quill's drawings: the yard fences, the hanging course of ropes, logs and platforms, and the ring for the last stand. Alfie checks the hanging course himself every spring, because young warriors fall off it and he would like them to fall off it on purpose.

docs.title: Archie
docs.text: Alfie's apprentice is Archie, who is seventeen, eager, careless and full of big ideas, and who starts three things before finishing one. Alfie took him on three years ago and has not regretted it, though he has frequently regretted particular afternoons. Archie wants to build a treehouse taller than the great one. Alfie wants him to finish a dovetail. They both think the other is missing the point, and both are a little right. Alfie is gentler with him than he lets the boy see, because he remembers being careless once himself, under Fennick, and remembers being forgiven.

docs.title: The carving
docs.text:
Early this spring, before the clock stopped, Alfie took down an old beam in the treehouse that had begun to split where it met the trunk. He had sent Archie off for nails. When the beam came away, he found that its hidden face, the side that had lain against the living tree for longer than anyone remembers, was carved. Not scratched: carved, carefully, by someone with a good blade and a steady hand. And in places the bark of the trunk had grown over the edge of the carving, which meant it was very old indeed.

He has not been able to explain it, and he has told only one person: Ewan, because Ewan knows how to keep a thing and listen to it. Ewan came, looked for a long time, and went away without a word, and he has been back to look at it since. Alfie put the old beam back in its place, cradled in new oak, so that the carving lies hidden again. He will not describe it in the Workshops, and if you ask him what it shows, he goes silent, which tells you that it is not going well.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Alfie wants the treehouse to stand another thousand years, and he would like to know who carved that beam, and why, and why there. He fears that the answer matters more than a carpenter has any business knowing. He also fears, in a smaller, everyday way, that Archie will one day hurt himself rushing, and that it will be Alfie's fault for not catching it.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: Alfie might one day ask a traveller to keep watch while he takes the beam down again, by lantern, to make a rubbing of the carving for someone wiser than himself. Or he might find, while mending the clock tower stairs, that another hand has been at the ladder, and have to decide whom to ask about it first.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Archie: apprentice
  • Ewan: friend

docs.title: Archie
docs.text:
Carpenter's Apprentice

Town Kaldemor Where Workshops Role Craftsman Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Eager, careless and full of big ideas, he starts three things before finishing one. He is very good at saying sorry.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Archie is going to build a treehouse taller than the great one. He has drawn it eleven times, on shavings, on the backs of Alfie's offcuts and once, unwisely, on the workshop wall. It has seven storeys, a rope lift, a lookout higher than Garrick's ledge and, in the latest drawing, a slide. He is seventeen, eager, careless and full of big ideas, and he starts three things before finishing one. He is also very good at saying sorry, which is just as well, because he gets a great deal of practice.

docs.title: Coming to the Workshops
docs.text:
Archie was born in a village down the Royal Road toward Selsior, the second of four children of a carter and his wife, who still live there and keep the cart going. He was the child who took things apart. He took apart the cart, the henhouse and, once, the neighbour's gate, and he was much better at the taking apart than the putting back. When he was fourteen his father drove a load of timber up to Kaldemor's Workshops, and Archie went along, saw the great treehouse for the first time, and refused to get back on the cart.

Alfie, who leads the town's carpenters, was persuaded to take him on as apprentice, partly because the boy would not leave and partly because, when Alfie handed him a plane to get rid of him, he planed a board truer than Alfie expected. That was three years ago. Archie lodges in a little room over a woodshed at the Park end of the Workshops lane, next door to Ewan the clockkeeper's cottage at the foot of the clock tower, so he hears the bell every hour of the night, and Ewan hears him coming home late.

docs.title: Alfie
docs.text:
Alfie measures three times and cuts once. Archie measures once, cuts, and then measures to see what happened. Alfie hums when the work is going well and goes silent when it is not, and Archie has learned to dread the silence more than any scolding. He thinks Alfie is the finest carpenter on Veligor and would rather be shouted at by him than praised by anyone else. He has not yet worked out that Alfie is gentler with him than he lets on.

Alfie did not tell Archie what he found in the old treehouse beam this spring. He sent the boy off for nails that morning, and by the time Archie came back the beam was cradled in new oak and Alfie was very quiet. Archie has noticed that Alfie and Ewan now talk in low voices at the foot of the tower. He has assumed, with a sinking heart, that they are talking about him.

docs.title: The rung
docs.text:
They are not. But they might be. Last spring Alfie sent Archie to the clock tower to replace a worn tread on the stairs. Archie finished the tread, and then, because he had always wanted to see the bell up close, he climbed the inside ladder, and on the way down he missed his footing and came down hard on a rung, and it cracked. He mended it himself, quickly, with glue and twine and a splint of ash, and it held. It is not a mend Alfie would ever have passed. Ewan, who notices everything in his tower, noticed. Archie knows he noticed, because Ewan has looked at him, once or twice, in a way that makes Archie's ears go hot.

Archie has meant to own up every day since. He is very good at saying sorry for small things. This is not a small thing; it is Ewan's ladder, and Ewan's clock, and the clock has since stopped once, though that was the Shroom and not Archie. He goes pale whenever anyone mentions the ladder, and he climbs the tower stairs, when Alfie sends him, as if they might bite.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Archie wants to build something people will still be climbing in a hundred years, and he wants Alfie to look at a joint of his and hum. What he fears is being sent home on the cart. He is afraid, too, that the rung will fail under Ewan one morning, and that it will be his fault, and that is the fear that keeps him up at night more than the bell does.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A traveller who earns Archie's trust might be asked to help him cut and fit a proper new rung in secret before dawn, and then to stand beside him while he finally tells Ewan. Another quest might begin when Archie, sent up the treehouse for something else, finds the new oak cradle around the old beam and cannot resist taking a look.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Alfie: master
  • Ewan: clockkeeper

docs.title: Bertie
docs.text:
Mushroom House Shaper

Town Kaldemor Where Workshops Role Craftsman Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Twinkly, unhurried and full of riddles, he treats every mushroom house like an old friend. He never measures; he says the mushroom tells him.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: "What grows a little every spring and is never once older?" asks Bertie, with a twinkle, and waits. He will not tell you the answer. He will tell you a different riddle instead, and then pat the mushroom house beside him as though it had laughed. Bertie is seventy-four, small, round and unhurried, with moss-green braces, a felt hat older than most of the town, and a satchel of curved knives and little saws that he has carried for fifty years. He hollows out the mushroom houses of Kaldemor, and he treats every one of them like an old friend.

docs.title: Fifty springs
docs.text:
Kaldemor's famous houses are real mushrooms, grown from the town's strangely generous soil, and every spring each one grows a little. Somebody has to hollow out the new room, cut the new window, rehang the door that the cap has lifted half a hand higher, and make sure the whole thing still stands straight. For fifty years, that somebody has been Bertie.

He was born in Kaldemor and came to the trade at twenty-four, when old Bracken, the shaper before him, caught him leaning on one of her houses and told him he was leaning on it wrong. She taught him for ten years and then died, peacefully, in the oldest mushroom house in town, and Bertie has had the work alone ever since. Bracken never measured, and neither does Bertie. He says the mushroom tells him where the window goes. He puts his hand flat on the cap, listens, and cuts, and he has never yet cut a window in the wrong place, though he admits a few were in surprising ones.

Every spring is his busy season. He goes from house to house with his satchel, greeting each one by its colour or its door, and by early summer he is tired, cheerful and sticky with sap. He knows every house in Kaldemor, which ones grow quickly and which slowly, which lean, which sulk, and which, he swears, have opinions.

docs.title: Daisy
docs.text:
Bertie married Heather, a seamstress, more than forty years ago; she died six years ago and he still talks to her hat, which hangs by the door. Their son grew up with no feeling for mushrooms at all, went to Selsior to keep a shop, and lives there still with his wife; they play no part in Kaldemor life and write at midwinter. Their daughter, Bertie's granddaughter Daisy, did not go. She was twelve, already painting everything that held still, and she announced that she was staying with her grandparents and the houses. She has stayed ten years.

Now Bertie shapes the houses and Daisy paints them, in colours so bright that he says he can find his way home in the dark by them. She paints half the shutters in Kaldemor, too, and is never seen without paint on her nose. Bertie thinks she is the best thing in the town, and tells everyone except Daisy, who cannot hear a compliment anyway. He has noticed that young Jem the fiddler turns up wherever Daisy is working, and has decided it is not his business, and enjoys watching it enormously.

docs.title: Fen
docs.text: Bertie's little helper is Fen, who is eight, who was born in a small round freckled mushroom house at the end of the lane from the Park to the Workshops, and who loves the houses even more than he does. She follows him all over town on fitting days and carries his tools with great ceremony. Fen measures everything, with knotted cords, one for every house she has adopted. Bertie never measures. They have argued about this for two springs, and he thinks she has the right answer for her, which is the best answer there is. She wants to fit a window, a real one. He keeps telling her "next spring". She has written it down, so he cannot forget. He has not forgotten. He is waiting for the right house to tell him.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Bertie wants to see Fen cut her first window and Daisy paint it. He would like one more spring, and then another, and he does not count them. What he fears he will only say in a riddle. This spring, for the first time in fifty years, several of the houses nearest the woods grew crooked, all leaning the same way, away from the trees. He has put his hand on their caps, and for the first time he could not hear what they were telling him.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: Bertie may ask a traveller to sit up with him one spring night beside a house that is growing too fast, to see what it does. Or he might at last decide which house is right for Fen's window, and need someone to fetch the frame from Alfie, the glass from the Market and Fen from wherever she is asking questions.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Daisy: granddaughter
  • Fen: little helper

docs.title: Bess
docs.text:
Herbalist

Town Kaldemor Where Kaldemor Market Role Healer Age Elder Sells Herbs, poultices and teas

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Brisk, practical and fond of telling people they should have come sooner. She trusts a leaf over a potion every time.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: "You should have come sooner," says Bess, before she has even looked at the wound. She is usually right. She is sixty-four, short, square and brisk, with grey hair cropped close so it never gets in the poultice, sleeves rolled to the elbow and a canvas apron whose pockets clink with little jars. She is the town's healer, and her stall in Kaldemor Market, under a green awning hung with drying bunches of yarrow, mint and feverfew, is where the cuts, bites, sprains and snail nips of Kaldemor come to be bound. She trusts a leaf over a potion every time, and she will tell you why at length while she cleans your arm, so that you hardly notice it stinging.

docs.title: Mother Sedge
docs.text: Bess and her younger brother Bram grew up in a narrow house on the lane behind the Market, the children of a Market porter and a woman who took in washing, both dead these many years. Bess is thirteen years older than Bram, and she half raised him, which she has never let him forget either. When she was fourteen she cut her hand to the bone on a sickle in a neighbour's field, and old Mother Sedge, the herb-woman who kept the green awning then, sewed it up, packed it with moss and comfrey, and told her she should have come sooner. Bess went back the next day to see how the comfrey worked, and the day after that, and Mother Sedge, who had no daughter, gave in and taught her everything: which leaf for which ill, how to dry them, when to pick, and when to send for help because no leaf will do. Mother Sedge died when Bess was twenty-six, and Bess has kept the green awning for thirty-eight years. She never married. She says she has been far too busy patching up other people's husbands.

docs.title: Bram
docs.text:
Her brother Bram keeps the potion stall under the striped awning at the far end of the same Market, and they have been arguing since he could talk. She tells him his potions are only herbs in a hurry. He tells her that her teas are only potions that gave up. They have both said it so often that the Market says it with them. Bess thinks Bram is a fine brewer who has never once listened to anyone in his life, and that he sends young people out to the fields with a bottle in their pocket and a false sense of safety. Bram thinks Bess is a fine healer who would let someone wait an hour for a poultice to draw when a red potion would close the wound in a breath. Each privately thinks the other is doing the more important work. Neither would say so under torture.

When a bad bite comes in, though, they stop. Bess cleans and packs and binds; Bram brings the potions and holds the lamp; and they work side by side without a word, and the whole Market goes quiet, because that is how everyone knows it is serious. Afterwards they go back to arguing, a little more gently, for about a day.

She knows all about Rosa and the green bread. She told Bram nine years ago that he should apologise, and has told him so every spring since. He has not. She buys Rosa's bread twice a week and, on one of those days, puts a slice on Bram's counter without a word.

docs.title: More nips than ever
docs.text: Bess has treated more snail nips this year than in any year she can remember, and she keeps count, the way her teacher did, in a little book with a mark for every wound. Most are simple: a green snail's nip is a bruise and a scolding. But the bites coming in from the far edge of the meadow, and from the woods past the hills, are worse than they were. They are deeper, they swell faster, and some of them do not want to close, even under comfrey, even under Bram's red potion. Bess has started keeping a separate page for those. She has shown it to Bram, and he did not argue, which frightened her more than anything on the page.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Bess wants the young people of Kaldemor to come to her sooner, and preferably not at all. She wants an apprentice with steady hands and the sense to listen. She fears the day a wound comes in that neither leaf nor potion can close, and she fears that her separate page is filling up faster every week.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: Bess needs fresh comfrey, marshwort and a moss that grows only on the shady side of the old stones past the hills, and she would send a traveller to gather them if she could trust them to pick the right leaves. Or she might ask a traveller to help her work out why some of this year's bites will not heal, and what has changed in the creatures that make them.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Bram: younger brother

docs.title: Bram
docs.text:
Potion Seller

Town Kaldemor Where Kaldemor Market Role Merchant Age Adult Sells Potions In the game Bram

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Friendly to every customer and stubborn with everyone else, he can talk about cauldrons for an hour. He admits he is wrong about once a year.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text:
Bram keeps the potion stall at the far end of Kaldemor Market, under a striped awning gone pale with steam, behind a row of bottles that glow red, orange, white and blue when the sun catches them. He is fifty-one, friendly to every customer and stubborn with everyone else, and he can talk about cauldrons for an hour without drawing breath. He admits he is wrong about once a year, usually in winter, and never about cauldrons.

Nearly every young adventurer in Kaldemor meets him in their first week out. Mayor Tobin sends them down to the Market before their first trip to the fields, and Bram greets each one as if Tobin had sent them personally, which he has. "Tell the mayor Bram says hello," he says, and sends them out to the fields with a few red potions and a warning not to drink anything blue on an empty stomach.

docs.title: Brewing
docs.text:
Bram learned to brew from the old potion seller who kept the stall before him, and he has kept it himself for more than twenty years. He sells red potions and orange, white and blue, warrior potions for strength and speed potions for the road, and scrolls to bring a traveller home in a hurry. This year he has sold more of all of them than ever before; the young warriors heading out to the fields come back with more bites, and go out again sooner.

He teaches brewing to anyone with the hands for it. A brew, he likes to say, is only a pot with a better reason. Two marjoram flowers and a mushroom spore make a red potion; lavender and the caps of orange mushrooms make an orange one. His spores come from Wilf, who gathers them in the woods, and Bram has been quietly anxious since Wilf came back from visiting his sister and said the Shrooms had grown too bold to gather alone.

docs.title: Bess
docs.text: His older sister Bess is the town's healer, and she has never once let him forget it. She tells him his potions are only herbs in a hurry. He tells her that her teas are only potions that gave up. They have been having this argument since before most of the Market was born, and both of them would be lost without it. Bess binds the cuts and snail nips that come back from the fields, Bram sells the potions that send people out to get them, and each privately thinks the other is doing the more important work. When a bad bite comes in, they stop arguing and work side by side, and that is how the Market knows it is serious.

docs.title: Rosa
docs.text:
Nine years ago, Bram's dearest friend in the Market was Rosa the baker. He ate at her table every week, tasted every new loaf, and argued with her about ovens and cauldrons as happily as he argued with his sister. Then, on the morning of the harvest fair, he "improved" a batch of her mushroom bread with a spore tincture of his own, certain it would make the loaves rise higher. They rose, and came out greenish and bitter, in front of the whole fair. Rosa told him to keep himself out of her kitchen. Bram said he had been right in principle.

He has missed her bread and her company every week since, and has never said so to anyone, least of all Rosa. He hears how she is doing from Wilf, who supplies them both, and from little Fen, who carries Rosa's flour and cannot keep a thing to herself. He knows, though he will not admit it, that he was the stubborn one. This is the one thing in nine years he has not been able to admit, even in winter.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Bram wants a steady supply of spores, a cauldron that does not crack, and an apprentice with real hands. What he wants most he will not name. He fears that the woods are closing to gatherers, and that the day will come when his potions are not enough for what comes back from the fields.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: If a traveller ever brings Bram word from the terrace oven, he will pretend to be surprised for exactly as long as it takes to set down his ladle. Another quest could send a brewer's apprentice into the woods with Wilf, to bring back the spores both Bram and Rosa depend on.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Bess: older sister
  • Wilf: spore supplier
  • Rosa: estranged friend

docs.title: Clem
docs.text:
Orchard Keeper

Town Kaldemor Where Farms Role Worker Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Shy, gentle and happiest up a ladder among the apples. He goes red whenever Lia waves.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: If you want to find Clem, look up. He is happiest at the top of a ladder among the apple boughs, where nobody can see him blush, and he blushes often. He is twenty-five, tall, shy and gentle, with leaves in his hair and grass on his knees, and he keeps the orchards that lie between the farms and the woods. He says more to his trees in a morning than to people in a week. When Lia waves at him across the square, he goes red to the ears, and the whole square has noticed, though the two of them pretend that nobody has.

docs.title: The orchards
docs.text:
Clem grew up in the orchard keeper's cottage at the end of the farm track, the only child of a mother who kept the trees before him. His father died when he was too small to remember him, and his mother taught him everything: how to graft and prune, how to tell a canker from a bruise, how to judge the day an apple is ready by the sound it makes when you twist it. She died five years ago, in the winter, and Clem has kept the orchards alone ever since. He has kept them well. Old Marta says his russets are the only apples worth the price, which from her is a medal.

The trees nearest the farms are the oldest, planted long ago by Kaldemor's first settlers, who brought the cuttings with them. The newest rows, the ones Clem's mother planted, run out toward the edge of the woods. His apples go to Old Marta's stall, to Rosa's oven for her tarts and, pressed, into the cider that rides the harvest carts down to Bain Harbour each autumn.

docs.title: Hattie's bees
docs.text: His neighbour across the hedge is Hattie the beekeeper, Wilbur's wife, and her hives stand at the edge of the farms where his orchard begins. Every spring her bees keep his blossom busy, and every autumn the apples prove it. Clem pays her in cider and in the first windfalls for her son Tam, who eats them with grim determination as a warrior should. Hattie is one of the few people Clem can talk to without going red, because she talks softly, the way he does, and because she has never once asked him about Lia.

docs.title: Lia
docs.text:
Everybody else has. Lia, the town guide, who greets every visitor in the square and knows every piece of news before anyone else, has been courting Clem since last autumn's harvest dance. She asked him to dance while Jem the fiddler was playing, and he said yes before he had time to be frightened. Since then she walks out to the orchards most evenings with the day's news, and he listens to all of it, and he finds he likes the news far better when she is the one telling it. They both believe they are being discreet. Jem has already written a song about them, which Clem has begged him not to play.

He means to ask her a question one day, a large one, and he has been practising it on a pear tree. The pear tree is very encouraging.

docs.title: The roots
docs.text: This spring something began gnawing the roots of the trees nearest the woods. Clem found the earth turned up around the trunks in the mornings and the roots beneath scored and stripped, deep down, deeper than any rabbit digs. It is not a snail. Snails eat leaves and fallen fruit; they do not dig, and they leave a silver trail, and there is none. Whatever it is comes at night, works from below, and leaves the bark above ground untouched. Two young trees have already died. Clem has told Hale, and Hale nodded, and Clem did not know whether the nod meant he understood or that he was worried. With Hale, it might mean both.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Clem wants a good crop, the old trees standing, and the courage to ask Lia his question somewhere other than a pear tree. He fears that whatever is under the orchard will work its way back from the woods row by row, toward the oldest trees, the ones the first settlers planted, and that he will not be able to stop it alone.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A traveller might be asked to sit up with Clem in the orchard on a moonless night, lantern shuttered, to see what comes for the roots. Or Clem, at last ready, might ask for help getting a single perfect apple from the topmost branch of the oldest tree in Kaldemor, the one he means to give Lia when he asks.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Lia: sweetheart
  • Hattie: neighbour

docs.title: Daisy
docs.text:
House Painter

Town Kaldemor Where Workshops Role Craftsman Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Lively, messy and never seen without paint on her nose, she thinks no colour is too bright. She is cheerfully deaf to compliments.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Daisy always has paint on her nose. Nobody knows how it gets there. She does not touch her nose while she works, she swears, and yet by mid-morning there is a dab of sunflower yellow on it, and by evening it has been joined by a smudge of sky blue and a fleck of something pink. She is twenty-two, lively, messy and quick, with her sleeves rolled up and her hair tied back in a rag that used to be a paint cloth, and she believes, with her whole heart, that no colour is ever too bright.

docs.title: The houses
docs.text:
Daisy paints the mushroom houses of Kaldemor that her grandfather Bertie shapes. Every spring, when the houses grow and Bertie cuts their new rooms and windows, Daisy follows a week behind with her pots and brushes, and by midsummer the whole town looks as if it has just been unwrapped. She paints the caps in spots and stripes and, once, in checks, which the owner asked her to undo and then asked her to put back. She also paints half the shutters in Kaldemor, the doors of the Sleepy Snail, the sign over Bram's stall and, every autumn, the harvest fair booths.

She mixes her own colours from whatever she can find: crushed petals from the meadow, clay from Mabel's bank, soot, egg, and once a handful of blue snail shell ground fine, which made the brightest blue she has ever had and which she has been trying to get again ever since. She names her colours, too. The yellow on the tall house by the Market steps is called Tuesday. Nobody has ever understood why.

docs.title: Bertie and the family
docs.text:
Daisy was born in Kaldemor. Her father, Bertie's son, never cared for mushrooms or for paint, and when Daisy was twelve he and her mother moved to Selsior to keep a shop. They live there still and write at midwinter. Daisy refused to go. She had already painted the henhouse, the gate and her grandmother's best chair, and she said the houses needed her. She stayed with Bertie and her grandmother Heather, and she has stayed ten years. Heather died six years ago, and now it is Daisy and Bertie, and the hat by the door that he still talks to.

She adores her grandfather and teases him without mercy. He never measures; she never plans. Between them, they say, they make one sensible craftsman. Lately she has watched him come home more tired from his spring rounds, and she has started carrying the heavy satchel herself without asking.

docs.title: Fen
docs.text: Little Fen, who carries Bertie's tools, once asked Daisy if she might paint a shutter. Daisy gave her a brush and three pots and walked away, and when she came back the shutter was a colour nobody has been able to name. Daisy thinks it is the best shutter in Kaldemor. She has hung it on her own window.

docs.title: Compliments and Jem
docs.text:
Daisy is cheerfully deaf to compliments. Tell her a house is beautiful and she will tell you the left shutter is too green. Tell her she is beautiful and she will ask you to pass the turpentine.

This has made life very hard for Jem the fiddler. For a year now, Jem has been writing a song for Daisy, and for a year it has never been good enough to play to her. He turns up wherever she is working and plays tunes that are nearly the song and then stops. Everybody in the Workshops knows. Bertie knows and is enjoying it enormously. Whether Daisy knows is the great question of the lane. She has never said a word about it. Once, though, she painted the shutters of the Sleepy Snail the exact colour of Jem's fiddle, and when Molly asked her why, she said she had had some brown left over, and then went pink under the paint.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Daisy wants to find that blue again, to paint every house in Kaldemor at least once and to paint something, someday, that nobody has ever seen before. She fears that Bertie will grow too tired for his rounds, and that the houses will grow crooked without him. The houses nearest the woods have started leaning, and she has noticed that the paint on them cracks in the mornings as though they had shivered in the night.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A traveller might be asked to gather blue snail shells from the meadow, so that Daisy can rediscover her lost colour. Another quest might begin the day Jem finally plays his song in the square, and Daisy, for once, does not have paint on her nose, and somebody has to find out where she has gone.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Bertie: grandfather
  • Jem: admirer

docs.title: Digby
docs.text:
Gauntlet Hopeful

Town Kaldemor Where Kaldemor Park Role Adventurer Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Earnest, clumsy and impossible to discourage, he gets up from every fall grinning. He believes hard work beats talent, and he has had to.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Digby has failed Quill's hanging course eleven times. He will tell you so himself, cheerfully, usually while rubbing a fresh bruise, and then he will tell you he means to pass it before the leaves turn. He is nineteen, earnest, clumsy and impossible to discourage. He falls more often than anyone who has ever run the Kaldemor Gauntlet, and he gets up from every fall grinning. He believes hard work beats talent. He has had to.

docs.title: From the east
docs.text:
Digby was born on a small farm far out in the eastern countryside, a long walk past the end of the Royal Road, where the fields are thin and the families are large. He was the fourth of six children, and by the time he was fourteen there was not enough work, or supper, for all of them. So he walked west to Kaldemor with a bundle on his back, a letter from his mother, and a firm belief that somebody in a town that big would need a pair of hands.

Wilbur did. The big farmer took one look at the skinny boy at his gate, gave him a bowl of soup and a bed in the barn loft, and put him to work the next morning. Digby worked for Wilbur for four years. He was not a natural farmhand. He tripped over rows, dropped baskets and once fell into the bean frames so thoroughly that it took two people to get him out. But he was always first in the field and last out of it, and by his third year he could bring in a harvest as fast as anyone in Kaldemor. His parents and his brothers and sisters still live out east; he sends them part of his pay each autumn with any carter heading east, and writes when he can.

docs.title: Becoming a warrior
docs.text:
Last year, watching the young warriors set out from the Park toward the meadow, Digby decided that he wanted to protect the fields rather than only plough them. He told Wilbur, expecting to be laughed at. Wilbur clapped him on the back, gave him a pair of good boots from Ned's shop, and told him to come back at harvest. Digby still does, every year, and Wilbur still pays him, though Digby keeps trying to refuse.

He joined Quill's recruits in the Park, and that is where the falling began. The monster yard he managed on his second try. The hanging course, ropes and swinging logs strung high above the ground, has beaten him eleven times. Quill, who never mocks a fall, has told him that his footwork is getting better, which Digby has decided to take as a promise. He practises in the evenings on the fence rails behind Wilbur's barn, and Tam, Wilbur's boy, sometimes watches and shouts advice, all of it wrong.

docs.title: Meg
docs.text: Digby's great rival is Meg, the snail hunter, who is quicker, bolder and better at almost everything, and who keeps a running tally of every snail she has beaten, plus a few. Meg passed the hanging course on her first try and has never let him forget it. Digby has never let her forget the time she fell in the Park fountain. They needle each other constantly. Each has, at least once, quietly made sure the other got home safe from the meadow, and neither has ever mentioned it.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Digby wants to pass the hanging course before the leaves turn, and then to walk out to the meadow as one of the warriors who keep the farms safe: Wilbur's fields first of all. He fears being sent home. He knows he will never be the fastest or the strongest, and he is afraid that one day, for the first time, he will fall and not want to get up.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: Digby's twelfth attempt at the hanging course is coming soon, and a traveller who has run the Gauntlet might be asked, very humbly, for help with his footwork. Another quest might begin when a letter comes from his family in the east, telling of trouble on the road past the end of the Royal Road, and Digby has to decide whether he is ready.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Wilbur: former employer
  • Quill: drillmaster
  • Meg: rival

docs.title: Dottie
docs.text:
Shepherd Girl

Town Kaldemor Where Farms Role Child Age Child

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Small, determined and very fond of her sheep, she counts them twice before bed. She does not like to be told she is too young for anything.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Dottie is ten years old and she is not too young. She would like that understood before anything else. She is small, sunburnt and very determined, with a crook taller than she is and a whistle on a string round her neck, and she minds her grandmother Elsie's flock of sheep on the hills above the farms all by herself. She counts them in the morning, counts them at noon, and counts them twice before bed, once for herself and once in case the first count was wrong.

docs.title: Grandmother Elsie
docs.text:
Dottie lives with her grandmother Elsie, the dairy farmer, in the stone farmhouse with the cheese room at the back. Her parents, Elsie's daughter Hyacinth and Hyacinth's husband Tom, died of a winter fever eight years ago, when Dottie was two, and she does not remember them, though she has her mother's crook and her father's whistle. Elsie raised her. Elsie is proud, plain and up before the sun, and has a firm opinion about everything and no patience for fuss, and Dottie is so like her that the farm hands say it is like watching the same woman at both ends of her life.

Elsie gave Dottie the sheep when she was seven, the year Elsie's knees decided they were finished with hills. The cows and the cheese are Elsie's. The sheep are Dottie's. Dottie takes this very seriously.

docs.title: The flock
docs.text: There are thirty-one sheep and, until a week ago, nine lambs. Dottie knows every one of them by face and most of them by voice. The big ewe with the black ear is Duchess. The ram is Mister Pike, who is not to be turned one's back on. The smallest lamb of the spring, a speckled one with a bent ear, is Button. She shears them each summer with Elsie watching from the gate, and sells the wool to Winnie the weaver in the Workshops, who spins it into yarn, some of which goes to old Wren in the Park to become caps for every child in Kaldemor, Dottie included. Winnie pays her fairly and never once has said she is too young, which is why Winnie is Dottie's favourite grown-up after her grandmother.

docs.title: Button
docs.text:
A week ago, on a misty morning, Button wandered off toward the woods while Dottie was counting the others, and has not come back.

Dottie went looking as far as she dared, which was further than she should have, and found nothing but a tuft of speckled wool on a bramble at the edge of the trees. She has gone back every evening since, and every evening she has turned round at the same bramble, because the woods are darker than they used to be and the grown-ups talk about Shrooms and something big in a hollow.

She has not told her grandmother. She means to. But Elsie gave her the sheep because she trusted her, and Dottie cannot bear to see her face when she hears that a lamb is lost. So she has said nothing, and counted forty every night out loud for Elsie, and thirty-nine under her breath. She has been so busy searching that she has brought Winnie less wool than usual, and Winnie has noticed, and so has Wren. Dottie knows they have noticed. She has decided that if she does not look at them, it does not count.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Dottie wants Button home and nobody ever to know he was gone. She wants to be allowed to drive the flock to the far hill pasture alone, and to have a dog, and to be taken seriously by Quill, though she does not want to be a warrior, only to be asked. What she fears is that Button is gone for good, and that it is her fault, and that her grandmother will say, kindly, that she is too young after all.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A traveller who finds Dottie at the bramble at dusk might be asked, very fiercely, to come with her into the woods to look for Button, and to promise not to tell. The tuft of wool on the bramble is not the only thing she found there: there were tracks beside it, large and round and damp, and she has not told anyone about those either.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Elsie: grandmother
  • Winnie: weaver

docs.title: Elsie
docs.text:
Dairy Farmer

Town Kaldemor Where Farms Role Worker Age Elder Sells Milk, butter and cheese

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Proud, plain and up before the sun, she has a firm opinion about everything and a name for every cow. She does not believe in fuss.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Elsie is up before the sun, and she would like to know why you are not. She is seventy-two, square-built and weathered, proud, plain and blunt, with forearms like a blacksmith's from sixty years of churning, and a firm opinion about everything from the weather to the proper thickness of a cheese rind. She does not believe in fuss. She keeps the dairy herd on the farm at the edge of Kaldemor's fields, and she has a name for every cow she has ever owned and can still tell you most of them.

docs.title: The dairy
docs.text: Elsie was born on the same farm she keeps now, the daughter of a dairyman and his wife, who taught her to milk at five and to make cheese at nine. She married Walt, a hedge-layer with a laugh like a cart going over cobbles, and they kept the dairy together for nearly forty years; he died fifteen years ago, and she ran it alone after that, without asking anyone for help and without anyone daring to offer. Her cheese is hard, pale and sharp, wrapped in cloth and kept in the cool back room of the farmhouse, and it is, in her opinion and in the opinion of most of Kaldemor, the best on Veligor. Her butter goes to Rosa's oven. Her milk goes to half the kitchens in town. The cows are called Bluebell, Hepzibah, Old Moll, Clover, Martha the Second and so on, through all fourteen of them, and Elsie talks to each one by name at the morning milking.

docs.title: Old Marta
docs.text: For twenty years, Elsie's cheese and Old Marta's pickles have fought for first prize at the harvest fair. Every autumn the judges go pale. Every autumn, one of the two old women wins, and the other says it was the judges' fault. Elsie keeps count of the years she has won; so, she is quite certain, does Marta, and neither of them has ever once agreed with the other's number. They have not said a civil word to each other at a fair in twenty years. They are, in the eyes of the rest of the Market, the closest of friends, and both would be appalled to hear it. When Elsie was ill one winter, a jar of Marta's best pickles appeared on her doorstep with no note. Elsie knows exactly who left it and has never mentioned it, and the next autumn she made her sharpest cheese in years, out of gratitude.

docs.title: Dottie
docs.text:
Elsie's only daughter, Hyacinth, and Hyacinth's husband, Tom, died of a winter fever eight years ago, and Elsie took their little girl, Dottie, who was two. It was the hardest winter of her life, and she got through it the only way she knew: she got up before the sun and milked the cows. Dottie is ten now, and so like her grandmother that the farm hands say they are the same woman at both ends of her life. Three years ago, when Elsie's knees finally gave up the hills, she gave Dottie the sheep. She has never once regretted it.

She has noticed, this past week, that Dottie counts the flock aloud at bedtime a little too loudly, and goes out every evening toward the woods. Elsie has not asked. She is waiting for the girl to tell her, because that is what she would have wanted at that age, and because she does not believe in fuss. It is costing her more than she shows.

docs.title: The cows
docs.text: This spring, Elsie's cows stopped grazing the far pasture by the woods. They will go to the gate, look across at the good grass, and turn back, every one of them, even Old Moll, who has never refused grass in her life. Elsie has driven them there twice; twice they have come home on their own, lowing, without being told. She has never known her cows to be wrong about anything, not weather, not water, not who is a bad sort. She has not said much about it. She has stopped sending Dottie's sheep that way, though, and she has told Hale, who nodded.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Elsie wants a good milk, a dry hay harvest and, just once more, the fair's first prize with Marta standing close enough to see it. She fears what her cows know. She fears even more, though she would never say it, that she will not see Dottie grown, and that the farm will be too much for the girl alone.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A traveller might be asked to bring back a cow that, for the first time, has wandered toward the far pasture instead of away from it, and to find out what is calling it. Or Elsie might need a rare herb from the woods' edge for this year's prize cheese, and refuse, out of pure pride, to admit to Marta that she cannot fetch it herself.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Dottie: granddaughter
  • Old Marta: old rival

docs.title: Ewan
docs.text:
Clockkeeper

Town Kaldemor Where Kaldemor Park Role Worker Age Elder In the game Ewan

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Fussy, gentle and proud, he talks to the clock as if it could hear him and listens to it as if it could answer. He cannot stand dust, or people touching things that swing.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: "Mind the dust," says Ewan, before anyone has so much as stepped through the door of the clock tower. "And mind the time." He is seventy-two, small, neat and fussy, with a soft brush in one pocket and an oil can in the other, and he has kept the clock tower in Kaldemor Park for forty years: winding it, oiling it and, most of all, listening to it. He talks to the clock as if it could hear him, and he listens to it as if it could answer. In his opinion, it usually does.

docs.title: How he came to the tower
docs.text:
Ewan was a boy in Kaldemor at the same time as Tobin, and the two of them have been friends since they were small enough to be chased out of the tower together. Tobin wanted to see the bell. Ewan wanted to see what made it ring. The clockkeeper of those days, old Absalom, caught them both on the stairs, sent Tobin home and let Ewan stay to watch the works, because Ewan had asked him a question about the escapement that Absalom had been waiting thirty years for somebody to ask. Ewan came back to watch every week after that, and when he was twenty-two Absalom took him on as his apprentice.

Ewan worked under Absalom for ten years, learning the great spring, the ladder of gears and the bell on top, and learning, harder than any of it, to listen. When Absalom died, Ewan was thirty-two, and the tower was his. Absalom left him a brass pocket watch that had never once stopped, and Ewan carried it every day of his forty years as keeper. He has never married. He says the clock does not like to share, and that he has never minded.

docs.title: The day it stopped
docs.text:
In all that time, the clock never stopped. Ewan was proud of it in a way he would never say aloud. Then, late this spring, he climbed the stairs one morning and heard nothing at all. Not a tick, not a tock. The works were whole. The great gear, the heart of the whole train, was gone, and there were damp, round tracks in the dust that led to the window. A Shroom from the woods had carried it off in the night; they take anything shiny.

Lia had the news all over town before breakfast. For nine nights Kaldemor went without its bell, and for nine nights Tobin climbed the tower stairs and sat up with his old friend in the dark, telling him stories he had heard a hundred times. Ewan has never told Tobin how much that meant. Tobin knows.

On the tenth day a young adventurer came back from the woods with the gear, not a scratch on it, and Ewan fitted it with shaking hands and listened to the clock start again. He gave the adventurer Absalom's pocket watch. He says it should go on being carried by someone, and that he no longer needs it to know what time it is. He still climbs up every morning, first thing, to check that the gear is where it belongs.

docs.title: Neighbours and nuisances
docs.text:
Ewan cannot stand dust, and he cannot stand people touching things that swing, which is why Garrick the climber is the bane of his life. Garrick has climbed the outside of the clock tower more often than Ewan would like, which is to say more than never, and once waved to him through the face of the clock. Ewan has written to Tobin about it four times.

He knows that one of the rungs on the inside ladder was cracked last spring and mended badly. He does not know who did it. He has noticed that young Archie, the carpenter's apprentice, goes very pale whenever the ladder is mentioned, and he has his suspicions, but he would rather the boy came and told him.

His good friend Alfie, who leads the carpenters and keeps the tower stairs in repair, has told Ewan one secret: while mending an old beam in the great treehouse, Alfie found a carving that nobody can explain. Ewan has been to see it. He has told no one, not even Tobin, and he goes back now and then to look at it, the way he would listen to a clock that was ticking slightly wrong.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Ewan wants the clock to run and the tower to stay clean. He fears that it will stop again, and that next time the gear will not come home. He also fears, though he has said it only to the clock, that whoever keeps the tower after him will not know how to listen.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might begin when Ewan, listening one morning, hears the clock running a fraction fast, every day a little faster, as though something under the Park is pulling at it. Or he might at last ask a trusted traveller to help him understand Alfie's carving, if they can promise to keep a secret.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Alfie: friend
  • Tobin: old friend
  • Garrick: uninvited climber
  • Archie: nervous young neighbour

docs.title: Fen
docs.text:
Mushroom House Fan

Town Kaldemor Where Kaldemor Park Role Child Age Child In the game Fen

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Wide-eyed and full of questions, she notices the small things everyone else walks past. She thinks every squirrel has a secret.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Fen notices things. She notices the beetle on the fountain's rim, the new crack in the bakery step, the squirrel that keeps vanishing behind the big birch in the woods, and the way the mushroom houses lean a little towards the morning sun. Then she asks about them, one question after another, until whoever she has caught either answers or runs out of breath. She is eight, wide-eyed, small for her age, and quite certain that every squirrel in Kaldemor has a secret.

docs.title: The mushroom houses
docs.text:
Fen loves the mushroom houses more than anything in town. She was born in one, a small, round, freckled one at the end of the lane that runs from the Park to the Workshops, and she has measured it every spring since she was old enough to hold a string. Now she measures dozens of them. She keeps a knotted cord for each house she has adopted, tied with a scrap of coloured thread so she knows which is which, and every spring she goes round with them, wrapping each cord around its cap and tying a new knot where it ends. She knows which house grew the most last year (the tall yellow one by the Market steps), which grew the least (the one with the green door, which she suspects is shy), and which grew crooked.

She does not entirely know why they grow, and neither does anyone else, which is the best part. Lottie told her the old story of the one seed and the generous soil, and Fen has been digging small holes in odd places ever since, to see whether the soil looks generous.

docs.title: Bertie and Rosa
docs.text:
Her great hero is Bertie, the old mushroom house shaper, who has been hollowing out the town's houses and fitting their doors and windows for fifty years. Bertie never measures; he says the mushroom tells him. Fen measures everything; she says the mushroom does not tell her anything yet, but it might if she pays attention. Bertie thinks this is the right answer and lets her carry his tools, which she does with enormous ceremony. She follows him all over town on fitting days, and her dearest wish is that he will let her fit a window one day, a real one, in a real house. He keeps saying "next spring". She has written it down so he cannot forget.

Bertie's granddaughter Daisy paints the houses afterwards, and once let Fen paint a shutter, which is now a colour nobody can name.

Fen also carries flour for Rosa the baker. Twice a week she brings bags up from Hob's windmills to the terrace oven, and Rosa pays her in buns, warm, and sometimes in the heel of the loaf, which Rosa saves only for friends. Fen knows this and is very proud of it.

docs.title: Friends and school
docs.text: Her best friends are Tam, who swings a stick at everything, and Nell, who counts the clouds. Fen is allowed to help Nell count, but only the small clouds. She asks Tam questions about being a warrior that he cannot answer, and she knows perfectly well he makes the answers up, and she likes them better that way. At Lottie's school in the great treehouse, she is the one who asks "but why?" until even Lottie has to go and look something up.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Fen wants to fit a window in a mushroom house, to find out where the squirrel behind the birch goes, and to know why the houses grow. She would like to grow up to be a shaper, like Bertie, and she has already decided she will measure.

She was frightened when the clock tower went quiet this spring. She had never heard the park without its ticking, and she says the silence was spooky, like the whole town holding its breath. She was very glad when the gear came home, but she still listens for the bell every hour, just to be sure.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: The squirrel behind the big birch is real, and it really does vanish. Fen is sure there is a hole, or a door, or something stranger, and she is only waiting for a grown-up brave enough to come and look. Another quest could follow her cords: one spring, one of her houses grows far more than it should, all in a single night, and Fen is the only one who has the knots to prove it.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Rosa: kindly baker
  • Bertie: hero
  • Tam: friend
  • Nell: friend
  • Lottie: teacher

docs.title: Gareth
docs.text:
Smith

Town Kaldemor Where Kaldemor Market Role Craftsman Age Adult Sells Swords, shields and armour In the game Gareth

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Broad, quiet and proud of a clean edge, he talks more to his anvil than to people. He thinks every smith should start with copper.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: The forge in Kaldemor Market is the only place in town that is hotter than Rosa's oven, and the man who works it does not say much. Gareth is forty-eight, broad as a barn door, with a leather apron scorched in a hundred places, forearms marked with old burns and a beard he keeps short so it will not catch. He is quiet and proud of a clean edge. He talks more to his anvil than to people, and the anvil, he says, is the better listener. When he does speak, it is usually to tell you that you are holding your sword wrong.

docs.title: The forge
docs.text:
Gareth was not born in Kaldemor. He came from a mining village in the hills toward Selsior, where his father dug ore (his parents are both long dead), and he walked to Kaldemor at sixteen because he had heard there was a smith in the Market who needed a striker. The smith was old Bryn, who had a temper like a quenching tub and the best hands Gareth has ever seen. Bryn made Gareth smelt copper for a whole year before he let him near iron. "Copper forgives," Bryn said. "Iron remembers." Gareth hated that year, and he has made every apprentice since do the same.

Bryn died eighteen years ago and left Gareth the forge, the anvil and a hammer whose handle has been replaced four times and whose head has not. Gareth has worked the forge alone since. He sells swords, shields and armour to the young warriors heading out to the fields, iron tyres and axle-pins to Percy the wheelwright, who is his best customer and the only man in the Market who can match him for gloom, and nails, hinges and brackets to the carpenters.

docs.title: Copper first
docs.text: Gareth teaches smithing to anyone who will listen and many who will not. He thinks every smith should start with copper, and he will not hear otherwise. When a young adventurer asks him to show them the forge, he sends them out to the fields to strike copper ore from the veins that glitter in the east and west, and when they bring it back and smelt their first ingot he looks at it a long time and says, "Copper is soft. But every smith starts there." Then, if they have done it well, he shows them how to make a bronze axe. He also teaches the use of upgrade scrolls, which he does not entirely approve of, because a scroll does in a moment what a smith should do in an afternoon. But a sword can be sharpened with one, and he would rather a young warrior went out with a sharper blade than a purer principle.

docs.title: More swords
docs.text:
This year he has been asked for more swords than in the five years before it put together. The young people of Kaldemor, who used to come to him for a hoe or a gate hinge, now come for blades; Quill's recruits come every week, and the warriors who go out to the meadow come back with notched edges and dented shields and go out again sooner. Gareth works later every night. He is proud of the work and does not like the reason for it.

Little Tam, Wilbur's boy, turns up at the forge door with his stick whenever his mother sends him to the Market, and asks for a real sword. Gareth tells him to come back when he can lift the hammer. Tam tries to lift the hammer every time. It is a long way off yet, but Gareth has quietly started a small blade, the length of a boy's arm, and keeps it under the bench.

docs.title: Neighbours
docs.text: Gareth's neighbour in the Market is Hilda, who keeps the town's storage and remembers where every single item sits. She has never lost a thing; he has never broken one on purpose. They nod to each other every morning across the lane, and once a year, at midwinter, he mends the hinges on her storage doors and she will not let him pay for the tea.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Gareth wants a good ore, a clean edge and a forge that is too quiet, because a quiet forge would mean nobody needed swords. He fears that the swords he makes will not be enough. He fears too, a little, that he will die like Bryn, with no one to hand the hammer to, though he would never say so to his anvil.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: Gareth has heard from Percy that some of the broken wheels coming off the Royal Road bear marks no beast should make, and he would like a traveller to bring him one of whatever made them, so that he can see what a blade must cut. Another quest might begin when he finally gives Tam the small sword, and asks someone to make sure the boy never uses it.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Percy: customer
  • Hilda: neighbour

docs.title: Garrick
docs.text:
The Climber

Town Kaldemor Where Kaldemor Park Role Adventurer Age Adult In the game Garrick

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Easygoing, odd and fond of a good saying, he is happiest anywhere higher than everyone else. He thinks up is just a direction.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: "Fine view from up here," says Garrick. "Fine view." He says it whether you have climbed up to him or are standing at the bottom of his ladder with your neck craned back, and he means it either way. He is thirty-eight, long-limbed and brown as a hazelnut, with chalk on his fingers, a coil of rope over one shoulder and the calm, slightly distant smile of a man who spends most of his day higher than everybody else. He is easygoing, odd and fond of a good saying. Up, he will tell you, is just a direction.

docs.title: The ledge
docs.text:
Garrick lives on a ledge of rock above the fountain in Kaldemor Park, reached by a long rope ladder that he pulls up after him when he does not want visitors and lets down when he does. He has a little shelter of canvas and old planks up there, a stove, a great many ropes, and a view over the Park, the windmills, the clock tower and, on a clear day, the hills to the west. Asked why he lives on a ledge, he says that fewer people ask him what he is doing up there, and that the fountain below makes a pleasant sound at dawn. Both are true. He has never given a third reason, and Kaldemor has stopped expecting one.

Nobody is quite sure where he came from. He walked into Kaldemor nine years ago over the hills, not along the road, with a rope and a pack and nothing else, and when Lia asked him where he had come from he pointed upward and smiled. He has climbed, by his own account, every cliff, tower and tall tree between here and the sea, and a few that were not his to climb. He has no family that anyone knows of, and he does not seem to miss one. If Mildred's ledger lists anything under his name besides "the ledge, Park", nobody has seen it.

docs.title: Teaching Rope Up
docs.text: Garrick teaches one thing, and he teaches it only to people who have earned it. Anyone who climbs his ladder has the hands for climbing, he says, but he will teach Rope Up, the leap that throws a climber onto the rope or ledge above, only to those who have seen the world from above. So he sends them west of the town square to Kaldemor Hills, to climb the long vine on the west side as far as the lookout on its high ledge, and look around, and come back. When they do, he looks at them carefully, says they have the look of someone who has seen the clouds up close, and teaches them. "Bend your knees, look up, and let go." Ropes, he says, are only stairs that forgot their steps.

docs.title: The clock tower
docs.text:
Garrick has climbed the outside of the clock tower more often than Ewan the clockkeeper would like, which, as Ewan has pointed out, is more often than never. Once, on a fine morning, he climbed up to the great clock face and waved to Ewan through it, and Ewan dropped his oil can. Ewan has written to the mayor about Garrick four times. Garrick knows, because Tobin read him the third letter aloud, laughing too hard to finish it. Garrick is genuinely fond of Ewan, and genuinely cannot understand the fuss. He never touches anything that swings. He only wanted to see the town from the top.

He sees a great deal from his ledge. He saw Meg walk the rim of the fountain on her hands and fall in, and he applauded, and she has not forgiven him. He sees Archie looking up at him from the Park with a pencil in his hand, drawing something taller.

docs.title: What he has seen
docs.text: From the lookout on Kaldemor Hills, on a clear morning, Garrick can see over the woods to the country beyond. This spring he saw something there that he did not like: a line through the trees, far past the hills, where the treetops had been pushed apart and some of them had fallen, leading toward the hollow where the old snail Mano has settled, and coming from somewhere much farther off. He has told Hale. Hale nodded. Garrick has not told anyone else, because nobody else has asked him what he sees from up there, and he has learned that people rarely want to know.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Garrick wants to climb things, and to be left alone while he does it, except when he wants company, which is more often than he admits. He wants one day to climb the great treehouse to its very top, if Alfie will ever let him. He does not fear heights. He fears, a little, the ground, and the things that are coming along it.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: Garrick will teach Rope Up to any traveller who reaches the lookout on Kaldemor Hills by the long vine on its west side. He might also ask a traveller who has learned it to go out with him past the hills and follow the line of broken trees back toward wherever it begins.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Ewan: exasperated clockkeeper

docs.title: Hale
docs.text:
Park Ranger

Town Kaldemor Where Kaldemor Park Role Guard Age Adult In the game Hale

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Quiet, watchful and slow to worry, which makes it serious when he does. He says more with a nod than most people say in a speech.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Hale stands at the park gate most days with his arms folded, looking out at the meadow. He is forty-seven, lean and weathered, quiet, watchful and slow to worry, and he says more with a nod than most people say in a speech. Visitors sometimes take him for unfriendly. They are wrong; he is listening. From the gate, he says, you can hear the whole meadow rustle, and if you listen long enough you can tell what is rustling it.

docs.title: The road years
docs.text:
Hale was born in Kaldemor, the son of a hedger who kept the field boundaries east of the square, and he spent his boyhood in the meadow and the woods. At twenty-two he went out on the Royal Road as a hired guard for the merchant caravans that ran between Selsior and the eastern countryside, and on his first trip he was paired with another young guard called Quill. They rode the caravans together for six years. They learned to sleep in shifts, to read tracks from a wagon seat, and to stand back to back when something came out of the dark at the edge of the firelight. Quill did the shouting. Hale did the watching. Each of them is fairly sure he saved the other's life at least once, and neither has ever agreed which time.

When Hale was twenty-nine, Mayor Tobin asked him to come home and look after the park gate and the meadow, and Hale has been Kaldemor's ranger for eighteen years. Quill came to Kaldemor too, in time, and now drills the young warriors on the Gauntlet in the Park, a short walk from Hale's gate. The two old comrades see each other most days and say very little, which suits them both.

docs.title: The meadow
docs.text:
Hale's work is the meadow beyond the gate and everything in it: green snails near the town, blue and red ones farther out, and lately a great many more of all three. He pays a bounty, out of the town's purse and sometimes his own, to anyone who thins them out, thirty at a time, and he pays it again whenever they come back with thirty more. He collected shells for the mayor's fence from the same young hunters. He teaches young hunters the basics at the gate, how to swing and when to drink a potion, and sends them out with the same three words every time: mind the meadow.

His scout is Meg, the cocky young snail hunter, who ranges further than anyone and boasts about it more. Hale has never told her how good she is, because she would never stop saying it, but he trusts her eyes more than anyone's but Quill's. He has noticed she has been out past the hills farther than she admits, and he is waiting for her to tell him herself.

docs.title: The hollow
docs.text:
The snails have been thick this year, and bold. Wilbur says they come at his fields in lines. Elsie's cows will no longer graze the far pasture by the woods. Hale has heard all of it, nodded, and said nothing, because he had heard something else first. One night this spring, standing at the gate after dark, he heard something huge settle in a hollow past the woods, a long, slow, grinding sound like a cart full of stone being tipped out, and since then the ground has shaken at night and the snails no longer stray that way.

Hale kept it to himself until he knew what it was. He told no one, not Meg, not Quill, not the mayor. When he finally sent a capable young adventurer out to the forest edge and they came back whole, he knew: the old giant snail called Mano had taken the hollow and made itself a king. Then he told Tobin, plainly, and the mayor went very quiet. Hale now leads the bravest hunters to the Snail King's hollow himself, and tells each of them the same thing: keep your potions close and your feet moving, jump the red marks, and do not stay still when it sweeps.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Hale wants the meadow quiet and the farms safe, and every hunter he sends out to come back. What worries him, and it is serious when Hale worries, is not Mano itself but why a creature that old should leave wherever it came from, and why the snails all across the meadow have grown so many and so bold since it came, as if something were stirring them all.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might follow Hale out past the hollow, to find where Mano came from and what drove it out. Another might begin when Meg comes back from beyond the hills with something she cannot explain, and Hale, for the first time, asks a traveller to go and look before he tells anyone.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Tobin: mayor
  • Meg: scout
  • Quill: old comrade

docs.title: Hattie
docs.text:
Beekeeper

Town Kaldemor Where Farms Sells Honey, beeswax and candles

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Wilbur: husband
  • Tam: son
  • Clem: neighbour

docs.text:
Storage Keeper

docs.title: Hob
docs.text:
Miller

Town Kaldemor Where Kaldemor Park Role Worker Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Easygoing and dusty from head to toe, he whistles along with the creak of the sails. He worries about the weather the way other people worry about money.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text:
You can hear Hob before you see him. He whistles along with the creak of the windmill sails, a tune that changes with the wind, and when the wind drops the whistling stops and he goes out to look at the sky. He is forty-four, easygoing, broad in the shoulder and dusty from head to toe; the flour has settled so deep into his eyebrows that his daughter says he was born with white ones.
