docs.title: The walking years
docs.text:
Mabbu was born in a hide tent on the high pastures in a hard, dry year, and she likes to say that she learned to walk so she could follow the goats to the next spring. The Tolmach have always lived by knowing where water is, and Mabbu learned it better than anyone of her generation. As a girl she lived through the driest year anyone in the camps can remember, when spring after spring failed along the south path, and she has never forgotten which ones kept running. The Greywater spring, in its cleft halfway down that path, was one of them. She has told that story so often that her grandchildren can recite it with her.

She married Garrak, a herder with a famous nose for weather, and they followed the herds together for over thirty years. Garrak died twenty years ago, of a long illness that kept him in the home camp for his last winter. Mabbu went back out with the herds the following spring, because, she said, the goats did not know he was gone and somebody had to explain it to them.

Their daughters are Sennu, now chieftain of the Tolmach, and Harra, who sells the herds' wool and cheese at the Trading Post. Mabbu raised Sennu on the paths, and Sennu has her patience. She raised Harra on the paths too, and Harra has her voice. Mabbu is proud of both and tells neither, except loudly to other people within their hearing.

docs.title: The home camp
docs.text:
About five years ago, Mabbu's knees gave out on a steep climb above the terraces, and she has not followed the herds since. She keeps the home camp now: the cluster of tents and stone shelters closest to town, where the Tolmach leave their elders, their youngest children and their stores. She runs it like a chieftain runs a family, and Sennu, who actually is one, has learned not to argue.

Mabbu remembers out loud. Every spring that ever ran in every dry year, every path that ever washed out, every herder who ever got lost and how they were found. Sennu listens, knowing that one day those memories will be the only map left. Her grandson Kesh, Harra's boy, asks her to tell it all again, which delights her. Her other grandson, Ennek, Sennu's son, became a canyon guide on her stories, and she considers every trader he brings up safely to be partly her doing.

Lessa, the Brenna bonesetter, walks out to the home camp every few days with salve for Mabbu's knees. Mabbu grumbles through every visit, tells her she is doing it wrong, feeds her far too much and asks after her daughter Neffa's singing. She would be deeply offended if Lessa ever stopped coming.

docs.title: What she fears
docs.text:
This year Sennu has kept the herds closer to town than ever before, and the home camp is crowded with animals that ought to be on the high pastures. Mabbu can see the grass thinning from her own tent. She says nothing to Sennu, who has enough to carry, but she has started walking a little farther each morning on her bad knees, testing them, in case the family needs her on the paths again.

She does not yet know that the Greywater spring has gone dry. When she learns it, she will know at once that it never failed in the worst year of her life, and she will want to know why it has failed now.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could carry Mabbu's memories of the old springs to a place no one has checked in years, or help her up a path one last time to see a pasture she has not seen since her knees gave out.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Sennu: daughter
  • Harra: daughter
  • Lessa: healer

docs.title: Neffa
docs.text:
Song Learner

Town Midbarium Where Brenna House Role Child Age Child Family Brenna

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Solemn, serious and proud; Neffa practises the long songs under her breath all day long.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Neffa is ten years old and practises the long songs under her breath all day long: while she eats, while she sweeps, while she walks to the cisterns for water, and, according to her mother, while she sleeps. She is solemn, serious and proud, and she has a plan. Before she turns twelve, she will stand up at a gathering of the four families in the great hall and recite the whole long song of the Old Ones without a single mistake.

docs.title: Brenna House
docs.text:
Neffa is the daughter of Lessa, the best bonesetter in the highlands, and the granddaughter of Odda, chieftain of the Brenna, and Thrun, who beats the great drum that calls the families together. Her father, Corrick, was a Brenna storyteller with a gift for voices. He died of a lung fever when she was two, and she does not remember him, though everyone tells her she has his ear for rhythm. She keeps that like a treasure.

She grew up in Brenna House among herbs, drums and stories, and she has always been the quiet one in a loud household. Her grandfather laughs from the belly and drums the same way; her grandmother can settle any quarrel with a story; her mother scolds patients for muddy boots. Neffa listens to all of them and remembers everything they say, which has made her, at ten, a slightly alarming person to argue with.

docs.title: Ahvi's pupil
docs.text:
Four years ago, Ahvi, the family's song-keeper and Odda's cousin, heard six-year-old Neffa repeat an entire evening's singing back to her mother the next morning, and took her as a pupil the same day. Ahvi had been chosen the same way when she was a child, and she told Neffa so, which Neffa considers the most important thing anyone has ever told her.

The long song of the Old Ones names every Old One of Midbarium back to the Age of Division, with their families, their deeds and the chieftains who stood beside them. It takes most of a night to sing. Ahvi is a demanding teacher: after any mistake at all, however small, Neffa must go back to the very beginning. Neffa has never once complained. She has, however, kept a private count of how many times she has started over, scratched on the underside of her bed, and it is well into the hundreds.

She can now sing three-quarters of the song without a slip. The last quarter holds the most recent Old Ones, and she stumbles in the same place every time: the verse for Old One Varra, Ahvi's sister, who died when Neffa was four. Neffa remembers Varra, a little, as a big laugh at the end of a table, and she is not sure why that verse is the one that trips her. Ahvi has not told her that she, too, finds it the hardest to sing.

docs.title: The other verse
docs.text: Neffa has noticed that Ahvi has been singing something alone in her room at night this summer, a short, strange verse from the oldest part of the song that Neffa has never been taught. She has heard enough of it through the wall to know it is about beasts. She has asked Ahvi about it once. Ahvi said it was not for learning yet, and Neffa, who has never been told that about any verse before, has not stopped thinking about it.

docs.title: What she wants
docs.text:
Neffa wants to recite the long song whole, before twelve, in front of everyone, and to see her grandmother pretend not to be proud. She fears stumbling in front of the families, and she fears, more quietly, that the song will one day have to name something she does not want it to.

A quest could help Neffa find the old meaning of a name or deed she cannot place in the song, or be in the great hall on the night she finally stands up to recite.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Lessa: mother
  • Odda: grandmother
  • Ahvi: teacher

docs.title: Odda
docs.text:
Chieftain of the Brenna

Town Midbarium Where Brenna House Role Ruler Age Elder Family Brenna

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Warm, shrewd and endlessly calm; Odda can settle a quarrel between two chieftains with one well-chosen story.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Odda has led the Brenna for twenty years, and in all that time nobody has seen her raise her voice. She is sixty-eight, warm, shrewd and endlessly calm, and she can settle a quarrel between two chieftains with one well-chosen story. The Brenna are Midbarium's healers, storytellers and drummers, the keepers of the families' memory, and Odda has always believed that a good story, told at the right moment, is a kind of medicine.

docs.title: The envoy and the teacher
docs.text:
Odda's friendship with Fairy Forest began forty-seven years ago. At twenty-one she was sent to the forest as a young Brenna envoy, carrying on a tie between the Brenna and the Magicians older than the kingdom itself. In her first week she got lost on the Lantern Paths after dark, and a young teacher from the Grove School named Calyra, then twenty-seven and in her third year of teaching, found her sitting under a lantern trying to look as though she had meant to be there. Calyra walked her home without a word of teasing, and only teased her about it for the next forty-seven years.

Odda stayed three winters in the forest. She taught Calyra Brenna bonesetting and the uses of highland herbs; Calyra taught her forest plant-lore and how to read the oldest Magician script, which Odda still reads slowly and proudly. When Odda came home, they agreed to keep the friendship alive. Every spring since, Odda has written a letter ahead to the forest and then followed it a few weeks later with a bundle of highland herbs, and she has come home each time with forest herbs for the Brenna healers. These days she travels with Uskari escorts on the worst roads, and grumbles that it makes the walk far less peaceful. Calyra is Eldest of the Grove now, and Odda says that suits her perfectly, because Calyra has been telling people what to do since she was twenty-seven.

docs.title: The Brenna and the choosing
docs.text:
Odda was chosen chieftain of the Brenna at forty-eight. She married Thrun, the drummer whose great drum calls the families to every gathering, and their daughter Lessa is the best bonesetter in the highlands. Lessa's daughter Neffa is learning the long song of the Old Ones from Odda's cousin Ahvi, and Odda listens to her practise with her eyes closed so the child will not see how proud she is.

The Brenna host every choosing. Six years ago, when Old One Varra died, Odda hosted the one that named Hask. Varra had been Ahvi's sister, and so Odda's cousin as well as her friend, and Odda remembers that night as both the saddest and the finest of her life: Ahvi singing the long song, Thrun drumming until dawn, Dorrek arguing for the Kragvar, and Hask, quiet as ever, accepting a title he had not asked for. Odda is Hask's adviser now and, he says, his friend. She does not tell him what to do. She tells him stories, and he works out the rest.

docs.title: What worries her
docs.text:
Lessa has treated more monster bites this year than in her first ten years of healing together, and the far-slope herbs she needs are running short. Ahvi is troubled by an old verse about beasts growing wild before the Burning came, and has asked Odda whether to sing it at the next gathering. Odda has not yet answered. She believes the families deserve the truth, and she knows what a verse like that might do to a frightened hall.

She fears, too, that one spring the road to the forest will be closed, and that she will have to send her letter and stay at home.

A quest might escort Odda's spring bundle of herbs to Fairy Forest, gather the far-slope herbs Lessa needs, or help her decide what to do about Ahvi's verse.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Thrun: husband
  • Lessa: daughter
  • Neffa: granddaughter
  • Ahvi: cousin
  • Hask: friend
  • Calyra: old friend

docs.title: Hask
docs.text:
The Old One

Town Midbarium Where Great Hall Role Ruler Age Adult Family Uskari

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Quiet, patient and hard to rattle; Hask listens to a whole loud council without a word, then speaks once and plainly.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Hask was born on the Uskari Rim, the younger brother of Zirra the bowyer, and he grew up the way Uskari children do: climbing before he could properly walk, tracking goats along the canyon edges and listening to his elders argue about everything. He was never the loudest of them. He was the one who waited until the arguing was done and then said, quietly, what everyone had been circling around. By the time he was thirty-three, that habit had made him chieftain of the Uskari, chosen around the family fire after old Chieftain Orvek died of a winter fever fifteen years ago.

docs.title: The choosing
docs.text:
Hask led the Uskari for nine years. Then Old One Varra of the Brenna died in her sleep at Brenna House, aged eighty-one, after twenty-five years as the voice of all four families. Varra had been patient, funny and very hard to argue with, and the families mourned her for a long time.

Six years ago, the four families gathered in the great hall around the council fire to choose who would follow her. Odda, chieftain of the Brenna, hosted the choosing as her family always does, and Thrun beat the great drum all night. By custom no family may hold the title twice running, so the Brenna could not follow Varra. Dorrek of the Kragvar argued long and hard for an Old One from his own family, and many listened, but by dawn the families had settled on Hask. He was forty-two, one of the youngest Old Ones the Brenna songs name. He gave up the Uskari chieftainship that same night, as custom asks, and the Uskari chose Tavi to lead them before the fire burned down.

docs.title: How he leads
docs.text:
Hask is quiet, patient and hard to rattle. He sits through a whole loud council without a word, lets every chieftain shout until they are hoarse, and then speaks once and plainly. Once he closes a council, the families stand by the decision, and that, more than anything, is what makes an Old One.

He leans on a small circle of people. Ulm, keeper of the council fire for forty years, is his most trusted counsel, and Hask often sits with him late at night watching the flames. Odda, who hosted his choosing, is his adviser and his friend; she can tell him in one story what he has been doing wrong for a month. Dorrek is his bluntest critic and, Hask has learned, one of his most loyal; the Kragvar chieftain never once complained about losing the choosing, and Hask respects him for it more than he can say. Tavi, his successor among the Uskari, still walks the worst stretch of trail personally, which Hask understands and worries about in equal measure. Sennu of the Tolmach is the one he watches most closely this year, because her herds are kept nearer town than ever and the high pastures are paying for it.

Zirra teases him mercilessly in private, calls him "little brother" in front of nobody and defends him fiercely to anyone else. Hask has never married. He says the Old One belongs to four families, and that is family enough.

docs.title: What troubles him
docs.text:
Hask's private worry is the canyon patrols. Every season they are stretched thinner, and every season the families are a little too proud to say so in council. The Uskari patrol the trails, the Tolmach guard the herds, the Kragvar mend the bridges, and the Brenna mend the people, and every one of them reports that all is well. Hask suspects none of them is telling the whole truth, because he knows he would not either.

He also carries the weight of being young for the post. An Old One can be any age, but Hask feels that he will be in the great hall for a long time, and that the hardest years of the Age of Disturbance may well fall within his.

A quest could begin with Hask quietly asking someone from outside the four families to walk the patrols and tell him the truth about them, or with a rope bridge gnawed through on the night before a gathering.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Zirra: older sister
  • Tavi: successor
  • Ulm: keeper of the fire and trusted counsel
  • Dorrek: blunt but loyal critic
  • Odda: host of the choosing and adviser

docs.title: Sennu
docs.text:
Chieftain of the Tolmach

Town Midbarium Where Tolmach Camps Role Ruler Age Adult Family Tolmach

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Weathered, wry and unhurried; Sennu has a herder's patience and a herder's habit of counting heads twice.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Sennu leads the Tolmach from a hide tent like any other herder's, pitched wherever the herds happen to be grazing, and she would not trade it for the finest house in the Kragvar Quarter. She is fifty, weathered and wry, and she has a herder's patience and a herder's habit of counting heads twice. The family chose her as chieftain thirteen years ago, after old Bekku died, because she had walked more of the high paths than anyone her age and because nobody had ever seen her lose her temper with a goat.

docs.title: A life on the move
docs.text:
Sennu was born in a camp on the high pastures and spent her childhood following her mother, Mabbu, from spring to spring. Mabbu has walked every herding path in the highlands at least a hundred times, and she taught Sennu where every one of them leads and where water can be found in a dry year. Mabbu's knees no longer let her follow the herds, so she keeps the home camp now and remembers, out loud and at length, every spring that ever ran. Sennu listens to all of it. She knows that one day those memories will be the only map left.

Her sister Harra takes the herds' wool, hides and cheese down to the Trading Post and drives famously hard bargains with lowland traders. The two of them argue about prices and agree about everything else. Sennu's son Ennek leads travelers up the old Tolmach paths, as the family has done since the founding, and she is quietly proud that the traders ask for him by name.

As chieftain, Sennu moves the camps with the seasons as the Tolmach always have, settles the family's disputes over grazing and water, and sits in council with the Old One and the other chieftains. She is not a talker in council. She lets Dorrek thunder and Tavi push, and then she says something dry that makes them both feel slightly foolish.

docs.title: This year
docs.text:
This year Sennu has kept the herds closer to town than ever before, because of the monsters in the low valleys. She has lost animals before to cats and storms and bad footing, but never like this: whole flocks scattered in a night, and herders who come back with stories they do not want to tell twice. Keeping the herds near town keeps them alive, but the high pastures closest to Midbarium are starting to suffer for it. The grass is thin, the ground is churned, and Sennu can count, as well as anyone, how many seasons the land can take this before it gives out.

That is where she and Tavi of the Uskari disagree. Tavi wants the herds close, where the trail patrols can guard them. Sennu wants the patrols pushed farther out, into the valleys, so the herds can go back to the pastures they have always used. They need each other and they know it, and they are uneasy allies on the trails because of it: each respects the other, and each thinks the other is asking too much. Sennu has told Hask, the Old One, that the arrangement will hold for one more year. She has not told him what happens after that, because she does not know.

docs.title: What she wants
docs.text:
Sennu wants the old paths open again. She wants Ennek to lead traders up the south path without looking over his shoulder, and she wants Mabbu to see the herds on the high pastures one more time. She fears the day a spring that has always run goes dry, because the Tolmach have survived every hard year by knowing where water is, and she does not know what they will do if the land starts forgetting.

She has no idea yet that Ennek has been keeping something from her.

A quest might help Sennu scout a safe route back to a high pasture, or carry a message between her and Tavi when the two of them are too proud to deliver it themselves.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Mabbu: mother
  • Harra: sister
  • Ennek: son
  • Tavi: uneasy ally on the trails

docs.title: Skarra
docs.text:
Captain of the Trail Watch

Town Midbarium Where Uskari Rim Role Guard Age Adult Family Uskari

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Stern, watchful and dryly funny once the patrol is safely home.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Skarra commands the Uskari trail watch, the patrols that guard Midbarium's highland trails, drive off the monsters that come up from the canyons and see travelers safely from one camp to the next. She is forty-one, stern and watchful on the trail, and nobody on the rim has ever heard her laugh while a patrol is still out. Once every patrol is safely home, she turns out to be the driest wit on the rim, and the scouts who have learned this stay late at her fire on purpose.

docs.title: The watch
docs.text:
Skarra was born on the Uskari Rim and was tracking goats along the canyon edges before she was ten. She never left to adventure, as so many young Uskari do; she says she could see all the trouble she wanted from the rim. She joined the trail watch at sixteen, became its best tracker by twenty-five, and was made its captain ten years ago by Hask, then chieftain of the Uskari, who chose her because she was the only scout who reported bad news before good.

She has served under two chieftains since. When Hask was chosen Old One six years ago, the Uskari chose Tavi, and Tavi doubled the patrols. Skarra approved of the doubling and argued with every route Tavi drew for it. The two of them have been friendly rivals since Tavi came home from adventuring, nearly twenty years ago, in everything from climbing races to arguments about patrol routes. Tavi still walks the worst stretch of trail personally, and Skarra has given up trying to stop it; she simply makes sure the scout walking behind Tavi is a good one.

docs.title: The hide map
docs.text:
In her tent, Skarra keeps a hide map of the highlands, painted with every trail, camp, bridge and cave the watch knows. Since the day she became captain she has marked every monster sighting on it with a dot of red ochre and the date. Ten years ago the dots sat mostly in the low valleys and the far canyons. Each season since, they have crept a little closer to town. This summer there are dots on the high pastures, on the south path and at the far end of the far canyon bridge.

She shows the map to Tavi and to no one else. In council the Uskari report that the trails are held, and they are; but Skarra knows exactly how few scouts are holding them, and she has stopped sending hunters out to the far slopes for game, hides or Lessa's grey herb, because she cannot spare them.

docs.title: Bekk
docs.text:
Skarra's son Bekk is eighteen, cocky, quick and the fastest climber on the rim, with a crowd of admiring children at his heels. His father, Haldo, went out alone onto the far slopes thirteen years ago to track a great horned beast and was gored and killed by it, and Skarra raised Bekk on the rim among the patrols. She is harder on him than on any scout she commands, and she knows he knows why.

Now Bekk wants to track the beast that has been raiding the high pastures, and he wants to do it alone. Skarra has forbidden it. She has not told him that she has measured the beast's tracks herself, and that they frighten her.

When Dorrek of the Kragvar came to her quietly last month to ask how young the Uskari take recruits, she told him sixteen, and asked whether this was about his small son who follows Bekk everywhere. Dorrek said it was a general question. Skarra has been smiling about it ever since, though only after dark.

docs.title: The stretch nobody walks
docs.text:
Skarra has noticed that Ketta, who came home last spring, always trades away the stretch of canyon trail that passes a certain deep cave. Skarra has let her, and has said nothing. But that stretch has a red dot on it now.

A quest could help Skarra check the newest dots on her map before the next council, or walk the canyon stretch Ketta will not.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Tavi: friendly rival
  • Bekk: son

docs.title: Tavi
docs.text:
Chieftain of the Uskari

Town Midbarium Where Uskari Rim Role Ruler Age Adult Family Uskari

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Restless, direct and competitive; Tavi would rather walk the trail than talk about it, and hates losing at anything.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Tavi has never been good at sitting still. Born on the Uskari Rim, Tavi learned to climb the canyon walls before learning to read, and left home at seventeen, like so many young Uskari, to see what the rest of Veligor had to offer. Tavi is thirty-nine now, chieftain of the Uskari for six years, and still restless, direct and fiercely competitive. Tavi would rather walk the trail than talk about it, and hates losing at anything.

docs.title: The season in the capital
docs.text:
At eighteen, Tavi walked into the Knights' Court in Selsior and asked to train with the capital's swordsmen. The Guard is open to anyone who can keep up, and the old Grand Swordmaster who ran the yard then took one look at Tavi and paired the newcomer with a nineteen-year-old recruit named Rhys, who was every bit as fierce and every bit as stubborn.

From spring until the first frosts of autumn, Tavi and Rhys fought a bout every evening after drill, eighty in all, and scratched the tally into a post in the practice yard. When Tavi left in the autumn, it stood at forty-one to thirty-nine in Tavi's favour, and Tavi has reminded Rhys of it in every letter since. Tavi left Selsior before the Guard's trials and took no rank, wanting the sword's lessons, not its titles. Tavi still fights with the capital's controlled cuts mixed into the Uskari way of the hunt, and says no one before or since has made Tavi work as hard as Rhys did.

They write once a year, around midwinter, and have met only a handful of times. The last was three years ago, when Tavi came down to Selsior with a party from Midbarium and the two of them fought one more bout in the old yard. The recruits' drill bell rang before either won. Both agree the bout is unfinished; Tavi is certain who would have won it, and suspects Rhys is equally certain of the opposite.

docs.title: Chieftain of the Uskari
docs.text:
After two more years of adventuring, Tavi came home to hunt, and spent the next years tracking beasts along the canyon rims, first under old Chieftain Orvek and then under Hask. Six years ago, when Hask was chosen Old One, the Uskari gathered around their fire the same night and chose Tavi to lead them. Hask and Tavi have always got on well; Hask is the patient one and Tavi the impatient one, and each finds the other useful. Hask worries that Tavi still walks the worst stretch of trail personally. Tavi has no intention of stopping.

Since becoming chieftain, Tavi has doubled the trail patrols. Skarra, captain of the trail watch, is Tavi's friendly rival in everything from climbing races to arguments about patrol routes, and the two of them keep each other sharp. Ketta, who came home last spring with a new scar and a pack full of stories, worries Tavi more than any monster, because she will tell every story but one, and Tavi knows that kind of silence from the inside.

Tavi and Sennu of the Tolmach are uneasy allies on the trails. Tavi wants the herds close to town, where the patrols can guard them; Sennu wants the patrols pushed farther out so the herds can return to the high pastures. Each respects the other. Neither has given ground.

docs.title: What Tavi wants
docs.text:
Tavi wants the trails safe enough that the patrols can go back to being hunters. Tavi fears that will not happen, and that the patrols are already stretched as thin as they can go. The monsters are creeping closer every season, Skarra's hide map says so, and Tavi hates nothing more than a fight that cannot be won by walking harder.

A quest might send someone along the worst stretch of trail with Tavi, find out what Ketta saw in the deep canyon cave, or carry a challenge down to the Knights' Court to finish an old bout.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Hask: former chieftain
  • Skarra: friendly rival
  • Ketta: worried-over hunter
  • Sennu: uneasy ally on the trails
  • Rhys: old training partner

docs.title: Thrun
docs.text:
Drummer of the Gatherings

Town Midbarium Where Great Hall Role Performer Age Elder Family Brenna

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Loud, warm and impossible to embarrass; Thrun laughs from the belly and drums the same way.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Thrun beats the great drum that calls the four families of Midbarium to every choosing and every feast, and you can hear him laughing from almost as far away as you can hear the drum. He is seventy, loud, warm and impossible to embarrass. He laughs from the belly and drums the same way, and there is not a child in the highlands who has not, at some point, been lifted onto his shoulders to watch a gathering over the heads of the crowd.

docs.title: The drummer
docs.text:
Thrun was born in Brenna House and started drumming on cooking pots before he could talk. The Brenna are the families' healers, storytellers and drummers, and Thrun was never much of a healer and only a fair storyteller, but the drum understood him from the start. He was made Drummer of the Gatherings at twenty-five, after the old drummer's hands grew too stiff to play, and he has drummed every gathering since: forty-five years of feasts, weddings, mournings and choosings, each with its own rhythm, all of which he can play in his sleep and some of which, his wife says, he does.

The great drum itself is far older than Thrun. Its frame is Kragvar-cut timber, bound with rope, and it stands taller than a man on a stand that Thrun's oldest friend, Vosk of the Kragvar, rebuilt for him when they were both young and has kept sound ever since. They have been friends since boyhood, the loud Brenna drummer and the dry Kragvar bridge-builder, and they still sit together at every feast, one talking and one listening, both enjoying themselves.

docs.title: Family
docs.text:
Thrun married Odda, now chieftain of the Brenna, the year after she came home from her three winters as an envoy in Fairy Forest. He says he married her because she was the only person in Midbarium who could make him stop talking, and she says she married him because she liked the noise. Their daughter is Lessa, the best bonesetter in the highlands, who inherited her mother's calm in a crisis and none of her father's tolerance for mud. Lessa's daughter Neffa, solemn and serious, is learning the long songs from Ahvi, and Thrun beats out the rhythms for her practice on the kitchen table, softly, which is the only thing he has ever done softly.

Lessa's husband Corrick was a storyteller and a great friend to Thrun, and his death eight years ago was the only time anyone in Brenna House can remember the drummer going quiet for a whole week.

docs.title: The finest night
docs.text: Six years ago, Thrun drummed through the whole night of the choosing that named Hask Old One, while Ahvi sang the long song and Odda hosted and Dorrek argued, and he swears it was the finest night of drumming in a generation. He drummed grief for Varra at the start, argument through the middle, and at dawn, when the families settled on Hask, he played the choosing beat so hard that the great hall's dust came down from the beams. He tells the story at every opportunity, and improves it each time.

docs.title: The split hide
docs.text:
This spring, at the first feast of the year, the drum's old hide split across its face with a sound like a branch breaking. Thrun has patched it, but a patched drum only mutters. A new hide must come from one of the great horned beasts of the plateau, the kind the Uskari hunted in the old days, and the hide on the drum now was taken in Thrun's grandfather's time. Few such beasts have been seen in years, and those that have been seen are wild and vicious in a way the songs Thrun knows never describe. Few hunters would dare to track one now.

Thrun fears the next choosing will be called by a muttering drum. He would never say it, but he also fears that the next choosing may come sooner than anyone thinks, the way the canyons are now.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could track the great horned beast whose hide the drum needs, or help Vosk and Thrun fit the new skin in time for the next gathering.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Odda: wife
  • Lessa: daughter
  • Vosk: old friend

docs.title: Ulm
docs.text:
Keeper of the Council Fire

Town Midbarium Where Great Hall Role Official Age Elder Family Kragvar

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Gruff, slow-moving and fiercely proud of his duty; he talks to the fire more kindly than to most people.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Ulm has tended the council fire in Midbarium's great hall for forty years, and in all that time he has never once let it burn low. He is seventy-four, gruff and slow-moving, with hands so scarred from the wood and the embers that he can lift a burning log without flinching. He is fiercely proud of his duty, and he talks to the fire more kindly than to most people.

docs.title: The fire that never goes out
docs.text:
The fire in the great hall is the heart of Midbarium. The four families choose their Old One around it, the chieftains meet in council beside it, and by custom it is never allowed to go out. The Kragvar, who raised the hall, have always kept it, and they count that as their proudest duty. The keeper sleeps in a small room behind the hearth, and in practice hardly sleeps at all.

Ulm was thirty-four when the old keeper died and the Kragvar asked him to take the fire. He had been a mason until then, and a good one, and some in the family thought he would make a chieftain one day. When the Kragvar chieftain of those years died, the family did look to Ulm first, and he refused them. A chieftain leads from the front, he said, and the keeper of the fire does not leave it. So the family chose his younger brother Baruk instead, and Ulm stayed by the hearth.

Eleven years ago Baruk died in the rockfall on the old north cliff stair, and Ulm's son Dorrek dug for him until his hands bled. Ulm did not go. Somebody had to keep the fire, and he kept it all that night with the whole hall empty and the sound of the digging carrying up the cliff. He has never said what that night cost him. The family chose Dorrek as chieftain the following evening, and Ulm, who had refused the post himself, was prouder than he has ever admitted.

docs.title: Family
docs.text: Ulm's wife Hessa, a Kragvar stone-carver who could cut a face into granite that looked ready to speak, died sixteen years ago, and Ulm rarely speaks of her except to the fire. Dorrek visits him most evenings, and the two of them sit by the fire and say very little, which suits them both. Gorra, Dorrek's wife, sends him a jug of the coldest cistern water every evening, which is the closest thing to fussing he will allow. His granddaughter Brakka brings him wood, when she remembers. His grandson Korrin is the only person allowed to sit on the woodpile while Ulm tends the fire, and the boy listens to the old songs with his mouth open.

docs.title: The Old One's counsel
docs.text: Old One Hask trusts Ulm more than anyone. Many nights, long after a council has shouted itself hoarse and gone home, Hask sits with Ulm and watches the flames, and the two of them talk about whatever the council would not. Ulm tells him plainly what the Kragvar are too proud to say, and Hask listens. Ulm thinks Hask is the best Old One he has served under, and the most tired, and he worries about both.

docs.title: The ones who stayed
docs.text:
Ulm knows every Kragvar song about the fighters who stood in the front line of the Balrog War and never came home, but stayed beneath the World Tree to keep watch. When he was young, those songs were simply history. Lately he finds himself wondering aloud, to the fire mostly, about the city of guardians that he knows lies beneath the Tree: whether any of its people are Kragvar, whether those fighters' children's children still keep watch among them, and whether they remember the names that Midbarium still sings for them. He does not know. Nobody in Midbarium does.

He fears that the families are forgetting how to ask for help, and that the fire will outlast the people who gather around it.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could carry a Kragvar song, and Ulm's question, down toward the World Tree, or sit up one night by the fire while Ulm tells the Old One what the council will not.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Dorrek: son
  • Korrin: grandson
  • Hask: the Old One he serves

docs.title: Vosk
docs.text:
Master of Bridges

Town Midbarium Where Kragvar Quarter Role Craftsman Age Elder Family Kragvar

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Careful, dry-humoured and suspicious of anything that sways; he trusts a knot only after he has tied it himself.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Vosk is the master of bridges, and every rope-and-plank bridge that swings across Midbarium's cliffs and canyons is sound because he has walked it, tested it and argued with it. He is seventy-one, careful, dry-humoured and suspicious of anything that sways, which he admits is an odd temper for a man who has spent his whole life on things that sway. He trusts a knot only after he has tied it himself, and he has been known to untie a perfectly good knot in front of its maker, retie it exactly the same way, and walk off satisfied.

docs.title: A Kragvar on a rope
docs.text:
Vosk was born in the Kragvar Quarter. His mother, Kelda, was the eldest sister of Ulm and Baruk, born so many years before her brothers that her son grew up nearer in age to his uncle Ulm than to anyone else in the family. That is how Vosk comes to be cousin to Dorrek, chieftain of the Kragvar, while being old enough to be his father. Kelda died long ago, and Vosk still uses her splicing awl, which has been reground so often it is half its old length.

Like every Kragvar child, he started on stone. But he was the boy who kept climbing out onto the bridges to watch the rope-masters work, and the old bridge-keeper of those days, tired of hauling him back, finally put a cable in his hands and told him to make himself useful. Vosk has been splicing cable ever since. He has taught three generations of Kragvar how to do it, and he can tell by the sound a plank makes underfoot whether the rope beneath it has a winter left in it.

docs.title: Friends and apprentices
docs.text:
Vosk's oldest friend is Thrun, the drummer of the gatherings. They have been friends since boyhood, the loud Brenna and the quiet Kragvar, and when they were both young Vosk rebuilt the stand of the great drum, which had begun to lean. He has kept it sound ever since, and he checks its lashings before every feast whether Thrun asks him to or not. They sit together at every feast, Thrun talking and Vosk listening, and both of them count it the best part of the evening. Since the drum's hide split this spring, Vosk has promised to help fit the new skin when one is found, and has privately begun to wonder whether one will be.

His apprentice for the last four years has been Brakka, Dorrek's daughter, who is eager, restless and would rather carve a new stairway than mend an old bridge. They began in mutual exasperation and have arrived, slowly, at mutual respect. She ties a knot he will trust, which he has told her is rare, and he has learned that the quickest way to get a long job out of her is to say it cannot be done. He has seen her stairway sketches on every flat stone in the quarter. He says nothing about them, which Brakka takes as disapproval. It is not.

Vosk never married. He says the bridges took all the patience he had, and that a wife would have wanted some of it.

docs.title: The gnawed ropes
docs.text:
Twice this season, Vosk and Brakka have climbed out to the far canyon bridge at dawn and found its ropes gnawed half through in the night. Not cut, not frayed by weather: gnawed, by teeth, on the side away from the town. He has spliced both breaks and doubled the lashings, and he has stopped sending the young ones out alone. Earlier this year one of the Kragvar masons working on that same bridge was bitten by something he never saw, and Lessa had to clean the wound with her bitter grey herb.

Vosk does not know what is doing it, and that is the part he cannot stand. He knows wind, rot, frost and the slow fatigue of rope. He does not know this. He has not said in council how worried he is, because he does not like to say anything until he is sure of it, and he is sure of nothing.

docs.title: What he fears
docs.text:
He fears a caravan on the far bridge on the night something finishes the job. He fears he is too old to sit up on it himself, and he suspects he will do it anyway.

A quest could keep watch with Vosk on the far canyon bridge after dark, or carry fresh cable down from the Trading Post before the next gnawing.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Brakka: apprentice
  • Dorrek: cousin
  • Thrun: old friend
  • Hallek: mason under him

docs.title: Yarrek
docs.text:
Goat Herder

Town Midbarium Where Tolmach Camps Role Worker Age Adult Family Tolmach

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Gentle, slow to speak and devoted to his goats, each of which he knows by name.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Yarrek leads the Tolmach goats between the high pastures and the camps, and he knows every one of them by name. He is forty-seven, gentle and slow to speak, and he can go a whole morning on the slopes without saying a word to a person while saying a great many quiet things to goats. The Tolmach say that if a goat ever learned to talk, it would talk like Yarrek: rarely, kindly, and only about the weather and the grass.

docs.title: On the paths
docs.text:
Yarrek was born in a hide tent in the Tolmach camps, the son of a herding family that has walked the same seasonal paths for longer than anyone can count. His parents are both long dead; his father taught him the herd, and his mother taught him to sing to it, which he still does under his breath on the steep stretches. He has never wanted any other work. When the herds go up to the high pastures in spring and down toward the valleys in autumn, Yarrek walks at the back, where the stragglers are, because that is where a herder learns the most.

He married Harra fifteen years ago. She is shrewd, cheerful and loud enough to be heard across the whole Trading Post, where she sells the herds' wool, hides and cheese and drives famously hard bargains with lowland traders. Everyone in the camps thought the match was a joke at first, the loudest woman in the family and its quietest man. They have been proved wrong for fifteen years. Harra talks for both of them, Yarrek listens for both of them, and each thinks the other got the better bargain. Harra's mother, Mabbu, approves of him in her own way, which is to scold him and feed him in the same breath.

docs.title: Kesh
docs.text: Their son Kesh is nine and has, his parents agree, inherited all of the talking and none of the quiet. Yarrek has trusted him with the kids of the herd since last year, and taught him to name every one, as his own father taught him. Kesh's names run to Grumble, Biter and Lady Snort, and Yarrek treats each with perfect seriousness. He is not yet ready to give the boy the grown goats, and he has explained why so gently that Kesh still thinks it unfair.

docs.title: The neighbour at the cisterns
docs.text: The Tolmach camps nearest town draw water from the same terrace cisterns as the Kragvar, and Yarrek's family shares its tanks with Gorra, the cistern keeper. Their arrangement is fair to the bucket and argued over weekly, Gorra counting and Yarrek nodding, and neither would give it up for anything. It was under one of Gorra's cistern lids that Kesh and her son Korrin first met, hiding from the pair of them.

docs.title: The three goats
docs.text:
This year Sennu, the Tolmach chieftain, has kept the herds closer to town than ever because of the monsters in the low valleys. But goats stray. Last month three of Yarrek's goats slipped away in the night and were found two days later, coming back up from the valley on their own. They were wild-eyed and biting, and they have not been right since. They will not eat from his hand. They butt the fence and stare at nothing. Yarrek keeps them penned apart from the herd, and every evening he sits beside their pen and talks to them softly, the way he talks to all his goats, hoping they will calm.

He does not know what happened to them in the valley. He has described them to anyone who will listen, which for Yarrek is a great deal of talking, and he has noticed that Ahvi the song-keeper listened harder than anyone, and then went very quiet.

docs.title: Hopes and fears
docs.text:
Yarrek wants his three goats back as they were. He fears they will not come back, and he fears, more quietly, that they will not be the last. He has started counting the herd twice each evening, as the chieftain does.

A quest could follow the goats' tracks down into the valley to find what they met there, or help Yarrek bring a calming herb up from the far slopes.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Harra: wife
  • Kesh: son
  • Gorra: water-sharing neighbour

docs.title: Zirra
docs.text:
Bowyer

Town Midbarium Where Uskari Rim Role Merchant Age Elder Family Uskari Sells Bows, arrows, climbing ropes and hunting knives

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Precise, sardonic and impossible to flatter; Zirra judges people by how they hold a bow.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Zirra is the bowyer of the Uskari Rim, and every bow the Uskari hunt and patrol with has passed through her hands. She is sixty-three, precise, sardonic and impossible to flatter. She judges people by how they hold a bow, and she will tell you what your grip says about you whether you asked or not. Compliments slide off her like rain off oiled horn. The only praise she trusts is a straight arrow.

docs.title: Big sister
docs.text:
Zirra is the older sister of Hask, the Old One, fifteen years his elder. Their mother died when Hask was six and Zirra twenty-one, and their father, a hunter, was out on the rims more than he was home, so Zirra did much of the work of raising her small, quiet brother. She taught him to string his first bow and told him his stance was a disgrace, which is what she tells everyone. Both their parents are long dead now.

She teases Hask mercilessly in private. She calls him "little brother" in front of nobody, reminds him of every childhood fall and sulk he would like forgotten, and refuses to stand when he enters a room. Let anyone else criticise him, though, and they will find out how sharp a bowyer's tongue can be. She thinks he is the best Old One in living memory and will never say so to his face. Hask, who knows her better than anyone, has never needed her to.

Zirra has never married. She says she has never met a man who held a bow well enough.

docs.title: The bowyer's craft
docs.text:
Zirra's workshop sits on the rim, open to the wind, hung with staves curing in the dry air. She makes bows, arrows, climbing ropes and hunting knives, and sells them to anyone with the coin, but the Uskari patrols come first. Since Tavi doubled the patrols, she has been making bows twice as fast as she likes to, and she has not lowered her standards by a hair, which means she sleeps less. Her climbing ropes are the best on the rim, and the one thing she and Vosk the bridge-master agree on is that nobody else's rope is quite good enough.

Her best staves come from the twisted trees that grow low in the canyon valleys, wood that has fought the wind and the drought for a hundred years and bends without breaking. She used to gather it herself each autumn. The valleys where the best stands grow are now marked on Skarra's map with red, and the patrols cannot spare anyone to walk her down there. Her stock of good wood is lower than it has been in her life.

docs.title: Pupils
docs.text: Zirra has taught many young Uskari the bow, and the pupil she is proudest of is Ketta. When Ketta's mother fell from the rim, Zirra watched the twelve-year-old shoot for an afternoon, told her her stance was a disgrace, and spent the next five years correcting it. When Ketta came home last spring from three years of adventuring, the first thing she did was show Zirra her new bow, and the second was to be told what was wrong with it. Zirra has noticed, as Tavi has, that Ketta goes quiet about one thing. Zirra has not asked. She has made Ketta a new bow instead, the best she has made in years, and left it at Ketta's fire without a word.

docs.title: What she fears
docs.text:
Zirra fears for her brother, who carries four families and sleeps too little. She fears running out of good wood in the very years the rim needs bows most.

A quest could escort Zirra down to the twisted trees in the canyon valleys to cut new staves, or carry a message from her to Hask that she would rather die than deliver in person.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Hask: younger brother
  • Ketta: former pupil

docs.title: Agatha
docs.text:
River Fisher

Town Selsior Where Riverside Role Worker Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Tough, practical and cheerful in any weather. She can gut a fish and an argument in one stroke.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Agatha is thirty-seven, a river fisher of the Riverside, and she is out on the water in any weather, cheerful in all of it. She can gut a fish in one stroke and an argument in another, and people who have watched her do both say the second is quicker. Her boat is small, flat and patched, her hands are hard as rope, and her laugh carries clear across the river to the far bank.

docs.title: Her father's nets
docs.text:
She was born on the river. Her father Osmund has poled the ferry across it since he was a boy, and in the years when the ferry did not keep him busy enough, he fished as well, with a set of heavy nets he had mended so many times that hardly a knot of the first ones is left. Her mother, Edda, died when Agatha was fifteen, and after that it was the two of them, Osmund and his daughter, on the water every day. He taught her to read the river the way he reads it: its colour, its smell, the way it moves before rain. He did it almost entirely without words. Agatha does the talking for both of them now, and she says she has never once misunderstood a nod.

When his hands grew too stiff for the nets, Osmund gave them to her. They are her father's old nets still, and she mends them every evening on the step of the house, the way he did.

docs.title: The market and the family
docs.text:
She sells her catch to her husband, Silas, who keeps a fish stall in the Crown Market and names every fish he sells. They met across that stall, when Agatha came up from the river with a basket of eels and told him his prices were a disgrace, and Silas, who is loud, salty and endlessly cheerful, told her hers were worse. They have been married eleven years and they still argue about prices, loudly and with enormous enjoyment, in front of anyone who happens to be buying.

Their son Robin is a mudlark who combs the bank at low water for treasure. He is muddy, curious and certain that every shiny thing is a lost crown, and Agatha is privately very proud of him. She makes him keep to two rules: never alone at the deep end of the bank, and never after dark.

docs.title: The torn nets
docs.text:
Lately the nets have been coming up torn. Not snagged on a sunken branch, not chewed by a pike, not frayed with age: torn. The rents are long and ragged, sometimes through three or four rows of mesh at once, and they come up empty around the hole, as if the fish had been taken out of the net before the net was taken out of the water. Agatha has fished this river her whole life and knows every fish in it. Whatever is doing this is none of them.

She has not made a fuss. She is practical, and making a fuss does not mend nets. But she has noticed that her father, who has crossed the river after dark all his life, no longer does, and she has noticed that he will not tell her why, and she has quietly moved her own fishing to the shallower water close to the bank. Silas has started hiring guards to ride with the harbour carts because of the monsters on the roads, and over supper, half joking, he has asked her whether the river needs guards too. She told him not to be daft. She has been thinking about it ever since.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Agatha wants her nets to come up whole and full, the way they did when she was a girl. She fears for her father, who is not as young as he behaves, and for Robin, who is braver than he should be at the water's edge.

A quest might begin with Agatha asking someone to watch the deep water with her from the boat one evening, or with a net that comes up holding something that is not a fish.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Silas: husband
  • Osmund: father
  • Robin: son

docs.title: Agnes
docs.text:
Palace Maid

Town Selsior Where Palace Role Service Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Cheerful, nosy and quick on her feet. She hears everything and repeats only half of it.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Agnes is nineteen, a maid of the palace, and she cleans the upper halls: the long gallery, the royal family's rooms, the stairs that nobody but the household ever sees. She is cheerful, nosy and quick on her feet, and she hears everything. She repeats only half of it. Osbert, the Royal Steward, says that is still half too much. Agnes says that if he knew what the other half was, he would thank her.

docs.title: The kitchen girl
docs.text:
She grew up in the palace kitchens, where her father Cuthbert is the royal cook. Her mother, Juliana, who kept the palace's stillroom and made its preserves, died of a winter fever when Agnes was six, and after that Agnes was raised among the pots, under the long table, on a stool by the bread oven, and by the whole kitchen at once. Cuthbert is loud, red-faced and generous; he shouts at the pots and sings to the bread, and Agnes learned to talk over both before she could reach the table. She also learned that a kitchen is the best place in any house to hear things. Everything comes through it in the end: the trays, the messengers, the gossip and the dirty boots.

At fourteen, five years ago, she asked Osbert for a place in the household rather than the kitchen. Cuthbert was hurt for about a day and then proud for the rest of the year. Osbert started her on the lower corridors, and two years ago, after watching her for three years without a word of praise, he gave her the upper halls. Agnes treasures this more than she lets him see, because she knows Osbert's praise is so rare that the staff count it.

docs.title: The upper halls
docs.text:
Her days start early and run at a trot. Fires laid, grates swept, beds made, floors polished, linen counted against the list Osbert checks, and all of it done without being seen, which is a palace maid's whole art. She has a friend in Peterkin, the page, who runs everywhere and tells her everything he carries, and she trades him news for biscuits from her father's kitchen. Sybil, the wardrobe mistress, is the one person in the palace Agnes cannot get a single story out of, and Agnes has decided to regard this as a challenge rather than a defeat.

She makes Princess Elinor's bed every morning. And every morning, by the time she gets there, the princess is back in it, or nearly, looking innocent, and there are boots by the door with fresh mud on them.

docs.title: The boots
docs.text:
Agnes noticed the boots in the autumn. She has been noticing them ever since. The mud is not garden mud; she has cleaned enough boots in her life to know the difference. It is the mud of a yard where a great many feet go round and round on the same ground. She has worked out that the princess goes out before dawn and comes back before breakfast, and she has three theories about why, and she likes all of them: a sweetheart, a secret, or a horse. She has told no one. Not her father, not Peterkin, not Osbert. Yet.

She has not decided why she is keeping quiet. Partly it is that she likes the princess, who has always been kind to her and has never once looked through her. Partly it is that a secret this good is worth more kept than spent. And partly, though she would not admit it, it is that she suspects Osbert already knows, and she would very much like to know what he is going to do about it before she does anything at all.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Agnes wants to be trusted with something that matters, and she wants, one day, to be the person in the palace who knows everything, as Osbert does now. What she fears is the day she repeats the wrong half.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might begin with Agnes finding something in the upper halls that should not be there, and needing someone from outside the palace to find out where it came from. Or it might begin with the princess's boots one morning not coming back at all.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Osbert: employer
  • Cuthbert: father

docs.title: Alaric
docs.text:
Young Prince

Town Selsior Where Palace Role Child Age Child

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Curious, chatty and always muddy. He asks why about everything and remembers every answer.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Alaric is nine years old, the younger child of Queen Aveline and Leofric, and very possibly the muddiest person ever to live in the palace. His tutors can usually find him by following the footprints. They lead, most days, either to the gardens or to the kitchens, and only rarely to the schoolroom where he is supposed to be.

docs.title: Why, why and why
docs.text:
Alaric asks why about everything. Why the Great Bell rings only for a crown. Why beetles have six legs and spiders eight. Why the cook sings to bread but shouts at soup. Why some envoys want the windows open and others want them shut. The remarkable thing is not the asking but that he remembers every answer, word for word, along with who gave it and whether they looked as if they believed it. His tutors find this exhausting. His father finds it delightful, and has been known to answer a single question about a road with a half-hour lecture and a sketch, which Alaric then keeps.

He collects three things: beetles, keys and rumours. The beetles live in a row of jars on his windowsill, each labelled in large, uneven letters. The keys come from everywhere: old ones from the bottoms of drawers, rusted ones dug out of flowerbeds, one that Cuthbert swears used to open a larder nobody can now find. He has never yet found the locks that most of them fit, and he is certain this is only a matter of time. The rumours he keeps in his head, and he brings the best of them to his mother along with the best of the beetles. Queen Aveline takes both seriously, and Alaric has noticed that she sometimes acts on the rumours.

docs.title: Friends in the garden and on the stairs
docs.text:
His two great friends are Godwin and Peterkin. Godwin, the old gardener, has tended the palace gardens since the old king's day, and he lets Alaric dig, water and ask questions as long as he is gentle with the roses. Godwin taught him which beetles help a garden and which ones eat it, and lately the two of them have been watching the wild bees, which Godwin says have turned mean this year. Alaric wants to know why, and for once nobody can tell him.

Peterkin, the palace page, is a little older and never walks anywhere. When he is not carrying messages, he and Alaric race the clock tower bells from the cellars to the roof, or take turns listening at doors in the name of practice. Peterkin is the only person Alaric has told about the passage.

docs.title: The secret passage
docs.text: Alaric is sure there is a secret passage behind the tapestries in the throne hall. He has evidence: a draught that moves the bottom of one tapestry when every door is shut, a hollow sound when he knocks on one stretch of wall, and a key in his collection that fits nothing else in the palace. Osbert, the steward, who knows where every spoon and every secret is kept, will neither confirm nor deny it, and to Alaric that is the best evidence of all.

docs.title: His sister
docs.text: Alaric adores Elinor and is a little afraid of her. He has noticed that she is gone from her room some mornings before even Peterkin is awake, and she has told him she goes riding. He believes her, mostly. He has filed it away with everything else.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Alaric wants to know things, all things, preferably first. He fears very little except being told he is too young to be told, and the nights when his mother does not sleep, which he has noticed too.

A quest might begin with one of his keys turning out to fit something important, or with a rumour he picked up in the kitchens that nobody else has heard yet.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Aveline: mother
  • Leofric: father
  • Elinor: sister
  • Godwin: gardening friend
  • Peterkin: friend

docs.title: Aldith
docs.text:
Herb Wife of the Riverside

Town Selsior Where Riverside Role Healer Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Earthy, warm and stubborn about old remedies. She swears by river mint for everything.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Aldith is seventy-two, the herb wife of the Riverside, and if you come to her door with a cough, a burn, a sprained wrist or a broken heart, she will give you river mint for it. She will give you other things as well, and some of them will be very good, but the river mint comes first. She is earthy, warm and stubborn about old remedies, and she has been treating the riverside folk from the same low cottage on the bank for most of her life.

docs.title: The garden on the bank
docs.text:
She was born in that cottage. Her mother, Elfrida, was the herb wife of the Riverside before her, and Aldith grew up among the drying racks, learning to tell feverfew from chamomile by the smell of her fingers. The garden behind the cottage runs right down to the water, and the best of it is the mint bed at the bottom, where the river laps at the roots in spring. Elfrida swore by that mint. Aldith swears by it louder. Her mother has been dead some thirty years, and Aldith has kept the garden exactly as she left it, except for the parts she has improved, which she will show you whether you ask or not.

Her brother Ansel went the other way. When they were young he crossed the city to study healing in the Scholars' Quarter, and he has served the palace as its physician for decades now, treating a queen and a scullery boy with the same cold hands. Aldith stayed on the river. Aldith never married; she says she had a garden to marry and it has never once disappointed her.

docs.title: Brother and sister
docs.text: The two of them argue about whose cures work best, cheerfully and at the tops of their voices, which suits them both, because Ansel is slightly deaf and Aldith was never quiet in her life. He says her mint is a superstition with a pleasant smell. She says his tinctures are mint with a Scholars' Quarter price. Neither of them will admit that they swap recipes in secret. Every so often a folded paper in Ansel's neat hand turns up tucked into her basket, and every so often a jar of Aldith's salve finds its way into the palace's medicine chest, unlabelled, and is used up faster than anything else in it.

docs.title: The riverside's healer
docs.text:
Her patients are the people of the river: fishers, ferrymen, millers, dyers, bargehands and their children. She knows them all from birth. She rubs a mint and comfrey salve into Osmund's stiff hands, which no longer manage the nets, and he nods his thanks, which from Osmund is a speech. She doses Robin's coughs and pretends not to notice the mud. Her oldest friend is Edwina, the midwife of the old quarters, who is as blunt as Aldith is warm; the two of them have shared patients, teapots and opinions for fifty years, and they still meet on Aldith's bench whenever Edwina can be spared.

Lately the river has been bringing her different work. She has seen cuts that no hook or net made, and a bargehand with a bruise on his leg in the shape of something that gripped him. Agatha's nets come up torn, and old Osmund will not cross after dark and will not say why. Aldith has begun keeping notes of her own, in a cheap book and a cramped hand, the way she knows her brother keeps his notes on the claw wounds that come to the palace. She has not told him. She suspects he would be pleased, and she is not ready for that.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Aldith wants to hand on the garden. She has no child to take it, and she has not yet found anyone patient enough to learn that mint must be cut in the morning and never in the rain. What she fears is the river itself changing: the water her mother's mint has drunk for seventy years turning into something she does not recognise.

A quest might begin with the mint bed at the bottom of the garden wilting at the water's edge for no reason Aldith can find, or with Ansel sending her, for the first time, a question rather than a recipe: a wound he cannot name, and a request to know whether the river has seen it too.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Ansel: brother
  • Edwina: old friend

docs.title: Ansel
docs.text:
Palace Physician

Town Selsior Where Palace Role Healer Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Calm, gentle and slightly deaf. He treats a queen and a scullery boy with the same cold hands.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Ansel is seventy-five, the Palace Physician, and he treats a queen and a scullery boy with the same cold hands. He warms them first, every time, on a little copper pan of water by his fire, and they are still cold, and his patients have stopped minding. He is calm, gentle and slightly deaf in his left ear, so that he tilts his head toward you as you speak, which makes everyone feel listened to and is, in fact, the only reason he hears them. He has served the palace for decades and has never once hurried at a bedside.

docs.title: The herb wife's son
docs.text:
He was born in the low cottage on the Riverside bank where his sister Aldith still lives, three years before her. Their mother, Elfrida, was the herb wife of the Riverside, and Ansel grew up among her drying racks with river mint under his fingernails. He loved the work and hated the guessing in it. He wanted to know why the mint worked, not only that it did, and at sixteen he crossed the city to study healing in the Scholars' Quarter, which Elfrida regarded as a kind of desertion and Aldith regarded as an excellent joke.

He studied and then practised in the Quarter until he was thirty, when he came to the palace as assistant to Master Corbin, the old king's physician. Corbin, long dead now, taught him that a physician's first duty is to be calm in the room, and that the second is to write everything down. Ansel took over the post when Corbin died, thirty-seven years ago, and has kept it through the rest of King Bertram's reign and all of Queen Aveline's. He sat with the old king through his last illness. He attended the births of both the royal children, and he set the princess's arm when she fell off a pony at seven, and has privately watched her collect bruises ever since with a professional interest he keeps to himself.

docs.title: The palace and the river
docs.text:
His rooms are at the bottom of a stair near the palace kitchens, so that the kitchen boys can reach him quickly with their burns. He treats the household, the Guard and anyone else who comes to the door. For many years his medicines came from the palace stillroom, kept by Juliana, Cuthbert's wife; when she died of a winter fever thirteen years ago he was with her, and he has never forgiven himself for the fever, though Cuthbert has never once blamed him.

He and Aldith argue about whose cures work best, cheerfully and at the tops of their voices, which suits his ear. He calls her mint a superstition with a pleasant smell. She calls his tinctures mint with a Scholars' Quarter price. Neither will admit that they swap recipes in secret. Every so often Ansel tucks a folded paper of notes into her basket when she is not looking, and every so often an unlabelled jar of her salve appears in the palace medicine chest. He tells his assistants it is a preparation of his own. It is used up faster than anything else on the shelf.

docs.title: The notes
docs.text:
Ansel writes everything down, as Corbin taught him. For thirty years he has kept a ledger of every wound that comes through his door: what it was, how deep, how it healed. For most of those years the ledger was burns, falls and broken fingers. Now, every season, more guards come to him with claw wounds and bites, and the ledger has grown a second volume just for them. He measures each wound, draws its shape to scale and notes what the guard says bit them, and where on the road it happened. Some of the shapes he can match to beasts he knows. More of them, lately, he cannot: claws spaced wrongly for any animal in the old books, a bite that closed from too many sides.

He does not know that Aldith has started keeping notes of her own on the river's wounds. If he did, he would be delighted, and very curious, and she knows it.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Ansel wants to understand what is out there from the marks it leaves, because a physician who understands a wound can treat it. What he fears is the day he opens his ledger to a wound he has no word for at all, and the guard on his table is one he once treated for a scraped knee.

A quest might begin with Ansel asking someone to carry a question, not a recipe, down to his sister on the river, or with him needing a fresh specimen of a creature from the roads, dead and whole, so that he can match it to the drawings in his ledger.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Aldith: sister

docs.title: Aubrey
docs.text:
Old Grand Swordmaster

Town Selsior Where Knights' Court Role Guard Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Wry, slow-moving and still frighteningly quick with a blade. He naps in the sun and wakes when a recruit holds a sword wrong.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Aubrey is seventy-six, the oldest Grand Swordmaster in the Royal Guard, and most mornings you will find him asleep. He has a bench against the warm south wall of the Knights' Court practice yard, and he sits on it with his hat over his eyes and his hands folded on his stomach, and he snores. He is wry, slow-moving and still frighteningly quick with a blade. Recruits who think he is asleep learn otherwise the first time they hold a sword wrong in his hearing, because he will say, from under the hat and without moving, "Your wrist is lying to you," and he will be right.

docs.title: Fifty-eight years at the Court
docs.text:
He came to the Knights' Court at eighteen, in the year King Bertram was crowned, a carpenter's son from the inner streets with long arms and no patience. He has said many times that he was the worst recruit of his intake and the only one too stubborn to leave. He earned the Swordsman's rank, then the Swordmaster's, and at thirty-five he passed the trial for Grand Swordmaster, the youngest in the Guard then. For the next three decades he was the finest blade at the Court and taught most of the warriors who now hold rank in it.

He was already an old Grand Swordmaster when Queen Aveline made her alliance with Cavelor, and he went down the Upper Stair with the other serving Swordmasters and Grand Swordmasters to swear the new oath in the Oath Hall. He complained about his knees the whole way down and never once about the oath.

He never married. He says the Court was his house and the recruits were noisy enough to count as children. He still keeps his old room off the cloister, and Helewise, the quartermaster, keeps his name on the roll because nobody has ever dared take it off.

docs.title: Rhys
docs.text:
Twenty-two years ago a young man called Rhys came to the Court with a borrowed sword and much more confidence than skill. Aubrey watched him swing for about a minute and told him he fought like a man chopping firewood. Rhys spent the next two years learning to stop, and Aubrey has never told him that he was the most promising recruit the old man had seen in twenty years. The spring after Rhys arrived, a young Uskari warrior came down from the highlands to train for a season, and Aubrey, who thought both of them were too fierce for their own good, paired them so they would wear each other down. They did not. They fought eighty evening bouts and scratched the tally on a post, forty-one to thirty-nine, and Aubrey still walks past that post on his way to his bench and taps it.

He gave up teaching nine years ago, a year after Rhys passed the Grand Swordmaster's trial, because he said he had seen what he was waiting for. When Rhys became Captain, Aubrey was the first to salute him and the last to stop calling him "boy". Rhys still listens to him with the patience of a pupil who owes his teacher everything, which Aubrey finds touching and slightly suspicious.

docs.title: The test
docs.text:
The old books name one rank beyond the Grand Swordmaster: the Sword Saint, earned by very few. Nobody alive at the Court has met one. Rhys sets that test as the old test, admitting he passes on something older than himself, and the books disagree about what it is. Tobe, one of this spring's recruits, has read six accounts of it, all different, and has started bringing them to Aubrey's bench. Aubrey pretends to be asleep through most of them.

He has spent his retirement looking for the real test. He has read every drill book in the Court's library, most of the sword books in the Academy's great library, and a great many crumbling papers nobody else wanted. Last autumn, in a chest of old Guard drill books that the storeroom was about to throw out, he found a single loose leaf of very old vellum, folded inside a cover where it did not belong. It is in an old hand, half faded, and it describes, he says, a part of the Sword Saint's test. He has shown it to nobody, not even Rhys. He will say only that it is not what anyone expected, and that it is not a fight with another swordsman, and he will not say how he knows the page is real. Rhys suspects that it is.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Aubrey wants to see one Sword Saint before he dies. He would prefer it to be Rhys, and he would settle for anyone holding their wrist right. What he fears is that the page is real, that the test it describes cannot be passed in an age of monsters, and that he will be the one to have to say so.

A quest might begin with Aubrey asking a traveller to find the rest of the book his page was torn from, or with him waking on his bench one morning, very suddenly, because someone he has never seen before is holding a sword in a way he last saw described in old ink.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Rhys: former pupil

docs.title: Avice
docs.text:
Recruit

Town Selsior Where Knights' Court Role Guard Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Fierce, proud and short with words. She trains harder when anyone is watching.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Avice is eighteen, a recruit of the Royal Guard, and she does not waste words. Ask her where she comes from and she says "the highlands." Ask her why she came and she says "the trials." Ask her what she wants and she says "Swordsman," and then she goes back to her drills, because she has already talked for longer than she likes.

docs.title: Down from the highlands
docs.text:
She grew up in the high dry country of Midbarium, among herders who move their flocks between the canyon pastures with the seasons. Her family is still there, a long way off, and they write to her rarely and play no part in her life at the Court. She learned early that the highlands respect what you can do, not what you say about it, and she has never seen any reason to change her mind.

This spring she walked to the capital. Not rode, not caught a cart: walked, for many days, down out of the highlands and along the roads to Selsior, with a pack on her back and a stick she cut for herself, because she wanted to arrive having already done something hard. She came through the gate dusty and footsore, asked the way to the Knights' Court, and stood in line with the other hopefuls for the Guard's trials. She passed. She was not surprised. She was annoyed that it had been easier than the walk.

docs.title: The fiercest of her year
docs.text:
She came in with the same intake as Pim and Tobe, and she means to be the first of that year to earn the Swordsman's rank. She is fierce, proud and very good, and she trains harder when anyone is watching, because she would rather be seen working than be seen failing. Pim has made it his strategy to watch her as often as possible, which means, though he has not worked this out, that Avice now trains hard nearly all the time. She has not worked out whether he is a rival or a friend. She has decided it does not matter, as long as she stays ahead of him.

Drill Sergeant Bertrand bellows at her less than at the others, and she minds this. She suspects it is because he thinks she does not need it, and she would like to prove him right in front of everyone. Captain Rhys says almost nothing to her, which she takes as a compliment.

Tobe she treats with a sort of impatient fairness. She once watched him miss the third cut four times running and told him what was wrong in five words: "Your back foot is lying." She was right, and she knew she was right, and she walked off before he could answer. She did not want thanks. She wanted the third cut done properly in her year.

docs.title: The stranger at dawn
docs.text: Avice comes to the practice yard earlier than any other recruit, and so she has seen what most of them have not: a cloaked stranger who trains at dawn with Rowena, the Swordmaster, before the drill bell. Avice does not know who it is. She has noticed only one thing, and she has noticed it very precisely: the stranger holds a sword like someone raised with fine manners, with a straight back and a polite grip that the drills have not yet beaten out of them. She has told nobody. It is not her business, she says, and besides, whoever it is will have to come to the trials in the end, and she would like to meet them there.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Avice wants the Swordsman's rank, then the next, then the next. She has watched what the wilds have started doing to herds in the highlands, and she wants to be the kind of sword that stands between a flock and whatever comes out of the canyons. What she fears is walking home without a rank. She has already decided she will not.

A quest might begin with Avice asking someone from outside the Court to spar with her where no recruit can watch, or with her following the cloaked stranger home one morning, purely to see which way they go.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Rhys: captain
  • Pim: rival

docs.title: Aylwin
docs.text:
Road Patrol Guard

Town Selsior Where Knights' Court Role Guard Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Brave, earnest and easily embarrassed. He writes poems he never shows anyone.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Aylwin is nineteen, a guard of the road patrol, and he blushes so easily that the older riders have made a game of it. He is brave, earnest and very good with a horse, and he has fought monsters on the royal roads without flinching.
