Ask him whether he writes poetry, though, and he will go red to the ears and change the subject. He does. He has never shown a line of it to anyone.

docs.title: Raised in the stables
docs.text:
Aylwin grew up above the Guard stables at the Knights' Court. His parents drowned when a river barge overturned in a spring flood when he was four, and his grandfather Wystan, the stablemaster, took him in. Wystan has kept the Guard's horses for forty years, grumbling at people and gentle with animals, and he raised his grandson much the way he raises a foal: patiently, with few words and a great deal of mucking out. Aylwin learned to ride before he could read, and he learned from Wystan to trust a horse's opinion of a stranger. He trusts it still.

He joined the Guard at seventeen and was put on the road patrol last year, under Lieutenant Edric. He loves it. He loves the dawn rides out of the Court, the long roads, the towns at the end of them and the way the whole patrol comes back in together at dusk. He even loves Edric's jokes, which nobody else admits to.

docs.title: The boars
docs.text: Earlier this spring, on the road to Kaldemor, a pack of wild boars came out of the trees at the patrol, more of them and wilder than any boar has a right to be. Aylwin's horse stood when others shied, and Aylwin stood with it, and between them they held the road while the rest of the patrol turned. He tells the story as if it were funny, mostly about how a boar ate his hat. Edric tells it differently, and so does Wystan, who says that the horses come back from the roads these days jumpy and wild-eyed, and who looked his grandson over very carefully that evening without saying anything at all.

docs.title: The princess
docs.text:
Elinor has been coming down to the Guard stables to see the horses since she was small. She and Aylwin grew up nodding to each other across the yard, then talking, then talking for far longer than anyone talks about horses. Somewhere along the way they fell for each other. Neither of them has told anyone, and both of them are sure nobody knows.

Aylwin also knows the other thing. On the first morning a cloaked stranger came to train at dawn with Rowena, Aylwin, saddling up for patrol, knew her by the way she walked across the yard. He has never said a word about it, to her or to anyone else, and he never will. But he worries. He knows what the roads are like now, and he knows Elinor wants to ride them, and he cannot decide whether he is more proud of her or more afraid.

docs.title: The poems
docs.text: The poems are mostly about her. Some are about the roads, the light over the Greenwood at dawn and the sound the patrol makes coming home. He keeps them in a bundle wrapped in oilcloth under a loose board in the hayloft, where he thinks no one will ever look. He has written one he thinks is good, and he has spent most of the spring deciding whether to give it to her.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Aylwin wants to be a guard Wystan can be proud of and a man Elinor deserves, and he thinks, earnestly, that these are probably the same thing. What he fears is the day the patrol meets something worse than boars, and he is not there to stand in front of it, or he is.

A quest might begin with Aylwin's bundle of poems going missing from the hayloft, or with him needing someone to carry a message to the palace that he cannot carry himself.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Edric: lieutenant
  • Wystan: grandfather
  • Elinor: sweetheart

docs.title: Baldwin
docs.text:
Lamplighter

Town Selsior Where Plaza Role Worker Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Quiet, unhurried and fond of the dark hours. He knows every lamp in the city by its flicker.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Baldwin is sixty-eight, the lamplighter of the plaza, and he is the last person in Selsior to go to bed and very nearly the first to see the stars come out. Every evening at dusk he crosses the plaza with his ladder over one shoulder, his oil can in one hand and his long brass taper in the other, and one by one the lamps around the Great Bell come alight behind him. He does not hurry. He has never hurried in his life, and the lamps, he says, have never minded waiting.

docs.title: Fifty years of dusk
docs.text:
He took up the work at eighteen, fifty years ago, as the helper of an old lamplighter called Odo, who carried the ladder for a season before he let Baldwin touch a wick. Odo taught him that every lamp has its own temper: this one smokes if you trim it short, that one gutters in an east wind, the one by the palace steps burns blue for no reason anyone has ever found. Odo has been dead for many years. Baldwin still trims the palace-steps lamp the way Odo showed him and still does not know why it burns blue.

He knows every lamp in the city by its flicker. Not only the plaza's: when the plaza is lit he takes the long way home, through the old quarters, and lights more as he goes, down the winding streets and under the skywalks, so that by the time he reaches his own narrow house near the gate end of the city he has left a thread of light behind him through half of Selsior. The children of the old quarters know that when Baldwin's lamps are lit, Winifred will be out on her doorstep with a story, and they run ahead of him to get there first.

docs.title: The people of the dark hours
docs.text:
He is quiet, unhurried and fond of the dark hours, and he has the dark hours' friends. Ida of the night watch passes him most nights in the old quarters with her lantern and her stick, and the two of them exchange a nod and, on a long night, a sentence. Gilbert the candlemaker supplies his oil and wicks and hums while he measures them out; lately Gilbert's bees have been short-tempered, and Baldwin, who has noticed that the night moths behave oddly too, has said so, once, and left it at that.

His brother Hugh is the Warden of the Great Bell, and so the two of them share the plaza: Hugh by day, polishing the bell's dais every morning, and Baldwin by dusk, lighting the lamps around it while Mirabel dances and Fulke plays. Baldwin has listened to his brother and the dancer argue about whether the Bell hums for years. He has never taken a side. He has noticed, on still evenings, that Hugh goes very quiet when the light fails, and he has never asked him why. They are brothers; some things you leave lit and walk past.

Baldwin never married. He says he has a few hundred lamps to look after and that is family enough.

docs.title: The lamps by the gate
docs.text: Lately Baldwin has started leaving extra lamps burning near the city gate. Nobody asked him to. He buys the oil from Gilbert out of his own pocket, sets the lamps on the last stretch of the road inside the gate and in the gatehouse's shadow, and lights them on his way home. He says it is for travellers who come in late, and it is. He does not say the rest of it, which is that he has spent fifty years watching the dark, and he has started to think the dark beyond the gate is not as empty as it used to be. Just in case, he says, and lights another.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Baldwin wants to find someone to carry the ladder, as he once carried Odo's. What he fears is a night when he reaches the gate and the lamps he left burning have been put out.

A quest might begin with one of the plaza lamps refusing to stay lit, the first in fifty years, or with Baldwin asking a traveller to walk the gate road with him after dark, just to see what is out there just past the light.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Hugh: brother
  • Gilbert: supplier

docs.title: Bartholomew
docs.text:
Master of the Royal Academy

Town Selsior Where Scholars' Quarter Role Scholar Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Grandfatherly, rambling and sharp as a tack beneath it. He answers questions with better questions.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Bartholomew is seventy-seven, the Master of the Royal Academy, and if you ask him a question he will answer it with a better one. He is grandfatherly, rambling and sharp as a tack beneath it. He will begin to tell you about the weather, wander through a story about a goat he knew as a boy and a disagreement he had with a stargazer in his forties, and arrive, quite suddenly, at the exact thing you were trying not to think about.

docs.title: A shepherd's boy among the Magicians
docs.text:
He did not grow up among books. He was a shepherd's son from the open downs beyond the capital, and he came to Selsior at fourteen with a letter from a village schoolteacher and no idea what an academy was. The Royal Academy was founded by the city's first Magicians, and in those days it still felt to a farm boy like a house full of old wizards who all knew something he did not. He decided, within a week, that the way to catch up was to ask them all questions. He has never stopped.

He studied there for ten years and began teaching at twenty-four. He was a teacher for most of his life before the other masters made him Master of the Academy, twenty-one years ago, and he still teaches a class every season, because he says a Master who does not teach is just a man with a large office. His office is indeed large, and it is buried under papers, and somewhere in it is a chair for visitors that nobody has found in years.

docs.title: The Academy's pride
docs.text:
He welcomes students from every town on Veligor and is fiercely proud that no two of them think alike. He has had highland students who argue with their fists, forest students who argue in riddles, harbour students who argue with the tide tables and Urbanograd students who argue with everything. He wants all of them. He says the Academy was made by people who once fought a war over whose way of thinking was right, and that the least it can do now is to keep every way of thinking in one building and make them eat lunch together.

He likes nothing better than a student who answers back. When Mariota's father died and the bindery went to pay his debts, Bartholomew made sure she kept the place she had won with an essay that argued with its own examiners. He has taken a long, patient interest in Thomasin, the historian, who is his protegee and who hates a good story that is not true, and he has watched with pleasure as she became the person the Academy sends for when someone wants to know what really happened in the Balrog War. He has also watched, with less pleasure, how often she is being asked.

docs.title: Morwen
docs.text: His oldest friend at the Academy is Morwen, who teaches its young mages. He has known her since she came to teach there twenty-eight years ago, a young teacher with very firm opinions, and the two of them have argued over supper about once a week ever since. She says he answers her questions with better questions and that it is infuriating. He says it is the only way to stop her answering them herself before she has finished asking. They would each defend the other to the death, and both of them know it.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Bartholomew wants the Academy to keep asking questions, even now, when the kingdom wants answers. He knows the roads are worse every season. He knows Morwen's work on the old seal-craft is no longer only history, and that Theobald's star charts and Mariota's reading of them are looking for something they have not yet named. What he fears is the day someone from the palace comes to the Academy and asks it for an answer it does not have, and his students, who have never once agreed with each other, all agree to go and find it.

A quest might begin with Bartholomew asking someone to deliver a question, not a letter, to a scholar in another town, or with a student who has stopped coming to class and left behind a notebook the Master would very much like to read.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Morwen: old friend
  • Thomasin: protegee

docs.title: Benedict
docs.text:
Head Librarian

Town Selsior Where Scholars' Quarter Role Scholar Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Hushed, fussy and passionately helpful. He can find any book except the one he lost himself.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Benedict is seventy-three, Head Librarian of the Royal Academy, and he can find any book in the great library in less time than it takes you to describe it. Any book, that is, except one. He is hushed, fussy and passionately helpful, and he moves between the stacks in soft shoes, straightening spines as he passes, like a shepherd counting sheep in the dark.

docs.title: A life among the shelves
docs.text:
He came to the library as a boy to fetch and shelve, and he has hardly left it since. He learned the catalogue before he learned the city, and by the time he was thirty he could tell you not only where a book was but who had last borrowed it, what they had spilled on it and whether they had bent the corners. He has been Head Librarian for thirty years. The great library is the Academy's oldest treasure, gathered over centuries from all four peoples: Magician treatises, Commons almanacs, Savage songs written down by people who were not supposed to write them down, and the long, dry chronicles of the Aristocrat families.

He also teaches. For decades Benedict has trained the copyists and scribes the palace needs, in a cold room at the back of the library with good north light, and he taught half the scribes now working in the palace to hold a pen properly. Petronella, the Royal Scribe, was the best pupil he ever had. She still sends him her finest pages to look at, and he still finds one letter on each to correct, which they both enjoy.

docs.title: Ermengarde
docs.text:
His sister Ermengarde mends and binds the Academy's books in a tiny shop beside the library, so close that Benedict can hear her laughing at her own jokes through the wall. She is placid where he is fussy, and fond of terrible puns, and she smells of glue and old leather. Every damaged book in the library goes through her hands, and every book comes back better, with a pun about it that Benedict pretends not to hear. They have worked side by side for most of their lives. He would not trust anyone else to touch a spine.

Ranulf the bookbinder, who did the Academy's larger binding work, was a friend of them both. When he died two winters ago and his bindery was sold, Benedict gave Ranulf's boy Tobe work fetching and shelving in the library, the same work Benedict had done as a boy. Tobe read every book on swordsmanship in the place and then went off to the Knights' Court with all of them in his head. Benedict disapproves of swords and was secretly rather proud.

docs.title: The missing volume
docs.text:
The book Benedict cannot find is a volume of the Aristocrat war chronicles, the long record the old Aristocrat families kept of the Balrog War. The library holds the rest of the set, and they are full of armies, marches and burned towns, and strangely thin on the thing that burned them. Benedict has always believed the missing volume fills some of that gap. He believes it because he read the first pages of it himself, eighteen years ago, at a desk by the window, and then was called away, and when he came back it was gone.

He lost it himself. That is the part he cannot bear. He has searched every shelf in the library at least once a year since, in order, with a list, and he has questioned every reader who was in the building that day, most of whom no longer remember being born. Thomasin, the historian, asks him about it more often than she used to, and lately she asks with a look he does not like.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Benedict wants the book back on its shelf before he dies, and then he wants to read it to the end. What he fears is that he has spent eighteen years looking in the right building for something that left it the same afternoon.

A quest might begin with a page in the right hand turning up somewhere it should not be, or with Benedict asking a traveller to look, discreetly, through the bookstalls and private libraries of another town for a binding he can describe down to the last stitch.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Petronella: former pupil
  • Ermengarde: sister

docs.title: Bennet
docs.text:
Boatwright

Town Selsior Where Riverside Role Craftsman Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Patient, wry and proud of his joinery. He can tell a boat's age by knocking on it.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Bennet is forty-nine, the boatwright of the Riverside, and he can tell how old a boat is by knocking on it. He raps the hull twice with a knuckle, listens with his head on one side, and says "eleven years, oak, mended badly once at the stern," and then he goes and looks at the stern to prove it. He is patient, wry and proud of his joinery, and he believes that most of the trouble in the world comes from people who will not wait for glue to set.

docs.title: The yard
docs.text:
His boatyard sits on the Riverside bank below the city bridge, a long slope of mud, timber stacks and sawdust running down to a slipway, with a shed at the top that smells of pitch and wet oak all year round. He lives in a loft over the shed. He learned the trade there, as a boy of twelve, from old Ebbe, the boatwright who had the yard before him, who never said a word more than he needed and could cut a joint so tight that water gave up trying. Ebbe left Bennet the yard when he died, twenty-four years ago. Bennet has never married. He says a boatwright is already married to the river, and the river is a demanding wife who leaks.

He builds and mends everything that floats on the city's stretch of the river: fishing skiffs, ferry planking, mill punts, and the big flat-bottomed barges that carry grain and stone and timber into Selsior. When Osmund's ferry needs a plank, Bennet fits it. When Agatha's skiff springs a seam, Bennet caulks it and charges her in eels.

docs.title: Lucan
docs.text: His oldest friend is Lucan, the bargemaster, who booms where Bennet murmurs and bets where Bennet measures. Bennet built two of Lucan's three barges and mends all of them, and he can tell from the sound of Lucan's voice coming round the bend whether a barge has hit something. They have a standing wager about which of them will retire first. It is older than either of them will admit, and the stake has grown so large and so strange over the years, with additions made in taverns and amendments made at weddings, that neither can now remember what it is. Bennet suspects it includes a goat.

docs.title: The fast barge
docs.text:
Bennet is designing a faster barge for the river trade. Since the roads turned dangerous, merchants send their goods by water, and the river has never been busier; a barge that runs faster carries more in a season and spends less of it on the water. That is what Bennet tells the merchants. The design is longer and narrower than any barge on the river, with a keel he has argued about with himself for a whole winter, and the half-built hull stands on the slipway under a tarpaulin.

The trouble is that he needs someone brave enough to take it out and run it hard. Lucan has said, loudly and in front of witnesses, that he will happily bet on Bennet's barge but will not be standing on it, and Bennet reminds him of this roughly every time they meet. The bargehands will not volunteer either. They are tired, and some of them are frightened, and one of them came out of the river last season with a bruise in the shape of a grip.

There is another reason for the speed, and Bennet keeps it to himself. Tristan, Lucan's scout, has started asking Lucan to pass one stretch of the river at speed, without saying why. Bennet has known Tristan since he was a boy lying in the reeds, and he knows the scout does not ask for things lightly. So when Tristan came down to the yard one evening this spring and stood a long while looking at the half-built hull without a word, Bennet did not ask him anything. He simply took the drawings back to his bench and made the keel a little deeper.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Bennet wants to see his barge launched, run flat out on the river and come home dry. He would also like to win the wager, whatever it is. What he fears is building the fastest boat on the river and finding that it still is not fast enough.

A quest might begin with Bennet needing seasoned timber from upriver, past the quarries, where the bargehands no longer like to go, or with him needing a crew, any crew, brave enough to test the new barge on its first run.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Lucan: friend

docs.title: Bertrand
docs.text:
Drill Sergeant

Town Selsior Where Knights' Court Role Guard Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Gruff, bellowing and fond of every recruit he shouts at. He has a voice that could crack a shield.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Bertrand is fifty-one, Drill Sergeant of the Royal Guard, and the first sound most recruits hear in the morning. It is not the drill bell. It is Bertrand, arriving at the practice yard of the Knights' Court before dawn and telling the barracks, at a volume that could crack a shield, that the day has started without them. He is gruff, bellowing and fond of every single recruit he shouts at, and he swears he can turn anyone into a guard given a year and enough porridge.

docs.title: A guard all his life
docs.text:
He joined the Guard at eighteen, thirty-three years ago, a big, loud youth from the Crown Market's back streets whose late father had unloaded carts there all his life. He was never the finest sword in the Court, and he knew it, but he had a gift nobody else had: he could see exactly what was going wrong in another person's feet and tell them in a voice they could not ignore. He walked patrols, stood at the gate and served on the walls for eighteen years, and fifteen years ago the Court gave him the dawn drills. He has had them ever since and has never once wanted a higher post.

He is married to Helewise, the Guard's quartermaster, who feeds, arms and clothes the whole Guard and knows how many arrows it has to the last fletching. They have been married nineteen years. They met over porridge: he was demanding more for his recruits, and she was explaining, to the last spoonful, exactly how much there was. She won. She usually does. They have no children, and Bertrand says that with a few hundred recruits through the yard, he has enough.

docs.title: The list
docs.text:
He keeps a list of every recruit he has trained. It started on a single sheet and is now three thick books, on the shelf above his bed, with more than six hundred names in his large, square hand. Beside each name is the date they came through the gate of the Court, and the rank they earned, and where they went.

Every week, when the patrol reports come in, Bertrand reads them before supper and checks the names in them against his list. Helewise knows not to talk to him while he does it. When a name comes up among the hurt, he makes a small mark in the margin and goes quiet for the rest of the evening, and the next morning he drills his recruits harder. There are more marks every season, and Bertrand is not a man who believes in coincidence.

docs.title: This year's recruits
docs.text:
This year's intake is the largest he has ever had. He bellows at Pim more than at anyone, because Pim is keen and clumsy in equal measure and never once asks to stop, and Bertrand has quietly decided that Pim is going to be his proof that the porridge works. He bellows at Tobe, who mouths the corrections along with him and still misses the third cut. He bellows at Avice least, which she resents, and he knows it, and he is waiting for the morning she gets angry enough to be better than she already is.

He has also noticed, most dawns, a small figure on a roof ridge above the old quarters, copying the drills with something long and thin. He has never said a word about it to anyone. He has just started bellowing the corrections a little louder.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Bertrand wants every name on his list to come home. He knows it is not a thing a drill sergeant can promise, and so he tries to make it true one cut at a time. What he fears is opening the patrol reports one evening and finding a name he taught to hold a sword, and knowing he should have shouted louder.

A quest might begin with Bertrand asking someone to check on a former recruit who has stopped appearing in the reports, or with a dawn when the figure on the roof ridge is not there and he finds he minds.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Pim: recruit
  • Helewise: wife

docs.title: Biscuit
docs.text:
Gate Dog

Town Selsior Where Selsior Gate Role Animal Age Adult In the game Biscuit

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Friendly, greedy and convinced every traveller has bread. He wags what he has of a tail at everyone.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Biscuit is the gate dog of Selsior, and he is quite certain that you have bread. You may not think you have bread. You may have searched your pockets and your pack and found nothing but a map and some lint. Biscuit will sniff you anyway, thoroughly and with great hope, and then he will wag what he has of a tail, and say "Woof," and forgive you. He forgives everyone. He is friendly, greedy and entirely without suspicion, which makes him the least useful watchdog at the busiest gate on Veligor.

docs.title: The winter he came
docs.text:
He turned up at the gate four winters ago, thin and hopeful, with snow in his coat and his ribs showing, and sat down in the shelter of the gatehouse as if he had an appointment. Nobody knows where he came from. He came in off the Royal Road, but that only means he came from somewhere along it, and the Royal Road is long. The guards tried to send him away, at first, the way they would send away any stray. He came back. They tried again. He came back again, slightly faster each time, and by the end of that winter nobody was trying any more.

He is a dog of no particular kind: middling in size, short in the coat, and the exact colour of a well-baked crust, which is the reason most people give for his name. Nobody agrees on who named him. Half the gate guards claim it, and Hollis claims it loudest. His tail is a short stub that wags his whole back end along with it. Whether he was born that way or lost the rest of it somewhere on the road before he found Selsior, nobody knows, and Biscuit has never seemed to miss it.

docs.title: A day in the life of a dog
docs.text:
Biscuit's day has a shape, and he keeps to it more faithfully than most of the Guard keep to theirs. He sleeps on an old sack by the gatehouse door, where the stones hold the warmth of the day. At first light he gets up, stretches front and back, greets Hollis at his post, sniffs the first travellers of the morning and checks the taxi stand, in case anyone has dropped anything near Tilda's cab overnight.

Then he follows his nose. The smell of the Crown Market's ovens reaches the gate a little after dawn, and Biscuit goes to meet it, trotting through the streets with his nose down and his stub of a tail going. He has a round. Margery the baker gives him her stale loaves and pretends she dropped them. Maud, Dame Orsa's housekeeper, keeps rinds and scraps in her apron pocket for him and tells everyone she is only getting rid of them; Biscuit has learned to recognise the sound of her baskets from the far end of the market and to be standing exactly where she will pass. He sniffs every stall, is chased off by some of them and is fed by more, and by the afternoon he trots back to the gate smelling powerfully of bread.

In the evening Brann, the Gate Sergeant, who trusts nobody, eats his supper on the gatehouse bench and slips Biscuit the crusts off his own plate when he thinks no one is looking. Everyone has seen him do it. Biscuit lies on Brann's boots afterwards and falls asleep, and that, as far as Biscuit is concerned, is a perfect day.

docs.title: What a dog knows
docs.text: Biscuit cannot tell anyone what he notices, but he notices a great deal. He knows every regular at the gate by smell. He knows which carters keep bread under the seat. He goes a little way out onto the Royal Road most days, to sniff the verges and the milestones and see who has passed, and comes back again; he has never gone far. Lately he comes back sooner, and some evenings, when the light goes and Baldwin's lamps are lit by the gate, he stands at the edge of their light with his nose to the dark and his ears up, very still, for longer than a dog who is only thinking about bread.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Biscuit wants bread, a warm sack and a friendly hand, in roughly that order. He is afraid of thunder, of the gate's great bar when it slams, and of very little else.

A quest might begin with Biscuit refusing, for the first time anyone can remember, to go out onto the road, or with him following a traveller's scent far past the gate and not coming back by supper.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Maud: soft touch for scraps
  • Brann: keeper

docs.title: Brann
docs.text:
Gate Sergeant

Town Selsior Where Selsior Gate Role Guard Age Adult In the game Brann

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Gruff, watchful and proud of his city. He welcomes everyone and trusts nobody until they have earned it.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Brann is forty-eight, Sergeant of the great gate of Selsior, and the first face most travellers see when they come in off the Royal Road. It is a gruff face, weathered and watchful, and it does not smile until it has decided to. "Welcome to Selsior," he tells everyone who comes through, and he means it. "Keep to the road and mind the Guard," he adds, and he means that too.

docs.title: The gate is his
docs.text:
Brann joined the Royal Guard at nineteen, twenty-nine years ago, and he has stood at the gate for twenty of those years and commanded it for the last twelve. He has never wanted to be anywhere else. Other guards dream of the road patrol or the Knights' Court; Brann has always thought the gate was the most important post in the city, because it is where Selsior meets everyone else. Every envoy, carter, pilgrim, performer and adventurer who comes to the capital along the Royal Road passes under his eye, and he is fiercely proud of what they find on the other side.

He is proud of the city in the way some people are proud of a family. He will tell any traveller who stands still long enough that Selsior has stood since before the roads were laid, that it grew out of the field where the treaty was signed, and that there is nothing on Veligor you cannot find inside its walls if you look long enough. He welcomes everyone. He trusts nobody until they have earned it. He sees no contradiction in this, and after twenty years at the gate, neither do most of his guards.

docs.title: The people at the gate
docs.text:
Hollis, one of his gate guards, stands twelve hours a day at the gate and still likes looking out over the Royal Road. He starts every greeting stern, the way Brann taught him, and ends it smiling, which Brann did not. Brann grumbles about it and has never once told him to stop, because travellers like Hollis, and a gate that travellers like is a gate that hears things.

Swithin, the gate clerk, has written down everyone who came and went since before Brann was a recruit. The two of them are old colleagues and, though neither would put it so, old friends: Brann watches the faces, Swithin keeps the names, and between them very little gets past the gate that they do not know about. Swithin imagines adventures for every traveller in his book. Brann pretends to find this ridiculous and then asks what Swithin has written about the interesting ones.

And then there is Biscuit. The dog turned up at the gate four winters ago, thin and hopeful, and the guards never managed to send him away. Brann says he is keeping the dog because a gate needs a watchdog. Biscuit has never watched anything but a bread roll in his life. He sleeps by the gatehouse, follows his nose to the Crown Market every morning and comes back smelling of bread, and Brann, who trusts nobody, slips him the crusts off his own supper and thinks no one has noticed.

docs.title: Quiet, until it is not
docs.text: Brann likes to say the road is quiet, until it is not. Lately it is not more often than it used to be. Swithin has noticed that fewer travellers come in on foot these days and more come in hurt, and Brann has noticed the same thing from the other end: more wagons riding in close together, more hired swords sitting on the tailboards, more caravans like Merrick's that pay well for guards because they have to. When a traveller comes in limping, Brann sends them to an apothecary first and asks his questions after, and he passes what he hears to the Knights' Court the same day.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Brann wants the gate to stay what it has always been: open, busy and safe. What he fears is the day he has to close it in daylight.

A quest might begin with a traveller who comes through the gate without appearing in Swithin's book, or with Biscuit refusing, for the first time anyone can remember, to go out onto the road.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Biscuit: dog
  • Hollis: gate guard
  • Swithin: old colleague

docs.title: Cecily
docs.text:
Singer

Town Selsior Where Theatre Row Role Performer Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Shy off stage and fearless on it. Her voice is bigger than she is.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Cecily is nineteen, a singer of the Gilded Stage, and offstage you could walk past her three times without noticing. She speaks quietly, looks at her shoes, and apologises to doors she bumps into. Then the house lights dim between the acts, she steps out alone in front of the curtain, and a voice comes out of her that fills the whole theatre to the gallery rail and seems to be looking for more room. She is shy off stage and fearless on it, and nobody, Cecily least of all, can quite explain how the same person manages both.

docs.title: The fishing village
docs.text:
She grew up in a fishing village on the coast, a long way from Selsior, a row of tarred cottages above a shingle beach where the boats were drawn up at night. Her family still live there, and still fish, and write to her when someone passes inland who can carry a letter. She learned to sing mending nets with the women on the shingle, hauling songs and long sea ballads with forty verses, and she sang loudest when the wind was strongest, because it was the only time nobody could hear her properly. Then one winter evening the wind dropped in the middle of a verse, and the whole beach heard her, and nobody spoke until she had finished.

She came to Selsior at sixteen, three years ago, riding inland on a fish carrier's cart with a bundle and a letter for a cousin of a neighbour who turned out to have moved away. She took work scrubbing pots in a Theatre Row cookshop. She sang while she scrubbed, very quietly, and one afternoon she sang a little less quietly in the queue for the Gilded Stage's cheap gallery, and Lavinia, who was passing and misses nothing that might sell a ticket, stopped, listened to an entire verse, and told her to come to the stage door at six.

docs.title: Between the acts
docs.text: For two years now she has sung between the acts at the Gilded Stage, while the stagehands change the scenery behind the curtain. It is meant to be the part of the evening when the audience buys oranges and talks. Lately the audience has stopped talking. Tibb, who works the ropes, gives her a nod from the fly rail when the scene change is nearly done, so that she always knows how many verses she has left, and she has never once run out. Marigold, Crispin and Rosamund's daughter, has told her she would be a great actress if she could only learn to be rude to people, and Cecily is thinking about it.

docs.title: Fulke's ballads
docs.text:
On her free afternoons she goes to the plaza to learn the old ballads from Fulke, the ballad singer, who sings the Balrog War four different ways and the rest of his songs mostly true. He teaches her the true verses first, he says, and then the good ones, and then she must decide for herself. Cecily has noticed that his voice goes up half a tone on some verses and not on others, and she is too polite to ask why. She thinks he is the finest singer in the city. Fulke thinks she will be better than him one day, and has told everyone on the plaza except her.

In return she has taught him the sea songs from her village. One of the newest of them, which her mother sent in a letter last winter, is about something the boats have started to see beyond the shallows at dusk. Fulke made her sing it three times and then sat very still.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Cecily dreams of singing at a royal feast, in the palace, for the queen, one song from every town of the kingdom one after another. She has not told anyone this except her mother, in a letter. She knows that Clement the herald must have a say in who performs at the palace, and she has walked past him on the plaza four times meaning to ask and has not managed to open her mouth. What she fears is that the shy half of her will win on the one night it matters.

A quest might begin with Cecily needing someone to carry a song from her village back to the coast and bring the rest of its verses home, or with her needing someone braver than herself to speak to the herald for her.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Fulke: teacher

docs.title: Clement
docs.text:
Royal Herald

Town Selsior Where Plaza Role Official Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Nervous in private and magnificent on the steps. He rehearses every proclamation to the pigeons first.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Clement is forty-one, the Royal Herald of Selsior, and on the palace steps he is magnificent. He stands at the top of the red carpet in his tabard, unrolls the proclamation, fills his chest, and his voice rolls across the plaza and silences the Crown Market three streets away. Then he rolls the paper up, walks back inside, sits down on the first bench he finds and shakes. He is nervous in private and magnificent in public, and he has given up trying to be either one all the way through.

docs.title: The market crier
docs.text:
He grew up in the inner streets, the son of a tallow seller, both his parents long dead, and at sixteen he found work as a crier in the Crown Market. He called the opening of the stalls each dawn, cried lost purses and found dogs, and, more than anything, cried lost children: their names, their ages, what they were wearing, where their mothers were waiting. He was very good at it. A crowd went quiet when he called, and the children came. One morning Gideon, the Royal Herald, was buying apples when Clement cried a lost boy back to his father in under a minute, and the old man walked over and said, "Ha! Who taught you to breathe like that?" Nobody had. Gideon did, from then on, every week, in the empty plaza at first light before the market opened, until Clement could make himself heard over a festival.

Sixteen years ago Gideon cried the death of the old king and then the crowning of Queen Aveline, and heard the Great Bell ring for the second time in his life, and that year he handed the post on. He gave Clement's name to the palace and the palace took it. Clement was twenty-five. His first proclamation was the date of a harvest fair. He rehearsed it to the pigeons on the roofs for three days and still nearly fainted.

docs.title: Standing in a giant's boots
docs.text:
He has been herald for sixteen years now, and he still feels he is standing in a giant's boots. Gideon cried the expedition to the World Tree, the finding of the Children of the Tree and Cavelor, a king's death and a queen's crowning. Clement has cried fairs, new roads, treaty days, the Guard's trials, and lately, more and more, notices from the Knights' Court: which roads the patrols ride, which hours travellers should keep, that royal couriers now ride with guards. He rehearses every one of them to the pigeons first, on the roofs below Gideon's perch, and Gideon hears him, and tells him he is far better than he believes in a voice that half the plaza hears.

Every week Clement climbs the long ladder to the old man's perch and pretends it is only a social call. He brings something to eat, sits on the windowsill and talks about the weather for a while. Then, as if by accident, a folded paper comes out of his sleeve. Gideon pretends not to notice that it is never only a social call. Clement pretends not to notice that the old man has been waiting at the window since noon.

docs.title: The plaza
docs.text:
Clement lives alone in two rooms above a saddler's shop off the plaza, with a window on the palace steps. He has never married; he says he talks for a living and would like to come home to silence, though the truth is nearer that he is too shy to have asked. Everyone on the plaza knows him and greets him, and he answers each one by name in his magnificent voice and then blushes.

People bring him requests, because they think the herald must decide who performs at the palace. He does not, quite, though his word is listened to. Lambert, the juggler, has asked him about juggling for the queen at the next festival, and Clement was kind about it and promised nothing, because he could not bear to promise something he might not be able to keep. He has noticed the young singer from the Gilded Stage walk past him on the plaza several times as if about to speak to him. He has not worked out what she wants, and he is too shy to ask.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Clement wants one day to cry a proclamation that the whole plaza cheers, the way Gideon says the crowd cheered on the day the Bell rang. What he fears is being handed news he cannot make a crowd believe, as the old man was handed the news of the expedition, or, worse, news that he can.

A quest might begin with Clement needing a proclamation carried to a crowd in another town, or with a sealed paper handed to him for crying at dawn that he is not sure the palace really sent.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Gideon: mentor

docs.title: Constance
docs.text:
Adventurer

Town Selsior Where Old Quarter Role Adventurer Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Cool-headed, studious and dryly funny. She plans every fight and is annoyed when it does not go to plan.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Constance is twenty-three, an adventurer of the old quarters, and the only lodger at the Crooked Lantern who comes home from a fight and sits down to write about it before she has washed the mud off. She keeps a stack of bound notebooks on the shelf above her bed, one for every season she has spent on the road, and every monster she and her partner Thurstan have faced is in them: where they met it, what it did, how it moved, what hurt it, and what did not.

docs.title: From the classroom to the road
docs.text:
She grew up on an orchard farm out along the Royal Road, toward Kaldemor, where her parents still keep the trees and write to her twice a year to ask when she is coming home. She was the kind of child who took the clock apart to see whether it would go back together, and who wrote down the answer. At fifteen she came to the Royal Academy in the Scholars' Quarter to study magic, and for five years she studied under Morwen, who teaches that magic is mostly patience and has no time at all for showing off.

Constance was not a show-off. She was something Morwen found nearly as trying: a student who wanted to know what a spell was for. She learned the forms precisely and cast them precisely, and then she asked, every time, what use they were against the things now coming down the roads. At twenty, three years ago, she left the Academy before her final year and took a room at the Crooked Lantern. Morwen did not stop her. She did say, at the door, that Constance would be back for the books one day. Constance has not decided whether that was a curse or a promise, and goes back to borrow books often enough that it may already have come true.

docs.title: Thurstan
docs.text:
She met Thurstan two years ago in the Lantern's common room, the evening he came back from his first bounty with a torn sleeve, a very small reward and a very large story. He charges first and plans later. She plans first and is annoyed when the plan does not survive the first charge. They have been partners ever since, and it works better than either of them will admit: he gets them into fights that she would have talked herself out of, and she gets them out of fights he would never have survived. She keeps him alive. He makes sure she sees daylight. Joan, who keeps the tavern, says she has never known two people argue so much over breakfast and agree so completely by supper.

Constance's humour is dry enough that Thurstan misses about half of it. She considers this one of the small pleasures of the job.

docs.title: The notebooks
docs.text:
The notebooks started as tactics and have become something else. The monsters on the roads are not the monsters in the Academy's old bestiaries. Creatures the books call shy now stand their ground; creatures the books call solitary now turn up in threes. Constance writes it all down with dates, because she noticed early that the changes seemed to come in waves, and she wanted to know whether that was true or only a feeling. She still does not know. She has not shown the notebooks to anyone except Thurstan, who says they are very tidy, and Joan, who read two pages and made her promise to be more careful.

She would like someone to ask why the monsters changed and to want her answer. She also fears that the answer, when it comes, will be one nobody can do anything about.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might begin with Constance needing a monster observed rather than killed, for once, which Thurstan finds very hard. Or it might begin with a notebook going missing from the shelf above her bed, and Constance discovering that somebody else in Selsior has been wanting her answer very much.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Morwen: former teacher
  • Joan: landlady
  • Thurstan: adventuring partner

docs.title: Crispin
docs.text:
Playwright

Town Selsior Where Theatre Row Role Performer Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Anxious, witty and always scribbling. He talks in half-finished lines.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Crispin is forty-two, the house playwright of the Gilded Stage, and he has not finished a sentence out loud since about the age of twelve. He starts them, certainly. He starts them beautifully. Then a better line occurs to him halfway through, and he stops to write it down on whatever is nearest: a playbill, a napkin, his own cuff. Theatre Row is used to it. Half the actors on the Row have, at some point, been handed a scrap of paper in the middle of a conversation and told, "No, wait, that's it, that's the one."

docs.title: A life backstage
docs.text:
He grew up in the wings. His father painted scenery for the theatres of the Row, and Crispin spent his childhood sitting on paint pots, watching rehearsals and learning, long before he could spell, that a good line lands on the third beat and a bad one never lands at all. His father is dead now, but Crispin still keeps one of his brushes in the jar on his desk.

He has written for the Gilded Stage for fifteen years, under Lavinia, its owner and once its greatest actress. His comedies fill the house. The Baker's Wager has been revived so many times that the city's bakers quote it at each other across the Crown Market. But Crispin has always wanted to write something large, and Lavinia, who wants one last triumph before she hands the theatre on, has finally given him the chance. She has bet everything on it. She tells him so roughly once a day, in case he forgets.

docs.title: The play
docs.text:
The play is about the Balrog War, the whole of it: the First Burning, the truce, the Last Stand at the Tree and the weaving of the seal. Crispin has the first four acts. He does not have an ending, and he cannot write the fifth act until he knows what the thing at the centre of the story actually is.

This is where Thomasin comes in. The historian of the Balrog War is Crispin's adviser and, despite everything, his friend. He goes to her in the Scholars' Quarter with questions, and she gives him the four peoples' accounts side by side and refuses to say which is right. A horned giant, a wound in the world, the Burning, a line in a chronicle: Crispin wants one of them, and Thomasin will not give it to him. He finds this very unhelpful, and says so, and she says that is precisely the point. He suspects she is right, which is worse.

He has drafted five endings so far. In one the Balrog speaks. In another it never appears on stage at all, and the audience only sees the light of it on the actors' faces. He likes that one best and is frightened of it, because Lavinia will hate it.

docs.title: The family business
docs.text: Crispin's wife is Rosamund, the most famous actress in Selsior, and their daughter Marigold has been on stage since she could walk. Rosamund is determined to play the play's Magician, who stands for the Magicians who wove the seal together, which Crispin had always imagined as a quiet part, and which is getting less quiet with every draft. She will not share the stage with Percival, who wants the play's Savage warrior, standing for the whole front line that held the Balrog at the Tree, and Crispin cannot see how to write the Last Stand without the two of them in it. Marigold, meanwhile, wants a part, any part, and has hinted that she knows where he keeps his discarded endings. Crispin loves all three of the people making his life impossible, and he writes better when he is anxious, so in a sense they are helping.

docs.title: What he fears
docs.text:
Crispin is afraid of getting it wrong. Lately, with monsters on the roads and Thomasin lecturing more often than she likes, the Balrog is not quite a legend in Selsior any more, and he has started to wonder whether a play about it should end with an answer or with a question.

A quest might begin with a missing draft of the fifth act, or with Crispin needing someone to travel out and ask what the other towns tell their children about the Balrog.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Lavinia: employer
  • Rosamund: wife
  • Marigold: daughter
  • Thomasin: history adviser

docs.title: Cuthbert
docs.text:
Royal Cook

Town Selsior Where Palace Role Service Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Loud, red-faced and generous. He shouts at the pots and sings to the bread.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Cuthbert is forty-eight, the royal cook, and you can hear his kitchen from the far end of the palace. He shouts at the pots. He sings to the bread. He is loud, red-faced and generous, and he runs the palace kitchens like a ship in a storm, with a great deal of noise, a great deal of steam and, somehow, every dish on the table at the moment it was promised.

docs.title: Thirty-four years of kitchen
docs.text:
He came to the palace at fourteen as a scullion, thirty-four years ago, in the middle of King Bertram's long reign, and he scrubbed pans for two years before anyone let him near a knife. He learned everything there was to learn about the palace kitchen by being in the way of it. By thirty he was royal cook, eighteen years ago, and two years after that he cooked the coronation feast for Queen Aveline, a feast for half the kingdom in the plaza and the throne hall at once. He did not sleep for three days. Osbert, the Royal Steward, still keeps the menu from that feast in his desk, and Cuthbert, who has found this out, has never once let him forget it.

Osbert has spent years trying to stop Cuthbert shouting at the pots and singing to the bread in the presence of envoys. He has failed. Cuthbert says the bread rises better for a song and the pots know what they did.

docs.title: Juliana and Agnes
docs.text:
Cuthbert married Juliana, who kept the palace stillroom and made its preserves, and for a few years the two of them filled the lower palace with the smell of jam and roasting meat. Their daughter Agnes was born in the rooms off the kitchen. Juliana died of a winter fever when Agnes was six, thirteen years ago, and Cuthbert, who had never been quiet in his life, was quiet for most of that winter. Then he picked up his ladle again, put Agnes on a stool by the bread oven, and raised her in the kitchen with every cook, scullion and pot boy in it helping. He still makes Juliana's plum preserve every autumn, from her book, and does not let anyone else touch the jars.

When Agnes asked Osbert for a place in the household at fourteen, rather than the kitchen, Cuthbert was hurt for about a day and proud for the rest of the year. He is proudest of all now that she has the upper halls. He still sends biscuits up with her, which she trades with Peterkin for news, and he pretends not to know.

docs.title: Every town's table
docs.text:
Cuthbert cooks for every envoy's feast the palace gives, and he insists on learning each town's dishes properly, not as the capital imagines them. He has argued with Kaldemor's bakers about crust, learned Midbarium's slow-roasted mutton from an envoy's own cook and nearly set the kitchen on fire learning to smoke fish the harbour way. He keeps a great stained book of every recipe he has been taught and who taught it. There are dishes from Fairy Forest that he has made only once, because the herbs did not travel, and there is a page for Cavelor that is still blank, because he has never yet tasted what the guardians below the Tree eat, and nobody in his kitchen knows.

His dream is a great harvest feast with one dish from every town on a single table, the whole kingdom passing plates. He has planned the menu many times over. Every year the roads get harder, the carts come in later and an ingredient or two simply does not arrive, and every year the feast slips a little further off.

He also swears that one of the old keys young Prince Alaric collects used to open a larder that nobody in the palace can now find. He remembers the larder from his scullion days. He cannot remember where it was.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Cuthbert wants his harvest feast, and he wants Agnes to be happy, and he is not entirely sure which comes first. What he fears is a winter when the carts stop coming altogether, and a kitchen with nothing in it to sing to.

A quest might begin with Cuthbert needing one ingredient from a town the carts no longer reach, or with Alaric's key, and an old scullion's memory of a door behind the cold store.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Osbert: employer
  • Agnes: daughter

docs.title: Dickon
docs.text:
Skywalk Carpenter

Town Selsior Where Old Quarter Role Craftsman Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Fearless, cheerful and a little reckless. He whistles while hanging over thin air.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Dickon is forty-one, the skywalk carpenter of the old quarters, and he does his best work hanging over thin air. He builds and mends the narrow wooden walkways that cross above the old quarters' streets from one upper storey to another, and he does it with a rope round his waist, a mallet in his belt, a mouthful of nails and a whistle that carries three lanes. He is fearless, cheerful and a little reckless. The people underneath his walks have learned to look up when the whistling stops, because that is when something is about to fall, and it is usually a nail and occasionally Dickon.

docs.title: Born under the walks
docs.text:
He grew up in the old quarters, in a garret room under a roof that had a skywalk running past its window, and as a small boy he spent more time on that walk than in the room. At thirteen he was apprenticed to old Godric, the skywalk carpenter of those days, who was then past sixty and no longer liked heights, and who stood in the street shouting instructions while Dickon did the climbing. Godric taught him which timbers bend before they break and which break without warning, how to hang a walk so it sways without twisting, and how to talk a frightened householder into letting a stranger nail a plank to their window. When Godric died, Dickon took over his tools and his walks, and he has kept them ever since.

There are more than forty skywalks in the old quarters now, a second city of planks and rails above the winding lanes. Dickon has built a dozen of them himself and mends all the rest. He knows each one by its creak.

docs.title: Ida
docs.text:
His wife is Ida, the night watchwoman of the old quarters. They have been married twelve years and have no children. He works by day and she works by night, so they meet twice a day, at dawn when she comes home and at dusk when she goes out, and they have made those two meetings into something better than most people's whole evenings. He married her, he says, because she can tell from the sound of a plank whether it will hold; she says she married him because he is the only man in Selsior who has never once asked her whether she is frightened on her rounds. He never will. He knows better than anyone how frightening the dark under the old quarters can be, because she tells him, at dawn, about the scratching under the drains that keeps pace with her and stops when she stops. He listens, and makes her tea, and has lately started building his walks with an extra brace, though he would deny it was for that reason.

Edwina the midwife came to their wedding uninvited, as she comes to everyone's, because she delivered Ida and has the name in her book. Dickon was delighted and gave her the best seat.

docs.title: The long walk
docs.text:
Dickon has a dream, and it hangs from the kitchen ceiling in the shape of a model made of matchwood and string. He wants to build a skywalk long enough to cross from the old quarters to Theatre Row without anyone touching the ground: one great span over the broad street at the foot of the Row, half as long again as any walk in the city, landing on the roof of the Gilded Stage itself. He has worked out the timbers and the bracing and most of the cost. He has climbed the theatre's roof with a measuring line twice, the second time with Tibb the stagehand holding the other end and asking pointed questions. He has not yet asked Lavinia, who owns the roof, and he suspects she will either throw him out or want her name painted along the whole length of it.

Lately he has had a smaller puzzle. On his rounds he has twice found small fresh footprints in the pitch on the newest walks, at dawn, before anyone should have been up there. Somebody young knows the roofs very well. Dickon has not told anyone. He would quite like to meet them.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Dickon wants the long walk built in his lifetime and Ida beside him on the day it opens, walking above the city in daylight for once. What he fears is not falling. It is the morning Ida does not come home at dawn.

A quest might begin with Dickon needing timber long and sound enough for the great span, from a forest the carters no longer like to visit, or with a skywalk found cut through in the night, from below.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Ida: wife

docs.title: Edith
docs.text:
Costumer

Town Selsior Where Theatre Row Role Craftsman Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Thrifty, patient and full of pins. She can make a king's robe from curtains.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Edith is sixty-six, the costumer of Theatre Row, and there is a pin in her mouth. There is nearly always a pin in her mouth. She talks around it, perfectly clearly, and she has been doing so for nearly fifty years. She is thrifty, patient and full of pins, and she can make a king's robe out of curtains, a dragon's wing out of an old umbrella and a queen's ball gown out of three petticoats and a grudge.

docs.title: The attic on the Row
docs.text:
She works in a long, low attic halfway down Theatre Row, under the roof of a building that has housed three different theatres in her lifetime and kept her through all of them. The attic is full: bolts of cloth, baskets of buttons sorted by size, rows of costumes hanging from the rafters like a crowd waiting to go on, and a great cutting table with Edith's chair at the end of it. She sews every costume on Theatre Row. The Gilded Stage is her biggest customer, and Lavinia, who runs it, has been arguing with her about budgets for longer than either of them will admit.

She came to the Row at eighteen, forty-eight years ago, as a girl who could sew a straight seam faster than anyone her mother knew, and she has been there ever since. She dressed Lavinia in the great parts when Lavinia still played them. She dressed Rosamund for her very first part, a maid with a line and a half, and she has dressed her in every part since. She once sewed a basket lining for a baby who was carried on stage in the second act of The Baker's Wager. The baby was Marigold, and Edith still has the scrap.

docs.title: Every thread haggled
docs.text:
Edith does not buy cloth. She haggles it. Every week she goes to the Crown Market with a list and a sharp eye, and most weeks she goes to Isabeau, the cloth merchant, who is elegant, impossible to cheat and the only person Edith enjoys losing to. They spend an hour over a bolt of linen the way other people spend an hour over a game, and both of them come away pleased. Isabeau sells to the palace too, and Edith likes to remind her that the palace's robes are only cloth, and the Row's are kingdoms.

Nothing is ever thrown away. A tired gown becomes a shepherdess's apron, then a bandage for a stage wound, then a dust rag, then stuffing for a giant's belly. Crispin, the house playwright of the Gilded Stage, has written a Balrog War play with no fifth act yet, and Edith has read enough of it to be worried about the budget for the fourth.

docs.title: Sybil
docs.text:
Her younger sister Sybil is the Royal Wardrobe Mistress at the palace, and dresses the royal family from the coronation robes down to the princess's riding boots. The two of them meet for supper once a week and trade gossip about who wore what: which envoy's wife wore last year's sleeves, which actor split his breeches in the third act, what the queen chose for the trade council and why. Edith says she and her sister dress the two halves of Selsior: the half that is real and the half that pretends, and that she is never quite sure which half is which.

Sybil is sharp-tongued and kind underneath, and she tells Edith things she tells nobody else in the palace. Lately, though, Edith has noticed that there is one subject Sybil goes quiet on, and Edith, who can tell a hem has been let down from across a room, has noticed exactly where the quiet begins.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Edith wants to train someone with clever hands before her own get too stiff, and she wants, just once, to make a costume from new cloth bought at full price, simply to see what it feels like. What she fears is the day the theatres go dark: the Row has never closed in her lifetime, and the audiences, lately, go home earlier.

A quest might begin with Edith needing a rare cloth that the carts from the highlands have stopped bringing, or with a costume stolen from her attic on the night before an opening, and nothing else touched.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Sybil: sister
  • Isabeau: supplier

docs.title: Edric
docs.text:
Lieutenant of the Road Patrol

Town Selsior Where Knights' Court Role Guard Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Weathered, plain-spoken and tired in a way sleep does not fix. He jokes to keep his patrols calm.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Edric is forty-six, Lieutenant of the Road Patrol, and he has the face of a man who has spent most of his life squinting into weather. He leads the riders of the Royal Guard who keep the royal roads open between the towns, and he has done it long enough to remember when the job was mostly about lost carters and lame horses. It is not about that any more.

docs.title: Born to the road
docs.text:
Edric and his younger brother Tristan grew up on the roads before either of them could ride them. Their father was a carter who hauled goods between the capital and the other towns, and the boys spent their childhood on the bench beside him, learning every milestone, ford and good place to water a horse. Their mother kept the house in Riverside, and both parents are dead now. Tristan took to the river, and scouts its banks for the barges. Edric took to the road. They still meet whenever they can to compare notes, and the notes, lately, are always about the same thing: what the wilds are doing, and how fast.

Edric joined the Guard at twenty, twenty-six years ago, and rode his first patrol three years later. He was already riding patrols when a young recruit called Rhys came to the Knights' Court with a borrowed sword, and he likes to remind the Captain of it when nobody else is listening. Rhys made him lieutenant eight years ago, in his first year as Captain, and Edric has never wanted any post but this one.

docs.title: The patrol
docs.text:
Every patrol Edric leads rides out of the Knights' Court before dawn and comes back, if things go well, before the gates close. Things go well less often than they did. Every season there are more monsters on the roads and bolder ones, creatures that used to scatter at the sound of hooves and now stand their ground. The young riders under him, Aylwin among them, have more courage than experience, and Edric has learned that the best thing he can do for a frightened patrol is make it laugh. He tells the same terrible jokes on every ride. The riders groan at them. That is the point: people who are groaning are not panicking.

He does not joke about the reports. After every patrol he writes down where they met trouble, what it was and how many, and the reports go to the palace, where the queen's consort marks them on his great map of the royal roads, and to his friend Gervase, the cartographer, who is drawing a map of his own of where monsters have been seen. Edric has stood in front of both maps. He does not need them to tell him what he already feels in his bones.

docs.title: Friends on the road
docs.text: His other great friend is Merrick, the caravan master, who prices danger like any other cargo and pays well for fighters because he has to. Edric and Merrick have shared more fires on the road than either can count, and they argue cheerfully about whether the patrol should guard caravans or the caravans should guard themselves. They both know the answer is that there are not enough swords for either.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Edric wants the Court to train faster than the wilds grow worse. He knows it cannot, quite, and that is the tiredness that sleep does not fix. He sees young riders like Aylwin, earnest and brave and fresh from fighting off a pack of boars on the road to Kaldemor, and he is proud of them and afraid for them in the same breath. What he fears most is the day a patrol rides out and he has to write a report that is not about monsters but about one of his own.

A quest might begin with the patrol short a rider on a road that cannot wait, or with a report Edric has not sent to the palace yet because he does not believe what it says.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Aylwin: patrol guard
  • Tristan: brother
  • Merrick: friend
  • Gervase: friend

docs.title: Edwina
docs.text:
Midwife

Town Selsior Where Old Quarter Role Healer Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Calm, blunt and unshockable. She has delivered half the old quarters and scolds them all.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Edwina is seventy-one, the midwife of the old quarters, and she has brought more babies into Selsior than anyone alive. She has also, by her own count, scolded every one of them at least once since. She is calm, blunt and entirely unshockable. She has seen everything that can happen in a small room at three in the morning, and when a frightened new father tells her something is wrong, she looks, says "No it isn't," and is right, and when something is wrong she says so just as plainly and gets on with it.

docs.title: Fifty-three years of night calls
docs.text:
She was born in the old quarters and has never lived outside them. At eighteen she was taken on by old Gunnhild, the midwife of those days, a woman with enormous hands and no patience who had delivered Edwina herself. Gunnhild taught her everything she knew in a single sentence, repeated for six years: "Wash your hands and watch." When Gunnhild died, Edwina simply kept answering the knocks on the door.

That was nearly half a century ago. She has delivered children in garrets and cellars, in the back rooms of shops and the upstairs of taverns, once in a cart, and once on a skywalk, which she still holds against the skywalk. She never married. She says she has more than two thousand children already and has no wish to feed any of them.

She treats the old quarters' cuts and fevers too, because there is no physician in the lanes and the palace one is a long way off. She sets fingers, stitches scalps, and doses whole households through the winter coughs. Lately she has been stitching other things: bites from cellar rats grown far too large, a scrape from something in a drain that Lettice the rat catcher would not name, and more than once a traveller who came in limping by the gate and could not afford anyone grander.

docs.title: The list
docs.text: Edwina keeps a list of every child she has delivered, written in four fat books on the shelf over her bed: the name, the date, the street, the parents, and a line of her own about the birth that nobody else is allowed to read. She has delivered Gytha, the washerwoman, and later both of Cristin's boys, Kenric and Wat. She delivered Ida, the night watchwoman, and when Ida married Dickon the skywalk carpenter twelve years ago, Edwina turned up at the wedding, uninvited, as she turns up at every wedding of every child in her books. She sits at the back, cries without apology, tells the bride she was a very long labour, and leaves before the dancing. Nobody has ever turned her away. Most people now save her a seat.

docs.title: Aldith
docs.text:
Her oldest friend is Aldith, the herb wife of the Riverside. They met fifty years ago, when Edwina was twenty-one and came running across the city in the night to Elfrida's cottage on the river for herbs for a hard birth. Elfrida was away. Her daughter Aldith, a year older than Edwina, packed the basket, would not let her go alone, and walked back with her through the dark lanes, and sat on the stairs till dawn. The mother and the baby both lived. The two women have shared patients, teapots and opinions ever since. They meet on Aldith's bench by the river whenever Edwina can be spared, which is less often than either would like, and they argue about everything, except each other.

Edwina knows Aldith is keeping notes on the river's strange wounds. She knows because she is keeping the same kind of notes on the old quarters', on the backs of pages in her fourth book. Neither has said a word to the other about it yet.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Edwina wants someone to take over the knocks on the door before her hands go, and she has not yet found anyone blunt enough. What she fears is the name in her books she will one day have to write a second line beside: a child she brought into the world, gone out on the roads and not come home.

A quest might begin with Edwina called out at night to a farm beyond the walls, on a road she is no longer sure of, and needing someone to walk beside her, or with a name in her books belonging to a child nobody in the old quarters remembers.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Aldith: old friend

docs.title: Elinor
docs.text:
Princess of Wonder Kingdom

Town Selsior Where Palace Role Resident Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Bold, restless and stubborn as a mule. She hates embroidery and loves anything with a blade or a horse in it.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Elinor is seventeen, the elder child of Queen Aveline and Leofric, and the only person in the palace who thinks a princess's day should begin before the bakers'. Most mornings, while the lamps in the upper halls are still cold, she slips out through the little door in the kitchen garden wall, pulls a plain grey cloak over her hair and walks across the waking city to the Knights' Court. By the time Agnes comes to make her bed, she is back, flushed and innocent, with mud on her boots.

docs.title: The girl who would not sit still
docs.text:
She was a restless child and has grown into a restless young woman. Her tutors could teach her history and the manners of every town, and did, but nobody could teach her to love embroidery, and after years of trying they stopped. What she loved instead was anything that moved fast: the horses in the Guard stables, the swordsmen drilling below the palace windows, the dancers in the plaza, her little brother Alaric when he was running away from his lessons. She is bold, stubborn as a mule and very much her mother's daughter, though neither of them would say so.

Elinor does not want to be given a sword. She wants to earn one. The Royal Guard is open to anyone from any town who can pass its trials, and she means to pass them exactly like anyone else, with no title and no favours. If the Court ever learned who she was before she had earned her rank, she is sure the trials would be quietly made easier, and the thought makes her furious.

docs.title: The cloak and the dawn lessons
docs.text:
Since last autumn she has trained at dawn with Rowena, the Swordmaster who teaches the Court's advanced classes. Elinor asked for private lessons with her hood up and her name unspoken, and Rowena agreed without asking it. Elinor believes this is because the disguise is good. It is not. The cloak itself belongs to Sybil, the wardrobe mistress, who lent it without a word and now pretends she has no idea where it went. Elinor's hands have blistered and healed and blistered again, and she has learned to keep them in her lap at breakfast.

She is not as invisible as she hopes. Avice, the fiercest of this year's recruits, has noticed that the cloaked stranger holds a sword like someone raised with fine manners, and Agnes has noticed the boots. Her mother has noticed the hands.

docs.title: Aylwin
docs.text: There is one person at the Court Elinor does not hide from. Aylwin, who rides with the road patrol, grew up above the Guard stables with his grandfather Wystan, and Elinor has been visiting those stables since she was small. Somewhere between the horses and the hay, the two of them fell for each other. He recognised her under the cloak the first morning she wore it and has never said so to anyone. She worries about him every time the patrol rides out, and she knows about the boars on the road to Kaldemor although he told the story as if it were funny. Both of them are certain no one knows. Both are wrong, though nobody has told them.

docs.title: What she wants and what she fears
docs.text:
Elinor wants the Swordsman's rank, earned in the open, and then she wants to ride the royal roads like Aylwin and the rest of the patrol. She knows the roads are getting worse. She has stood in front of her father's great map and watched the marks spread, and she thinks a kingdom whose roads are full of monsters needs every sword it can get, including hers.

What she fears is being found out before she is ready. She is not afraid of her mother's anger so much as her mother's worry, and of the look her father would give her, gentle and disappointed. She has no idea that the queen already suspects.

A quest might begin with a hooded recruit asking for a sparring partner who will not hold back, or with the princess needing someone to cover her absence on the morning of the trials.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Aveline: mother
  • Leofric: father
  • Alaric: brother
  • Sybil: secret keeper
  • Aylwin: sweetheart
  • Rowena: secret teacher

docs.title: Emmeline
docs.text:
Flower Seller

Town Selsior Where Plaza Sells Flowers, garlands and festival ribbons

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Lambert: sweetheart

docs.title: Ermengarde
docs.text:
Bookbinder

Town Selsior Where Scholars' Quarter Role Craftsman Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Placid, careful and fond of terrible puns. She smells of glue and old leather.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Ermengarde is seventy, the bookbinder of the Scholars' Quarter, and she smells of glue and old leather from a street away. She mends and binds the Academy's books in a tiny shop beside the great library, so close that her brother Benedict, the Head Librarian, can hear her laughing at her own jokes through the wall. She is placid, careful and fond of terrible puns. Bring her a book with a broken back and she will look at it sorrowfully, say, "Spineless, I see," and then mend it so well that it outlives you.

docs.title: The shop through the wall
docs.text:
She and Benedict were born in the Scholars' Quarter, three years apart, he the elder, the children of a laundress who washed for the Academy's masters. Their parents are long dead. Benedict went to the library as a boy to fetch and shelve; Ermengarde went next door at thirteen, to old Master Quentin, the bookbinder whose shop leaned against the library wall, and asked if he needed someone to sweep. He needed someone to stir the glue pot, which is worse. She stirred it for three years before he let her sew a single signature, and she has said ever since that it taught her everything important about bookbinding, mainly that it is mostly waiting.

Quentin left her the shop when he died, forty years ago. It is one room and a loft, with a sewing frame, a press as old as the Academy, racks of leather and boards, and a back door that opens straight into the library's mending room, so that the damaged books can come to her without crossing a street. Every damaged book in the library goes through her hands, and every one comes back with a pun about it that Benedict pretends not to hear. She never married. She says she has been bound to her work so long that she would not know how to come unstitched.

docs.title: Benedict and the missing volume
docs.text: She and her brother have worked side by side, through a wall, for most of their lives. He is fussy where she is placid; he frets over a bent corner while she shrugs and fixes it. She knows better than anyone how much the missing volume of the Aristocrat war chronicles weighs on him, eighteen years after he read its first pages at a desk by the window and came back to find it gone. She has helped him search the shelves every year, with his list. Once, years ago, she told him that books go where they are needed, and he did not speak to her for a week, so she has not said it again, though she still believes it.

docs.title: Ranulf
docs.text: The larger binding work of the Academy, the great ledgers and the presentation volumes, went for many years to Ranulf, who kept a bindery in the Quarter, and he was a friend of hers and Benedict's both.
