When he died two winters ago and his bindery was sold to pay what he owed, Ermengarde went to the sale and bought his finishing tools, his brass rolls and stamps and his good bone folder, so that strangers would not have them. She keeps them in a cloth on the shelf in her loft for his children, Mariota and Tobe, if either of them ever wants them. Neither has asked yet. She has not offered. She thinks it should be their idea.

docs.title: The letter
docs.text: Thirty-three years ago Ermengarde took apart the binding of an old book to resew it, and found, folded small and sewn into the spine where it did not belong, a letter. She read it. Then she folded it again, sewed it back exactly where she had found it, bound the book up better than before, and sent it back to its shelf. She has never told anyone what it said, not Benedict, not anyone, and she has never told anyone which book it was in. People who know the story ask her about it often. She smiles placidly and says it was a matter of some delicacy, and that she would not want to give anything away, which is, she points out, a bookbinder's whole job.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Ermengarde wants to see her brother's missing volume back on its shelf, mostly for his sake. What she fears is the day someone takes that old book off its shelf to rebind it after she is gone, and finds the letter, and does not understand it, or worse, does.

A quest might begin with Ermengarde needing a rare leather or a particular glue from another town to mend a book that must not leave her shop, or with the old book she rebound thirty-three years ago being borrowed from the library, for the first time in decades, by someone she does not know.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Benedict: brother

docs.title: Everard
docs.text:
Academy Student

Town Selsior Where Scholars' Quarter Role Scholar Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Lazy, charming and secretly brilliant. He sleeps through lectures and passes every exam.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Everard is eighteen, a student of the Royal Academy, and he is asleep. Not always, but often enough that Morwen, who teaches him, has stopped waking him and started asking him questions instead, on the theory that he cannot possibly know the answer. He always knows the answer. He is lazy, charming and secretly brilliant, and he sleeps through lectures and passes every exam, and he would very much like everyone to go on believing that the second fact is luck.

docs.title: From the harbour to the Academy
docs.text:
He grew up in one of the harbour towns, in a house that smelled of tar and salt, and his family still lives there; they write now and then, mostly to ask about his marks, and play no part in his life in the capital. He was the sort of child who could do sums in his head before he could swim, which in a harbour town is a scandal. When a small light started coming to his fingers at night, the kind of thing a young mage notices before anyone else does, he hid it for a year. Then his family found out, and at fifteen he was put on a cart to Selsior with a letter for the Academy and a great deal of hope pinned to his coat.

He has been at the Academy three years now. He studies the mage's art under Morwen, who is intense, precise and impatient with anything flashy, and who is convinced he could be a great mage if he tried. She is right. He knows she is right. That is the whole trouble.

docs.title: Theatre Row
docs.text:
Everard spends more of his time on Theatre Row than in the classroom. He likes the theatres for the same reason he dislikes lectures: on the Row, nobody expects anything of him except that he laughs at the right moments. He sits in the cheap gallery of the Gilded Stage, knows half the company by name, has opinions about every play on the Row and argues them over late suppers in the Row's taverns. He can quote most of The Baker's Wager. He has a suspicion, from overheard rehearsals, that the new Balrog War play has no ending, and he has been tempted, more than once, to suggest one.

He likes the light, too. Stage light is a craft of its own, lamps and mirrors and coloured glass, and Everard has spent more hours than he would admit watching how the stagehands make a dawn out of a candle. He has never done anything about it. Probably.

docs.title: Mariota
docs.text: His friend Mariota, who studies under Theobald the stargazer and corrects his arithmetic, has worked out that Everard is far cleverer than he lets anyone see, and she has made it her business to catch him at it. She has come close twice. He enjoys this game enormously and would be lost without it, and he has never told her that she is the only person at the Academy whose opinion of him he actually minds.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Everard wants to be left alone to be good at things quietly. What he fears is being great. He has read enough of the news from the roads, and seen enough of the worry on Morwen's face when she comes back from the Master's rooms, to understand what a kingdom does with a great mage in a time like this one: it needs them. It sends them somewhere. It puts the weight of something very large on their shoulders and expects them to carry it. He has seen what that look does to Morwen. He is eighteen, and he would rather be thought lazy.

He also fears, a little, that if he ever tried with everything he had, he would find out where his limit was, and it would not be as far away as everyone believes.

A quest might begin with someone noticing that a small theatre on the Row has had remarkably beautiful lighting this season, with no lamps anyone can find, or with Morwen asking a traveller to take Everard somewhere he will have no choice but to try.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Morwen: teacher
  • Mariota: friend

docs.title: Fulke
docs.text:
Ballad Singer

Town Selsior Where Plaza Role Performer Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Charming, theatrical and a terrible liar. Every ballad he sings is mostly true.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Fulke is thirty-seven, a ballad singer of the plaza, and every song he sings is mostly true. He is charming, theatrical and a terrible liar, and the two facts are closely connected: whenever a ballad of his strays from the truth, his voice goes up half a tone and his eyebrows go up with it, and the regulars on the plaza have learned to tell exactly which verses he made up. They do not mind. They say the made-up verses are often the best ones.

docs.title: A plaza child
docs.text:
He was born a street off the plaza and has never lived anywhere else for long. As a boy he sat on the steps by the Great Bell and listened to the old singers who worked the square in those days, and by twelve he had learned every ballad they knew and was improving on them, out loud, to their faces. A lute came to him second-hand from one of those old singers, who said it had more songs in it than he had years left to sing them. Fulke has been trying to get them all out of it ever since.

He sings for coin on the plaza most afternoons, wherever the crowd is thickest, and he has the plaza performer's gift of making a crowd of strangers feel like an audience of friends. He bows too low, flourishes too much and tells the story behind every song at greater length than the song itself. People stay anyway.

docs.title: Mirabel and the Bell
docs.text: Every evening, when Baldwin the lamplighter has lit the lamps around the Great Bell, Fulke plays his lute for Mirabel's dances. Mirabel dances for the pleasure of it, dreamy and impossible to hurry, and Fulke has learned to follow her rather than lead, playing faster when she spins and slower when she drifts. They have played the plaza together for years. Mirabel swears the Bell sings at dusk when the wind is kind, and Hugh, the Bell Warden, insists it has not rung since the coronation. Fulke refuses to take sides. He has written a verse about the Bell humming at dusk, which Mirabel loves and Hugh pretends not to hear, and when he sings it his voice does not go up at all, which has started one or two arguments of its own.

docs.title: Ballads of the Balrog War
docs.text:
His favourite songs, and his best-paid, are the ballads of the Balrog War: the First Burning, the truce at one table, the Last Stand at the Tree with the warriors holding the line while the Magicians worked the seal. He knows the four peoples tell the war four different ways, and he sings all four, sometimes in the same evening, sometimes in the same song. He sings of what the Balrog was the way the old stories do, and never the same way twice, because he does not know, and he would rather sing three guesses than pretend to one answer.

He also collects new songs. Most mornings he stops at the city gate and asks the travellers coming in what they sing at home: highland herding songs, harbour shanties, forest rounds, the strange marching songs of Urbanograd. Lately, the travellers' songs have more monsters in them than they used to, and some of them are not old songs at all.

docs.title: Cecily
docs.text: Fulke has a pupil. Cecily, who came from a fishing village on the coast and sings between the acts at the Gilded Stage, is shy off the stage and fearless on it, with a voice far bigger than she is. She comes to him to learn the old ballads. He teaches her the true verses first, he says, and then the good ones, and then she must decide for herself. He thinks she will be better than he is. He has told everyone except her.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Fulke wants to write one song that the whole kingdom sings: a song they hum in the harbours and the highlands and under the Tree, long after they have forgotten who wrote it. What he fears is that the song he is meant to write is not a ballad about the old war at all, but about something that has not finished happening yet.

A quest might begin with Fulke hearing a song at the gate about a place he has never heard of and needing someone to find out whether it is real, or with him asking a traveller to carry a new ballad to another town and bring back what they think of it.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Mirabel: dancer he plays for
  • Cecily: pupil

docs.title: Gervase
docs.text:
Cartographer

Town Selsior Where Scholars' Quarter Role Scholar Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Restless, chatty and allergic to blank spaces on maps. He paces when he thinks.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Gervase is forty-nine, the kingdom's cartographer, and he cannot stand still. He paces when he thinks, which is always, and he talks while he paces, which is also always, and he is allergic to blank spaces on maps in a way that makes him itch. Show Gervase a map with an empty corner and he will want to know what is there, and then he will want to go and look, and then he will want to draw it.

docs.title: The road years
docs.text:
He grew up in the Scholars' Quarter and was drawing maps of his own street at six, with every door, drain and cat marked on them. At twenty-two, twenty-seven years ago, he set out on the royal roads with a quiet young surveyor called Leofric, who was two years younger than him and the only person Gervase had ever met who was more careful than he was restless. For the better part of seven years the two of them walked, measured and argued their way between the towns. Gervase talked and paced and could not bear a blank space on a page. Leofric would walk the same mile three times to be sure of it. Between them they got the roads right.

The survey ended twenty years ago, the year Leofric met the woman who would become queen over a disputed map in the Scholars' Quarter, and married her before the year was out. Gervase likes to say that the road Leofric was defending that afternoon was one they had walked together, and that he would have been less polite about it. He and Leofric are still old colleagues and old friends, and Gervase is one of the few people in the city who still calls the queen's consort by his name and sends him maps with rude notes in the margins.

docs.title: The monster map
docs.text:
Gervase works in a narrow house in the Scholars' Quarter with maps on every wall, maps on the ceiling over his worktable and maps laid out on the floor so that visitors must walk on the margins. He draws the kingdom's maps for the Academy, the palace, the Guard and anyone else who will pay, and he has never yet drawn one he thought was finished.

For some years now he has been making a different kind of map: a map of where monsters have been seen. It began as a curiosity, a few marks in the wild places where everyone knew there was trouble. It is a curiosity no longer. His friend Edric, Lieutenant of the Road Patrol, sends him a copy of every patrol report, and comes round in person when he can, to stand in front of the map with a cup of something and tell a terrible joke or two before they both go quiet. Gervase marks every sighting with a dot of ink and the date. Leofric keeps his own map of the same reports on a wall in the palace, and when the two of them compare, the marks agree.

The map is getting crowded. Places that were blank spaces in Gervase's youth, the safe stretches between towns that nobody bothered to draw in detail because nothing ever happened there, are filling up with dots. He has had to start a second sheet for the roads near the towns themselves. He paces in front of it for hours.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Gervase wants to finish a map of the whole kingdom, every road and ford and ridge, with no blank space anywhere, before he is too old to walk. He also wants, for the first time in his life, a map with fewer marks on it than the year before. What he fears is the shape the dots are making. He is not a scholar of the Balrog War and does not pretend to be. But he knows what a map looks like when something is spreading, and he has started, very quietly, to measure how fast.

A quest might begin with Gervase needing someone to walk a stretch of road that is blank on his monster map, to find out whether it is truly quiet or simply unwatched, or with a dot appearing somewhere on his map that should be impossible.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Leofric: old colleague
  • Edric: friend

docs.title: Gideon
docs.text:
Retired Herald

Town Selsior Where Plaza Role Resident Age Elder In the game Gideon

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Booming, nostalgic and a little lonely. He laughs loudest at his own stories.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Gideon is seventy-eight, the retired Royal Herald of Selsior, and he still has the loudest voice in the city. He does not use it as often as he would like. These days he lives in a perch high above the plaza, a little room under the eaves at the top of a long ladder, and when someone does climb up to see him, he greets them with a great booming "Ha!" that sends the pigeons off the sill. He is booming, nostalgic and a little lonely, and he laughs loudest at his own stories, which is just as well, because he tells a great many of them.

docs.title: Forty years on the steps
docs.text:
Gideon cried King Bertram's news in the plaza for forty years. He was twenty and standing in the crowd on the day Bertram was crowned, fifty-eight years ago, when the Great Bell rang over the square, and he has said ever since that the sound went straight into his chest and stayed there. Two years later the herald's post fell vacant, and Gideon, who had been practising proclamations to the river for most of his youth, walked up the palace steps and asked for it. He got it, he says, because nobody else in the city could make himself heard over the Crown Market on a busy morning.

From then on, every piece of royal news in Selsior came out of Gideon's mouth first: new laws and new roads, harvest fairs and treaty days, the births and deaths of great people. Fifty years ago, a young man of twenty-eight, he cried the setting out of the Great World Tree Expedition from the palace steps to the biggest crowd he had ever seen. Later he cried the news of what it found, the Children of the Tree and the guardians of Cavelor beneath the roots, and he says no news he ever gave was harder to make a crowd believe.

His last two proclamations came in the same year, sixteen years ago. He cried the death of the old king, and a little while later he cried the crowning of Queen Aveline, and he heard the Great Bell ring for the second time in his life. He handed the post on that year, and he has never stood on the steps in an official capacity since.

docs.title: The perch
docs.text:
He chose the perch because from up there he can hear every bell in Selsior: the clock tower bells that the palace children race, the drill bell at the Knights' Court, the market's opening bell, the bell on the gatehouse, and of course the Great Bell on its dais, which does not ring. He knows them all by voice, the way other old men know birds. If he has ever heard anything from the Great Bell in the long years since the coronation, he has not said so, and for a man who says everything, that is a little unusual.

The trouble with a perch is the ladder. Nobody climbs it to hear Gideon any more. Clement, who took over the herald's post, climbs up every week, and pretends it is only a social call, and then asks his advice on a proclamation. Gideon pretends not to notice that it is never only a social call. He has heard Clement rehearsing to the pigeons on the roofs below, and he thinks the young man is far better than he believes, and tells him so in a voice that half the plaza hears. Clement says he is standing in a giant's boots. Gideon, privately, remembers being exactly as nervous on those steps himself, and has never quite admitted it.

His oldest friend is Aldous, the Keeper of the Royal Vault, who counts twice and smiles once and does not climb ladders. So once a month Gideon climbs down instead, slowly, and walks to the palace to sit with Aldous when the vault closes. They have served the crown for most of their lives, and they talk about the old king's reign the way other people talk about a favourite play.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Gideon wants a visitor. He has sixty years of stories about the plaza and the people in it, and he would like to tell them to someone who has not heard them, and he would like that someone to laugh in the right places, or at least after he does. What he fears is that the stories will go when he does, and that nobody will remember how the square sounded on the day the Bell rang.

A quest might begin with Gideon asking a traveller to carry a message down to Clement that he is too proud to deliver himself, or with the old herald hearing, from his perch, a bell he does not recognise.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Aldous: old friend
  • Clement: pupil

docs.title: Gilbert
docs.text:
Candlemaker

Town Selsior Where Old Quarter Role Craftsman Age Adult Sells Candles, lamp oil and wax seals

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Mild, methodical and very fond of bees. He hums at the same pitch as his hives.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Gilbert is forty-four, the candlemaker of the old quarters, and he hums. He hums while he dips wicks, while he pours wax, while he climbs the ladder to his roof, and above all while he works among his hives, where the hum he makes and the hum the bees make are so close in pitch that the neighbours below cannot always tell which is which. He is mild, methodical and very fond of bees. Ask him about candles and he will tell you politely what you need to know. Ask him about bees and you may as well sit down.

docs.title: The rooftop
docs.text:
His shop is a narrow, sweet-smelling room on a crooked lane in the old quarters, with a dipping frame by the window, racks of candles hung up by their wicks like sleeping bats, and a counter where he sells lamp oil and wax seals as well. Above it, up a ladder and through a hatch, is the part of his life he actually cares about: a flat stretch of roof, fenced with a low rail, where nine hives stand in a row among pots of lavender, thyme and borage. From up there he can see across the jumbled roofs and skywalks of the old quarters to the palace towers, and on a clear morning he says he can watch his bees fly out over half the city and come back with all of it in their legs.

He learned candlemaking from his mother, who sold tallow dips from a tray and has been dead these many years, and he learned bees from nobody at all. At fifteen he caught a swarm that had settled on a washing line, in a basket, with his bare hands, because no one else would go near it, and he has kept bees ever since. Beeswax made from his own hives is the whole of his pride. It burns clean and slow and smells faintly of summer, and it is why the better households of the city buy their candles from a crooked lane rather than a grand street.

docs.title: Customers and friends
docs.text: His steadiest customer is Baldwin, the lamplighter, who has bought oil and wicks from him for years. Gilbert measures them out humming, and Baldwin waits without hurrying him, and neither of them finds this strange. Lately Baldwin has been buying more oil than the city pays for, to burn extra lamps by the gate. Gilbert has noticed. He has quietly started charging him less for it, and Baldwin has quietly noticed that.

docs.title: The bees
docs.text:
This year his bees have turned short-tempered. They have always been gentle, gentle enough that he works them in his shirtsleeves with no veil, and he has been stung more times since spring than in the ten years before it. They come off the hives at nothing, at a shadow, at the sound of a door, and they come back from their flights restless, as though they have been somewhere that upset them. He has moved the hives, changed the flowers, smoked them more and smoked them less. Nothing helps.

He is not the only one. Other beekeepers on the city roofs say the same, and he has heard that the wild bees in the palace gardens have turned mean as well. Baldwin has mentioned that the night moths behave oddly too. Gilbert does not know what any of it means. He has a feeling, which he does not like, that the bees are answering something, the way a hive answers a storm long before anyone sees the clouds.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Gilbert wants his bees calm again and his rooftop full of the old, contented hum. What he fears is going up the ladder one morning and finding the hives empty, the bees gone somewhere he cannot follow.

A quest might begin with Gilbert needing someone to take a frame of comb to a beekeeper outside the city and bring back word of how the bees are there, or with a swarm of his own that leaves the roof and settles, of all places, on the Great Bell.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Baldwin: customer

docs.title: Godwin
docs.text:
Palace Gardener

Town Selsior Where Palace Role Worker Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Slow, patient and full of proverbs. He talks to his roses more than to people.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Godwin is seventy-four and the gardener of the palace, and he is never in a hurry. He moves along the garden paths at the speed of a growing thing, he answers questions after a pause long enough to plant something in, and when he does speak it is usually in proverbs: a rose remembers the hand that pruned it, weeds come to those who wait, a garden is only ever finished on the day the gardener is. He is slow, patient and kind, and he talks to his roses more than he talks to people. He says the roses listen better. Nobody who has seen him with them is sure he is wrong.

docs.title: Since the old king's day
docs.text:
He came to the palace at sixteen, fifty-eight years ago, in the year King Bertram was crowned, to push a barrow for the old head gardener, Gerold, a stern man who believed that a boy should learn every bed in the gardens by its smell before he was allowed to touch a pair of shears. Godwin learned them all. When Gerold died, thirty-eight years ago, the gardens passed to him, and he has tended them ever since, through the rest of the old king's reign and the whole of Queen Aveline's. Osbert, the steward, arrived as a boot boy a few years after Godwin and has never once managed to make him come indoors for a household meeting.

He has never married. He lives in a small brick lodge against the kitchen-garden wall, with a stove, a cot, a shelf of seed packets labelled in a shaky hand, and a window that looks out on his roses.

docs.title: A flower from every town
docs.text: His great work is a long bed below the palace terrace that he calls the kingdom border. In it he grows a cutting from every town's favourite flower, begged from envoys, carters and travellers over many years and coaxed along in the capital's soil, which suits some of them and sulks at others. He tends it as if it were a treaty, which in a way he thinks it is. One place in the border is still empty. He has never been able to learn what Cavelor's favourite flower is, or whether anything flowers down there at all, and he keeps the space weeded anyway, just in case someone tells him.

docs.title: Alaric
docs.text: His friend in the gardens is Prince Alaric, who is nine and wants to know everything. Godwin lets him dig, water and ask questions, so long as he is gentle with the roses, and he taught him which beetles help a garden and which ones eat it. The boy keeps the good ones in labelled jars on his windowsill and brings the bad ones to Godwin for judgment. Godwin finds him the best company in the palace, after the roses.

docs.title: The mean bees
docs.text: This year the wild bees in the gardens have turned mean. In fifty-eight summers Godwin has never been stung in the rose walk; since spring he has been stung four times, once on the eyelid. The bees fly hard and low and seem angry at the flowers themselves. He and Alaric sit on the bench by the lavender and watch them, and Alaric asks why, and for once Godwin has no proverb for it. He has heard the candlemaker's roof hives in the old quarters are the same, and he does not like the sound of that at all.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Godwin wants the empty place in his border filled before he is too old to plant it, and the bees gentle again. What he fears is a garden he does not understand any more.

A quest might begin with Godwin asking a traveller bound for the World Tree to bring back a cutting of anything that grows near Cavelor, or with a rose in the kingdom border that has started, quite suddenly, to wither from the root.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Alaric: gardening friend

docs.title: Gytha
docs.text:
Washerwoman

Town Selsior Where Old Quarter Role Worker Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Tough, sharp-tongued and quick to laugh. She can scrub a stain and a reputation clean.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Gytha is thirty-five and runs the washing yard in a courtyard of the old quarters, where the lines are strung so thick between the walls that on a fine day you walk through the yard under a ceiling of other people's sheets. She has scrubbed the linen of half the lanes around her, and she can tell a household's whole week from its washing: who has been ill, who has been courting, who has been at the tavern, who has a guest they would rather the neighbours did not hear about. She does not repeat most of it. She does not need to. Knowing is enough, and everyone in the old quarters knows that she knows, which keeps a great many of them honest.

docs.title: A yard full of voices
docs.text:
She grew up in the lane where her father Simkin still mends shoes, the only child of Simkin and Winifred, and she learned early that the way to hold your own in a house with a storyteller and a grumbler in it is to talk faster than both of them. She is tough, sharp-tongued and quick to laugh, and the washing yard suits her: it is loud, hot, wet and full of women who talk while they work. Gytha talks loudest. She can scrub a stain out of a collar and a rumour out of a reputation with about the same effort, and she has done both for neighbours who needed it.

Her days start before light, with water hauled and fires lit under the coppers, and end after dark, when the last baskets go back to their houses. In between she argues prices, settles quarrels over whose shirt is whose and keeps the coppers from boiling dry.

docs.title: Hodge
docs.text:
Her son Hodge is ten. Hodge's father is gone, and Gytha does not talk about him. Not to Hodge, not to her neighbours, not even to her mother, who has a story for everything and has never once tried to tell that one. If someone in the yard is foolish enough to ask, Gytha changes the subject so briskly that they do not try twice. Whatever happened, she has decided it is hers to carry, and she carries it the way she carries a full basket, without complaint and without putting it down.

She is raising Hodge with her parents' help. Simkin gives him scraps of leather and lectures on the proper care of heels; Winifred gives him stories every evening on her doorstep. Gytha gives him rules, a great many of them, and the rule she means most is the one about the Royal Guard. Hodge wants to be a guard. Gytha has forbidden it, flatly and more than once. She wants him to learn a trade: something with tools in it, something that keeps him inside the city walls and brings him home every night. Her father's trade would do. So would any other. What will not do is a sword.

She has heard plenty about Hodge on the rooftops. Half the old quarters have told her, usually while handing over their washing. She has never once caught him at it, and she has her suspicions about how he gets home so fast. What she does not know, for all that she knows everyone else's secrets, is what he does up there at dawn. It has never crossed her mind to wonder what became of the old broom handle that used to lean in the corner of her own yard.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text: Gytha wants Hodge safe, fed and apprenticed, in that order. She fears the roads, which have taken more people out of the gate than they have brought back lately, and she fears the day her son is old enough to walk out of it without asking her. Underneath that is a smaller fear that she keeps even quieter: that Hodge will one day ask the question she has never answered.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest might begin with Gytha finding a stain on someone's linen that she cannot place and does not like, or with her son finally being caught, and Gytha needing someone to help her decide what to do about it.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Simkin: father
  • Winifred: mother
  • Hodge: son

docs.title: Hamon
docs.text:
Keeper of the Gate Inn

Town Selsior Where Selsior Gate Role Service Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Hearty, nosy and a natural host. He greets guests by name on their second visit.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Hamon is fifty, the keeper of the Gate Inn, and he has never met a stranger he did not intend to know better by morning. The Gate Inn stands just inside Selsior's great gate, where the Royal Road ends and the city begins, and for most travellers it is the first bed they sleep in when they arrive and the last they leave from. Hamon makes sure they remember it. He is hearty, nosy and a natural host, with a voice that fills the common room and a memory that fills the rest. Come in once and he will ask your name, your road and your business. Come in a second time and he will greet you by name at the door, and ask after the cousin you mentioned.

docs.title: The inn by the gate
docs.text:
The Gate Inn is a tall, broad house of timber over stone, with a yard for wagons behind it, a stable for a dozen horses, a long common room with a fire at each end, and rooms upstairs for every kind of purse. Hamon was born in it. His mother, Ethelind, kept it for thirty years and taught him that an innkeeper's real stock is not beer or beds but names. She died twenty years ago, and he has kept the inn alone since, with a cook, two maids, a stable lad and a great many opinions.

He has never married. He says the inn is a wife who never sleeps, and that he would not ask a second one to put up with the first.

docs.title: Regulars
docs.text:
His favourite guests are the ones who come back, and his favourite of those is Merrick, the caravan master, who has slept in the same back room every time he has been in the capital for longer than Hamon has kept the inn. Hamon keeps that room for him. When Merrick's wagons come up the road and his voice comes through the gate ahead of them, shouting at the oxen, Hamon has his supper on the table before he is down off the box. They argue about everything, prices most of all, and Hamon would not miss it for the world.

The gate's people are his neighbours. Swithin the gate clerk takes his supper at the inn's corner table most evenings, Brann's guards drink there off duty, and Tilda waters Thistle at the inn's trough before her first fare.

docs.title: The board
docs.text:
Hamon hears every road story first. It is the nature of the place: tired travellers want a fire, a meal and someone to tell, and he is always the someone. For years he simply remembered them. Lately there have been too many to remember, and too many that someone else ought to hear, so this spring he nailed a broad board by the inn door and began writing them up on it in chalk: which bridge is down, which ford is high, where the wolves were seen and how many, which stretch of the Royal Road a wagon should not be on after dusk.

Travellers read it before they set out and add to it when they come in, and Merrick reads it before he reads anything else. The Guard sends a rider down to copy it some mornings. Hamon is proud of the board and a little afraid of it, because he has noticed that the stories on it grow worse each month, and that he now rubs out the old ones faster to make room.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Hamon wants a full house, a long supper and every guest back again. What he fears is a name he has learned and will never get to say a second time.

A quest might begin with a story on Hamon's board that no traveller admits to writing, or with Hamon asking someone to ride out and find a regular who is three days late.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Merrick: regular guest

docs.title: Hawise
docs.text:
Dyer

Town Selsior Where Riverside Role Craftsman Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Bright, impulsive and stained to the elbows. She talks about colours the way others talk about friends.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Hawise is thirty-three, the dyer of the Riverside, and she is stained to the elbows in a colour that changes with the day of the week. On Mondays it is woad blue, on Wednesdays the yellow of weld, on Fridays the rust of madder; and on Tuesdays, for reasons she will explain to anyone at great length, it is purple. She is bright, impulsive and talks about colours the way other people talk about friends. She will tell you that madder is moody and must be coaxed, that weld is cheerful but unreliable, that a good black is the most difficult friend a dyer can have, and that she is still waiting to meet the colour she has always wanted.

docs.title: The vats on the bank
docs.text:
Her dye yard sits on the riverbank a little upstream of the great mill: a row of vats steaming over low fires, poles hung with dripping cloth, and baskets of roots, bark, lichen and petals drying on every flat surface. She came to it at fourteen as the apprentice of the old dyer who worked the yard before her, a stooped, silent woman with permanently blue fingernails who taught her that a colour is half recipe and half patience, and that Hawise had none of the second. The old dyer died when Hawise was twenty-two and left her the yard, the vats and a box of recipes written in a code Hawise took two years to crack. She has run the yard alone ever since, with a girl or two to stir.

She dyes for the tailors of the old quarters, the theatres of the Row, and, through Isabeau the cloth merchant, for a good part of the city. Isabeau sells highland wool and fine cloth to tailors, theatres and the palace itself, and she can tell good wool by its smell. She is elegant, sharp-eyed and impossible to cheat, and Hawise, who is none of those things, adores her. Isabeau sends cloth down to the yard with notes in her elegant hand, and Hawise sends it back with the notes answered in purple.

docs.title: Hereward and the purple river
docs.text:
Her husband is Hereward, the miller, who runs the great water mill that grinds flour for half the city. He is steady, dusty and slow to anger, and he measures his words like flour, and they have been married nine years. He met her the first Tuesday she let a purple vat drain into the race, and he walked along the bank, slowly, to tell her that his wheel was turning purple. She told him it suited it. He thought about that for a long time and then asked her to supper.

He still complains that the river runs purple on Tuesdays, and it does, for about an hour, all the way past the mill. He says it frightens the fish and stains the flour sacks. Hawise says the fish have never looked better. It is their oldest joke and they both enjoy it far more than they let on. What Hereward does not joke about is the mill wheel, which needs rebuilding before winter and which he cannot afford alone. Hawise has been quietly putting by every coin the yard spares, and she has not told him, because she knows he would refuse it.

docs.title: The new colour
docs.text: Isabeau is planning a festival of colours in the market square, and she needs a dyer who can make a colour no one has seen. Hawise intends to be that dyer. She has tried crushed beetle wings, river weed, dried mussel shell, the bark of a tree from the edge of the Greenwood, and a lichen a carter swore came from the highlands. She has made seven new browns and one green so ugly that Hereward asked her to bury it. She has not yet made anything no one has seen, and the festival is coming.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Hawise wants her colour, and she wants to see it hung across the Crown Market with all of Selsior looking up at it. What she fears is that every colour has already been found, and that she will spend her life making slightly better versions of other people's.

A quest might begin with Hawise needing a rare dyestuff that grows somewhere dangerous outside the city, or with a vat that turns a colour overnight that she did not put in it, and that no one on the bank can name.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Hereward: husband
  • Isabeau: cloth merchant

docs.title: Helewise
docs.text:
Guard Quartermaster

Town Selsior Where Knights' Court Role Official Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Practical, thrifty and unshakeable. She knows how many arrows the Guard has to the last fletching.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Helewise is forty-nine, Quartermaster of the Royal Guard, and she knows how many arrows the Guard has to the last fletching. She also knows how many boots, helms, blankets, horseshoes, spoons and sacks of oats it has, and which of them are wearing thin, and who signed for the last whetstone and has not brought it back. She feeds, arms and clothes the whole Guard from a long storeroom under the Knights' Court, behind a counter with a ledger chained to it, and nothing leaves that room without her knowing. She is practical, thrifty and unshakeable, and the only person in the Court whom even Captain Rhys knocks before disturbing.

docs.title: Counted from a cradle
docs.text:
She grew up in the Crown Market, behind a dry-goods stall where her mother sold beans, lentils and dried peas by the scoop. Her mother, dead these many years now, had her counting scoops before she could read and haggling with carters before she could reach the counter, and Helewise has never lost the habit of believing that every coin is worth arguing for. She came to the Knights' Court at twenty as a clerk to the stores, because the Guard needed someone who could count, and she rose through the storeroom the way other guards rise through the ranks. She has been Quartermaster for fourteen years.

She haggles with the Crown Market's armourers as if the gold were her own. Her chief victim, and favourite opponent, is Vessa the armourer, who fits mail, helms and boots while her customers wait and who runs one of the two busiest forges in the market. The other belongs to Vessa's sister Selene, the weaponsmith, and the two sisters compete over everything. Helewise knows it and uses it shamelessly. She buys the Guard's mail from Vessa while mentioning, once, lightly, what Selene charges for blades; she buys the blades from Selene while wondering aloud what Vessa would say. Vessa calls her a bandit. Helewise calls it housekeeping.

docs.title: Bertrand
docs.text:
Her husband is Bertrand, the Drill Sergeant, who bellows at recruits at dawn and swears he can make a guard of anyone given a year and enough porridge. They met nineteen years ago over that porridge. He was demanding more for his recruits; she explained to him, to the last spoonful, exactly how much there was. She won. She usually does. They married that same year, and they have no children, and both of them say, separately and in the same tone, that a few hundred recruits through the yard is plenty.

She knows him better than anyone. She knows not to speak to him on the evenings when the patrol reports come in and he checks the names against his list, and she knows what it means when he goes quiet and marks a margin. On those evenings she makes his supper without asking and sits with him without talking, and the next morning she quietly sends a new pair of boots to the recruit he will shout at hardest.

docs.title: The boots
docs.text: Lately the numbers will not come right. Patrols ride further and fight more, and they are wearing out boots faster than Helewise can buy them, along with saddle leather, shield straps and cloaks torn by things that are not branches. The Guard has more recruits than it has ever had, and every one of them needs fitting. She has stretched the budget, patched what can be patched and haggled Vessa down until even Vessa looked tired. It is still not enough, and Helewise, who has never in her life let a column of figures beat her, is beginning to suspect that this one might.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Helewise wants every guard who rides out of the Court to ride out properly shod, properly fed and properly armed, and to come back the same way. What she fears is the day she has to tell Rhys that the Guard cannot equip the next intake, and see in his face that he already knows.

A quest might begin with Helewise needing a cartload of leather brought in from outside the city, because the market has run short, or with a crate of arrows that her ledger says was delivered and her storeroom says was not.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Bertrand: husband
  • Vessa: armourer

docs.title: Hereward
docs.text:
Miller

Town Selsior Where Riverside Role Craftsman Age Adult Sells Flour, meal and bran

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Steady, dusty and slow to anger. He measures his words like flour.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Hereward is forty-two, the miller of the great water mill on the Riverside, and he is dusty all the way through. Flour lives in his eyebrows, in the creases of his knuckles, in the seams of his coat; when he claps someone on the shoulder they come away white. He is steady, patient and slow to anger, and he measures his words the way he measures flour, carefully, by weight, with nothing spilled. He would rather say one true thing than three quick ones, and people who are used to Selsior's chatter sometimes mistake his silences for slowness. They are not. He is simply weighing.

docs.title: The great mill
docs.text:
The mill stands on the riverbank below the city, a tall stone-and-timber building with a race cut off the river and a great undershot wheel that turns, day and night, through every season but the hardest freeze. Inside, two pairs of stones grind wheat, rye and barley for half the bakers in Selsior, and the whole building shakes gently with them, so that Hereward says he cannot sleep anywhere that holds still.

His father ran the mill before him, and taught him to dress a millstone by the time he was fourteen, to hear a bearing going dry from the next room, and to read the river's height by the note of the wheel. His father died fifteen years ago and left him the mill, the debts and the wheel, and Hereward has paid off the debts. Lucan's barges bring him grain from upstream, and they have done business for years in the way two careful men do: few words, a firm hand, and neither ever short.

docs.title: Hawise
docs.text:
His wife is Hawise, the dyer, whose yard of steaming vats sits on the bank a little upstream of the mill. Nine years ago, on the first Tuesday she drained a purple vat into the river, Hereward watched his wheel come round the colour of a plum. He walked along the bank, slowly, and told her his wheel was turning purple. She told him it suited it. He thought about that for some time, and then he asked her to supper.

The river still runs purple past the mill for about an hour every Tuesday. He complains that it frightens the fish and stains the flour sacks, and she says the fish have never looked better, and it is the oldest joke in their house. He is the quiet half of the marriage, and he knows it, and he likes it. Hawise talks about colours the way he thinks about grain, and he listens to all of it. When she made a green so ugly he asked her to bury it, it was the longest speech he had made in a month.

docs.title: The wheel
docs.text: The wheel is the trouble. It is older than Hereward, and old timber in running water does not last forever. Paddles have split this year that he has patched twice, the shaft groans in a new place, and he knows, as surely as he knows the note of the stones, that it will not see another winter. He wants it rebuilt before the frosts. He cannot afford it alone, and he has said so to no one but Hawise, and he has said it to her only once, because he will not burden her with it. He does not know that she has been putting by every spare coin the yard makes for that very wheel. She knows he would refuse it.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Hereward wants the new wheel turning before winter and the mill grinding for another lifetime. What he fears is the morning the wheel stops and half the city's bread stops with it.

A quest might begin with Hereward needing great oak timbers floated down from upstream, past stretches of river the bargehands no longer like, or with something in the race at night that is strong enough to stop the wheel for the space of a breath.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Hawise: wife

docs.title: Hodge
docs.text:
Lane Child

Town Selsior Where Old Quarter Role Child Age Child

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Adventurous, sneaky and loyal to his friends. He climbs anything that holds still.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Hodge is ten years old and has never in his life used a door when a wall would do. He lives in a crooked house off a courtyard in the old quarters, where his mother Gytha runs the washing yard, and he knows the rooftops above it better than most people know their own street. If a thing holds still, Hodge will climb it. If it does not hold still, he will wait until it does.

docs.title: The old quarters from above
docs.text:
The old quarters grew without a plan, and from street level they are a maze of winding lanes, narrow passages and hidden courtyards. From above they are something else: a second city of ridges, chimney stacks, gutters and the skywalks that cross over the streets, and Hodge has made it his own. He knows which tiles are loose, which skywalks sway, which chimneys are warm in winter and which roofs belong to people who will shout. He can cross half the old quarters without touching the cobbles, and he is quite proud of the fact that his mother has never once caught him at it, even if she has heard plenty about it.

He is sneaky, adventurous and fiercely loyal. His two best friends are Mab, the pie seller's daughter, who practises cartwheels by the Great Bell and wants to be the most famous performer in Selsior, and Wat, the errand boy, who used to pick pockets in the Crown Market and still knows every alley shortcut in the city. Between the three of them there is no corner of Selsior they cannot reach. Mab handles the crowds, Wat handles the ground and Hodge handles everything above it. When one of them is in trouble, the other two turn up, usually from an unexpected direction.

docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Gytha is tough, sharp-tongued and quick to laugh, and she is raising Hodge with help from her family. Hodge's father is gone. Gytha does not talk about him, and Hodge has learned not to ask. His grandmother Winifred tells stories on her doorstep every evening, and Hodge grew up on them, as half the children of the old quarters did. He likes the ones about the Last Stand at the Tree best, the Savage warriors holding the line, and he has noticed that Winifred tells that one a little differently every time and never says which version is true.

What Gytha wants for her son is a trade: something with tools in it, something that keeps him in the city and brings him home every night. What Hodge wants is the Royal Guard.

docs.title: The broom handle
docs.text:
Gytha has forbidden it, flatly and more than once. So Hodge trains in secret. Most dawns, while the washing yard is still dark, he crosses the rooftops to a ridge where he can see down into the practice yard of the Knights' Court, and he copies the recruits at their drills, cut for cut, with an old broom handle. He has watched Drill Sergeant Bertrand bellow at the same recruits so often that he can bellow the corrections along with him, quietly, so nobody hears. He thinks he is getting good. He is not wrong, exactly, but he has never held a real sword, and he has no idea how heavy one is.

He has also noticed, from his ridge, a cloaked stranger who trains in a corner of the Court at dawn with one of the Swordmasters. Hodge has decided this stranger must be someone very important in disguise, and he is determined to find out who.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Hodge wants to be a guard, to wear the Guard's colours down the middle of the street instead of across the roofs above it. What he fears is disappointing his mother, and, more privately, that she is right.

A quest might begin with Hodge spotting something on the rooftops of the old quarters that nobody on the ground has seen, or with the broom handle finally being found.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Mab: friend
  • Wat: friend
  • Winifred: grandmother
  • Gytha: mother

docs.title: Hollis
docs.text:
Gate Guard

Town Selsior Where Selsior Gate Role Guard Age Young In the game Hollis

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Friendly, chatty and a little too fond of the view. He starts every greeting stern and ends it smiling.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Hollis is twenty-four, a gate guard of Selsior, and he has the best view in the city and knows it. He stands twelve hours a day at the great gate, where the Royal Road runs out east past the Greenwood toward Kaldemor, and he still likes looking out over it. Most guards stop seeing the road after their first season. Hollis has not. He watches the light move across the fields, the carts come over the rise, the weather walk in from the east, and he would tell you, if you stood still long enough, that it is never the same road twice.

docs.title: The stern start
docs.text:
"State your business," he tells every traveller who comes up to the gate, in a voice as stern as he can make it. Then he looks at them properly, sees a tired face and a dusty pack, and the sternness falls off him like a cloak. "Ah, a traveller. Welcome." He cannot help it. Brann, the Gate Sergeant, taught him to start every greeting stern, because a gate guard who smiles first is a gate guard who gets lied to, and Hollis took the lesson to heart. He just never learned to finish the same way. Brann grumbles about it. He has never told him to stop, and Hollis has noticed that travellers tell him things they would never tell the Sergeant, and that Brann always wants to hear them.

He grew up in a narrow house in the inner streets of the city, where the only view from his window was the wall of the house opposite, close enough to touch. Perhaps that is why he loves the gate. His parents, a bricklayer and his wife, moved out to the farming country past the Greenwood when he was nineteen, to a cottage with a garden, and they write to him twice a year to tell him how far they can see from their door. He joined the Royal Guard the same year, scraped through his trials, and was sent to the gate a year later. He has asked for no other posting since.

docs.title: Mind the step
docs.text:
There is a worn step under the arch of the great gate, hollowed by centuries of feet, and it catches every third traveller who is looking up at the walls instead of down at the road. Hollis warns them all. "Mind the step," he says, "and the Sergeant," and the travellers laugh, and Brann, if he is in earshot, does not. It is the closest thing the gate has to a motto.

His friends are the gate's regulars. Tilda drives the Selsior cab from the stand just outside, and on slow afternoons she leans against her cab and Hollis leans against the gate and they trade news of the road: who came in hurt, which carters are late, which towns the cab will not go to because the passenger has never walked there. Tilda has never driven into the wilds and says that rule has never seemed wiser, and Hollis has started to agree with her. Then there is Biscuit, the gate dog, who greets Hollis every morning before he greets anyone else. Half the gate guards claim to have named the dog. Hollis claims it loudest, and has a long story about it that changes a little every time.

docs.title: The road, lately
docs.text: Hollis likes the view, but he is not a fool, and the view has been changing. There are fewer travellers on foot, more wagons riding close together with hired swords on the tailboards, and more people coming in limping. Some evenings, when Baldwin's lamps are lit by the gate, Biscuit stands at the edge of their light with his ears up, staring into the dark, and Hollis finds himself staring too.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Hollis wants to walk the Royal Road himself one day, all the way to the end of what he can see and past it, just to know what is there. What he fears is that by the time he gets the chance, the road will not be safe to walk.

A quest might begin with Hollis asking a traveller what is just over the rise to the east, because something has been moving there at dusk, or with a traveller he greeted stern and welcomed warmly who turns out to have been lying.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Brann: sergeant
  • Tilda: friend

docs.title: Hugh
docs.text:
Warden of the Great Bell

Town Selsior Where Plaza Role Guard Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Solemn, stubborn and proud of a duty most people forget. He polishes the bell's dais every morning.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Hugh is seventy-one, the Warden of the Great Bell, and every morning before the plaza wakes he is on his knees on the bell's dais with a cloth and a tin of polish. The dais is stone and does not strictly need polishing. Hugh polishes it anyway, every step and every edge, and then he stands beside the Bell with his hands behind his back and his chin up, and he stays there until dusk. He is solemn, stubborn and proud of a duty that most of the city has forgotten exists.

docs.title: The Bell and the man who keeps it
docs.text:
The Great Bell stands on its dais in the middle of the plaza, on the spot where the founding treaty was signed, cast from metal given by all four peoples. It rings only when a new monarch is crowned. Hugh will tell anyone who asks that it rings for no one else: not for festivals, not for victories, not for weddings, and certainly not for children who want to hear what it sounds like. He has said it so many times that the plaza's regulars can say it along with him, and some of them do.

He served in the Royal Guard as a young man, on the walls and at the palace, and thirty years ago, at forty-one, in King Bertram's reign, he was given the Bell when the old Warden died. In all that time it has rung once. Sixteen years ago, at Queen Aveline's coronation, Hugh stood on the dais and rang it himself, and he says it was the proudest morning of his life and also the most frightening, because the whole city was listening and the Bell was louder than he had ever imagined. He was a boy of thirteen at King Bertram's coronation and heard it then too, from the back of the crowd. He has not heard it ring since Queen Aveline's coronation.

He has never married. He says the Bell does not leave a man much time for courting, and that it is, at least, a very good listener.

docs.title: Baldwin and the plaza
docs.text:
His younger brother Baldwin is the lamplighter, and between them they keep the plaza by day and by dusk: Hugh at the Bell from dawn, Baldwin with his ladder and taper when the light goes. They are not men of many words with each other. They do not need them. Baldwin lights the lamps around the dais last, and Hugh waits until they are lit before he goes home, and that is how most of their evenings have ended for thirty years.

Mirabel dances by the Bell every evening and swears she hears it sing at dusk when the wind is kind. Hugh tells her it has not rung since the coronation and that the wind makes many noises. They have argued about it, happily, for years; it is one of the best parts of his day, and he suspects it is one of the best parts of hers. Fulke, who plays for her, has written a verse about the Bell humming at dusk, and Hugh pretends not to hear it. Then there is Mab, the pie seller's daughter, who turns cartwheels at the foot of the dais. Hugh tells her off every afternoon. He has never yet actually stopped her, and he has caught himself watching to see if she lands.

docs.title: What he does not say
docs.text: Here is the thing Hugh has never admitted to anyone: on still evenings, when there is no wind at all, he sometimes thinks he hears it hum. Not ring; hum, very low, the way a cup hums when you run a wet finger round its rim, so faint he is never sure it is not his own blood in his ears. Mirabel hears the Bell sing when the wind is kind. Hugh hears it when there is no wind at all, and that is what frightens him, because the wind would be an explanation. He has not told Mirabel, because she would be delighted. He has not told Baldwin, though he knows his brother has noticed him going quiet when the light fails.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Hugh wants the Bell to mean what it has always meant, and to ring only for a crowning. What he fears is that it is trying to say something else, and that he is the only one standing close enough to hear.

A quest might begin with Hugh asking a traveller to sit with him by the Bell one still evening and tell him honestly what they hear, or with a hairline crack in the lip of the Bell, one morning, that was not there the evening before.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Mirabel: friend and sparring partner in argument
  • Baldwin: brother

docs.title: Ida
docs.text:
Night Watchwoman

Town Selsior Where Old Quarter Role Guard Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Watchful, dry and unafraid of the dark. She knows the old quarters by sound alone.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Ida is thirty-eight, the night watchwoman of the old quarters, and she knows them by sound alone. Put her blindfolded in any lane between the plaza and the river and she will tell you where she is from the echo of her own footsteps, the drip of a particular gutter, the creak of a particular sign. She walks the old quarters every night for the Royal Guard with a lantern in one hand and a stout stick in the other, and she has never once been afraid of the dark. She is watchful, dry and very hard to surprise.

docs.title: Born under the skywalks
docs.text:
She grew up in the old quarters, in a cramped house at the bottom of a lane so steep it has steps instead of cobbles. Her father, long dead now, worked the old drains under the lanes, clearing them and mending the brickwork, and as a girl Ida carried his lamp. She learned the city from below before she learned it from above: which lanes have water running under them, where the old channels join, which gratings carry a voice and which swallow it. Her mother kept a mending stall. Both are gone, and Ida has no brothers or sisters.

She joined the Royal Guard at twenty, eighteen years ago, and asked for the night watch within two years. Nobody else wanted it. Ida took it gladly, because the old quarters at night are quieter, stranger and more honest than they are by day, and because she could hear them properly at last. She has walked the night watch for sixteen years.

docs.title: Days and nights
docs.text:
Her husband is Dickon, the skywalk carpenter, who builds and mends the walkways that cross above the old quarters' streets. He works by day and she works by night, so they meet twice a day, at dawn when she comes home and at dusk when she goes out, and have done for the twelve years they have been married. Dickon whistles while hanging over thin air and Ida has long since stopped watching him do it. She says she married him because he is the only man in Selsior who has never once asked her whether she is frightened on her rounds, and he says he married her because she can tell from the sound of a plank whether it will hold.

She has the night's friends. Baldwin the lamplighter passes her most nights on his long way home, and they trade a nod and, on long nights, a sentence. Lettice the rat catcher and her terrier sometimes walk a lane with her, and Ida trusts the terrier's nose as much as her own ears. Each morning she reports to the Knights' Court, and Captain Rhys reads every word.

docs.title: The scratching
docs.text: For some months now, on her rounds, Ida has heard something scratching under the old drains. Not rats: she grew up among rats and knows every sound they make. This is slower, heavier, and it seems to move along the old channels from one grating to the next, keeping pace with her, then stopping when she stops. She has knelt at the gratings with her lantern and seen nothing but black water. She has told Rhys, plainly and without decoration, and he did not laugh, which worried her more than if he had. Lettice says the rats in the deep tunnels have grown bigger and bolder lately and that she now charges double to go down there. Ida does not think it is the rats. She thinks the rats are leaving.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Ida wants to know what is down there, and she would like to find out before it finds a way up. What she fears is not the dark; it is the morning she comes home and cannot tell Dickon that the old quarters are safe.

A quest might begin with Ida asking for someone to go down into the old drains with her father's old map, which she still keeps, or with a grating in a quiet lane found pushed up from below.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Rhys: captain
  • Dickon: husband
  • Tancred: her late father's drain-mending partner

docs.text:

Town Selsior Where Crown Market Sells Highland wool, linen and dyed cloth

docs.text:

Town Selsior Where Crown Market Sells Urbanograd inventions, gadgets and curiosities
