docs.title: Edgar Penhallow
docs.text:
Guild Apprentice from Selsior

Town Urbanograd Where Workshops Row Role Craftsman Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Polite, earnest and slowly loosening up. Edgar still says please to doors.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Edgar Penhallow still says please to doors. He does it under his breath, especially to the heavy ones, and he has been in Urbanograd long enough now to be embarrassed by it and not long enough to stop. He is nineteen, polite, earnest and very tidy, a guild apprentice from Selsior with ink on his cuffs and a satchel that holds four full notebooks and a fifth he started last week. He is, everyone on Workshops Row agrees, slowly loosening up. Last week he was seen without a collar.

docs.title: The guild boy
docs.text:
Edgar was born in Selsior, in a narrow house near the Crown Market, the second son of a family that has belonged to the Cordwainers' Guild, the capital's guild of shoe- and bootmakers, for as long as anyone has kept count. His parents and elder brother are still there, cutting leather to the guild's patterns, and they are proud of him in a careful, guild-approved way. At twelve Edgar was apprenticed in the guild hall, where he learned to cut, stitch and last a shoe exactly as it had been done for generations, and to ask permission before trying anything else.

This spring the guild sent him to Urbanograd for a season. Selsior's guilds, which once wanted the Walkers brought home, now send their apprentices to see what the city's workshops have come up with, and Edgar's masters wanted a report: what the bootmakers of Urbanograd do differently, and whether any of it is respectable enough to copy. Edgar arrived with a clean notebook and very firm ideas about what he would find.

docs.title: Four notebooks
docs.text:
He has filled four notebooks since. The first is careful and full of measurements. The second is mostly drawings of Rivet's rope-and-pulley lift, which he cannot stop looking at. The third contains a list of every color of Dyna's coats he has no name for, a diagram of how Jinx keeps five balls in the air, and a page of notes on the Open Table headed "Who is in charge?" with nothing written under it. The fourth is about boots, because of Cobble.

Cobble makes the soft-soled boots the rooftop runners swear by, and Edgar has never seen anything like them: no guild pattern, no stamp, just a sole that grips a wet slate and an upper that will outlive its owner. Edgar wants, more than he has wanted anything, to learn how they are made. He has asked Cobble to take him on as an apprentice for the rest of the season. Cobble looked at his hands, said they were the wrong sort, and went back to work. Edgar has asked twice more since, very politely, and now sweeps the doorstep of Cobble's shop every morning in case it helps. Cobble has not said no a fourth time, which Edgar has decided to treat as progress.

docs.title: Rivet
docs.text: Rivet, who built the lift, is the first friend Edgar made in the city, and the most unexpected. Rivet is cocky where Edgar is careful, loud where Edgar is polite, and builds things without asking anyone's leave. Edgar admires all of it. He follows Rivet about asking how things work, and Rivet pretends to be annoyed and answers every question. Lately Rivet has started letting him hold the tools, and once, on a windy evening at the top of the lift, told him he would make a decent builder if he stopped apologizing to the ropes.

docs.title: What he has not written home
docs.text:
Edgar's season ends when the summer does, and then he is due back at the guild hall with his report. He has begun to suspect he does not want to go. He has not written home about it. His letters to his parents are cheerful, detailed and entirely about boots, and every one of them leaves out the only thing he actually wants to say. He fears disappointing them, and fears even more becoming someone who never found out what he might have made.

A quest might carry Edgar's letter home, or the honest one he has not yet sent, help him prove his hands to Cobble, or fetch good leather through the dangerous roads for a pair of boots he wants to make himself.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Rivet: friend
  • Cobble: unimpressed teacher

docs.title: Bastian 'Bellows' Krell
docs.text:
Loudest Voice at the Table

Town Urbanograd Where Great Hall Role Council Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Enormous voice, enormous opinions, enormous heart. He changes his mind loudly and without shame.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Bastian Krell has spoken at every Open Table for twenty years, and he has never once been short. He has an enormous voice, enormous opinions and an enormous heart, and all three arrive in a room before the rest of him does. He is fifty, broad as a door, with a beard he trims for important debates and forgets about the rest of the time. Everyone calls him Bellows. He is the loudest voice at the Table, and the most generous, and he changes his mind loudly and without the slightest shame.

docs.title: Where the voice came from
docs.text:
Bastian was born in Urbanograd, the son of a Night Market crier, long dead now, who could sell a stale bun across three streets, and he grew up learning to throw his voice off the old fortress walls for fun. The nickname came first, for the voice. The trade came later and, he says, to make the nickname honest: he makes and mends bellows for the forges, kilns and glass furnaces of Workshops Row, from a cramped leather-smelling shop whose door is always open so he can join in any argument passing by. Ferro and Tinsel both keep their fires going with his bellows, and both have learned that buying one includes an opinion on whatever the Table debated the night before.

He first stood up at the Open Table at thirty, to object to a new tax on lamp oil, and found he liked it far too much to sit down. He has not missed a gathering since.

docs.title: At the Table
docs.text:
Bastian is Rook's favorite heckler, and Rook is his most patient listener. He interrupts, applauds, groans, quotes the Charter and sometimes, gloriously, argues both sides of a question in one speech. He is also the first to clap for a good point made against him, and the first to stand up and say, at full volume, "I was wrong, and that was an excellent argument." The Table has learned to wait an hour before treating anything Bastian says as final.

This year he is campaigning, at length, for a covered bridge over Lantern Square, so that the Night Market can run in the rain. He has drawings. He has costings. He has a speech about the dignity of a dry pepper bun. The bridge has filled so many evenings that Rivet, who wants the Table's leave for a second rooftop lift, has twice been talked over waiting for a turn, and Bastian, when he noticed, was so mortified that he has privately promised to give up his own time at the next gathering. He has not yet told Rivet.

docs.title: Mags
docs.text:
Bastian married Mags, the cook of the Great Hall, seventeen years ago, after spending most of a winter praising her stew in the middle of debates about something else entirely. He still maintains that it was the most persuasive campaign of his life. Mags kept her own name and still claims she married him to stop him talking about the stew; Bastian says she has not succeeded.

He tries out every new speech on her while she stirs the great pot, and when he changes his mind she is always the first to hear it. She supports the bridge in public and teases him about it at home, and her opinion is the only one in the city that can make Bastian lower his voice.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Bastian wants the bridge, and a city that stays loud. He fears, though he hides it under the noise, that the Table is too slow for the trouble on the roads, and that one day it will talk until dawn while something at the gate will not wait. Lately his speeches have started to end with Brindle's call for volunteers, whatever they began with.

A quest might gather the timber, measurements or signatures Bastian needs for his bridge, help him make amends to someone his voice has drowned out, or carry one of his famous speeches to an audience who badly needs persuading.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Rook: patient listener
  • Mags: wife

docs.title: Bolt
docs.text:
Tinker's Apprentice

Town Urbanograd Where Workshops Row Role Craftsman Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Eager, clumsy and full of ideas that almost work. Bolt apologizes to every machine he breaks.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Bolt is sorry. He is sorry to the kettle he overfilled, sorry to the spring-trap that snapped shut on his sleeve, sorry to the clockwork bird whose wing he bent, and very sorry indeed to the door of Margo Venn's workshop, which he has not yet blown off but has come close to. Bolt is sixteen, gangly, eager and clumsy, with soot on his nose, a pencil behind each ear and a head so full of ideas that they keep falling out half-finished. He apologizes to every machine he breaks, out loud and sincerely, and Workshops Row has long since stopped laughing about it, because it is clear that he means it.

docs.title: From the harbour to the Row
docs.text:
Bolt grew up in Bain Harbour, the youngest son of a net-mender, in a house full of rope and gull noise and brothers. His parents and brothers still live there; they write when a cart gets through, and play no part in his life here. As a boy he took apart everything on the quay that had a moving part: winches, pulleys, a ship's bell, a pump that was working perfectly well until he got to it. Nobody in the harbour quite knew what to do with him. When he was fourteen, a carter told him about a street in Urbanograd where people built whatever they liked and blew their own doors off, and Bolt was on the next wagon inland.

He arrived on Workshops Row two years ago with a bag of tools and no plan, and stood outside the scorched door of Margo's workshop for most of a morning. When she came out to see what he wanted, he asked if she needed someone to sweep. She did. He has been her apprentice ever since.

docs.title: The apprentice
docs.text:
Bolt does most of the sweeping and all of the testing. When Margo builds something, Bolt is the one who turns it on first, stands where she says to stand, writes down what it does and, more often than not, puts out what it set alight. He has tested a self-stirring pot that stirred itself out of the window, a door-knocker that answered back, three versions of a spring-trap and, this year, Margo's spark lamp, which he has fired at a broom, a barrel and, once, by accident, himself. He says it is very bright. His eyebrows say the same.

Margo explains every invention three ways, with drawings, with her hands and by shouting, and Bolt loves all three. She thinks he has good hands and better instincts, and does not tell him so nearly often enough. He thinks she is the cleverest person on Veligor, and he is nearly right.

docs.title: The secret
docs.text:
Bolt's secret is Rivet. Across the Row, at the end by the old granary, stands the rope-and-pulley lift Rivet built to haul crates up to the Rooftops, and Bolt thinks it is the most beautiful machine in the city. Not because it sparkles; it does not. Because it works, every day, simply, for everyone. Margo and Rivet argue across the street about gears against ropes and sparks against sense, and Bolt, sweeping, finds himself agreeing with Rivet more often than he should. He thinks some of Rivet's ideas are better than Margo's. He has a notebook of drawings of the counterweight, hidden under his sleeping mat, and he has never told a soul.

He is afraid to say it. Margo has been kind to him, and he cannot bear the thought of hurting her. And he is fairly sure Rivet would never stop gloating. So he keeps quiet, and watches the lift whenever he is sent out for parts, and takes the long way back.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Bolt wants to build one thing of his own that works the first time, and he has an idea, half-drawn, for a machine that would combine Margo's springs with Rivet's counterweights. He fears that showing it to either of them would mean choosing between them.

A quest might help Bolt test an invention somewhere safe, carry a message across the Row that he is too nervous to deliver, or find the parts for his first machine of his own.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Margo 'Sparks' Venn: mentor

docs.title: Brindle
docs.text:
Captain of the Gate Watch

Town Urbanograd Where Gate Walk Role Guard Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Steady, plain-spoken and dryly funny. Brindle believes in good boots, good lanterns and checking twice.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Brindle is Captain of the Gate Watch, which sounds grander than it is. The Watch is a small band of volunteers who keep the old fortress gate at the end of the Gate Walk, and its captain is the volunteer who has stayed longest and complained least. Brindle is thirty-nine, steady and plain-spoken, with a dry wit that surfaces at the worst moments and rescues most of them. Brindle believes in three things: good boots, good lanterns and checking twice.

docs.title: How Brindle came to the gate
docs.text: Brindle grew up in Urbanograd, the child of a family of rope-makers, and was meant to make rope. Brindle tried, and was good at it, and found it unbearably quiet. At twenty-two Brindle signed on with the Watch for a single season, for something to do on summer nights, and never left. In those days the Watch was mostly a matter of greeting late carts and settling quarrels over tolls nobody actually paid. Seven years ago the old captain, Garran Holt, hung up his lantern and moved to a cottage near Kaldemor to keep bees, and the volunteers turned to Brindle without a vote, because Brindle was already doing the job.

docs.title: The Watch now
docs.text:
The job has changed since then. Monsters come closer to the walls every year. Carts arrive scratched, late or not at all, and travelers stumble in with bites that Patch and Ivo spend the night cleaning. Brindle keeps a slate by the gate with the number of sightings each week, and the numbers only go one way.

Knox is the backbone of the Watch, a big, gentle guard who has kept the gate for ten years, three longer than Brindle has been captain, and who knows every regular traveler by face. Brindle trusts him completely and often asks his advice. Dagny takes the night watch with her two lamps and her nervous chatter, and Brindle has noticed, as she has not, that she is the one who never steps back from the dark. Brindle is trying to find a way to tell her without frightening her off.

Shade, Hatch, Torvi and the other adventurers who drift through the Gate Walk are not part of the Watch, but Brindle counts on them anyway, and buys more of their drinks than the Watch's purse can afford.

docs.title: At the Table
docs.text: Brindle reports to the Open Table and is a good friend of Rook, the Caller. This year Brindle has stood up at the Table again and again to ask for more volunteers. People listen, nod, cheer, and then mostly go back to their workshops. Brindle does not blame them; the city was built by painters and players, not soldiers. But Brindle has begun to wonder what happens the night something gets past the gate before anyone has decided whose turn it is to stop it.

docs.title: What Brindle wants
docs.text:
Brindle wants twenty more volunteers, a second lantern on every post and a full night's sleep, in roughly that order. Brindle fears losing someone on the road, and fears even more being the person who sent them out.

A quest might help Brindle recruit volunteers from the workshops and stages, scout what has been coming closer to the walls at night, or deliver word to the Watch from a cart that never arrived.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Knox: guard
  • Dagny 'Two-Lamps' Roe: guard
  • Rook: friend

docs.title: Cobble
docs.text:
Bootmaker

Town Urbanograd Where Workshops Row Role Craftsman Age Elder Sells Boots, rooftop slippers and repairs

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Grumpy, honest and proud. Cobble says a boot should outlive its owner and means it.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Cobble says a boot should outlive its owner, and means it. There are boots walking about Urbanograd today that Cobble made before their wearers were born, resoled, restitched and handed down, and Cobble can tell you whose feet each pair was cut for. He is seventy-six, grumpy, honest and proud, with a voice like a creaking stair and hands so hard and sure that he can feel a flaw in a hide with his eyes shut. His shop on Workshops Row is small, dark and smells of leather and beeswax, and it has no sign. Anyone who needs to ask where it is, Cobble says, does not yet need his boots.

docs.title: The soft-soled boot
docs.text:
Cobble was born in Urbanograd, in a house on the Row, and at fourteen went to work for an old bootmaker named Henrike Tull, a Walker's daughter who had never belonged to any guild and was proud of it. She taught him that a boot is made for one pair of feet and one kind of ground, and nothing else matters. When she died, fifty-two years ago, she left him the shop, the lasts and her bad temper, and he has kept all three in good repair.

Urbanograd has a kind of ground no other town has: slate roofs, wet tiles, plank bridges and chimney ledges. Cobble spent his first years on his own perfecting a boot for it, with a soft, grippy sole sewn in a pattern of his own invention and an upper that bends like a glove and wears like iron. The rooftop runners took to it at once. It is the boot they swear by still.

docs.title: Three generations of Kites
docs.text:
Cobble has made boots for three generations of Kites. He made the first pair for Kite's grandmother, who ran messages across the city when he was a young man, and later the first pair for Kite's mother, and a few years ago the first pair for Kite, who holds the record for the run from the Gate Walk to the Great Hall and tells Cobble about it every visit. Cobble pretends not to listen and keeps a note of every record on the back of his shop door. Kite is his most loyal customer, and the only one allowed to criticize the stitching, because Kite has earned it.

Rooftop folk come to him for slippers and repairs too, and so do the actors of the Old Barracks, who need shoes that will not slip on a cart. He is fair in his prices, scathing in his opinions, and never once late with a pair.

docs.title: The wrong sort of hands
docs.text:
Cobble wants an apprentice. He is old enough to know that the soft-soled boot will die with him otherwise, and the thought frightens him more than anything on the roads. But he has rejected every one who has asked, for having the wrong sort of hands: too soft, too quick, too impatient, too eager to be finished. He cannot explain what the right sort looks like, only that he will know them.

This year the most persistent candidate is Edgar Penhallow, a guild apprentice visiting from Selsior, who has asked three times and been refused once out loud and twice with a grunt. Edgar's hands are guild hands, neat and careful and used to cutting by pattern, and Cobble said so. Edgar now sweeps Cobble's doorstep every morning. Cobble has not told him to stop, and lately has started leaving a scrap of hide and an awl by the door, as if by accident, to see what the boy does with them.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Cobble wants to hand on the boot before his hands give out. He fears dying with it, and fears almost as much choosing wrong. Good leather comes in from outside the walls less often each season, and the hides that do arrive are poorer; he hoards the best for the runners.

A quest might bring a load of good hides safely through the roads, find Cobble the right sort of hands, or recover a pair of old Kite boots that has gone missing from the shop door.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Kite: loyal customer
  • Edgar Penhallow: would-be apprentice

docs.text:

Town Urbanograd Where Night Market Sells Healing tonics, mana draughts and remedies

docs.title: Dagny 'Two-Lamps' Roe
docs.text:
Night Watch Guard

Town Urbanograd Where Gate Walk Role Guard Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Jumpy, sharp-eyed and talkative to fight off the dark. She carries two lamps because one went out once.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Dagny Roe keeps the gate on the night watch, and she carries two lamps. One hangs from her belt and one from her hand, both trimmed, both full, both lit before the sun is properly down. She carries two because one went out once. Everyone at the Gate Walk calls her Two-Lamps, and she has stopped minding. She is twenty-one, jumpy and sharp-eyed, and she talks: to the other guards, to the gate, to the moths, to the dark itself. It keeps the dark from getting the last word.

docs.title: From the harbour
docs.text:
Dagny grew up in Bain Harbour, on the Waterfront, where her family has rendered lamp oil from fish for three generations and sold it to every lamp, lantern and galley stove along the quay. Her parents and her two older brothers are still there, stirring the vats, and they write to her twice a year, mostly about the weather. Dagny was meant to stir the vats too. She was good at it, and could not bear the smell or the sameness, and at eighteen she came inland to see the city everyone sang about. She meant to stay a summer. She has stayed three years.

She found work hauling oil for the lamp-sellers of the Night Market, and a year later, when Brindle stood up at the Open Table asking for volunteers for the Gate Watch, Dagny surprised herself by putting her hand up. Brindle gave her the night watch, because nobody else wanted it, and because a girl who had trimmed and filled every kind of lamp on the Waterfront already knew more about keeping a flame alive in the wind than anyone else in the Watch.

docs.title: The night the lamp went out
docs.text: In her first month on the gate, on a wet night in late autumn, her lamp guttered and died, and for a long minute she stood in pitch darkness with the road in front of her and something moving on it. It turned out to be a lost goat. She has never forgiven it. The next evening she came to the gate with two lamps, and she has carried two ever since.

docs.title: What she has seen
docs.text:
This year Dagny has seen eyes in the dark beyond the road more often than last year. Pairs of them, low in the brush, catching the lamplight and holding still. Some nights they come close enough to the walls that she can hear them breathing. She reports every sighting to Brindle, who chalks them on the weekly slate by the gate, and she has noticed the numbers only go one way.

What Dagny has not noticed is that she is the one who never steps back. When something moves out there, she raises both lamps, steps forward to the edge of the light and calls out to it, talking all the while. She thinks this is because she is too frightened to think of anything else. Brindle has seen it, and thinks it is courage, and is trying to find a way to tell her without frightening her off. Knox, who has kept the gate for ten years, brings her a carved wooden owl now and then to keep her company, and has started to call her the bravest of them, which she assumes is a joke.

docs.title: Patch
docs.text: Patch, the herbalist of the Gate Walk, is Dagny's friend. She tends travelers who stumble in through the gate with monster bites and scrapes, and on bad nights Dagny is the one who brings them to her door. Patch scolds the patients while bandaging them and scolds Dagny for standing too near the road, and then makes her a cup of something hot and bitter that Dagny swears is the only reason she survives until dawn. In return Dagny walks Patch home after late patients, two lamps lighting the way.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Dagny wants to see what the eyes belong to, and in daylight, please. She fears the night both lamps go out, and, more than that, the night something comes out of the dark that talking will not stop.

A quest might stand the night watch beside Dagny, track whatever leaves its prints by the road in the morning, or gather the herbs Patch needs from fields Dagny can see from the gate but cannot leave it to reach.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Brindle: captain
  • Patch: healer

docs.title: Dex
docs.text:
Plays the Grandee

Town Urbanograd Where Old Barracks Theatre Role Performer Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: A born clown with a booming voice and an ego to match, but generous with every laugh he gets.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Dex has played the pompous grandee in Juna Marrow's play for fifteen years, and every Walkout Day the whole square waits for his entrance the way children wait for snow. He is forty-one, big and booming, a born clown with a voice that can rattle the shutters on the far side of Lantern Square and an ego to match. He is also the most generous actor in the Old Barracks Troupe. He will take a laugh anywhere he can find one, and then hand it straight to whoever is standing next to him.

docs.title: The part
docs.text:
The grandee is the villain of Juna's comedy: a puffed-up Selsior worthy who bans everything fun, falls off things and is finally chased off the cart by the market crowd. It is the second-best part in the play, and Dex would argue the best. Old Bellamy Stroud, who directed the troupe for decades, cast him in it fifteen years ago, when Dex was twenty-six and had been playing the back end of a mule for three seasons. Two years later Bellamy died and Dina Finch took over the troupe, and she inherited Dex the way one inherits a beloved, noisy dog. They shout at each other at every rehearsal and would walk into fire for each other.

Dex knows every line of every part in the play, not just his own, and mouths along with the whole thing from the wings. When Rue won the part of Juna this spring, he took her aside and taught her where the laughs fall, how to wait for them and how to stand so the grandee's hat does not block her face. Thimble keeps that hat, an absurd tower of purple felt and feathers, locked away between shows, and Dex has never once been allowed to take it home.

docs.title: Sprout
docs.text:
Dex's son, Sprout, plays the market urchin who cheers for Juna in the first scene, and steals the show every year. He is eight, giggly, loud and never still, and he has learned every part in the play by accident, from growing up backstage. He wants to play the grandee one day so that he can wear the hat. Dex pretends to be outraged by the ambition and is secretly the proudest man in Urbanograd.

Sprout's mother, Lark, sang in the troupe's chorus and died of a fever when Sprout was barely a year old. Dex has raised the boy since among costume baskets and painted flats, with half the troupe as aunts and uncles, and has never once let him see his father sad in daylight. On the anniversary he takes Sprout up to the Rooftops to watch the lanterns come on, and they sing one of her songs, badly, together.

docs.title: A serious role
docs.text:
What Dex wants, just once, is to play something serious. Not a grandee, not a fool, not a man who falls off a cart. A grieving king, perhaps, or an old soldier, or a father who has lost something. He has learned the great tragic speeches by heart and recites them to the empty theatre in the early mornings. Nobody will take him seriously. The moment he steps on stage, audiences start smiling in anticipation, and the moment he opens his mouth they laugh, whatever comes out of it.

Dina knows he wants it. She has not yet found a part he could play without the audience laughing, and she worries about telling him so. Dex suspects she worries, and that hurts more than a refusal would.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Dex wants one night in which a whole audience goes silent because of him. He fears he is only ever funny, and that Sprout will grow up thinking his father was nothing but a hat.

A quest might find Dex a serious play worth staging, carry a script to the Old Barracks from a writer in another town, or help him rehearse in secret somewhere nobody will laugh.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Dina Finch: director
  • Sprout: son

docs.title: Dimity 'Inkpot' Ash
docs.text:
Scribe of the Open Table

Town Urbanograd Where Great Hall Role Official Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Precise, ink-stained and secretly delighted by every argument. She writes down the jokes as carefully as the decisions.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Dimity Ash sits at a small sloping desk beside the Caller's chair in the Great Hall, and she writes down everything. Every motion, every vote, every speech, every heckle, every joke. Especially the jokes. She is forty, precise and permanently ink-stained, with a pen behind each ear and a third in her hand, and the whole city calls her Inkpot because she once knocked one over onto a visiting guild master from Selsior and recorded the moment in the minutes, word for word. She looks severe. She is, in fact, secretly delighted by every argument the Table has ever had.

docs.title: The record
docs.text:
Dimity has kept the Table's record for twelve years. The Open Table has no lord and no chieftain, only a Caller chosen each year and whoever turns up with something to say, so the record is the closest thing the city has to a memory. If someone claims the Table agreed to something nine years ago, it is Dimity who goes to the shelves and finds out whether it did. Rook, this year's Caller, leans on her constantly, and Dimity is fond of Rook, who listens properly and never asks her to leave the rude bits out.

Her rule is simple: the record keeps what was said, not what people wish they had said. So the jokes go in as carefully as the decisions. Bastian Krell has filled more pages than anyone alive, and she has a private tally of the times he has changed his mind mid-speech. Tonight's quarrel over the covered bridge and Rivet's lift will be written up by dawn in her small, square hand, heckles and all.

docs.title: How she came to the desk
docs.text: Dimity was born in Urbanograd, the daughter of a sign-painter and a printer's devil, both dead now, and grew up reading anything with letters on it, including the backs of other people's posters. At twenty she began copying out speeches for the old scribe, Mortimer Reed, whose eyesight was failing, and found she loved the Table more as a record than as a crowd. When Mortimer died twelve years ago, the Table did not argue about who should take the desk, which Dimity still considers the only unanimous decision in its history. She wrote that down too.

docs.title: The crumbling books
docs.text:
Her shelves hold every heckle and every vote since the city's early years. But the record books begin only after the first winter. Of the first winter itself there is nothing, and nobody knows why. The oldest books that do survive, from the city's first winters after that, were written on whatever the Walkers could find: scavenged paper, cheap ink, old ledgers turned upside down. They are crumbling. Pages come away at the spine, and ink has faded to brown ghosts, and nobody has ever copied them out.

Dimity is quietly worried about it, more than she lets on. She has started copying the oldest volume herself, a page or two after each session, but it is slow work, and the Table keeps producing new arguments faster than she can save the old ones. Ozzie Lantry, the historian, is her fellow keeper of records, and the two of them fret over those books together. He wants the first winter; she wants to save what is left of the ones after it. They have agreed that if either finds anything in an old attic, the other hears first.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Dimity wants the oldest books copied before they turn to dust, and a scribe's apprentice with a neat hand and a sense of humor. She fears opening a volume one day and finding a page gone, and with it a joke nobody alive remembers.

A quest might bring her good paper and ink from outside the walls, help copy a crumbling book before it falls apart, or look into a strange gap she has noticed in one of the oldest volumes.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Rook: colleague at the Table
  • Ozzie Lantry: fellow keeper of records

docs.title: Wendel 'Dog-Ear' Tuck
docs.text:
Seller of Old Books and Banned Plays

Town Urbanograd Where Night Market Sells Second-hand books, play scripts and song sheets

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Ozzie Lantry: frustrated would-be buyer

docs.title: Drum
docs.text:
Bucket Drummer

Town Urbanograd Where Lantern Square Role Performer Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Says almost nothing and lets the rhythm talk. Drum smiles only when someone in the crowd starts dancing.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Every evening, just as the lanterns come on, Drum sits down on an upturned crate at the edge of Lantern Square, inside a ring of upturned buckets, pans, a washtub and one cracked kettle, and begins to play. The night market sets its pace by the beat. Stall-keepers hang their lamps in time to it, Ladle turns her skewers to it, and by the second hour half the square is walking in step without noticing. Drum says almost nothing and lets the rhythm talk. Drum smiles only when someone in the crowd starts dancing, and then the smile is so sudden and wide that people dance on purpose, just to see it.

docs.title: A cooper's yard
docs.text:
Drum is thirty-one and grew up in Goa Harbour, in a cooper's yard above the Inlet Quay, among stacks of buckets, barrels and tubs. Drum's parents still make them there, and send a new bucket inland now and then, by carter, with no note; Drum knows what it means. As a small child Drum was the quiet one in a loud family, and found that a stave struck just so said more than any words, and that the sound of the whole yard at work, hammers and mallets and hoops, was a kind of song if you listened for it.

At seventeen Drum walked inland with a sack of mallets and three nested buckets, and arrived in Urbanograd on a night market evening. Nobody was playing. Drum sat down on the edge of the square and started, and has been there ever since, fourteen years now. Ivo Sable, the street healer, still argues with patients about whether Drum's buckets count as an instrument. Drum has never joined the argument, and has never needed to.

docs.title: Partners
docs.text:
Jinx, the juggler of Lantern Square, is Drum's street partner. Jinx talks enough for both of them, which suits Drum perfectly. Together they have worked out an act in which every throw lands on a beat and every drop lands on a rimshot, and nobody watching can tell which drops are deliberate. Jinx counts it a good night when Drum smiles twice. Drum has never said so, but counts it a good night when Jinx is there at all.

Saffi, the fiddler who plays everything twice as fast, is Drum's bandmate. She has been writing a tune for every street in the city, and Drum has found a rhythm for each of the nine she has finished. They rarely discuss music; Saffi starts, Drum follows, and a few bars later Saffi is following Drum. She laughs at her own mistakes before anyone else can, and Drum, unusually, laughs with her.

docs.title: The rhythm for the roads
docs.text: Lately Drum has been working on something new, late at night after the market closes, in an empty corner of the Old Barracks yard. It is a rhythm loud enough, steady enough and strange enough to keep monsters away from the roads. Drum says this is half a joke. It is also half not. The travelers Drum sees stumbling past to Ivo's awning, bitten and shaking, are more every season, and Drum has noticed that on nights the beat is loudest the lanterns facing the wilds tend to survive till morning. It proves nothing. Drum keeps playing anyway, and keeps a tally of which patterns seem to make the stray dogs at the gate fall silent.

docs.title: What Drum wants and fears
docs.text:
Drum wants to find out whether rhythm can do more than make people dance, and to play once for the whole square on Walkout Day. Drum fears silence: the night the square is too empty, or too frightened, to need a beat.

A quest might test Drum's rhythm on the road outside the gate, gather new pans and buckets that ring true, or carry word from Drum's family on the quay at Goa Harbour.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Jinx: street partner
  • Saffi: bandmate

docs.title: Dyna
docs.text:
Tailor of Loud Clothes

Town Urbanograd Where Workshops Row Sells Patchwork coats, bright scarves and stage clothes

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Thimble: haggling customer

docs.title: Ferro
docs.text:
Smith of Odd Metals

Town Urbanograd Where Workshops Row Role Craftsman Age Adult Sells Daggers, throwing stars, claws and knuckle guards

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Gruff, exacting and secretly sentimental. Ferro names every blade before it leaves the forge.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Ferro's forge stands near the far end of Workshops Row, and you can find it by the sculptures. A heron made of old hinges guards the door. A copper fox curls on the roof. A great spiral of fortress chain, gate bolts and cart springs, which Ferro calls nothing at all, rises out of the yard like a frozen whirlwind. Ferro is forty-six, gruff and exacting, broad in the shoulder and scarred on both forearms, and has the patience of iron and roughly the same warmth on first meeting. The warmth comes later, and it is real. Ferro names every blade before it leaves the forge, and is more sentimental about them than anyone would guess.

docs.title: Sculptor first
docs.text:
Ferro was born in Urbanograd, the child of a tinker who mended pots door to door and died when Ferro was twenty, leaving a handcart full of scrap metal and no instructions. Ferro looked at the scrap for a long time and then began welding it together into shapes. The odd metals of the city became Ferro's materials: bronze from broken bells, copper from old pipes, salvaged iron from the fortress's own rusted gates, tin, pewter and whatever the carts brought in. For years Ferro made only sculptures: birds, beasts, strange spirals, a fiddler for the corner of Lantern Square that the children still climb on.

Bastian Krell made the bellows that keep Ferro's forge alive, and still mends them, with an opinion thrown in free each time.

docs.title: How the knives began
docs.text:
Hatch, the monster hunter, came in one day about sixteen years ago with a bent spear-head and nowhere else to take it. Ferro said it was not that kind of forge. Hatch said a forge was a forge. Ferro mended it, grumbling, and mended it well, and Hatch came back a month later and talked Ferro into forging him a pair of hunting knives. That was long before the other adventurers came asking. Hatch still claims he started Ferro's weapon trade, and says it to anyone in earshot. Ferro still replies that Hatch ruined a perfectly good sculptor. Neither of them has ever wanted the argument to end.

Then the roads grew worse, and the adventurers came. They wanted daggers, throwing stars, claws, knuckle guards, things that are light and quick and do not miss. Ferro makes them now, and makes them very well, and grumbles about every one. But each blade gets a name before it goes, scratched small on the tang where nobody but a very careful owner will ever find it: Small Errand, Last Lantern, Mind the Step. Ferro believes a named blade is more careful in the hand, and will not be argued out of it.

docs.title: Shade
docs.text: Shade, the knife-thrower and road guide, is Ferro's best customer and favorite. Their dealings are short and nearly wordless: Shade holds out a worn knife, Ferro looks at it, and a week later a new one is ready. Ferro has never told Shade the knives' names, and Shade has never told anyone, but Ferro knows Shade has found them, because Shade once returned a chipped knife and asked, quietly, that it be mended and not replaced.

docs.title: Walkout Day
docs.text: Every Walkout Day, Ferro welds one new sculpture and gives it away. Nobody knows in advance what it will be or who will get it: a newcomer, a child, a stall-keeper who had a bad year. Last year it was a small iron cat for Perch's loft, and Pounce has slept beside it every afternoon since. The gift is Ferro's way of remembering that the forge was for making things beautiful first.

docs.title: What Ferro wants and fears
docs.text:
Ferro wants a season with no weapon orders at all, and time for one great sculpture for the Gate Walk. Ferro fears hearing that a named blade failed someone on the road.

A quest might fetch an odd metal Ferro needs from outside the walls, help choose who receives this year's Walkout Day sculpture, or return a named knife that has turned up far from its owner.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Shade: customer
  • Hatch: old customer

docs.title: Figgy
docs.text:
Chalk Artist

Town Urbanograd Where Lantern Square Role Child Age Child

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Bright, bossy and stubborn, with chalk dust up to the elbows. Figgy insists every drawing is finished only when it rains.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Figgy is eight years old and has chalk dust up to her elbows, on her nose, in her hair and, according to her mother, in places chalk should not be able to reach. She draws on the flagstones of Lantern Square every day that it is dry, and she is very clear about the rules. Anyone may look at her pictures for free. Anyone who steps on one owes her a copper. She collects the fee with an outstretched hand and a stare that has made grown carters dig in their pockets, and she has never once let anybody off.

docs.title: A painter's daughter
docs.text:
Figgy is the daughter of Ochre, the muralist who has painted half the walls around the square. She grew up under scaffolding, handing up brushes, getting splashed, and falling asleep on drop cloths while Ochre talked to a wall about its feelings. She learned to draw before she learned to read, and she learned to argue about drawing even earlier. Ochre gives her the stubs of chalk and the dregs of the paint pots, and Figgy gives Ochre a great deal of advice that nobody asked for.

She is bright, bossy and stubborn, and she has opinions about everyone's work. She thinks her mother's colours are too careful. She thinks the night paintings on the backs of the chimneys, which everyone knows are Splash's and which nobody can prove are Splash's, are the best pictures in the city, and she says this loudly whenever Ochre can hear. She has not yet worked out why it makes Ochre laugh and sigh at the same time.

docs.title: The rain rule
docs.text: Figgy insists that no drawing of hers is finished until it rains. Then she sits on the edge of the square, under the lip of Ivo Sable's awning if he will let her, and watches the colours run together, slide between the stones and go down the gutters in long bright ribbons. That, she says, is the end of the picture. Everything before it was just the beginning. Grown-ups find this either very wise or very annoying, depending on how much they have just paid to step on a dragon.

docs.title: Her audience
docs.text:
Jinx the juggler is Figgy's favourite performer in the city, and Figgy is Jinx's harshest critic. She sits on the edge of her own drawings every evening and shouts advice: higher, faster, more apples, fewer apologies. When a ball lands on one of her pictures, she holds out her hand, and Jinx always pays. She suspects Jinx drops them on purpose and has decided not to mind, because a copper is a copper.

Nana Gristle, on her bench at the side of the square, tells Figgy which of her drawings are the best and which are rubbish, with equal confidence, and keeps a honey cake in her pocket for the good days. Figgy pretends she does not care what Nana thinks and always checks.

docs.title: What she wants
docs.text:
Figgy wants a real wall of her own. Not a flagstone that the rain takes, not a corner of one of her mother's murals, but a whole wall, as tall as possible, that stays. She is saving her coppers for it in a jar under her bed, though she has not worked out who sells walls. Ochre has explained that the old walls around the square belong to the Walkers' pictures and cannot be painted over. Figgy has explained that the Walkers are not using them.

She is afraid, secretly, of being told she is only good for a child. She would rather be told she is terrible.

A quest might find Figgy a wall that nobody is using and persuade its owner to let her have it, carry a box of good coloured chalk safely in from outside the walls, or settle a dispute over an unpaid copper with a very large and very stubborn carter.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Jinx: favorite audience
  • Ochre: mother

docs.title: Hambone
docs.text:
Keeper of the Theatre Cart

Town Urbanograd Where Old Barracks Theatre Role Worker Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Sentimental, stubborn and a very bad liar. Hambone polishes the cart wheels while humming the play's songs.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Hambone keeps the old cart that the Old Barracks Troupe performs on every Walkout Day, and he loves it the way other people love a grandparent. He is seventy-two, broad and slow, with big careful hands and a voice that is always humming one of the play's songs, usually slightly flat. Every morning he polishes the wheels, checks the axle, oils the hinges of the fold-down steps, and tells the cart what kind of day it is going to have. He is sentimental, stubborn and the worst liar in Urbanograd, and everyone who has ever asked him a question he did not want to answer knows it.

docs.title: A life behind the cart
docs.text:
Hambone was born in the city and joined the troupe at twenty as a cart-pusher, back when old Bellamy Stroud was a young director. He got his name in his second season, playing the back half of a prize pig in one of Bellamy's farces with such commitment that the crowd threw sausages. The name stuck. He has not answered to any other in more than fifty years, and very few people remember what the other one was.

He never wanted big parts. What he wanted was the cart. Its keeper in those days was Fenwick Corliss, a wheelwright who had joined the troupe for the same reason, and Fenwick taught Hambone everything: how to true a wheel, how to swap a plank so the audience never notices, how to brace the stage for a crowd that will climb onto it at the end. When Fenwick died, forty years ago, the cart passed to Hambone without anyone needing to say so. When a nineteen-year-old called Dina Finch joined the troupe seven years later, it was Hambone who showed her how to push it.

docs.title: Juna's planks
docs.text: The cart has been mended so many times that very little of it is very old. But Hambone swears that some of its planks come from Juna Marrow's own cart, the one Selsior's theatre guild hauled out of the market square a hundred years ago. Fenwick told him so, and someone told Fenwick, and Hambone can point to the boards in question: three dark, worn planks in the middle of the stage, darker than the rest. He cannot prove it, and Ozzie Lantry, who has looked, has found no letter either way. Hambone does not need proof. He lets Pip Marrow, Juna's great-granddaughter, sit on those planks during rehearsals, humming, while she pretends not to be moved.

docs.title: His friends
docs.text: Thimble, the troupe's costume maker, is his oldest friend. They have shared a bench backstage for thirty years, Thimble with pins in her mouth, Hambone with a polishing rag, and they argue about everything from hat feathers to the right speed for the Walkers' song. This spring, when Rue froze in the wings at her audition, it was Hambone who went to fetch her water, and he has been quietly proud of her ever since. Little Sprout rides on the cart's tailboard whenever Hambone is not looking, which is whenever Sprout is on it.

docs.title: The wheel
docs.text:
One of the cart's wheels is cracking. It is the left rear one, the oldest, and Hambone found the crack in early spring. He has bound it with wire and told everyone it is perfectly fine, and every time he says so his ears go red. Dina knows. Thimble knows. Sprout knows. Hambone knows they know, and still cannot bear the thought of taking it off and burning it. A wheel like that should come from good seasoned wood, and good wood arrives from outside the walls less often each year.

He wants the cart to roll into the main square this Walkout Day the way it always has, and he fears, more than he can say, the day it breaks under the play in front of the whole city.

A quest might bring seasoned timber safely through the roads for a new wheel, find a wheelwright willing to keep the old hub, or discover some proof, one way or the other, about Juna's planks.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Thimble: old friend
  • Pip Marrow: friend

docs.title: Hatch
docs.text:
Monster Hunter

Town Urbanograd Where Gate Walk Role Adventurer Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Weathered, blunt and full of stories he tells only after the second cup. Hatch trusts his nose more than any map.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Hatch has hunted monsters on Veligor's roads for thirty years, and he looks it. He is sixty-three, weathered as an old saddle, with a nose that has been broken twice and still, he swears, works better than any map. He is blunt to the point of rudeness until the second cup of something warm, after which the stories start, and once they start they do not stop until the lamps are low.

docs.title: From the carts to the hunt
docs.text:
Hatch was not born in Urbanograd. He grew up on the roads, the son of a carter who hauled goods between the towns, and by sixteen he was driving a wagon of his own. He learned the land from the driver's bench: which fords flooded, which woods held boar, which hills smelled of rain a day before it fell. The wilds were changing even then, but slowly, and in those years a careful carter could go a whole season without trouble.

At thirty-three he lost a wagon and a good pair of horses to something in a ravine that should not have been there. He came back on foot, sold what was left of the cart, and bought a spear. He has hunted ever since, taking work from caravans, farmers and towns, and he settled in Urbanograd twenty-odd years ago because, as he puts it, it was the only town that never asked him to wipe his boots.

docs.title: What has changed
docs.text: Hatch says the monsters of his youth were animals that had turned mean. The ones on the roads today are something else: bolder, stranger, harder to read, and coming closer to the towns every season. He does not claim to know why. When the young ones repeat old tales about the Balrog, he grunts and changes the subject, but he has started keeping notes on what he sees, which he never used to do.

docs.title: People
docs.text:
Shade was Hatch's pupil, years ago, for four seasons on the roads, and is the best he ever taught. These days Shade guides travelers along routes Hatch first walked, and finds many of them unsafe now; the two meet at the Gate Walk to trade what they have seen, and Hatch is prouder of Shade than he will ever say aloud.

Ferro, the smith of odd metals, has been taking Hatch's money for years, first for mending a bent spear-head when Ferro still made only sculptures, and later for the knives Hatch talked Ferro into forging long before the other adventurers came asking. Hatch likes to claim he started Ferro's weapon trade. Ferro likes to reply that Hatch ruined a perfectly good sculptor.

Tick, Knox's son, follows Hatch about with a notebook and asks for stories at every hour. Hatch pretends to find it tiresome and answers every question. He respects Knox too much to encourage the boy toward the roads, and he is losing that argument with himself as surely as Knox is losing his.

docs.title: What he wants
docs.text:
Hatch is too old to go out alone now, and he knows it; his knees told him first. He wants someone worth teaching before the knowledge in his head is lost: someone patient, who listens to the land and does not hunt for glory. He fears dying in a chair with nobody knowing what he knows.

A quest might earn Hatch's respect by tracking a beast he can no longer follow, retrieve his notes from a camp he had to abandon, or prove a young hunter worth teaching.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Ferro: smith
  • Tick: admirer
  • Shade: former pupil

docs.title: Hex
docs.text:
Puzzle-Box Maker

Town Urbanograd Where Workshops Row Role Craftsman Age Adult Sells Puzzle boxes, locks and clever latches

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Sly, playful and secretive. Hex answers every question with a riddle unless you are buying something.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Ask Hex a question on Workshops Row and you will get a riddle back. Ask the way to the Great Hall and Hex will tell you it is "where the loudest voice sits down and the quietest stands up". Ask Hex's age and Hex will say "older than my oldest box and younger than its secret". Ask the price of something, on the other hand, and Hex answers at once, plainly and to the copper, because, as Hex likes to say, a riddle is a gift but a sale is a promise. Hex is fifty-two, thin, sly and playful, with long nimble fingers, a jeweller's glass screwed into one eye and a smile that suggests Hex knows something you do not, which is usually true.

docs.title: The boxes
docs.text:
Hex makes puzzle boxes, locks and clever latches, in a narrow shop on the Row with a door that has no visible handle. (Knock twice, slide the third board left, knock once more.) The boxes are small, beautiful things of inlaid wood and brass, and every one of them opens only for the right sequence of taps and turns: press the bird's eye, turn the base a quarter, tap the lid twice and lift. Some take three moves. The great ones take forty. Hex sells them to travelers, to lovers who want a place to keep letters, to merchants who want somewhere better than a pocket for their coin, and to the occasional visiting guild master from Selsior, who goes home baffled and delighted.

Hex learned the trade at twelve, sweeping for a locksmith named Esmond who kept the same shop and refused to answer any question at all, riddle or not. Hex learned by watching, by taking apart Esmond's spare locks at night and by putting them back together before morning, and when Esmond finally noticed, he gave Hex the shop's oldest pick and said nothing else. Esmond died when Hex was twenty-six. Hex has kept the shop since, and the riddles are, Hex says, a kindness Esmond never showed.

docs.title: The box that came back
docs.text:
Hex's oldest shame sits on the workbench, where everyone can see it. It is one of Hex's earliest boxes, made about twenty-eight years ago, a dark walnut cube with a tiny brass key-shaped inlay on each side and no keyhole anywhere. Hex sold it at the Night Market to a traveler whose face Hex no longer remembers. This spring it came back, delivered by a carter who did not know where it had come from, wrapped in sacking, with a note tied around it in a careful hand: the buyer had tried for years and could not solve it, and would the maker kindly open it.

Hex cannot remember the trick.

Hex did not write down the sequences in those days, believing a true maker never forgets. Hex has tried every evening since, and has worked out eleven moves, then lost them, then found nine others. Something inside rattles faintly when the box is tipped. Hex does not know whether it is something the buyer put in, or something Hex built in and forgot. Hex has told everyone who asks that it is a riddle Hex set for Hex's own future, and it is the only riddle Hex tells that is not quite a joke.

docs.title: Velvet
docs.text: Velvet, the curio trader at the Night Market, is Hex's closest friend. They are two of a kind: both theatrical, both secretive, both convinced that a good story improves anything it is attached to. Velvet sells some of Hex's smaller boxes at her stall with a tale for each, and Hex has never once asked which tales are true. Most nights after the market closes they share a pot of something hot and trade secrets they never quite tell. Velvet has a dark stone that stays warm to the touch and will not say what she thinks it is; Hex has guessed at it in riddles for months, and Velvet has answered every riddle with another.

docs.title: What Hex wants and fears
docs.text:
Hex wants to open the box that came back, and has begun, quietly, writing every new sequence down in a little book locked in another box. Hex fears that a maker's hands can forget, and that the next thing forgotten will matter more.

A quest might solve the returned box, find the traveler who bought it, or carry one of Hex's boxes to a buyer in another town and bring back the answer to the riddle written on its lid.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Velvet: friend
  • Leland: old customer and friend

docs.title: Ozzie Lantry
docs.text:
Historian of the Walkers

Town Urbanograd Where Great Hall Role Scholar Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Gentle, rambling and easily sidetracked by a good anecdote. He keeps three pairs of spectacles and can never find any of them.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Ozzie Lantry is the Historian of the Walkers, a title nobody gave him and everybody uses. He is seventy-four, gentle and rambling, and he cannot answer a simple question without first telling you about a woman who once answered a similar one in a letter ninety years ago. He keeps three pairs of spectacles, one for reading, one for distance and one for emergencies, and he can never find any of them. They are usually on his head.

docs.title: A grandson of the Walk
docs.text:
Ozzie was born in Urbanograd. His grandfather was one of the Walkers, a fiddler who left Selsior with nothing but his instrument and a pocketful of songs that the theatres there had refused to hear. Ozzie grew up on those songs, sung badly by his grandfather at bedtime, and it was the songs that first made him curious. Who wrote them? Who sang them on the road? What did the Walkers eat, where did they sleep, and what did they say to each other on the first night in a roofless fortress?

For most of his life Ozzie taught reading to the city's children in his front room, and collected stories on the side. Eighteen years ago, when his last class grew up, he moved his papers into a corner of the Great Hall and began writing the history properly: Urbanograd's first hundred years, told through the letters, diaries and songs of the Walkers and their children.

docs.title: The work
docs.text:
Ozzie's corner of the hall is a landslide of boxes. He has copied hundreds of letters, written down songs from the city's oldest grandmothers before they could be forgotten, and borrowed diaries from attics all over the city, always returning them, usually late. Nana Gristle has told him her mother's story so often that he could recite it, and he still writes it down every time in case she adds something.

But there is a hole in the middle of the book. Every account of the first winter is missing. The Walkers wrote about the road, and they wrote about the spring that followed, but of the first winter itself there is nothing, not a letter or a page. Ozzie has a dozen theories. Perhaps they were too cold and hungry to write. Perhaps the pages were burned for warmth. Perhaps somebody hid them. He does not know, and it nags at him every day. He would pay well for anyone who finds one in an old attic.

docs.title: Friends and foes
docs.text:
Quint, keeper of the Charter Scroll, has been Ozzie's friend since they were boys stealing apples on the same rooftops, and they still argue over supper about which of them was the worse thief. Dimity Ash, the Table's scribe, is his fellow keeper of records; the Table's books begin only after that first winter, and the two of them fret together over the oldest volumes, which are crumbling faster than anyone is copying them.

And then there is Dog-Ear Tuck, who sells old books at the Night Market and claims to own a script of Juna's play in her own hand. For ten years Ozzie has asked to see it. For ten years Dog-Ear has teased him, quoted a line or two, and changed the subject. Ozzie half believes the script is real and half suspects it is the best joke in the city.

docs.title: What he wants
docs.text:
Ozzie wants to finish the book before his eyes give out, and he fears he will not. Above all he wants the first winter, in the Walkers' own words.

A quest might search the city's attics for a first-winter diary, persuade Dog-Ear to show the script at last, or track down a lost song only the oldest Walker families remember.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Dimity 'Inkpot' Ash: fellow keeper of records
  • Quint: old friend
  • Wendel 'Dog-Ear' Tuck: teasing bookseller

docs.title: Ivo Sable
docs.text:
Street Healer

Town Urbanograd Where Lantern Square Role Healer Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Unhurried, gentle and very hard to rattle. He talks to patients about music to take their minds off the stitches.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Ivo Sable runs a little clinic under a patched green awning on the edge of Lantern Square, with a cot, a stool, a cabinet of jars and a kettle that is always warm. He is forty-four, unhurried and very hard to rattle, and his patients agree that the worst part of having a cut stitched by Ivo is the conversation. He talks to every one of them about music, which songs they like, which fiddler is best, whether Drum's buckets count as an instrument, and by the time they have finished arguing, the stitches are in.

docs.title: Coming to the square
docs.text: Ivo grew up on a farm in the orchard country outside Kaldemor, the youngest child of a family of apple growers, and came to Urbanograd at nineteen to be a singer. He was not a good singer. He was, it turned out, very good at patching up the other musicians after they fell off things, and an old street healer called Henna Bright, who kept the awning on the square in those days, noticed. She took him on, taught him to set bones and clean wounds, and scolded him for humming while he worked until she gave up and started humming along. When she died fifteen years ago, she left him the awning, the cabinet and the kettle, and he has kept all three going ever since.

docs.title: Everyday work
docs.text:
For most of those years, Ivo's work was the city's own small disasters: rooftop tumbles, burnt fingers from the workshops, sprained ankles from the dancing at the Night Market, and the occasional actor who took a stage fight too seriously. Tinder, the fire-eater, is his most frequent patient by far. He has treated her blistered lips and singed hands more times than he can count, and he likes her far too much to stop scolding her about the water bucket she already checks three times.

But that has been changing. More and more of the people on Ivo's cot are travelers hurt on the roads: bitten, clawed, thrown from frightened horses. The wounds are worse than they used to be, and they come in faster than his supplies do. The bandages, salves and dried herbs he relies on come in from outside the walls, and every season fewer carts bring them.

docs.title: Colleagues
docs.text:
Patch, the herbalist at the Gate Walk, sees the road's wounded first, and Ivo sees them second. The two healers send patients back and forth, share whatever supplies they have and trade remedies over tea. Patch scolds her patients and Ivo soothes his, and between them they think they cover most kinds of person.

Crow sells tonics at the Night Market, and Ivo does not doubt they work. What he doubts is that anyone, including Crow, knows which bottle is which. He has asked Crow to label them properly perhaps a hundred times. Crow has ignored him perhaps a hundred times. They have settled into an exasperated friendship in which Ivo sends Crow his patients and Crow sends Ivo the ones who drank the wrong bottle.

docs.title: Hopes and fears
docs.text:
Ivo wants a steady supply of clean bandages and a quiet week. He fears, more than he admits, the night someone comes in from the road whom he cannot help.

A quest might escort a cart of medical supplies to the city, gather herbs for his salves in fields too risky for him to visit, or finally sort and label Crow's bottles.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Crow: stubborn colleague
  • Patch: fellow healer
  • Tinder: frequent patient

docs.title: Jinx
docs.text:
Juggler of Lantern Square

Town Urbanograd Where Lantern Square Role Performer Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Restless, cheeky and terrible at keeping secrets. Jinx drops things on purpose to make children laugh, and almost never by accident.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Jinx juggles in Lantern Square every evening, and will juggle anything handed over: apples, boots, teacups, a cabbage from Old Parsnip's tubs, and once, memorably, three of Margo Venn's spare parts, one of which turned out to be a spring that went off in mid-air. Jinx is eighteen, restless and cheeky, with quick hands and a grin that never quite switches off. Jinx drops things on purpose to make children laugh, and almost never by accident, though nobody watching can ever tell which is which.

docs.title: A runaway from the capital
docs.text:
Jinx was born in Selsior, to a family of respectable clerks who expected their child to become a respectable clerk. Jinx spent most of childhood juggling the household inkpots instead, and at fourteen hitched a ride on a carter's wagon to Urbanograd with a bag of clothes and three wooden balls. That was four years ago. Jinx's parents still live in Selsior, write once a season and hope it is a phase; Jinx writes back cheerfully, and is fairly sure it is not.

The first winter was hard. Jinx slept in a stairwell and juggled for coins in the cold until Tinder, the fire-eater, took pity, shared her supper and showed Jinx which corners of the square stay warm after dark. They have been friends ever since. Tinder is swaggering on stage and nervous off it, and Jinx is the opposite, and both of them find this very funny.

docs.title: Life on the square
docs.text:
Jinx's street partner is Drum, who plays a ring of upturned buckets and pans and says almost nothing. Jinx talks enough for both of them, and the two of them have worked out an act in which every throw lands on a beat. Drum smiles only when someone starts dancing, and Jinx counts it a good night when Drum smiles twice.

Jinx's favorite audience is Figgy, the chalk artist's daughter, who sits on the edge of her own drawings and shouts advice. Figgy is Jinx's harshest critic and loudest fan. Jinx sometimes drops a ball onto one of her chalk pictures on purpose so that she can demand the one-copper fee, which Jinx always pays.

Afterwards Jinx passes the hat, counts the takings, and spends most of it at the Night Market within the hour.

docs.title: Secrets and torches
docs.text:
Jinx is terrible at keeping secrets. Not out of malice: secrets simply feel like something too good to keep in one pair of hands. Half the city has learned to stop telling Jinx anything, and the other half tells Jinx things precisely because they want them spread.

Jinx's great dream is to juggle burning torches on top of the theatre cart on Walkout Day. The Old Barracks Troupe has firmly refused, every year, and Dina Finch has told Jinx in front of witnesses that it will happen over her dead body and the cart's. Tinder refuses to teach the trick, too, at least for now; she says Jinx does not yet check the water bucket even once, let alone three times.

docs.title: What Jinx wants
docs.text:
Jinx wants a crowd that fills the whole square, one night on the cart, and never to go back to Selsior for good. What Jinx fears is being ordinary, and, though Jinx would never admit it, being sent home.

A quest might help Jinx win the troupe's permission for the torch act, recover something Jinx juggled onto a rooftop, or stop a secret Jinx has just overheard from reaching the whole city.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Drum: street partner
  • Figgy: favorite juggler
  • Tinder: friend
