docs.title: Kite
docs.text:
Rooftop Runner

Town Urbanograd Where Rooftops Role Worker Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Fast, boastful and impossible to keep on the ground. Kite talks while running and never runs out of breath.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Kite carries messages across Urbanograd by rooftop, and does it faster than anyone alive. Kite is nineteen, wiry and sunburnt, with a runner's long legs and a mouth that never stops: Kite talks while running, talks while jumping, talks while hanging by the fingertips from a gutter, and arrives at the far end of the city still in the middle of a sentence and not remotely out of breath. Kite is fast, boastful and impossible to keep on the ground, and would tell you so, at length, if you could keep up.

docs.title: A family of runners
docs.text:
Urbanograd grew upward, not outward, and its streets are a tangle of stairs, bridges and passages that lead to three places at once. A message sent through the streets can take an hour. A message sent over the roofs takes minutes, if the runner knows the way. Kite comes from a family that knew it. Kite's grandmother ran messages over the roofs when Cobble the bootmaker was a young man, and Kite's mother ran them after her. Both wore Cobble's soft-soled rooftop boots, and so does Kite.

Kite's grandmother died when Kite was small, but not before teaching Kite the names of the old runners' routes: the long jump over the Night Market, the gutter run below the Crooked Tower, the stretch of slates that sings under a fast foot. Kite's mother ran until a bad fall on a wet roof left her with a knee that would not bend on slates. She moved away to live with flat ground under her, in the farmlands near Kaldemor, and writes now and then when the carts get through. Kite misses her and says so to no one, and runs her old routes every day.

docs.title: The record
docs.text:
Cobble made Kite's first pair of boots four years ago, when Kite was fifteen. Kite went back to the shop the next week to complain about the left heel, and has been Cobble's most loyal customer ever since, and the only one allowed to criticise the stitching. Every record Kite sets is told to Cobble first, and Cobble pretends not to listen, and writes it on the back of his shop door.

The record that matters is the run from the Gate Walk to the Great Hall. Kite took it last summer, beating a mark that had stood for years, and has bettered it twice since. The runners time it with a sand-glass at each end, and Kite has made sure every person in the city knows the count. Tick, Knox's son, who runs messages from the gate along the streets, is convinced he will beat Kite one day. Kite encourages this, mostly so there will be someone to beat.

docs.title: Splash
docs.text: Kite's sweetheart is Splash, the night painter who leaves murals on the backs of chimneys and the undersides of bridges where only rooftop folk can see them. Splash never signs anything. Kite is the only one who knows for certain which pictures are Splash's, because Kite carries the paint pots across the roofs at night and keeps watch while Splash works. Kite has promised to help Splash paint something big enough to be seen from the Gate Walk, and has already worked out three ways to get the paint up there, two of them nearly legal.

docs.title: What Kite wants and fears
docs.text:
Kite wants to keep the record forever, and to run one day from the top of the Crooked Tower to the gate without touching a single stair. Kite fears very little on the roofs, but has noticed that Nana Gristle's warnings about which rooftops to avoid are, irritatingly, always right. What Kite fears most is a fall like the one that took the roofs from Kite's mother.

Kite also teaches Rooftop Dash, the quick dash along the ground that runners use to cross a gap before a roof edge stops them, to anyone who can follow Kite across three rooftops without being told which ones to avoid.

A quest might race Kite across the rooftops, carry an urgent message when Kite is laid up, or help Kite and Splash get a mural up where the whole Gate Walk can see it.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Cobble: bootmaker
  • Splash: sweetheart

docs.title: Knox
docs.text:
Gate Watch Guard

Town Urbanograd Where Gate Walk Role Guard Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Big, gentle and slow to anger. Knox carves little wooden animals during quiet watches.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Knox is the biggest member of the Gate Watch and the gentlest. He is forty-four, broad as a doorway, with a short beard going grey at the chin and hands that look as if they could lift a cart, which they occasionally do. He speaks slowly and seldom raises his voice, and in ten years at the gate nobody has ever seen him truly angry. Travelers who arrive frightened from the roads find him standing at the gate with a lantern, saying their names, and most of them feel safe before they are through it.

docs.title: Before the gate
docs.text:
Knox was born in Urbanograd and spent his young years as a joiner's labourer on Workshops Row, carrying beams up the city's endless stairs and fitting the bridges that run between its rooftops. He learned to work wood there, and kept the habit of carving when the work dried up. He married Jessamy, a stall-keeper's daughter with a loud laugh, and they had a son, Tick.

Ten years ago, when Tick was a baby, Knox signed on with the Gate Watch. He says he did it for something steady and quiet to do on long evenings. In those days the gate was steady and quiet. Old Garran Holt was captain then, and a young volunteer called Brindle had already been keeping the gate for seven years. Two years later Jessamy died after a fall on an icy stair one winter, and Knox raised Tick at the Gate Walk, where the boy learned to walk between the guards' boots and to talk to every traveler who came through.

docs.title: The watch
docs.text:
Knox has guarded the gate for ten years, three longer than Brindle has been captain, and he knows every regular traveler by face: the carters, the peddlers, the hunters, the cider sellers, the woman who brings eggs and the man who brings bad jokes. When a regular stops coming, Knox notices first, and he is noticing more of that every season. Brindle trusts him completely and asks his advice on most things. Knox gives it slowly and briefly and is usually right.

During quiet watches Knox carves little wooden animals with a short knife: foxes, hares, goats, and owls. The owls go to Dagny, who keeps the night watch with her two lamps. Knox has started calling her the bravest of them. She thinks he is joking. He is not. Brindle has seen the same thing and is still hunting for the right words to tell her; Knox has decided that owls will do in the meantime. Patch, the herbalist further along the Gate Walk, has pulled more of his carving splinters than either of them can count, and scolds him every time.

docs.title: Tick
docs.text: Knox's son Tick is ten, eager and always out of breath, and runs messages from the gate to the rest of the city. Tick salutes everyone, including the cat. He keeps a notebook of every strange story travelers tell him, and above all he follows Hatch, the old monster hunter, asking for more. Tick wants to be an adventurer. Knox wants him to be anything else: a joiner, a baker, a fiddler, a clerk. They have this argument at supper most nights, and Knox is losing it, and knows it. Hatch respects Knox too much to encourage the boy, and answers every one of Tick's questions anyway.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Knox wants Tick to grow up safely and choose a gentler life, and if that cannot happen, he wants Tick to be taught well by the right people. What Knox fears is the evening a regular face does not come back up the road, and it is Tick who goes looking.

A quest might find a regular traveler who has failed to arrive, help Knox make his peace with Tick's dream, or carry one of his carvings to a child in another town.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Brindle: captain
  • Tick: son

docs.title: Leland
docs.text:
Keeper of the Low Door

Town Urbanograd Where Great Hall Role Worker Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Quiet, careful and endlessly curious about what lies under things, he talks to stone as if it might answer. He keeps a chalk map of everything he has dug.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Leland is seventy-six, an old well-digger, and he knows more about what lies under Urbanograd's streets than anyone alive. He is quiet, careful and endlessly curious about what lies under things: floors, cobbles, hillsides, other people's questions. He talks to stone as if it might answer, in a low, reasonable voice, the way you might talk to a horse you were not quite sure of. He says it usually does answer, if you are patient, and that the answer is generally "not there".

docs.title: Born to the shovel
docs.text:
Leland was born in Urbanograd, in a lean-to against the old fortress wall, the son of Caleb, a well-digger who had come to the city in its early years, when the Walkers were still learning that art does not draw water. Old Grad had been built for a garrison, and its wells had silted up in the generations it stood empty. Caleb spent his life opening the old ones and digging new ones, and Leland went down the shafts with him on a rope from the age of nine. Caleb died when Leland was thirty, and Leland has dug alone ever since.

For more than sixty years he has dug, cleared, lined and capped the wells of the city, and in all that time he has kept a map. It is drawn in chalk on the long wall of his cellar, under his house near the Great Hall: every well he has dug, every shaft he has cleared, every old drain and cellar and buried wall he has met on the way down, each in the right place and at the right depth. When the wall filled up he started on the floor. He never married. He says he spent his courting years at the bottom of holes, and that the holes were better company than he deserved.

docs.title: The well that went through
docs.text:
Forty years ago, digging a new well in the yard behind the Great Hall kitchens, Leland's shaft broke through into nothing. He lowered a lantern on a long rope and saw, far below, dark water, the tops of stone pillars and the curve of a vaulted roof, much older than anything he had met before. He sat at the top of that shaft for a whole afternoon, looking down. Then he went to the Open Table of the day, which told him, after a long argument, to cap it. He capped it with a stone slab and a ring bolt, and has been thinking about it ever since. It is the reason his map has a great blank space under the Great Hall, edged in careful dotted chalk.

The other reason is the iron door. Under the Great Hall, behind the kitchens, is an iron door that the Walkers found locked a century ago and never had a key for. Leland has knelt at its keyhole more times than he can count. For years he has carried his questions about it to Hex, the locksmith on Workshops Row, who has made the latches on his well covers for twenty years, and who has looked through the keyhole with Leland's lantern and pronounced the lock "Aristocrat, and very proud of it". They are old friends. Leland is the only person in the city who does not mind Hex's riddles, because he takes as long to answer them as Hex takes to tell them.

docs.title: Keeper of the Low Door
docs.text: When the Open Table at last agrees to open that door, there is really only one person it can name to keep it. It was Hex, kneeling at the lock with his picks, who said aloud that the Table should name Leland its keeper, and nobody argued. Leland is Keeper of the Low Door. He keeps the door, the ropes and the map, and he adds to the map every evening, in chalk, from what the people who go down tell him: the old keep's halls, the flooded cisterns, the long tunnels running out under the hills, and the quarry at the bottom where the stone is warm. He lets anyone with the nerve go down, as often as they like, and he asks every one of them the same question when they come back up: what did the stone feel like?

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text: Leland wants to finish the map. He knows he will not, and he does not mind, so long as someone carries it on after him. What he fears is the warm stone at the bottom. Sixty years of digging have taught him that stone underground is cool to the hand, always, everywhere, and the stone down there has not heard the rule.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text: A quest could follow Leland's chalk map down into the levels below the door, or help him rig a rope down his old capped well shaft. Another might bring him back a piece of the deepest stone, so that he can put his hand on it and listen.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Hex: the locksmith he asks about old doors

docs.title: Lux
docs.text:
Keeper of the Lanterns

Town Urbanograd Where Lantern Square Role Official Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Calm, watchful and fond of heights. Lux speaks softly and notices every lantern that has gone out.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Every evening at dusk, Lux climbs. Up the stairs of the first tower, out along the wall, up the ladder bolted to the second, and so on around the old fortress, relighting the lanterns strung between Old Grad's towers. By full dark the whole city glows, and Lux is somewhere high above it, sitting on a parapet with legs dangling, counting the lights. Lux is thirty-six, calm and watchful, speaks softly and notices every lantern that has gone out, often before it has quite finished going.

docs.title: The twelfth keeper
docs.text:
The Walkers hung the first lanterns between the towers in their first year, partly to see by and partly, the old songs say, to show the rest of Veligor that someone lived in the ruin now. The job of keeping them lit has passed through a dozen hands since then. Lux is the twelfth Keeper of the Lanterns, and knows the names of all eleven before, because they are scratched into the oldest beam of the lamp store at the foot of the first tower.

Lux grew up in the city and was always climbing something: drainpipes, washing lines, the theatre cart. At twenty, Lux began carrying oil for the old keeper, Lionel Callow, whose knees had started to fail; when Lionel died eight years ago, nobody even suggested anyone else. Lux was already up there most nights.

docs.title: The lanterns and their people
docs.text:
The lantern glass comes from Tinsel, the glassblower on Workshops Row, who makes the colored panes that give Urbanograd its glow. Lux is Tinsel's best customer and most patient one, willing to wait while each pane is held up to the sun and admired before it is wrapped. Between them they argue cheerfully about which colors carry furthest in fog.

Perch, who keeps pigeons on the Crooked Tower, is Lux's closest friend. The loft is on Lux's nightly round, and most evenings Lux stops there on the way down for tea and an exchange of reports: Perch on which routes the birds refused, Lux on which lanterns are out. They are both people who prefer heights to crowds, and they can sit for an hour together without needing to say much.

Prism, the young light-painter from the forest who works the Gate Walk, has become another friend. Prism is fascinated by the lanterns and asks more questions about them in an evening than Lux usually answers in a year. Lux pretends to be worn out by it and secretly enjoys it, and has promised to help with Prism's light show on Walkout Day.

docs.title: The smashed lanterns
docs.text: Lately, some of the lanterns that face the wilds have been found smashed in the mornings. Not stolen, not blown down: smashed, the frames bent and the glass scattered. It happens only on the outward side of the walls, and never on the same night twice in a row. Lux has sat up three nights waiting, saw nothing, and found a broken lantern the morning after the fourth. Lux would very much like to know by what, and is beginning to fear the answer.

docs.title: Hopes and fears
docs.text:
Lux wants every lantern lit every night, and an apprentice with a good head for heights. Lux fears the night the outer lanterns go dark and stay dark, and what it would mean for travelers looking for the city in the dark.

A quest might keep watch on the outer walls at night, fetch replacement panes from Tinsel through a busy market, or follow whatever smashed the lanterns back into the wilds.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Tinsel: glass supplier
  • Perch: friend
  • Prism: friend

docs.title: Mags
docs.text:
Cook of the Great Hall

Town Urbanograd Where Great Hall Role Service Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Brisk and bossy in the kitchen, soft as bread dough everywhere else. She judges people by whether they wash their own bowl.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Mags cooks for the Great Hall, which means she cooks for the Open Table, which means she cooks for anyone in Urbanograd who has something to say and is prepared to say it until dawn. She is forty-eight, square and red-cheeked, brisk and bossy in her kitchen and soft as bread dough everywhere else. She judges people by one thing only: whether they wash their own bowl. Those who do are welcome forever. Those who do not are remembered.

docs.title: The pot
docs.text:
At the heart of the Great Hall's kitchen, over a fire that never quite goes out, sits one enormous iron pot of stew. Mags claims it has never been fully emptied since her grandmother's day. Each night she adds whatever there is: Old Parsnip's rooftop vegetables, beans, barley, a ham bone from the Night Market, whatever the farm carts brought in. Each night the Table eats most of it, and each morning she starts again on what is left. Some people in the city swear they can taste a hundred years of arguments in it.

Her grandmother, Bettany Ferrow, cooked for the Table for nearly forty years and taught Mags everything in that kitchen, from how to keep a fire low all night to how to stop a hungry orator from talking with his mouth full. When Bettany's knees gave out twenty-two years ago, Mags took over the ladle; Bettany sat beside the fire and gave orders for four more years, until she died. Mags still talks to the pot as if her grandmother were listening.

docs.title: Bastian
docs.text:
Mags is married to Bastian Krell, the loudest voice at the Table, a man with an enormous voice, enormous opinions and an enormous heart. They married seventeen years ago, after he spent most of a winter's sessions arguing in favor of her stew in the middle of debates about something else entirely. She still claims she married him to stop him talking about it.

These days he is campaigning, at length, for a covered bridge over Lantern Square so the Night Market can run in the rain. Mags supports the bridge in public and teases him about it at home. When he changes his mind, which he does loudly and without shame, she is the first to know, because he tries the new speech on her while she stirs.

docs.title: Friends at the Table
docs.text: Rook, the Caller, is a grateful regular, and Mags is fond of Rook in the bossy way she is fond of everyone she feeds: she makes sure the Caller eats before the session, not during it. Old Parsnip, who grows vegetables in tubs and troughs across the rooftops, supplies most of her greens and talks to his cabbages as though they had opinions, which Mags finds perfectly reasonable.

docs.title: The smoke
docs.text:
The kitchen's chimney is as old as the fortress and draws badly, and on cold nights the whole hall fills with smoke. Mags would dearly like someone to invent a stove that does not smoke, and has said so loudly in the direction of Workshops Row more than once.

She worries, too, about the farm carts. Fewer reach the city every season, and a pot that has never been empty takes a great deal of feeding. More and more of what goes in comes from the rooftop gardens.

A quest might bring a cart of supplies through to the Great Hall's kitchen, carry Mags's challenge to an inventor on Workshops Row, or hunt down a lost ingredient from her grandmother's recipe.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Rook: grateful regular
  • Bastian 'Bellows' Krell: husband
  • Old Parsnip: vegetable supplier

docs.title: Margo 'Sparks' Venn
docs.text:
Inventor of Sparking Things

Town Urbanograd Where Workshops Row Role Craftsman Age Adult Sells Gadgets, spring-traps and sparking lamps

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Brilliant, scatterbrained and slightly singed. Margo explains every invention three ways before she lets anyone touch it.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Margo Venn's workshop is easy to find on Workshops Row: it is the one with the smoke stains around the door, the scorch marks on the lintel and, on a good day, a faint smell of burnt hair. Margo, called Sparks by everyone who has stood too close to one of her inventions, is thirty-eight, brilliant, scatterbrained and slightly singed. Her eyebrows have grown back so many times that she no longer worries about them.

docs.title: Learning to make sparks
docs.text:
Margo was born in Urbanograd and spent most of her childhood underfoot in the shop of her aunt, Odile Venn, a clockmender with a cramped shop at the top of a staircase that led to three different places. Odile taught her to take things apart, and, more slowly, to put them back together. By twelve Margo had built a music box that played backwards; by fifteen, a kettle that whistled a different note for every temperature. Odile died when Margo was twenty-three and left her a bench full of tools, and Margo opened her own workshop on the Row soon afterwards. She has blown its door off twice in fifteen years.

Margo explains every invention three ways before she lets anyone touch it: once with drawings, once with her hands, and once by shouting, usually while the invention is already doing something unexpected. Spring-traps, sparking lamps and odd gadgets fill her shelves, and she sells enough of them to keep buying parts for the next idea.

docs.title: The spark lamp
docs.text:
Her great project this year is a lamp that throws sparks, bright and loud enough, she hopes, to frighten off the monsters that make the roads so dangerous now. It works beautifully in the workshop. Whether it works on a real monster outside the walls, she has no idea, and she needs someone brave enough to test it.

Zinnia Calloway, called Zip, has volunteered with alarming enthusiasm. Zip has never refused a dare and came home from her first adventure with a broken arm and a great story, and Margo is torn between gratitude and the uneasy feeling that she is handing an untested invention to the least careful person in the city.

docs.title: Bolt and Rivet
docs.text:
Bolt is Margo's apprentice. He does most of the sweeping, all of the testing and a great deal of apologizing to machines. Margo thinks he has good hands and better instincts, and does not tell him so often enough. She has no idea that he secretly admires some of Rivet's ideas, though if she found out she would be more hurt than she would admit.

Rivet built the rope-and-pulley lift that hauls crates up to the Rooftops, and is Margo's rival in everything. Rivet builds things that work; Margo builds things that sparkle, and then, eventually, work. They argue across the Row about gears, ropes, springs and the proper use of lamp oil, and each would be lost without the other. When Rivet's lift jammed last winter, Margo was the first one up the ropes to help, complaining the whole way.

docs.title: What she wants
docs.text:
Margo wants the spark lamp to work outside the walls, and she would quite like to invent the smokeless stove Mags keeps demanding, if only to stop Mags shouting about it in the street. What Margo fears is that one of her inventions will hurt someone who trusted it.

A quest might test the spark lamp on a real monster beside Zip, gather rare parts from beyond the walls, or settle one of Margo and Rivet's arguments with a fair trial.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Bolt: apprentice
  • Rivet: rival
  • Zinnia 'Zip' Calloway: gadget tester

docs.title: Moth
docs.text:
Keeper of the Night Market Stalls

Town Urbanograd Where Night Market Role Official Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Wry, tireless and allergic to mornings. Moth knows which stall is where by smell alone.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Moth wakes at noon, under protest, and is properly awake by dusk. That suits the job. Moth is the Keeper of the Night Market Stalls, the person who decides each evening who sets up where, and the Night Market does not begin until Moth arrives with a battered felt hat full of folded names. Moth is forty-nine, lean and rumpled, with ink on one thumb and a voice like a door that needs oiling. Moth is wry, tireless and allergic to mornings, and has been heard to say that sunrise is the city's only real mistake.

docs.title: The hat
docs.text:
The first traders of Urbanograd, in the Walkers' early years, quarrelled so badly over the best corners of the market that somebody put everyone's name in a hat and drew them out one by one, first name, first pick. It worked so well that nobody ever stopped. Every evening since, someone has drawn the names, so that no stall owns the best corner for long and newcomers have the same chance as old hands. The hat itself has been replaced more than once; the one Moth carries is the third that anyone remembers, and it is held together mostly by habit.

Moth took over the hat sixteen years ago from old Bramble, a rope-seller who had kept it for most of a lifetime and who could recite every stall's position from the last thirty years. Bramble taught Moth the rules, which are few, and the exceptions, which are many: who must not be put next to whom, which stall needs to be near water, whose smoke goes where when the wind turns. Moth learned the rest by walking the market every night. Moth can now tell where every stall stands with eyes shut, by smell alone: Ladle's pepper and grilling meat, Saucer's spiced tea, the dusty paper of Dog-Ear's books, the sharp, odd smells of Crow's tonics, and, at the very end of the row, the warm wax of Glim's candle stubs.

docs.title: Glim and Ladle
docs.text:
Glim is Moth's daughter, and she runs her own little stall of paper lanterns and candle stubs at the far end of the market. Her name goes into the hat like everyone else's. Moth has never once fixed a draw for her, and she has never once asked, and both of them are proud of that. Glim is saving to buy a cart and dreams of taking her lanterns to other towns. Moth is proud of that too, and terrified of it, and has not yet found a way to say both at once.

Hester Cray, whom the whole market calls Ladle, is Moth's friend, and her skewer stall is always the first lit and the last dark, wherever the hat puts it. The two of them share the last cup of hot cider most nights while the market packs up, and Moth pretends not to notice how many rooftop children Ladle feeds for nothing.

docs.title: The empty corners
docs.text:
Lately the draw has been getting shorter. Fewer traders are arriving from outside since the roads turned dangerous: the salt sellers, the wool carters, the spice peddlers who once came every month. Some corners now go empty for nights at a time, and Moth has started counting the names in the hat before each draw, which never used to be necessary. The Night Market feeds a good part of the city through the winter, and Moth is worried about what happens if the outside carts stop altogether. Moth has even wondered, privately, whether to break the old rule and promise the best corners to any outside trader brave enough to come. Moth has not done it yet, and is not sure the hat would forgive it.

A quest might escort a trader's cart safely to the gate before winter, find out why a regular peddler has stopped coming, or recover the old hat when it vanishes on the night of the draw.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Glim: daughter
  • Hester 'Ladle' Cray: friend

docs.title: Nana Gristle
docs.text:
Bench-Sitter of Lantern Square

Town Urbanograd Where Lantern Square Role Resident Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Sharp-tongued, sweet-toothed and impossible to shock. She knows everyone's grandparents and all their embarrassing stories.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text:
Nana Gristle sits on the same bench on the sunny side of Lantern Square every day of the year, rain or shine, from mid-morning until the lanterns come on. She is seventy-nine, tiny, wrapped in three shawls in all weathers, and sharp enough to cut bread with. She knows everyone's grandparents, and everything their grandparents ever did that they would rather forget, and she is happy to share it. Nothing shocks her. She has seen the city do all of it before, usually on a Walkout Day, usually on a roof.

Nobody is quite sure when she became Nana. She has no grandchildren and never had children of her own; the square simply started calling her that some forty years ago, and Gristle came with it, because she is tough as gristle and twice as hard to get rid of. She outlived a husband and two sweethearts and speaks fondly of all three, though never in the same breath.

docs.title: The basket
docs.text:
Nana Gristle's mother, Posy, was carried out of Selsior in a basket on the day of the Long Walk. Posy was a baby then, a few months old, and her mother, a lace-maker called Marguerite who had never been allowed into a guild, carried her the whole way in a laundry basket on one hip, with her lace bobbins packed in around the baby to keep her warm. Posy grew up in the roofless fortress among the first Walkers and lived to be very old, and died eighteen years ago still able to recite which songs her mother sang on the road.

Nana treats this as the most important fact in the city, and in a way she is right: Posy was one of the very last people alive who had been on the Long Walk, and through her, Nana is one of the very last people who heard about it first-hand. Nana tells the story to anyone who sits on her bench for longer than a minute. Ozzie Lantry, the city's historian, has heard it so often that he could recite it, and still writes it down every time in case she adds something. Sometimes she does. Ozzie suspects some of the additions are new; Nana says the basket was hers to remember, not his.

docs.title: The bench
docs.text:
From her bench Nana watches everything. She tells newcomers which rooftops to avoid, and she is always right, because she knows which ones fell in during her childhood, which were patched badly afterwards, and by whom. Kite, the rooftop runner, finds this deeply irritating. She judges Figgy's chalk drawings with a critic's eye and keeps a honey cake in her pocket for the good ones. She scolds Rook, the Caller of the Open Table, every time Rook passes, for skipping meals, for speaking too softly and for letting Bastian go on, and Rook stops to listen anyway.

Saucer, who has kept the tea stall at the Night Market for forty years, is Nana's oldest friend. Each evening, as the market opens, Nana leaves her bench and walks across for a cup of spiced tea and a honey cake, and the two of them sit with their heads together, saying terrible things about everyone and laughing at their own jokes. Saucer reads her leaves every evening and always predicts something nice; Nana always says it is nonsense, and always asks what it said.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Nana Gristle wants the city to remember where it came from, and to remember that it came from people carrying babies and bobbins, not from heroes. She fears, though she would never say so, that when she goes, the basket goes with her.

A quest might find one of Marguerite's lace pieces in an old attic, help Ozzie test which parts of Nana's story are new, or fetch something sweet enough to bribe a story out of her.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Rook: fond listener

docs.title: Ochre
docs.text:
Muralist

Town Urbanograd Where Lantern Square Role Craftsman Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Big-hearted and messy, always speckled with paint. Ochre talks to walls as if they were old friends.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Ochre has painted half the walls around Lantern Square, and talks to all of them. "Morning, old girl," Ochre says to the long wall by the steps, and "You're looking peeling," to the one behind Ivo Sable's awning, and passers-by have long since stopped finding it strange. Ochre is thirty-eight, big-hearted and messy, speckled from head to boots with every colour in the city, and so often up a ladder that children in the square think of Ochre as a sort of weather.

docs.title: Learning the walls
docs.text:
Ochre was born in Urbanograd and grew up in the square, a child who drew on everything and was forgiven for it. At twelve Ochre started grinding colours for old Rosalba, the muralist who looked after the square's painted walls in those days, and at sixteen was trusted with a brush. Rosalba had learned from someone who had learned from the Walkers themselves, and she taught Ochre the most important rule of the square: the oldest pictures are not anybody's to improve. They are only to be kept. When Rosalba died, fifteen years ago, the walls came to Ochre the way such things come in Urbanograd, because Ochre was already up the ladder.

When the Walkers first came to Old Grad, they painted every bare wall they could reach, and some of those first pictures still survive around the square: a cart full of laughing people, a long line of walkers with bundles, a lantern hung between two towers, a very rude cartoon of a guild master that the city would not part with for anything. Every spring, Ochre repaints them, stroke by stroke, over the faded lines, so they never vanish. It takes most of the season. Ochre has never once changed a line, though the guild master's nose is, Ochre admits, a great temptation.

docs.title: Figgy
docs.text: Figgy, Ochre's daughter, is eight and draws on every flagstone in the square. She has chalk to the elbows, an opinion about everything and a fee of one copper for stepping on her pictures, and she thinks Ochre's colours are too careful. Ochre thinks she may be right. Figgy wants a real wall of her own, and Ochre has had to explain that the old walls belong to the Walkers' pictures. Figgy has pointed out that the Walkers are not using them. Ochre is still working on an answer, and is secretly looking for a wall to give her.

docs.title: Splash
docs.text: Ochre's rival is Splash, the night painter whose unsigned murals turn up on the backs of chimneys and the undersides of bridges, where only rooftop folk can see them. Ochre says painting where nobody can see is like singing into a sack. Ochre also climbs up to look at every new one, usually the morning after, and stands there a long while. The two of them have never had a proper conversation, only a long exchange of pointed remarks passed through Figgy, who loves Splash's paintings and says so loudly whenever her mother can hear.

docs.title: The Gate Walk
docs.text:
Ochre's great ambition is to paint the whole history of the city along the walls of the Gate Walk, from the cart in Selsior's market square to the present day, so that every traveler who comes in through the gate walks through Urbanograd's story before reaching the city. Ochre has the drawings ready, a hundred sheets of them. What Ochre lacks is red. Good red paint is made from a red earth dug outside the walls and carted in, and with the roads dangerous the carts bring less every season. A history of Urbanograd without red, Ochre says, would be a history with all the shouting left out.

Ochre has heard that Splash wants a painting seen from the Gate Walk too. Ochre is pretending not to have heard.

A quest might bring a load of red earth safely in through the roads, broker a truce between Ochre and Splash over the Gate Walk, or help Ochre find Figgy a wall of her own.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Figgy: daughter
  • Splash: rival painter

docs.title: Dina Finch
docs.text:
Director of the Old Barracks Troupe

Town Urbanograd Where Old Barracks Theatre Role Performer Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Commanding, theatrical and warm under the bluster. Dina gives notes even at breakfast.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Dina Finch directs the Old Barracks Troupe, and she directs everything else within earshot too. She gives notes at breakfast, notes on the stairs and notes to people who are not in the play at all, usually about their posture. She is fifty-two, broad-shouldered and loud, with a voice trained to reach the back of a market square without a single raised hand. Under the bluster she is one of the warmest people in Urbanograd, and every actor she has ever shouted at knows it.

docs.title: Growing up in the crowd
docs.text:
Dina was born in the city and saw her first Walkout Day play from her father's shoulders. She joined the troupe at nineteen as a stagehand who pushed the cart, moved up to small parts, and spent nine years playing Juna herself. When old Bellamy Stroud, who had directed the troupe for decades, died thirteen years ago, the company turned to Dina before the funeral bread was cold. She has run the Old Barracks Theatre ever since, from a cluttered office in what was once the fortress quartermaster's store.

The troupe performs Juna Marrow's play every Walkout Day on a cart in the main square, as it was first performed, and Dina guards that tradition fiercely. The rest of the year the Old Barracks puts on whatever she likes: new comedies, old farces, and once, regrettably, a tragedy in which the dagger fell apart in the first act.

docs.title: Her company
docs.text:
Dex has played the pompous grandee for fifteen years, two years longer than Dina has been in charge, and she inherited him the way one inherits a beloved, noisy dog. She knows he wants a serious role. She has not yet found one he could play without the audience laughing, and she worries about telling him so. Rue won the part of Juna this spring, beating several older actresses, because Dina saw her freeze in the wings at the audition and then walk on and own the stage. Piper rewrites the songs every year, which drives Dina to despair; she cuts half of them in rehearsal and secretly hums the other half all summer. Thimble, Hambone and little Sprout round out the company that Dina calls her family, and she means it.

Every Walkout Day morning, Quint opens the day by reading the Open Charter aloud before the play begins. Dina treats his reading as the overture and times the first entrance to the moment he rolls up the scroll.

docs.title: Pip
docs.text: Dina's dearest project is not a play but a person. She has watched Pip Marrow grow up backstage and taken her on as a protégée, teaching her to cut a scene, to hear a joke land and to survive a bad night. Dina believes Pip may write something better than her great-grandmother's play one day, and she is careful never to say so aloud, because she knows the whole city already says it too often.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Dina has announced, every year for a decade, that this year's play will be the funniest in ten years. She would like, just once, to be right. Under that she carries a quieter fear: fewer travelers reach the city each summer, and she remembers the year the queen stood in the crowd six years ago. She wonders how many more seasons the square will be full.

A quest might help Dina recover a lost prop before Walkout Day, coax Dex into a serious audition, or carry a letter to a touring player who could join the troupe if the roads allowed it.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Pip Marrow: protégée
  • Dex: lead actor
  • Piper: songwriter
  • Rue: lead actress
  • Quint: opening speaker

docs.title: Old Parsnip
docs.text:
Rooftop Gardener

Town Urbanograd Where Rooftops Role Worker Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Slow, earthy and stubbornly hopeful. Old Parsnip talks to seedlings and swears they listen.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Old Parsnip has a garden that nobody on the ground can see. It runs across three rooftops near the Crooked Tower, in tubs and troughs and split barrels and a bathtub that has not held a bath in living memory: beans up strings, cabbages in rows, onions, carrots, rhubarb, lettuces that bolt in a hot week, and of course parsnips. He is eighty-one, slow and stooped, brown as a turnip from a lifetime of sun on the roofs, and he moves among his tubs at the pace of the plants themselves. He talks to his seedlings, kindly and at length, and swears they listen. Given how they grow, few people argue.

docs.title: Why the city grows on its roofs
docs.text:
Urbanograd's rooftop gardens go back to the Walkers' first winter, when the founders of the city, who knew a great deal about art and very little about farming, nearly starved in the old fortress. Nobody now knows the details of that winter, but everybody knows the lesson: the city should never again depend entirely on what the carts bring. From the next spring on, people grew what they could wherever there was sun, and in a city built upward, the sun is on the roofs.

Old Parsnip has kept that habit longer than anyone living. He began as a boy, carrying buckets of soil up the stairs for the old rooftop growers, and by twenty had tubs of his own. He has outlived every one of the gardeners who taught him, and the habit he learned from them has outlived several fashions for buying everything at the market instead.

docs.title: Neighbours and customers
docs.text:
Perch, whose pigeon loft sits atop the Crooked Tower, is Old Parsnip's neighbour on the next roof over. They trade: Parsnip's cabbage leaves for Perch's pigeon droppings, which Parsnip insists are better than gold for his tubs. Pounce, the big grey cat who sleeps in Perch's loft, uses Parsnip's warmest trough as a second bed on sunny afternoons, and Parsnip has given up and planted that one with catmint.

Mags, the cook of the Great Hall, buys most of her greens from him for the great pot of stew that feeds the Open Table. She finds his habit of talking to cabbages perfectly reasonable, and he finds her habit of shouting at stew equally so. Scrap, the rooftop girl who practises sneaking on everyone, practises on him among the tubs, and he has never once let on that he hears her coming. Jinx once juggled one of his cabbages in Lantern Square, and he has asked for it back, as a joke, every time they meet since.

docs.title: The seeds
docs.text:
Every autumn Old Parsnip saves seed from his best plants, dries it and keeps it in twists of paper in an old chest of drawers in his rooftop shed, each twist labelled in a shaky hand. For most of his life this was a hobby. Now, with fewer food carts reaching the city, people come up the stairs every week to ask him for seeds: workshop families, stall-keepers, a grandmother with a window box, a young couple with a single tub on a balcony. He gives them seed, and advice, and a stern lecture about watering, and he has started to worry that the drawers are emptying faster than he can fill them. Some of his oldest kinds came from Kaldemor's farms long ago, and he has no fresh seed of them at all.

He is stubbornly hopeful all the same. Seeds, he says, are just patience in a paper twist.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Old Parsnip wants every roof in the city green before he dies, and someone young to learn to keep the seed. He fears a hard winter with an empty chest of drawers.

A quest might carry a parcel of fresh seed from Kaldemor's farms through the roads, help him build tubs on a new roof, or find out what has been digging up his beans at night.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Perch: rooftop neighbour
  • Mags: customer

docs.title: Patch
docs.text:
Herbalist of the Gate Walk

Town Urbanograd Where Gate Walk Role Healer Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Brusque, practical and quietly tender. Patch scolds patients while bandaging them.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Patch keeps a narrow herb house on the Gate Walk, a few steps inside the old fortress gate, where bundles of dried leaves hang so thickly from the rafters that tall visitors have to stoop. She is sixty-eight, small, quick and sharp-elbowed, with grey hair cropped short so it will not get in the way and spectacles she only admits to needing in bad light. She is brusque and practical, and she scolds every patient from the moment they sit down until the last bandage is tied. Then she sends them away with a jar of salve and strict instructions, and, if they are young or frightened, a boiled sweet. People who have been patched by Patch speak of her the way they speak of a hard winter they came through: with a wince and real affection.

docs.title: A healer by the gate
docs.text:
Patch was born in Urbanograd and grew up near the Gate Walk. As a girl she went out every summer morning into the meadows beyond the gate with her mother, who sold herbs, and learned to tell yarrow from hemlock, feverfew from chamomile, and which roots to dig in spring and which in autumn. By twenty she was treating the scrapes and sprains of the carters and peddlers who came through the gate, because her house was the first one they reached, and the name Patch stuck to her long before anyone thought to call her a healer. She has kept the house by the gate for more than forty years.

For most of that time her patients were what a gate brings: carters who had dropped a barrel on a foot, peddlers with blisters, travelers with a cough from the road. That has changed. Now they come in with bites, gashes and claw marks, sometimes in the middle of the night, sometimes carried, and there are more of them every season.

docs.title: Her colleagues
docs.text:
Dagny Roe, who keeps the night watch with two lamps, is Patch's friend. On bad nights Dagny brings the wounded straight to Patch's door. Patch scolds the patients while she bandages them and scolds Dagny for standing too near the road, and then makes her a cup of something hot and bitter, mostly willow bark and something Patch will not name, that Dagny swears gets her through till dawn. When the last patient has gone, Dagny walks Patch home, a lamp in each hand, which Patch says is unnecessary and has never once refused.

Ivo Sable, the street healer under the green awning on Lantern Square, is her fellow healer. Patch sees the road's wounded first and Ivo sees them second. They send patients back and forth, share supplies and trade remedies over tea. She scolds and he soothes, and they agree that between them they cover most kinds of person. Knox, the big gentle guard at the gate, brings her carving splinters to pull, and his son Tick brings her skinned knees and long stories, and she treats both with the same sour face and the same care.

docs.title: The empty shelves
docs.text:
Patch's herbs come from outside the walls. For forty years she gathered most of them herself, in the meadows and hedgerows beyond the gate, and bought the rest from farm carts and travelling herb-sellers. Her knees have slowed her, and the fields are risky now: things move in the long grass at dusk, and Brindle has asked her, politely and then not politely, to stop going out alone. The carts bring less every season. Her jars are emptying, and some of the herbs she needs most, for cleaning bites and stopping fevers, grow only in places nobody sensible walks any more.

She needs someone to gather fresh herbs for her, someone who can tell yarrow from hemlock and keep their head when the grass moves. She has not yet found anyone she trusts to do both.

She fears the night a patient comes through the gate whom she cannot help, and the morning after, when the jar she needed turns out to be empty.

A quest might gather fresh herbs from the fields beyond the gate, learn from Patch which plant is which, or find the one rare root she needs that grows only along a road Shade no longer walks.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Ivo Sable: fellow healer
  • Dagny 'Two-Lamps' Roe: friend

docs.title: Perch
docs.text:
Pigeon Keeper

Town Urbanograd Where Rooftops Role Resident Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Soft-spoken, patient and covered in feathers. Perch understands birds better than people and admits it.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Perch lives at the top of the city, in a pigeon loft on the highest roof in Urbanograd, and comes down as seldom as possible. The loft sits on the Crooked Tower, the tallest and leanest of Old Grad's fortress towers, and the climb to it would wind most people half Perch's age. Perch is seventy-one, soft-spoken and patient, and nearly always dusted with feathers. Perch understands birds better than people and says so without embarrassment, because it is simply true.

docs.title: A life with birds
docs.text:
Perch was born in a stacked house below the tower and began feeding the old loft's birds as a child, when an elderly keeper named Isolde Spurr still ran it. Isolde taught Perch to read a pigeon's mood from the set of its wings and to tell every bird apart by its call. When Isolde died, Perch was twenty and already doing most of the work, so the loft simply became Perch's. That was fifty-one years ago.

The birds carry short messages to other towns and back: orders for goods, news of births and deaths, notes between friends who cannot make the journey. Rooftop runners like Kite carry messages within the city; Perch's birds carry them beyond it. Each bird is trained to one or two homes, and Perch knows which is which the way other people know their neighbours' faces.

docs.title: The list
docs.text:
A few years ago, a steady old bird named Greyfeather refused to fly a route she had flown a hundred times. She circled the tower once and came straight back. Perch thought she was ill. Then another bird refused, and another, always on routes that cross certain stretches of wild country. Since then Perch has kept a careful list: which bird, which route, which day, which way the wind blew. The list is long now. Some routes the birds will still fly in the morning but not at dusk. A few they will not fly at all.

Perch does not know why. Perch has guesses, and keeps them modest. Starling, who stargazes on a nearby roof and sometimes sees the horizon toward the middle of the island flicker, has begun bringing a notebook of dates to the loft, and the two of them sit with their lists side by side late at night, not quite saying what they are both wondering.

docs.title: Neighbours
docs.text: Lux, the Keeper of the Lanterns, is Perch's closest friend. Both of them spend their evenings higher than anyone else in the city, and Lux often stops at the loft on the way down from the towers to share a pot of tea and a report of which lanterns are out. Old Parsnip gardens on the next roof over and trades cabbage leaves for pigeon droppings, which he insists are better than gold for his tubs. Pounce, a large grey cat nobody invited, sleeps in the loft every day. The pigeons have accepted him with deep reluctance, and Perch suspects he has never once tried to catch one because it would be too much effort.

docs.title: Hopes and fears
docs.text:
Perch wants the birds to fly freely again, and fears the day the last open route closes and the loft goes quiet. Perch also worries, privately, about who will keep the birds afterwards; no young person has yet asked to learn.

A quest might carry a message the birds refuse to take, find out what waits along one of the refused routes, or find Perch an apprentice who listens to birds.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Lux: friend
  • Pounce: uninvited lodger
  • Old Parsnip: rooftop neighbour
  • Starling: friend

docs.title: Pip Marrow
docs.text:
Juna's Great-Granddaughter

Town Urbanograd Where Old Barracks Theatre Role Performer Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Witty, self-doubting and quick with a comeback. Pip hates being introduced by her surname.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Pip Marrow is nineteen, sharp-tongued and quick with a comeback, and she hates being introduced by her surname. It happens constantly. "This is Pip Marrow," people say, with a meaningful pause, and then they wait for her to say something brilliant, because she is Juna Marrow's great-granddaughter, and Juna Marrow's play is the reason the city exists. Pip usually says something rude instead. It is generally funnier than whatever they were hoping for, which only makes it worse.

docs.title: The Marrow line
docs.text:
Juna Marrow, the young playwright whose banned comedy sparked the Long Walk, had one daughter, Hazel, born in Urbanograd in the city's early years. Hazel had a son, Corin, and Corin had Pip. When Pip was three, a winter fever took both her parents within a week, and she was raised by her grandmother in a crooked little house near the Old Barracks.

Hazel Marrow was not a writer and never pretended to be. She was a seamstress with a dry wit and no patience for fuss, and she told Pip, often, that Juna had been a person and not a statue. She died four years ago, at eighty-eight, and Pip still misses her daily. Hazel was the one person in Urbanograd who never expected anything from the Marrow name.

docs.title: The weight of a play
docs.text:
Everyone else does. Pip grew up hearing her great-grandmother's lines from the cart every Walkout Day and being asked, from the age of seven, when she would write one of her own. So she did. She has written three plays and burned two of them. The third sits in a drawer, finished, and she has not decided yet whether it is good or merely not embarrassing.

Now she is working on a new comedy, and she will not show it to anyone: not her friends, not the troupe, not even Dina. She writes it late at night in a cheap notebook that she keeps on her person at all times. Even its title is a secret, and the only thing anyone knows about it is that she laughs at it sometimes when she thinks she is alone.

docs.title: The people around her
docs.text:
Dina Finch, director of the Old Barracks Troupe, has been Pip's mentor since Pip was small enough to hide in the costume baskets. Since Hazel died, Dina has kept a closer eye on her, teaching her to cut a scene, to time a joke and to survive a bad night, and never once telling her she has to be as good as Juna. Pip has noticed that, and is more grateful than she says.

Hambone, who keeps the old theatre cart, is a good friend. He swears some of the cart's planks come from Juna's own cart, and he lets Pip sit on them during rehearsals, humming the songs, while she pretends not to be moved.

Nix the mask maker has been asked to make a new Juna mask for this year's play and is terrified of getting her face wrong. Since the old pictures of Juna all disagree with one another, Nix has asked Pip to sit as the model. Pip has agreed, and complains about it constantly, and turns up early for every sitting.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Pip wants to write something that is entirely hers, that people love without knowing her surname. She fears that whatever she writes will only ever be judged against a play written a hundred years ago, and that it will lose.

A quest might find a lost page of Juna's that tells Pip something about her great-grandmother as a person, recover Pip's notebook when it goes missing, or help her stage the new comedy in secret.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Dina Finch: mentor
  • Hambone: keeper of her ancestor's cart
  • Nix: mask maker

docs.title: Piper
docs.text:
Songwriter of the Troupe

Town Urbanograd Where Old Barracks Theatre Role Performer Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Romantic, scatterbrained and always humming something new. Piper falls in love with a melody a week.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Piper writes the songs for the Old Barracks Troupe, and is never not humming one. Piper is twenty, thin and untidy, with ink on both hands, a tin whistle in one pocket and a stub of pencil behind each ear, because one always goes missing. Piper is romantic, scatterbrained and helplessly in love with music, and falls in love with a new melody about once a week: a tune whistled by a carter, the rhythm of a loose shutter, the creak of the theatre cart as it turns. Each one is the most beautiful thing Piper has ever heard, until the next.

docs.title: Songs for the play
docs.text:
Juna Marrow's play has been performed on a cart every Walkout Day for a hundred years, and the words have barely changed. The songs are another matter. The troupe has always let them drift with the times, and for the last four years they have been Piper's. Every year Piper rewrites them: new tunes, new verses, new jokes about whatever the city has argued about at the Open Table that spring. Dina Finch, the director, despairs. She cuts half of them in rehearsal, threatens to cut the rest, and then hums the survivors all summer when she thinks nobody is listening. Piper has heard her and has never said a word, which may be the most tactful thing Piper has ever done.

The crowd loves the new songs. By the end of Walkout Day half the square is singing them, and by the autumn the Night Market is still singing them, slightly wrong. Hambone, who keeps the cart, hums the old versions at the same time, on purpose, and the two of them have a long, friendly war over which ones the city will remember. Sprout, Dex's son, knows all of them, old and new, and sings them in whichever order annoys both sides most.

docs.title: Where it began
docs.text: Piper grew up in Urbanograd, in the narrow streets behind the Old Barracks, and began hanging about the theatre at twelve, carrying ladders and listening at the doors. Piper learned to read music from scraps and to play the whistle from anyone who would put up with it. Ozzie Lantry, the historian, once sang Piper the old Walker songs his grandfather had taught him, very badly, and Piper wrote every one of them down and still keeps them, tied with a ribbon. At sixteen Piper played a new tune for the grandee's entrance during a rehearsal, without being asked; Dina shouted, then laughed, and then kept it. That was the beginning.

docs.title: Saffi
docs.text: There is one melody Piper has loved for longer than a week. Saffi, the fiddler of Lantern Square, plays everything twice as fast as anyone else and is writing a tune for every street in the city. Piper has heard all nine she has finished, from the back of the crowd, more times than can be counted, and has written a second part for each of them, to be played on the whistle underneath her fiddle. Piper wants, more than anything, to play them with her. Piper has not asked. Every evening Piper walks to the edge of the square with the whistle, listens to Saffi and Drum play until the lanterns are bright, and walks home again without saying a word.

docs.title: What Piper wants and fears
docs.text:
Piper wants to hear one song of Piper's own sung by the whole square on Walkout Day, and to play one tune, just one, beside Saffi. Piper fears that the moment Saffi hears the whistle part, she will laugh, and not in the kind way.

A quest might carry Piper's written-out second parts to Saffi, find a lost Walker song for the play, or help Piper rescue a favourite song from Dina's cuts.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Saffi: admired musician
  • Dina Finch: exasperated director

docs.title: Pounce
docs.text:
Rooftop Cat

Town Urbanograd Where Rooftops Role Animal Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Lazy by day, dignified by night and certain that every roof belongs to him.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Pounce is a big grey cat, broad in the shoulder and broader in the middle, with a torn left ear, a tail like a feather duster and the unhurried walk of somebody who owns everything he can see. From the Rooftops of Urbanograd he can see a great deal, and he is quite certain that all of it is his. By day he is magnificently lazy. By night he is dignified, watchful and very hard to find, and rooftop folk who meet him on a ridge after dark sometimes step aside for him without quite deciding to.

docs.title: The uninvited lodger
docs.text:
Nobody knows where Pounce came from. He was simply there one wet autumn, years ago, asleep in the straw of Perch's pigeon loft at the top of the Crooked Tower, the highest roof in the city. Perch tried, briefly, to discourage him. Pounce ignored this, as he ignores most things, and has slept in the loft every day since. The pigeons have accepted him with deep reluctance. They mutter when he arrives and settle, eventually, when he does not move. Perch suspects he has never once tried to catch one, because it would be too much effort, and has come to find his company restful. He is the only lodger Perch has ever had who never asks a question.

Last Walkout Day, Ferro the smith gave Perch's loft a small iron cat, and Pounce has slept beside it every afternoon since, as though he has finally been given a portrait of himself and approves of it.

docs.title: His rounds
docs.text:
Pounce has a round, as fixed as a lamplighter's. In the morning he sleeps in the loft. Around midday he crosses to Old Parsnip's rooftop garden next door and sleeps in the warmest trough, which Parsnip has given up on and planted with catmint. In the afternoon he goes back to the loft and the iron cat. At dusk he wakes, stretches, and goes out over the roofs, and where he goes then is his own business. He has been seen on the chimneys above the Night Market, on the ridge of the Great Hall, and once, to general astonishment, riding Rivet's lift.

Rue, who is to play Juna on Walkout Day, rehearses her lines on the Rooftops, usually to Pounce. He is not much help. He yawns at the best speeches and walks away during the climax, and she has decided that this is good training for a real audience. Tick, Knox's son, salutes everyone, including Pounce, and Pounce returns the salute by not leaving, which Tick counts as a great honour.

docs.title: The weather cat
docs.text: Rooftop folk say Pounce always knows when the weather is about to turn. Before a storm he comes in early and curls up in the deepest corner of the loft with his back to the wind; before a long dry spell he sleeps flat out on the slates in the open. Old Parsnip waters by him. Kite plans runs by him. Figgy, down in Lantern Square, has been known to ask Kite whether Pounce has come in yet, because she likes to know when the rain will finish her drawings. Nobody has ever caught Pounce being wrong, though Perch points out that nobody has ever kept a list.

docs.title: What he wants
docs.text:
Pounce wants the warm trough, the sunny ledge, the quiet loft and the respect of the pigeons, roughly in that order. He fears nothing he will admit to, though he does not like the evenings when the wind blows from the middle of the island, and on those nights he does not go out at all.

A quest might find Pounce when he goes missing before a storm, coax him down from somewhere he should not be before Rue's rehearsal, or follow him on his night round to find out where he really goes.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Perch: keeper
  • Rue: rehearsal partner

docs.title: Prism
docs.text:
Light-Painter from the Forest

Town Urbanograd Where Gate Walk Role Performer Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Curious, earnest and delighted by everything. Prism asks questions faster than anyone can answer them.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text:
On most evenings, travelers who come up the last stretch of road to Urbanograd's gate find a picture waiting for them in the air. A heron made of soft blue lights lifts off from nothing and flaps once, twice, over their heads. A little lit cart rolls across the dusk with tiny glowing passengers waving. A lantern blooms between two invisible towers. Then the lights drift apart like sparks off a fire and are gone, and a young person by the gate is beaming at them and asking where they have come from, what the road was like, whether they have ever been to the sea, and how long they are staying, all before they have answered the first question.

That is Prism, the light-painter from the forest. Prism is nineteen, slight and bright-eyed, with leaf-green threads braided through dark hair and fingertips that glimmer faintly after a long evening's work. Prism is curious, earnest and delighted by everything, and asks questions faster than anyone can answer them.

docs.title: A little magic
docs.text:
Prism grew up in Fairy Forest, among the branch-bridges and lantern-lit paths, in a family of basket-weavers who live there still; they write often and play no part here. Prism's gift showed early but stayed small. A few years of lessons at the Grove School taught Prism what that gift could do and, mostly, what it could not: no great workings, no healing, nothing that would ever matter to a scholar. What it could do was make light. Small lights, soft and coloured, that move where Prism moves them and last a few breaths before they fade.

The forest has many people who can do more, and Prism never minded. What Prism minded was the forest's way of thinking that magic must be useful or sacred. Prism wanted to make pictures with it, for no reason except that they were lovely, and had heard of a city where nobody needs a reason. Two springs ago Prism walked out of the forest with a caravan of glass-carters and came to Urbanograd, and has been painting the air at the gate ever since.

docs.title: The Gate Walk
docs.text:
Prism chose the gate on purpose. The roads are frightening now, and travelers arrive tired, dusty and often shaken. Prism wants the first thing they see in Urbanograd to be something beautiful made just for them. The Gate Watch were doubtful at first, because lights in the dusk can be mistaken for other things, and Prism agreed to paint only inside the walls and never toward the road. Now the guards stop to watch, and Tick, Knox's son, who runs the gate's messages, salutes the herons.

The pictures are of the city's own stories: the Walkers' cart, the line of people with bundles, the first lanterns going up between the towers. Prism learned them by asking everyone in Urbanograd to tell them, which took a year and is not finished.

docs.title: Lux
docs.text: Lux, the Keeper of the Lanterns, is Prism's friend. Prism is fascinated by the lanterns, by the colours of their glass and the way they make the old towers float in the dark, and asks Lux more questions about them in one evening than Lux usually answers in a year. Lux pretends to be worn out and, Prism suspects, secretly enjoys it. Some nights Prism climbs part of the round with Lux and paints small moths of light that follow the lantern-pole from tower to tower.

docs.title: Walkout Day
docs.text:
Prism's great hope is a light show for Walkout Day: after the play, when the square is full, a great picture painted across the whole dark sky above Lantern Square, the story of the Long Walk told in light. Lux has promised to help, dimming the lanterns at the right moment so that Prism's lights can be seen. The trouble is size. Prism has never made more than a handful of lights at once, and the show needs hundreds. Prism has been practising every night and has managed forty, briefly, before having to sit down.

Prism fears standing in front of the whole city on Walkout Day and making only a few small sparks. Prism also, quietly, worries about the forest; the news that comes from home is mostly cheerful, and not entirely.

A quest might find a way to make Prism's lights reach across the whole square, fetch something from the forest that could help, or keep the Walkout Day crowd from mistaking the show for something in the sky that should frighten them.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Lux: friend

docs.title: Quint
docs.text:
Keeper of the Charter Scroll

Town Urbanograd Where Great Hall Role Official Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Solemn about exactly one thing, the Open Charter, and cheerfully unserious about everything else.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Quint is the Keeper of the Charter Scroll, and he is solemn about exactly one thing. Ask him about the weather, the price of bread, Bastian's bridge or the state of his own knees and he will make a joke of it; he is seventy-seven, wiry and white-whiskered, and he finds almost everything at least a little funny. But mention the Open Charter and his face changes, his back straightens, and for a moment he looks every inch the old fortress's last sentry.

docs.title: The scroll
docs.text:
The Great Hall keeps a copy of the Open Charter, the ruling in which the royal court declared that the founding treaty's promise protects any people who choose to live differently, so long as they keep the kingdom's peace and laws. It is the reason Urbanograd exists as it does, and the hall's copy is kept in a cedar case in a niche behind the Caller's chair. Quint dusts the case every morning, checks the scroll for damp every week, and lets nobody touch it but himself.

He has been Keeper for twenty-six years. Before that he was a bookbinder with a shop off the Night Market, and the old keeper, Mercy Oakes, chose him to succeed her because, she said, he was the only person in the city who handled paper as if it might bruise. She died the following winter, and Quint has kept the scroll ever since.

docs.title: Walkout Day
docs.text:
Every Walkout Day morning, Quint carries the scroll out into the square and reads the Charter aloud, from beginning to end, before the play begins. The crowd is noisy right up until he starts and silent the moment he does. Dina Finch, who directs the Old Barracks Troupe, treats his reading as her overture and times the cart's first entrance to the moment he rolls the scroll closed. They have worked together this way for thirteen years and argue every single year about whether he reads too slowly. He does, on purpose.

Quint likes to remind the city's young hotheads that the kingdom chose to welcome the Walkers, when it could have sent them home, and that this is worth being proud of. Urbanograd's rebellion, he tells them, has always been about how its people live, never about tearing down the realm that let them. He says it gently, and he says it often.

docs.title: Old friends
docs.text:
Ozzie Lantry, the Historian of the Walkers, has been Quint's friend since they were boys stealing apples on the same rooftops. They eat supper together most weeks and argue about which of them was the worse thief, and Quint is the only person who can reliably find Ozzie's spectacles.

Rook, the Caller, is another old friend. Quint remembers Rook as a child sitting under the Table's benches, listening to arguments with shining eyes, and he was not at all surprised when the Table chose Rook this spring. Rook comes to him when the Table cannot decide whether something is a matter of principle or merely of noise, and Quint answers honestly, which usually means it is noise.

docs.title: What he fears
docs.text:
Quint fears that the city will forget why the Charter matters, once nobody alive remembers anyone who remembered the Walk. He also worries, quietly, about who will keep the scroll after him.

A quest might find a worthy successor for Quint, recover a page from the old court records about the ruling, or keep the scroll safe on a Walkout Day when something goes wrong.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Rook: friend
  • Ozzie Lantry: old friend
  • Dina Finch: director

docs.title: Rivet
docs.text:
Builder of the Rooftop Lift

Town Urbanograd Where Workshops Row Role Craftsman Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Cocky, competitive and very practical. Rivet would rather build something that works than something that sparkles.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Rivet built the lift. Ask anyone on the Rooftops how the crates get up there now, and they will point at the rope-and-pulley tower bolted to the side of the old granary at the end of Workshops Row, and say the name with the same mix of gratitude and exasperation that Rivet seems to inspire in everyone. Rivet is twenty-two, cocky, competitive and very practical, with rope-burned palms and a belt of tools that clank on every step. Rivet would rather build something that works than something that sparkles, and says so, usually within earshot of Margo Venn.

docs.title: Why a lift
docs.text:
Rivet was born in Urbanograd, in a stacked house four floors above the Row, and grew up watching the city carry itself upstairs. Urbanograd grew upward rather than outward, and everything the Rooftops need, from Old Parsnip's soil to the glass for the lanterns, used to go up on somebody's back. Rivet's mother, Hedda, was one of those somebodies: a porter who hauled crates up the rooftop stairs for twenty years until her back gave out. She died when Rivet was sixteen, and Rivet spent the following winter drawing pulleys on every scrap of paper in the house.

The lift went up three years ago, when Rivet was nineteen. It is not pretty. It is ropes, a counterweight of old fortress stones, a hand-winch and a platform that sways in a high wind, and it hauls a full crate from the street to the Rooftops in the time it takes to climb a single flight. Porters who once carried those crates now work the winch instead, and nobody's back gives out.

docs.title: Margo
docs.text:
Margo Venn and Rivet argue about everything: gears against ropes, springs against counterweights, sparks against sense. Margo builds things that dazzle and then, eventually, work; Rivet builds things that work and never sees the point of dazzling. The whole Row has heard them shouting across the street, and the whole Row knows that neither would manage without the other. When the lift jammed last winter, with a crate of lantern glass stuck halfway up, Margo was the first one up the ropes to help, complaining the whole way. Rivet has never quite thanked her, and has quietly rehung her workshop door the last time she blew it off, without being asked.

Rivet has no idea that Margo's apprentice, Bolt, thinks some of Rivet's ideas are better than his teacher's. If Rivet found out, the gloating would last a month.

docs.title: Partners and admirers
docs.text:
Vane, who builds and mends the plank bridges between the rooftops, is Rivet's partner on every project above the second floor. Vane tests the planks by jumping on them; Rivet tests the ropes by hanging off them; together they have opinions about every roof in the city. Vane's daughter, Scrap, rides the lift platform whenever Rivet is not looking, and sometimes when Rivet is.

Edgar Penhallow, the guild apprentice visiting from Selsior, has filled a whole notebook with drawings of the lift and follows Rivet about asking how things work. Rivet pretends to find this annoying, answers every question, and has started letting Edgar hold the tools. They have become friends, which surprised them both.

docs.title: The second lift
docs.text:
Rivet wants to build a second lift, on the far side of the city near the Old Barracks, so that the theatre's scenery and the western roofs' supplies can go up as easily as the eastern ones. It needs timber, rope and the Open Table's agreement, because the lift would hang over a public stair. Rivet has stood up at the Table twice, been talked over by Bastian Krell's bridge campaign both times, and is learning, slowly and resentfully, that building something is easier than persuading people to let you.

What Rivet fears is the lift failing with someone on it. Rivet checks every rope at dawn, and replaced the whole counterweight line after last winter's jam, but the rope that comes in from outside the walls is scarcer and worse than it used to be.

A quest might bring a load of good rope safely into the city, help Rivet win over the Open Table for the second lift, or find out who keeps riding the platform at night.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Margo 'Sparks' Venn: rival
  • Edgar Penhallow: admirer
  • Vane: partner on rooftop projects

docs.title: Rook
docs.text:
Caller of the Open Table

Town Urbanograd Where Great Hall Role Ruler Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Dry, patient and quick to laugh, with a voice that can cut through a shouting hall without ever sounding angry. Rook hates making speeches and loves listening to them.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Rook Tallow makes candles. That is the first thing Rook tells anyone who calls Rook the leader of Urbanograd, and it is meant as a correction. Rook is forty-one, a chandler with a narrow workshop on Workshops Row that smells of beeswax and lamp oil, and this year the Open Table chose Rook as its Caller. Being Caller means convening the Table, keeping order and making sure the quiet ones get a turn. It does not mean ruling anyone, and Rook reminds people of that often, usually just after someone has asked Rook to rule on something.

docs.title: A Walker's great-grandchild
docs.text:
Rook was born in Urbanograd and has never wanted to live anywhere else. Rook's great-grandmother was one of the Walkers who left Selsior a hundred years ago and patched the roofs of Old Grad, and the family has made candles and lamp wicks in the same workshop ever since. Rook grew up sitting under the benches at the Open Table, listening to arguments that ran until dawn, and found them more exciting than any play at the Old Barracks.

Rook is dry, patient and quick to laugh, with a voice that can cut through a shouting hall without ever sounding angry. Rook hates making speeches and loves listening to them, which is exactly why the Table chose Rook this spring; this is the first time Rook has been Caller, and Rook has said loudly that it will be the last.

docs.title: The Table and its people
docs.text: The Great Hall is where Rook spends most evenings now. Dimity Ash, the Table's scribe, sits beside the Caller's chair and keeps the record; Rook and Dimity are colleagues in the truest sense, and Rook leans on her memory of twelve years of votes. Bastian Krell, the loudest voice at the Table, has spoken at every gathering for twenty years and is currently campaigning, at length, for a covered bridge over Lantern Square. He is Rook's favourite heckler, and Rook is his most patient listener. Quint, keeper of the Charter Scroll, is Rook's old friend and adviser, and the person Rook goes to when the Table cannot decide whether something is a matter of principle or merely of noise. Mags feeds the Table from her endless pot of stew, and Rook is grateful for every bowl. Brindle, captain of the Gate Watch, reports to the Table and is Rook's friend, and Rook has heard Brindle's request for more volunteers more times this year than any other. Rook buys tea every night from Saucer at the Night Market, and is fond enough of Nana Gristle on her bench in Lantern Square to listen happily while she scolds.

docs.title: Letters to the capital
docs.text:
Nine years ago, before Rook was anything but a chandler with opinions, Rook wrote an indignant letter to Queen Aveline about Guard patrols that stopped short of the road to Urbanograd. Rook expected no answer. Instead the queen wrote back herself, three pages, agreeing with half of it and arguing with the rest. The patrols were extended the next year, and the letters never stopped.

They write roughly every fortnight and argue about nearly everything: guilds, theatre, the Great Bell, whether a kingdom needs a crown at all. Rook thinks Aveline is the only person who argues fairly, conceding a point the moment it is fairly made, and the best correspondent Rook has ever had.
