They have met in person only once, on Walkout Day six years ago, when the queen came to watch Juna Marrow's play standing in the crowd like anyone else. Rook found her an upturned crate to sit on and has never let her forget it. Rook reads the funniest parts of her letters aloud at the Table, with her blessing, and suspects she now writes some of them on purpose.

docs.title: What Rook fears
docs.text:
Fewer food carts reach the city each year, and the Gate Watch reports monsters closer to the walls than ever. Rook fears the day the Table has to decide something hard and fast, because the Table was never built to be fast.

A quest might deliver a late letter to the capital, help the Table find volunteers for the Gate Watch, or settle Bastian's bridge once and for all.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Dimity 'Inkpot' Ash: colleague at the Table
  • Bastian 'Bellows' Krell: favorite heckler
  • Quint: old friend and adviser
  • Mags: friend
  • Saucer: tea seller
  • Nana Gristle: scolding elder
  • Brindle: captain who reports to the Table
  • Aveline: frequent correspondent

docs.title: Rue
docs.text:
Plays Juna on Walkout Day

Town Urbanograd Where Old Barracks Theatre Role Performer Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Quiet, observant and stricken with stage fright until the very moment she steps on. Then she is fearless.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Rue will play Juna Marrow on Walkout Day this year, on the cart in the main square, in front of the whole city. She still cannot quite believe it, and some mornings she wakes up certain it was a dream. She is twenty, quiet and observant, the sort of person who notices which board on the stage creaks and who in the audience is about to sneeze. Until the very moment she steps on, she is stricken with stage fright: pale, cold-handed, sure she has forgotten every word. Then she walks into the light, and she is fearless.

docs.title: From the farmlands
docs.text:
Rue grew up on a farm in the farmlands around Kaldemor, the third of five children, in a family that grows barley and keeps geese. Her parents and siblings are still there, busy with the harvest, and write to her when the carts are running. Nobody in her family has ever acted, and none of them quite understands why she wanted to, though her mother sends a cake every Walkout Day for luck.

What Rue loved, as a child, was watching. She would sit at the back of the harvest fair and study how the storytellers held a crowd, and then go home and do it all again for the geese. Three years ago, at seventeen, she rode into Urbanograd on a cider cart with a bag of clothes and no plan beyond seeing a real play.

She found work with the Old Barracks Troupe the way Dina Finch once did: pushing the cart, fetching pins for Thimble, sweeping the stage after rehearsals. For two years she never said a line. She learned all of them anyway.

docs.title: The audition
docs.text:
This spring Dina held auditions for Juna, and Rue put her name down on a dare from herself. Several older actresses tried for the part. When Rue's turn came, she froze in the wings, so completely that Hambone went to fetch her a cup of water. Then she walked on and owned the stage, and Dina, who had watched it all, gave her the part before the end of the day. Nobody was more surprised than Rue.

Dina is her director now, and gives her notes even at breakfast. Rue writes every one of them down. Dex, who has played the grandee for fifteen years, has been generous with her, teaching her where the laughs fall and how to wait for them; little Sprout has decided she is his favorite Juna ever, and tells everyone so. Pip Marrow, Juna's great-granddaughter, is sitting as the model for the new Juna mask Nix is making, which means Rue will spend Walkout Day wearing a likeness of Pip's face on her own. The two of them have not yet worked out whether that is funny or strange, and suspect it is both.

docs.title: Pounce and Crumb
docs.text:
Rue practices her lines on the Rooftops, usually to Pounce, the big grey cat who sleeps in Perch's pigeon loft. Pounce is not much help. He yawns at the best speeches and walks away during the climax, which Rue has decided is good training for a real audience.

Crumb, the baker from the farmlands, is her friend in the city. They met at the Night Market in her first week, when she recognized the shape of his rolls from the harvest fairs back home, and they have looked out for each other ever since. He saves her the burnt buns she prefers, and she listens when he is homesick, because she is too.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Rue wants to get through Walkout Day without freezing for good, and, secretly, to write home that she was good. She fears the day the fright does not lift when she steps on, and the whole square sees it.

A quest might carry a letter or a lucky cake from her family through the dangerous roads in time for Walkout Day, coax Pounce down from somewhere he should not be before a rehearsal, or help Rue find a quiet place to practice that nobody knows about.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Crumb: friend from the farmlands
  • Dina Finch: director
  • Pounce: unimpressed audience

docs.title: Saffi
docs.text:
Fiddler of Lantern Square

Town Urbanograd Where Lantern Square Role Performer Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Fierce, fast and impatient with anything slow, including her own fingers. She laughs at her own mistakes before anyone else can.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Saffi plays the fiddle in Lantern Square every evening, and she plays it twice as fast as anybody else in the kingdom. She is twenty-two, small and fierce, with a cloud of dark hair tied back in a strip of red cloth and a bow that has lost half its hairs to sheer speed. She is impatient with anything slow, including carts, queues, long speeches at the Open Table and her own fingers, which never quite keep up with the tune in her head. When she fumbles a run, she laughs out loud before anyone else can, and then plays it again, faster.

docs.title: A respectable family
docs.text:
Saffi was born in Selsior into a family of respectable musicians. Her parents and grandparents played at banquets, guild dinners and grand houses, and they played slow court dances above all: stately, careful tunes for people in heavy clothes to turn in circles to. Saffi was handed a fiddle at four and expected to play those dances for the rest of her life. She learned them perfectly. Then she started playing them faster, just a little at first, and then a lot, until the dancers at one guild dinner gave up and simply ran.

There was a great deal of shouting after that. At seventeen Saffi packed her fiddle and walked out to Urbanograd, which is what Selsior's restless young people have been doing for a hundred years. Her family are still in the capital, still playing slow dances, and they write once a year to ask whether she has calmed down. She writes back that she has not. They play no part in her life here, and she likes it that way, though she still plays one of their slowest dances, very, very fast, every time a letter arrives.

docs.title: Lantern Square
docs.text: Saffi plays at the edge of the square near Ferro's climbable fiddler sculpture, usually sitting on its iron knee. Her bandmate is Drum, who plays a ring of upturned buckets and pans and says almost nothing. They rarely talk about music. Saffi starts, Drum follows, and a few bars later Saffi is following Drum. She laughs at her own mistakes and Drum, unusually, laughs with her. Ivo Sable, from his awning nearby, says she is the best fiddler in the city and argues about it with any patient who disagrees.

docs.title: A tune for every street
docs.text:
Saffi is writing a tune for every street in Urbanograd. Not just the famous ones, the Gate Walk, Workshops Row, the Night Market, but every crooked lane, stair and passage: each one with a tune that sounds the way the street feels to walk down. She has finished nine. Workshops Row clatters, the Gate Walk marches and keeps looking over its shoulder, and the Night Market tune changes key every time it turns a corner. Drum has found a rhythm for all nine. Saffi has a list of the rest pinned inside her fiddle case, and it is very long, because the city keeps building new stairs.

She has no idea that Piper, the troupe's songwriter, has been standing at the back of her crowd for months, and has written a second part for each of her nine tunes. She has noticed a thin person with a tin whistle who never quite plays it, and has wondered about that once or twice, and then started another tune.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Saffi wants to finish every street before the city builds any more, and to play the whole set straight through, all of them, one Walkout Day night. She fears slowing down: growing old, growing careful, and one day playing a court dance at its proper speed without noticing.

A quest might help Saffi map a street she has never found, carry a letter home to Selsior that says more than "not yet", or bring a shy whistle player close enough to be heard.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Piper: admirer
  • Drum: bandmate

docs.title: Saucer
docs.text:
Tea Stall Keeper

Town Urbanograd Where Night Market Sells Spiced tea, honey cakes and fortune leaves

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Rook: regular customer
  • Nana Gristle: old friend
  • Glim: helper

docs.title: Scrap
docs.text:
Rooftop Scamp

Town Urbanograd Where Rooftops Role Child Age Child

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Nimble, nosy and fearless in all the wrong places. Scrap collects lost things and gives them names.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Scrap has never once used the stairs. Not to go to the market, not to visit the Great Hall, not even the time she was carrying a bowl of soup. Scrap goes by rooftop, by plank bridge, by drainpipe, washing line and, when Rivet is not looking, the lift. She is nine years old, nimble and nosy, small enough to fit through gaps that grown-ups have forgotten exist, and fearless in all the wrong places. The rooftop folk have long since stopped shouting when they see her balanced on a chimney pot; they just shout her name, so she knows someone is watching.

docs.title: Vane's daughter
docs.text:
Scrap is the daughter of Vane, who builds and mends the plank bridges between the rooftops and knows every one of them by name. Scrap learned to walk on those bridges, and to read a plank by the sound it makes underfoot before she could read a word. She tests planks the way Vane does, by jumping on them, which is the part of her upbringing Vane most regrets.

Vane is trying very hard to raise her well, with regular meals, clean ears and a sense of where the edge of a roof is. Scrap agrees with the first of these and has opinions about the others. She loves Vane fiercely and shows it by turning up at every bridge Vane is mending, handing over nails nobody asked for and asking why the job is taking so long.

docs.title: Lost things
docs.text:
Scrap collects lost things and gives them names. A brass button called Sir Wobble. A single glove called Lefty, who is still waiting for Righty to turn up. A cracked lantern pane from one of the outer towers, which she found in the gutter one morning and named Bad News without being able to say why. Her collection lives in a biscuit tin under a loose slate on Vane's roof, and she will show it to anyone who promises not to tell, which means everyone has seen it.

She is also, for her size, an extremely good finder. If something has rolled under a bridge, fallen down a chimney or been lost on a rooftop since last spring, Scrap probably knows where it is, and might give it back if it has not been named yet.

docs.title: Ladle
docs.text: Hester Cray, called Ladle, runs the skewer stall at the Night Market, the first one lit and the last one dark. Ladle feeds a few of the rooftop children for free and pretends not to know she is doing it. Scrap is one of them. She is not hungry for want of supper; she is simply always hungry, and Ladle's pepper buns are better than anything else on Veligor. Scrap pays her back with gossip from the Rooftops, delivered upside down from the awning frame, and considers Ladle one of her best friends.

docs.title: Shade
docs.text: Above all, Scrap wants to be an adventurer like Shade, the knife-thrower who guides travelers along the roads into the city. Shade never misses and never brags, and Scrap has decided this is the most impressive way a person can be. She practices sneaking on everyone: on Perch's pigeons, on Old Parsnip among his tubs, on Kite and Splash, and on Shade most of all. She has never once caught Shade unawares. Shade pretends not to have noticed her following, and has quietly taught her how to fall without breaking anything.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Scrap wants to go out through the gate and see the roads Shade talks about. Vane dreads the day she tries. What Scrap fears, though she would never say it, is that the grown-ups will decide she is too big for the rooftops one day and make her use the stairs.

A quest might find something Scrap has lost and not yet named, follow her across the rooftops after she slips away on a dare, or ask her where to find an object nobody else can locate.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Hester 'Ladle' Cray: secret feeder
  • Vane: mother
  • Shade: hero

docs.title: Shade
docs.text:
Knife-Thrower and Road Guide

Town Urbanograd Where Gate Walk Role Adventurer Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Cool, quiet and secretly soft on children. Shade never misses and never brags.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Shade guides travelers and traders safely along the roads into Urbanograd, for a fee and a hot meal, and has never lost one. Shade is thirty-five, cool and quiet, dressed in road-dust greys with a belt of throwing knives across the chest, and has a way of standing so still at the Gate Walk that newcomers do not notice Shade until spoken to. Shade never misses and never brags. The first is a matter of practice; the second, Shade says, is a matter of not needing to.

docs.title: A rooftop child
docs.text:
Shade grew up in Urbanograd, on the Rooftops, the child of two street musicians who died within a year of each other when Shade was twelve. The rooftop folk fed Shade between them, the way they still feed their strays, and Shade learned early to be quiet, quick and difficult to find. It was a useful education. By sixteen Shade could cross the city from the Gate Walk to the Great Hall without touching a street, and could hit a weathervane with a pebble from three roofs away.

At twenty, restless and too good at sneaking for city life, Shade went to Hatch. The old monster hunter was already settled at the Gate Walk and already grumbling about the roads, and he took Shade on for four seasons, spring to winter, on the roads between the towns. Hatch taught Shade to read tracks, to smell weather, to sleep light and to tell an animal that was hungry from one that was something worse. He says Shade is the best he ever taught. Shade says Hatch talks too much after the second cup, and goes to the Gate Walk every few days to listen to him do it.

docs.title: The work
docs.text:
Shade's trade is the last and most dangerous stretch of every journey: meeting caravans and travelers on the roads outside the walls and bringing them in by routes Shade has walked and trusts. Many of those routes were first walked by Hatch. That is the trouble. The routes Shade trusted a few years ago are not safe anymore: a ford where something now waits at dusk, a wooded cutting where the birds have gone silent, a hill path where the tracks have grown too large. Shade has been scouting new ones, longer and stranger, and comparing notes with Hatch when they meet.

Shade's knives come from Ferro, the smith of odd metals, who names every blade before it leaves the forge. Shade has never told anyone the knives' names, but uses them, and Ferro knows it. Their dealings are short and wordless and very satisfactory to both.

docs.title: Scrap
docs.text: Shade is secretly soft on children, and one child in particular has noticed. Scrap, the rooftop scamp who is Vane's daughter, wants to be an adventurer exactly like Shade, and practices sneaking on Shade daily. She has never once caught Shade unawares. Shade pretends not to see her anyway, leaves a careful gap in the conversation for her to overhear, and has quietly taught her how to fall from a low wall without breaking anything. Shade sees a good deal of a younger self on those rooftops, and would like Scrap to have a safer road to the same place, or a different place altogether.

docs.title: What Shade wants and fears
docs.text:
Shade wants one road into the city that stays safe for a whole year. Shade fears the day a traveler trusts Shade's route and the route has changed overnight, and, though Shade would never say it, the day Scrap follows Shade out of the gate.

A quest might scout a new route along the roads with Shade, find out what has made an old ford unsafe, or bring in a caravan that set out before Shade could reach it.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Ferro: smith
  • Scrap: admirer
  • Hatch: old mentor

docs.title: Splash
docs.text:
Night Painter

Town Urbanograd Where Rooftops Role Craftsman Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Restless, playful and allergic to permission. Splash never signs a painting and never stops grinning.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Splash paints at night, on walls nobody is supposed to be looking at. The backs of chimneys, the undersides of plank bridges, the blind side of a water tank, the inside curve of a gutter: if a surface can only be seen from the Rooftops, there is a fair chance Splash has already put a picture on it. Splash is twenty, restless, playful and allergic to permission, paint-spattered to the wrists and never without a grin. Splash has never signed a single painting, and denies painting any of them, grinning the whole time.

docs.title: A painter of the Rooftops
docs.text:
Splash was born in Urbanograd, in a stacked house so high up that the front door opened onto a roof, and grew up on the slates the way other children grow up in the street. Splash's parents, a pair of sign-painters, moved to Selsior when Splash was sixteen, because sign work pays better in the capital. Splash refused to go, stayed behind with a bag of brushes and a borrowed attic, and has been painting the city's hidden walls ever since. The parents write now and then, mostly to ask whether Splash has found proper work yet.

Splash taught painting to Splash. There was no master, no ground colours for anyone, no rule about which pictures may be touched. Splash paints fast and loose and big, in whatever colours are to hand: dregs bought cheap from the sign shops, mixed with brick dust, soot and anything else that will stain. The pictures are of whatever the night suggests: a heron fishing in a rain barrel, a giant asleep with a town on its chest, the moon dropping a coin into a chimney. Rooftop folk come across them on their morning rounds and stop to look, and everyone knows they are Splash's, and nobody can prove it.

docs.title: Kite
docs.text: Kite, the fastest rooftop runner in the city, is Splash's sweetheart. Kite carries the paint pots across the roofs at night and keeps watch while Splash works, talking the whole time in a whisper that is not much of a whisper. Kite is the only person who knows for certain which paintings are Splash's, and keeps that list strictly to Kite. Splash says it is the most romantic thing anyone has ever done, and also that Kite is the worst lookout on Veligor, because Kite keeps turning round to watch the painting instead of the stairs.

docs.title: Ochre
docs.text: Ochre, who keeps the old murals around Lantern Square, is Splash's rival. They have never had a proper conversation. What they have instead is a long exchange of pointed remarks passed through Figgy, Ochre's daughter, who loves Splash's paintings and says so at the top of her voice. Ochre says painting where nobody can see is like singing into a sack. Splash says Ochre paints like someone afraid the wall will tell. Splash also knows, because Kite has seen it, that Ochre climbs up to look at every new picture the morning after, and stands in front of it for a long time. Splash has never said a word about that, and is secretly more pleased by it than by anything Figgy shouts.

docs.title: The Gate Walk
docs.text:
What Splash wants is one painting that can be seen from the Gate Walk. Not hidden, not tucked under a bridge: a picture high on the city's face, big enough that a tired traveler coming up the road at the end of a long and frightening day lifts their head, sees it, and knows they have arrived. Kite has promised to help, and has worked out three ways of getting the paint up there, two of them nearly legal. Splash has worked out what the picture will be and will not tell anyone, Kite included.

The trouble is that the Gate Walk is Ochre's dream too, and Splash knows it. Splash has heard about Ochre's hundred sheets of drawings for a history of the city along those walls, and is pretending not to have heard, in exactly the way Ochre is pretending about Splash. The other trouble is paint. A picture that size needs more colour than Splash has ever had at once, and the good earths and pigments come in from outside the walls, on carts that come less often every season.

Splash fears being made respectable more than falling. Splash would hate to be given a wall, with a ladder and a blessing, and find the picture would not come.

A quest might help Splash and Kite get a mural up where the Gate Walk can see it, bring a load of pigment in safely from the roads, or carry a message between Splash and Ochre that is not, for once, an insult.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Ochre: rival painter
  • Kite: sweetheart

docs.title: Sprout
docs.text:
Troupe Urchin

Town Urbanograd Where Old Barracks Theatre Role Child Age Child

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Giggly, loud and never still. Sprout has learned every part in the play by accident.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Sprout is never still. He is eight years old, small, freckled and loud, with hair that sticks up whatever anyone does to it and a giggle that can be heard from the far side of Lantern Square. He lives at the Old Barracks Theatre, among costume baskets, painted flats and folded scenery, and he has run, climbed, hidden and fallen asleep in every corner of it. Every Walkout Day he plays the market urchin who cheers for Juna in the first scene of Juna Marrow's play, and every year, with one line and a cartwheel nobody asked for, he steals the show.

docs.title: Growing up backstage
docs.text:
Sprout is the son of Dex, the big booming actor who has played the grandee for fifteen years. His mother, Lark, sang in the troupe's chorus and died of a fever when Sprout was barely a year old. He does not remember her, but he knows her songs, because his father sings them, badly, and because on the anniversary of her death the two of them climb up to the Rooftops to watch the lanterns come on across the city and sing one of them together. Sprout thinks of it as a good night, not a sad one. His father has made sure of that.

Dex raised him backstage, with half the troupe for aunts and uncles. Dina Finch, the director, calls the company her family, and to Sprout that is simply true. Hambone, who keeps the old cart, lets him ride on the tailboard, or rather, does not notice him riding on it, which Sprout counts as the same thing. Thimble, the costume maker, has pins in her mouth at all times and has stitched every one of Sprout's urchin costumes, letting each one out a little more every spring and complaining about how fast he grows. Sprout knows about the crack in the cart's left rear wheel, because he knows everything that happens backstage, and he has kept the secret, which for Sprout is a heroic effort.

docs.title: Every part, by accident
docs.text:
Sprout has learned every part in the play without ever meaning to. He has heard the rehearsals so many times that the lines simply stayed in his head: Juna's speeches, the grandee's bluster, the market crowd's jeers, the songs. He sings Piper's new songs and Hambone's old versions of them both, in whichever order annoys both sides most, and he does the grandee's fall off the cart on any raised surface available, including, once, the Great Hall's table during a quiet moment in a debate.

He has decided that Rue, who plays Juna this year, is his favourite Juna ever, and tells everyone so, including the older actresses who have played her before. When Rue froze in the wings at her audition this spring, Sprout told her afterwards that he freezes too sometimes, but only when he is about to do something brilliant. Rue says it was the most useful note she got all year.

docs.title: The hat
docs.text:
What Sprout wants most in the world is to play the grandee one day, and the reason is the hat. The grandee's hat is a tall tower of purple felt and feathers that Thimble keeps locked away between shows, and that even Dex is not allowed to take home. Sprout has seen it, been near it and once, for nearly a whole breath, touched it. He has a plan, roughly, involving growing up. Dex pretends to be outraged that his son wants his part, and is secretly the proudest man in Urbanograd.

Sprout fears very little except being told to sit still. He sometimes worries, though, that his father is sad when nobody is looking, and he has started making him laugh on purpose, just in case.

A quest might find Sprout when he has hidden somewhere in the Old Barracks right before his cue, help him get a look at the locked hat, or carry a song of Lark's that someone else in the city remembers back to Dex and Sprout.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Dex: father

docs.title: Starling
docs.text:
Rooftop Stargazer

Town Urbanograd Where Rooftops Role Scholar Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Distracted, kind and wildly enthusiastic about anything in the sky. Starling sleeps through every afternoon.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Starling lives upside down to the rest of Urbanograd. When the Night Market is closing and the last fiddlers are packing up, Starling is wide awake on a flat roof not far from the Crooked Tower, eye to a brass tube, murmuring numbers into the dark. When the city is at its busiest in the middle of the afternoon, Starling is asleep, usually in a hammock slung between two chimney stacks, with a notebook open on Starling's chest. Starling is thirty-four, distracted, kind and wildly enthusiastic about anything in the sky, and will explain a comet to anyone who stands still for long enough, including people who were only trying to get past.

docs.title: How it started
docs.text:
Starling was born in Urbanograd and was the sort of child who fell asleep on the roof and had to be carried in. Starling's parents, a pair of quiet bookbinders, are both dead now; what they left was a narrow house with a flat roof and a shelf of old almanacs, one of them a battered star chart drawn by somebody in the city's early years, with the constellations given Walker names nobody else uses: the Cart, the Fiddle, the Open Door. One of them has faded from the sky since the chart was drawn, or was never quite there: a crooked line of faint stars the chart calls the Lost Bow, which Ozzie Lantry thinks the Walkers named for something they left behind in Selsior. Starling learned the sky from that chart and from lying on the slates, and has spent the years since correcting it, adding to it, and growing fonder of it with every mistake found.

The telescope came later. It is built out of Tinsel's spare lenses: the slightly wrong ones, the ones with a bubble near the edge, the ones Tinsel held up to the sun and decided were not quite good enough to sell. Tinsel, the glassblower on Workshops Row, gives them to Starling instead of melting them down, and over the years they have become a long brass tube, three eyepieces and a finder made from a bottle bottom. Tinsel comes up to look through it on clear nights and talks about the colour of starlight for hours, which suits Starling perfectly. They are friends of the kind who can lose a whole evening agreeing about something beautiful.

docs.title: The flickers
docs.text:
About two years ago, on a clear night with no moon, Starling noticed something wrong with the horizon. Not the sky: the very edge of the land, toward the middle of the island, where the distant country meets the stars. For a few breaths it seemed to waver, the way air wavers above a hot stove, though the night was cold. Then it was still again. Starling thought it was tired eyes. It happened again a month later, and again.

Starling has started writing down the dates, and the hours, and the weather, without knowing what any of them mean. The flickers are not regular. They do not follow the moon or the seasons, as far as Starling can tell. They do not show on every clear night, and they never show from anywhere in the city lower than the Rooftops.

Perch, who keeps pigeons on the Crooked Tower and is Starling's friend, keeps a list of the routes the birds have begun to refuse. Last autumn Starling brought the notebook of dates up to the loft for the first time, and now the two of them sit late at night with their lists side by side, comparing. Some of the days seem to match. Some do not. Neither of them knows what that means, and neither has yet quite said aloud what they are both wondering.

docs.title: What Starling wants and fears
docs.text:
Starling wants to understand the flickers, and also, more simply, to finish the chart: every star over Urbanograd named and placed, in a book anyone could use. Starling fears that the flickers mean something everyone ought to know about, and that by the time anyone believes a person who sleeps all afternoon, it will be too late to matter.

A quest might watch the horizon with Starling on a night of flickers, carry Starling's dates and Perch's routes to someone who might read them, or bring Tinsel's newest lens safely up through the crowded streets.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Tinsel: lens maker
  • Perch: friend

docs.title: Thimble
docs.text:
Costume Maker

Town Urbanograd Where Old Barracks Theatre Role Craftsman Age Elder

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Fussy, sharp-eyed and secretly sentimental. Thimble has pins in her mouth at all times and still talks.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Thimble has pins in her mouth. She has had pins in her mouth, as far as anyone at the Old Barracks can remember, for thirty years, and in all that time she has never once stopped talking around them. She is sixty-six, small, sharp-eyed and fussy, with spectacles on a ribbon, a tape measure round her neck and a pincushion strapped to her wrist like a bracer. She can tell from across the stage that a hem has dropped by the width of a fingernail, and she will say so, through the pins, during the most moving speech in the play.

docs.title: Coming to the troupe
docs.text:
Thimble was born in Urbanograd and grew up sewing. For years she worked for a dressmaker off the Night Market, turning out party clothes for half the city, and on Walkout Days she stood in the crowd and watched the troupe's costumes come apart at the seams in front of everyone. One year she went backstage after the play to tell them so. The troupe's costume maker then, an old woman called Wilhelmina Gage, listened to the whole complaint, handed her a needle and a split doublet, and said that if she knew so much she could start now. Thimble was thirty-six. Wilhelmina died a few winters later, and the baskets were Thimble's.

That was thirty years ago, back when Bellamy Stroud still directed, and Thimble has sewn every costume the troupe has worn since: the market crowd's patched coats, Juna's famous green jacket, the chorus's ribbons and the absurd, glorious, feathered nonsense of the grandee. She keeps them in wicker baskets labelled in a hand nobody else can read, and she knows which patch on which coat came from which year's play.

docs.title: The hat
docs.text:
The grandee's hat is her particular charge: a tall tower of purple felt and feathers, rebuilt a little every spring, that gets the biggest laugh in the play before Dex has even opened his mouth. Thimble keeps it locked away between shows, in a box with a key she wears on the same ribbon as her spectacles. Dex has asked to take it home every year for fifteen years. She has said no every year, and she will go on saying no, because she knows exactly what Dex would do with it at the Night Market.

Little Sprout, Dex's son, wants to play the grandee one day so that he can wear that hat. Thimble tells him it would sit on his shoulders. She has also, without telling anybody, started keeping the feathers she trims off each spring in a separate packet, in case a smaller hat is ever needed.

docs.title: Friends and fabric
docs.text:
Hambone, who keeps the cart, is her oldest friend. They have shared a bench backstage for thirty years, Thimble sewing and Hambone polishing, and they argue about everything: feathers, the speed of the Walkers' song, whether the cart needs a new coat of paint. She knows about the cracked wheel, and has not said a word to anyone, because Hambone's ears go red whenever it comes up and she cannot bear to watch. For two years Rue fetched Thimble's pins and swept her scraps before anyone knew Rue could act. Thimble is now telling everyone that she knew all along. She did not.

Thimble buys her brightest fabric from Dyna, the tailor on Workshops Row who dyes cloth in colours no guild would allow. She complains about the price every single time, at length, with pins, and Dyna compliments her spectacles and does not move a copper. Both of them enjoy it enormously. Lately the cloth from outside the walls has grown scarcer, and Dyna's prices have risen for real, and the haggling has a sharper edge than it used to.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Thimble is secretly sentimental. She has kept a scrap from every Juna jacket she ever made, sewn into the lining of her own coat. She wants the troupe to look splendid on the cart every Walkout Day for as long as she can thread a needle, and she fears the year her eyes are not good enough to see the dropped hem, and nobody tells her.

A quest might bring a bolt of good cloth safely through the roads, find a lost basket of costumes before the play, or help Thimble track down the oldest Juna jacket, which she has never been able to find.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Dyna: supplier
  • Hambone: old friend

docs.title: Tick
docs.text:
Gate Messenger

Town Urbanograd Where Gate Walk Role Child Age Child

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Eager, earnest and always out of breath. Tick salutes everyone, including the cat.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Tick is ten years old and always out of breath. He runs messages from the city gate to everywhere else in Urbanograd, by street and stair and alley, and he arrives at every door panting, red-faced and saluting, because Tick salutes everyone: the guards, the carters, the herbalist, the Caller of the Open Table, the stray dogs at the gate and Pounce, the big grey cat, who returns the salute by not leaving. Tick is eager, earnest and completely sincere, and the only person in the city who takes his salutes for granted is his father.

docs.title: A boy of the Gate Walk
docs.text:
Tick is the son of Knox, the biggest and gentlest guard of the Gate Watch. Knox signed on with the Watch when Tick was a baby, and when Tick's mother, Jessamy, died after a fall on an icy stair eight years ago, Knox raised him at the Gate Walk. Tick was two. He does not remember her face, only a laugh, and he is not sure whether he remembers it or has been told about it so often that it feels like remembering.

So Tick learned to walk between the guards' boots, to count wagons before he could count to twenty, and to talk to every traveler who came through the gate. Brindle, the captain, lets him read the weekly sightings slate aloud, slowly, with feeling. Dagny, who keeps the night watch with two lamps, lets him hold one of them until bedtime. Patch, the herbalist a few steps inside the gate, treats his skinned knees with a sour face, great care and a boiled sweet, and listens to the long story of how each knee got skinned.

docs.title: The messages
docs.text: Tick began running messages when he was seven, because there was always someone at the gate who needed to tell someone in the city that they had arrived. Now the Gate Watch sends him with word for the Great Hall, carters send him to the Night Market traders, and travelers send him to whoever is expecting them. He knows the streets the way Kite knows the roofs, and he is convinced that one day he will beat Kite's record from the Gate Walk to the Great Hall. Kite's record is run over the rooftops. Tick means to beat it by the streets. Everyone tells him this is impossible, and Tick writes down each of their names, so he will know whom to tell.

docs.title: The notebook
docs.text:
Tick keeps a notebook of every strange story a traveler tells him. It is on its third volume. In it are a talking crow on the road from Kaldemor, a ford where the water ran backwards for an evening, a stag with antlers like a burnt tree, and lights seen moving in a wood where nobody lives. Tick does not judge the stories; he writes them all down, with the teller's name and the date. Some are obviously nonsense. Some, Tick is sure, are not, and those have been arriving more often.

Zip Calloway's broken arm is in the notebook three times, in three different versions, all told by Zip.

docs.title: Hatch
docs.text: Above everyone, Tick admires Hatch, the old monster hunter who has walked Veligor's roads for thirty years. Tick follows him about the Gate Walk with the notebook, asking for stories at every hour, and Hatch pretends to find it tiresome and answers every question. Tick wants to be an adventurer like Hatch, out on the roads, tracking things nobody else can follow. His father wants him to be anything else at all, and they have that argument at supper most nights. Tick knows he is winning it, and does not quite understand why winning makes his father look so tired.

docs.title: What he wants and fears
docs.text:
Tick wants to beat Kite's record, to fill his notebook, and one day to walk out through the gate as an adventurer with Hatch's blessing. What he fears, though he has never told anyone, is coming back from a message one evening and finding his father's place at the gate empty.

A quest might race Tick through the streets against the clock, follow up one of the strange stories in his notebook, or carry an urgent message from the gate when Tick has run himself off his feet.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Knox: father
  • Hatch: reluctant hero

docs.title: Tinder
docs.text:
Fire-Eater

Town Urbanograd Where Lantern Square Role Performer Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Swaggering and showy on stage, careful and nervous off it. Tinder checks the water bucket three times before every show.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text:
On stage, Tinder is magnificent. She struts into the middle of Lantern Square in a scarlet waistcoat, bows to the crowd as if they ought to be bowing to her, lights a torch, tips her head back and swallows the flame whole, then breathes it out again in a roaring orange plume that sends the front row stumbling backwards and the children shrieking with delight. She juggles burning clubs, walks a line of hot coals and lights a stranger's pipe with a kiss of flame from her own lips. She is thirty-three, broad-shouldered and loud, and she makes the whole thing look like the easiest trick in the world.

Off stage, she checks the water bucket. Then she checks it again. Then, just before she begins, she checks it a third time, and anyone who has watched her for long knows that the swagger only starts after the third check.

docs.title: A life on the road
docs.text:
Tinder was born into a traveling show, a string of painted wagons called Brightwater's that went from town to town across Veligor with acrobats, a dancing goat and a fire-eater. Her parents were tumblers with the show; both are dead now. The fire-eater was an old man called Cassius, with no eyebrows and very steady hands, and he took Tinder on when she was eleven because she kept trying to copy him with candles. He taught her the trick, the breath, the oils and the order of things, and above all he taught her the bucket. Fire, he said, is a guest that never goes home on its own.

Cassius also taught her his superstitions, and one of them she has never shaken. He would not perform anywhere near the old stories of the Burning: not on a stage where someone had just been telling them, not in a square where a balladeer was singing them, not even in a town where the children played at being it. He said it was bad luck to play with fire while the fire was listening. Tinder does not know whether he believed it. She does.

The show came to Urbanograd eleven years ago, when Tinder was twenty-two. Cassius had died the winter before, and the wagons were older and the roads slower than they used to be. Tinder performed in Lantern Square for a week, and nobody told her to stop, and nobody told her to move on, and nobody told her a fire-eater ought not to be a woman, as people had in other places. When the wagons left, she stayed. The show did not come back.

docs.title: Lantern Square
docs.text:
Tinder's pitch is a stretch of flagstones in the middle of the square, well away from the awnings. If a storyteller starts in on the Burning nearby, she packs up and moves, mid-show if she has to, and the regulars have learned to follow her. Ivo Sable, the street healer whose green awning stands at the edge of the square, has treated her blistered lips and singed hands more times than either of them can count. He scolds her every time about the bucket, even though she already checks it three times, and she brings him the first coins of every good night.

Jinx, the juggler, is her friend. Four winters ago she found a skinny fourteen-year-old from Selsior juggling for coins in the cold, shared her supper and showed Jinx the corners of the square that stay warm after dark. Jinx wants more than anything to learn to juggle burning torches, and Tinder refuses to teach the trick, at least for now. Jinx does not yet check the water bucket even once, let alone three times. Tinder will teach Jinx the day Jinx checks it without being told, and she has not said so, because then Jinx would only do it to be taught.

docs.title: What she wants and fears
docs.text:
Tinder wants to grow old in this square, eyebrows and all, and to pass the trick on properly before her hands stop being steady. She fears a fire she cannot put out, and, more quietly, that the old stories Cassius would not perform near are not only stories.

A quest might fetch the special lamp oil Tinder's act needs from outside the walls, move a Burning storyteller along before her show, or persuade her that Jinx is finally ready.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Jinx: friend
  • Ivo Sable: healer

docs.title: Tinsel
docs.text:
Glassblower

Town Urbanograd Where Workshops Row Role Craftsman Age Adult Sells Lantern glass, bottles and glass beads

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Dreamy, slow-spoken and fascinated by light. Tinsel holds every bit of glass up to the sun before selling it.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Tinsel's furnace is the warmest place on Workshops Row and the slowest. Customers who come for a box of beads or a dozen bottles find the glassblower in no hurry at all: Tinsel takes each piece down from the shelf, carries it to the open door, and holds it up to the sun, turning it slowly, watching the light come through, before wrapping it in straw and naming a price. It can take a long time to buy a jar. Tinsel is forty-two, dreamy and slow-spoken, with burn-freckled forearms and pale, patient eyes, and is fascinated by light in a way that makes other people stop and look at their own windows.

docs.title: The glass that lights the city
docs.text:
Urbanograd glows at night because of Tinsel. The lanterns strung between Old Grad's towers burn behind coloured panes, amber and rose and sea-green and a deep cornflower blue, and nearly every one of those panes came out of Tinsel's furnace. Tinsel learned the craft as a child from an old glassblower called Ignatius Fenn, who kept the same furnace before Tinsel and who used to say that glass is only sand that has been told a secret. Ignatius died when Tinsel was twenty-five, seventeen years ago, and the furnace has been Tinsel's since.

Lux, the Keeper of the Lanterns, is Tinsel's best customer and the most patient one, willing to stand in the doorway while each pane is held up to the sun and admired before it is wrapped. The two of them argue, cheerfully and endlessly, about which colours carry furthest in fog. Lux says amber. Tinsel says it depends on the fog. Lately there has been less time for arguing: some of the lanterns on the outward side of the walls have been found smashed in the mornings, frames bent and glass scattered, and Lux needs new panes faster than Tinsel can make them. It was a crate of Tinsel's lantern glass that stuck halfway up Rivet's lift when it jammed last winter. Tinsel stood at the bottom the whole time, perfectly calm, and only afterwards had to sit down.

Bastian Krell made the bellows that keep Tinsel's fire hot, and mends them, and charges for every repair with an opinion about the last night's Table. Tinsel listens to all of it with a dreamy nod and has never been known to disagree.

docs.title: Starling
docs.text: The lenses are where Tinsel's work goes strangest. Tinsel grinds them on winter evenings, for the joy of it: lenses for spectacles, lenses for magnifying glasses, and, more and more, lenses for Starling, the stargazer who lives on the roofs near the Crooked Tower. The ones that come out slightly wrong, with a bubble near the edge or a curve a hair too deep, Tinsel cannot bear to melt down, and gives them to Starling instead. Over the years they have become a telescope. On clear nights Tinsel climbs up to look through it, and the two of them talk about the colour of starlight until the lanterns burn low. They are each the only person the other has met who thinks that is a reasonable way to spend a night.

docs.title: The glass that glows
docs.text:
Tinsel's great experiment is a glass that glows on its own: no oil, no wick, no flame, just light caught inside it and given back slowly in the dark. Tinsel has tried powdered shells, rare sands, river stones, a pinch of everything in the street apothecaries' jars, and once, unwisely, some of Margo Venn's leftover spark-powder. So far the results have been very pretty paperweights. They sit in a row on the windowsill, dozens of them, swirled and bubbled and catching the light beautifully, and not one of them glows after sunset. Tinsel sells a few to visitors and keeps the best.

The sands Tinsel needs for good clear glass come in from outside the walls, and the carts are fewer every season. Tinsel has begun reusing broken glass, which Tinsel dislikes, because remelted glass is never quite as clear.

docs.title: What Tinsel wants and fears
docs.text:
Tinsel wants to make one piece of glass that shines in the dark, and to hang it in a lantern where the outer walls face the wilds. Tinsel fears, without saying so, the night there is no glass left to give Lux.

A quest might carry a load of good sand safely in from the roads, gather some strange mineral from the wilds for the glowing glass, or deliver a crate of new panes to Lux before the outer lanterns go dark.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Lux: customer
  • Starling: friend

docs.title: Torvi Brask
docs.text:
Axe-Fighter from the Highlands

Town Urbanograd Where Gate Walk Role Adventurer Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Proud, honest and bemused by city manners. Torvi laughs like a rockslide.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Torvi Brask is the axe-fighter from the highlands, and anyone on the Gate Walk can find Torvi by ear. Torvi laughs like a rockslide: a long, rolling roar that starts somewhere low and keeps going, startles carters' mules, and makes the Gate Watch grin before they know what the joke was. Torvi is proud, honest to the point of rudeness, and still, after six years, bemused by city manners.

docs.title: From the high slopes
docs.text:
Torvi was born thirty-one years ago on the Brask homestead, a stone shelter and a few goat pens on the far slopes of the highlands, a long walk from any town. Torvi's parents still keep the herd there; they send word down with the wool carters now and then and play no part in Torvi's life in the city. Whether the Brasks count themselves among any of Midbarium's four families is a question Torvi answers differently depending on who is asking.

It was Torvi's grandmother, Hulda Brask, who put an axe in Torvi's hands. She split wood with it, cleared scrub with it, and once, in a story Torvi has told in every tavern on the Gate Walk, drove off a hill cat with it while still holding a pail of milk. Hulda taught Torvi to fight the way the slopes teach anything: plainly, with no flourishes, for the sake of the herd. She also taught the lesson Torvi values most, that a fighter who never runs is a fighter who only gets one bad day. Hulda died when Torvi was twenty-two, and her axe, its handle replaced twice, is the one Torvi carries now.

docs.title: Down to the city
docs.text:
Six years ago, at twenty-five, Torvi walked down out of the hills to see the city everyone at the highland fires talked about. Torvi meant to stay a week. On the first night, in Lantern Square, someone was hammering out a rhythm on buckets and pans while half the square danced, and Torvi, who had grown up on drumming, joined the dancing and did not stop until the lanterns guttered. Torvi stayed because the music was good, and it has stayed good: Torvi stamps along to Drum's buckets, and calls Saffi's fast fiddle tunes the only thing in the city that moves like a mountain wind.

The manners are another matter. In the highlands, anyone who comes to your fire in peace is given water, food and a place to sleep. In Urbanograd, Torvi has learned, you do not invite strangers in off the street, you queue at Night Market stalls, and you do not settle an argument by wrestling. Torvi went to the Open Table once, listened to a whole evening of speeches end in an agreement to talk more next week, and laughed so loudly that the Caller had to wait. Torvi likes the Table anyway, because anyone may speak there, and Torvi respects that more than Torvi can explain.

docs.title: Caravan guard
docs.text: Torvi earns a living by hiring out as a caravan guard on the roads to Kaldemor, Selsior and the harbours. Torvi charges a fair price, refuses to promise a safe road when there isn't one, and tells caravan masters plainly which stretches have gone bad. More caravans want guards every season. Shade often brings Torvi's caravans in over the last stretch to the gate, and the two of them compare tracks. Hatch and Torvi trade stories over cups at the Gate Walk; Hatch only starts after the second cup, Torvi after the first. Brindle buys Torvi more drinks than the Watch's purse can afford, and Torvi has carried more than one bitten traveler straight to Patch's door.

docs.title: Zip
docs.text:
Last spring Torvi guarded the caravan to Kaldemor that Zip had talked her way onto. Two days out, something large and tusked crashed out of the brush, and Zip ran at it. Torvi splashed across the stream too late to stop her falling off the top of the bank, found her on the rock with her arm broken in two places, looked her over, laughed, and told her that bravery was wasted on someone who could not fight. Then Torvi carried her back to the wagons over one shoulder while she shouted about the tusks, and bound the arm the way Hulda taught.

Back in the city, Zip followed Torvi around the Gate Walk until Torvi gave in. Now they train most mornings on the open ground inside the gate: footwork, guard, when to stand and, above all, when to run. Torvi is proud of how fast she learns everything except the running.

docs.title: Wants and fears
docs.text:
Torvi wants the roads open, because the music needs them: fewer outside traders come every year, and Torvi knows a city that cannot trade will stop dancing first. One day Torvi wants to walk home with the city's tunes in Torvi's head and play them badly at a highland fire. What Torvi fears is the day Zip stands when she should run, with Torvi too far away to carry her back.

A quest might guard a caravan with Torvi and Zip while she tries Margo's spark lamp on the road, or go back to the stream bank where the tusked beast vanished. Torvi only saw tracks at the top of the bank, larger than any boar's, and has wondered ever since what made them.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: • Zinnia 'Zip' Calloway: student

docs.title: Vane
docs.text:
Rooftop Bridge-Builder

Town Urbanograd Where Rooftops Role Worker Age Adult

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Fearless, practical and calm in a high wind. Vane tests every plank by jumping on it.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Vane is the reason you can cross Urbanograd without touching the ground. The plank bridges that run between the city's rooftops, from chimney to chimney, gable to gable, tower to stacked tower, are Vane's to build and Vane's to mend, and Vane knows every one of them by name. Vane is thirty-seven, lean and weathered, with a coil of rope over one shoulder, a hammer through the belt and a habit, alarming to anyone watching, of testing every new plank by jumping on it as hard as possible. Vane is fearless, practical and calm in a high wind, and has been seen standing on a ridge in a gale, eating an apple, while the bridge beside it bucked like a horse.

docs.title: Learning the bridges
docs.text:
Vane was born in Urbanograd, high up, and was carrying nails for the old bridge-builder Corbett before Vane could carry anything else. Corbett had kept the bridges for most of his life and named every one he built: the Long Lean, Grandmother's Step, the Fiddler's Crossing above Lantern Square, the Wobbler, which does not wobble and never has, and the Kiss, which is short. He taught Vane that a bridge is only as good as the worst plank in it and that the wind is never your friend, only an honest enemy. When Corbett died, Vane was twenty-four and already doing the heavy work, and the bridges simply passed to the one who knew them.

Vane has added a good many since. The new ones get names too, chosen with care, because a rooftop runner has to be able to shout "not the Gutter Queen, take Old Copper" across three roofs in a hurry. There are more than two hundred bridges now, and Vane walks some part of them every morning, listening to the planks underfoot. A bad plank sounds different. Vane can hear it from the next roof.

docs.title: Rivet
docs.text:
Rivet, who built the lift at the end of Workshops Row, is Vane's partner on every project above the second floor. Rivet tests ropes by hanging off them; Vane tests planks by jumping on them; between them, there is not a roof in the city they do not have an opinion about. They have been arguing about the second lift Rivet wants near the Old Barracks for a year now, about where the platform should land and which bridge it would make redundant, and both are enjoying it. Bastian Krell's covered bridge over Lantern Square is another matter. Vane has told Bastian, more than once, that it would need more timber than reaches the city in a year. Bastian keeps campaigning anyway, and Vane keeps quietly measuring the gap, just in case.

Vane sometimes finds pictures on the undersides of the bridges in the morning, painted overnight: a heron, a laughing moon, a giant asleep. Vane knows perfectly well whose they are, and has said nothing, except to point out that paint does not keep the rain off a plank as well as tar.

docs.title: Scrap
docs.text:
Scrap is Vane's daughter, nine years old, who has never used a staircase in her life. She learned to walk on Vane's bridges and to read a plank by its sound before she could read a word, and she tests planks by jumping on them, which is the part of her upbringing Vane most regrets. Vane is trying very hard to raise her well: regular meals, clean ears, bed before the lanterns are all lit and a firm sense of where the edge of a roof is. Scrap agrees with the meals. Her collection of named lost things lives in a biscuit tin under a loose slate on Vane's roof, and Vane has been shown it many times, always under oath.

What frightens Vane, who is frightened of almost nothing, is the road. Scrap wants to be an adventurer like Shade, the knife-thrower who guides travelers into the city, and one day she will want to go out through the gate and see the roads for herself. Vane is grateful that Shade taught her how to fall safely, and dreads the day she wants to learn something more.

A quest might bring good timber safely into the city for a bridge, find out who has been loosening planks on the Long Lean at night, or follow Scrap when she slips out toward the gate.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Scrap: daughter
  • Rivet: partner on rooftop projects

Town Urbanograd Where Night Market Sells Curios, trinkets and oddities from across Veligor
