docs.title: Zinnia 'Zip' Calloway
docs.text:
Young Adventurer

Town Urbanograd Where Gate Walk Role Adventurer Age Young

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Reckless, sunny and determined to be famous. Zip has never met a dare she would refuse.

docs.title: Lore
docs.text: Zinnia Calloway has never met a dare she would refuse, and the whole Gate Walk knows it. Nobody calls her Zinnia except, very occasionally, in a tone of warning. She is Zip: eighteen, sunny, sunburnt, with a shock of copper hair she cuts herself with whatever is sharpest, a sword she has not yet earned the right to swing and an arm that still aches when the weather turns. Zip is reckless, cheerful and absolutely determined to be famous, and she has decided that the quickest way to fame is to go and stand next to something terrifying and see what happens.

docs.title: A city girl
docs.text:
Zip grew up in Urbanograd, in her grandmother's laundry at the bottom of the Gate Walk, among copper tubs, wet sheets and steam. Her parents died when she was too small to remember them, and her grandmother, Ottoline Calloway, raised her: a big, slow-voiced washerwoman who had walked to every town on Veligor as a girl and told Zip about all of them while wringing out shirts. Ottoline died two winters ago. Zip kept the laundry going for one season, and then, as she puts it, had to admit that she was not a laundry sort of person. She gave the tubs to the woman next door and moved into the room above the shop with a pack, a borrowed sword and Ottoline's old road map.

Growing up at the foot of the Gate Walk, Zip watched every adventurer who came through the gate, and decided early that she would be one of them, and the best one, and that people would sing about her in the Night Market.

docs.title: The broken arm
docs.text:
Last spring, Zip went on her first adventure. She talked her way onto a caravan bound for Kaldemor as an extra pair of hands, and two days out, when something large and tusked crashed out of the brush and the carters reached for their spears, Zip ran at it. She did not catch it. She chased it across a stream and up a steep bank and fell off the top of the bank onto a rock, and broke her arm in two places. The caravan's guard, Torvi Brask, carried her back to the wagons over one shoulder, still shouting about the tusks.

That is the true version. Zip has told the story in a good many other versions since, and Tick, the gate messenger, has written three of them down in his notebook, each one featuring a slightly bigger monster. The arm has healed. The story keeps growing.

docs.title: Torvi
docs.text: Torvi Brask, the axe-fighter from the highlands who hires out as a caravan guard, looked at Zip on the bank that day, laughed like a rockslide and said that bravery was wasted on someone who could not fight. Back in the city, Zip followed Torvi around the Gate Walk until Torvi gave in. Now Torvi is teaching her to fight properly: footwork, guard, when to stand and, above all, when to run, which is the lesson Zip finds hardest. They train on the open ground inside the gate most mornings, and the Gate Watch lean on their spears and watch.

docs.title: The spark lamp
docs.text: Margo Venn, the inventor on Workshops Row, has built a lamp that throws sparks, bright and loud enough, she hopes, to frighten off the monsters that make the roads so dangerous. It works beautifully in the workshop, where Bolt, Margo's apprentice, has tested it on a broom, a barrel and himself. Nobody knows whether it works on a real monster. Zip volunteered before Margo had finished asking. Margo is grateful and uneasy in equal measure, and has made Zip promise to bring the lamp back even if she does not bring back the story.

docs.title: What Zip wants and fears
docs.text:
Zip wants a song. She wants a tune at the Night Market with her name in the chorus, and to come home through the gate one day to a crowd. What she fears, and has told nobody, is that she will turn out to be ordinary, and that the broken arm was the most interesting thing that will ever happen to her.

A quest might go out with Zip and Margo's spark lamp to find a real monster, keep Zip from accepting a truly stupid dare, or find out what really happened to the tusked beast she chased.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• Margo 'Sparks' Venn: inventor
  • Torvi Brask: teacher

docs.title: Bain Harbour
docs.text:
The Coastal Town

Bain Harbour is a rich and sunlit port on the east coast of Veligor, a proud merchant town of the sea that governs itself through its harbour council. Canals run in from the harbour between houses of pale stone and terracotta, merchants trade under the arcades of Merchant Street, and on the square before the Harbour Hall it is never quiet. It still feels a little like Selsior and a little like Kaldemor, with the capital's fine stone and the countryside's warmth, but its pride is its own: ships, trade and the sea.

docs.title: The Fishermen's Cove
docs.text: Bain Harbour began as a cove of Commons fishing families, who found that the deep, sheltered bay was the one place on that coast where boats could ride out a storm. Through the Age of Division, the cove stayed small and kept its head down, selling fish to whichever side came to buy and trying hard to stay out of the wars.

docs.title: The Shipwrights' Century
docs.text:
After the founding, peace changed everything. With the island united, goods needed to move from one end of Veligor to the other, and the sea was often the fastest road. The fishing families took up shipbuilding, and the cove's sheltered water became the island's busiest shipyard. Merchants followed the ships, craftsmen followed the merchants, and the cove grew into a town.

The shipwrights dug as well as built. To float timber and cargo to the yards and warehouses they cut canals in from the harbour, and the town grew up along them, its streets following the water. Their greatest work was the Old Cut, a canal across the neck of the headland to the open sea beyond it, so that ships could leave for the north without rounding the point in bad weather. By the century's end the fishermen's cove had become a town of trading houses, and the money that came in by sea was spent on stone.

The town takes its name from Old Bain, a fisherwoman remembered as the first to build a ship big enough to sail around the island. Her boat-hook still hangs above the door of the harbour hall.

docs.title: A Town of Its Own
docs.text: As it grew, both Selsior and Kaldemor did a great deal of business through Bain Harbour, and more than once someone in the capital suggested that the port ought to answer to the crown's own officials. The people of Bain Harbour politely refused every time. The harbour is run by its own harbour council, made up of its captains, shipwrights and merchants, and the town is proud that no one else has ever had a say in its affairs.

docs.title: Environment and Identity
docs.text:
Bain Harbour is a town built on its water. Canals run in from the harbour through every quarter, crossed by humped stone bridges and lined with water doors where boats unload straight into the warehouses. Its houses are of pale stone under terracotta roofs, washed in the soft colours of sand, shell and sunset, with flowers in their window boxes and washing strung between them over the water. The sun is almost always on it.

Its heart is the square before the Harbour Hall, the grandest building on the coast, with a colonnade along its front, a bell tower over it and broad steps down to the square, where the council's business spills out among the market awnings. From the square, Merchant Street runs along the town's main canal under shaded arcades, lined with trading houses, counting rooms, spice and cloth merchants, and the halls of the trades. Below them lie the Docks and their warehouses, the Shipyard with its slipways and timber stacks, and the Waterfront of quays, inns and sailors' houses. The Fish Market stands where the old cove was, by the fishermen's steps, the oldest and plainest corner of the town, and Bain Harbour never forgets that it began there. On the headland to the north the Lighthouse watches over it all.

It is a town that loves to trade, to bargain, to show off a little and to make visitors welcome. Its merchants are proud of their ledgers and its captains of their ships, and it smells of tar, salt, spice and fresh bread.

Since the Age of Disturbance began, the sea around Veligor has grown rougher and stranger, and Bain Harbour's sailors tell of creatures in the deep water that were never there before. The harbour's ships still sail, but its captains now hire adventurers to sail with them.

docs.title: Independence
docs.text:
Bain Harbour is not Selsior's port, nor Kaldemor's. It is a town in its own right, with its own history, people and identity. What it shares with those towns is a feeling, not a chain of command, and it belongs to Wonder Kingdom on equal terms with every other settlement.

It lies on the east coast, on the opposite side of the island from Goa Harbour on the west. The two ports are very different, but they are friends, not rivals, and they hold a friendly boat race between them every summer that goes all the way around Veligor.

docs.title: The Lands Around Bain Harbour
docs.text:
Two roads come down to Bain Harbour and one more comes in beside them: the royal road from Selsior over the eastern downs, the Southern Coastal Road along the island's south shore from Goa Harbour, and the Verdant Coast Road, which comes down from Kaldemor's countryside and reaches the town by the Strand, the long beach at its south end. None of them is as safe as it was, but all are travelled every day, and the real change is not on the roads at all. It is in the water: along the Old Cut, where the open sea now comes in, and under the headland, where the sea has turned strange in recent years.

The headland closes the bay on the north side, with the lighthouse on its point. Below the lighthouse lies the Clatterstones, a beach of great round boulders where harbour children have always caught crabs in the rock pools. Beyond the harbour wall, running out from the headland's foot, is the Long Reef, the reef that the pearl diver Nerissa and her grandmother before her have dived all their lives. Below and beyond the reef a wide underwater shelf runs north under the headland, and at its edge, the Drop, the sea floor falls away into water that no diver has ever seen the bottom of.

docs.title: The royal road from Selsior
docs.text:
From the capital's great gate the road to Bain Harbour soon parts from the Royal Road and bears east, onto the Chalk Downs, a long country of short grass and white tracks where the wind first begins to smell of salt. On the downs' eastern edge the road runs through copses of holm oak and cork, and scrub wolves, lean and grey, have come out of the thickets to follow travellers and snatch at anything left on a cart. Drovers and carters still use the road every day, but they keep together.

The last stretch is Baysight Hill, where the road comes out of the trees onto a sunny bluff and the whole bay of Bain Harbour opens below: the lighthouse on its headland, the masts in the harbour, the terracotta roofs and the shining lines of the canals. Travellers stop there to look. The bluff's wildcats, which have always raided the gulls' nests on its ledges, have grown big and bold enough to raid travellers instead, and they will leap on anyone who stops long enough to unwrap a meal. From the foot of the hill the road runs down past the shipyard into town, and a lane runs north along the back of the town to the first lock of the Old Cut.

docs.title: The Southern Coastal Road
docs.text:
Travellers for Goa Harbour follow the Strand south to Shellbrook Mouth, where the Verdant Coast Road comes down over the dunes from Kaldemor, and there the Southern Coastal Road begins. It carries on south and then west along the island's south shore, all the way to Goa Harbour without passing the capital. It is the longest road out of Bain Harbour and the emptiest, used by drovers, pedlars, fishing families going between the coves, and every summer by people walking out to watch the race boats go by.

Its first stretch is the Dune Reach, low sunny dunes and marram grass along the shore, where the dune cats that once lived on the fishermen's leavings have grown bold and quarrelsome and follow walkers for miles. Where the coast turns west, the road comes down to Marram Cove, a fishing hamlet of a dozen houses in a sheltered bend of the shore, where travellers rest, fill their water bottles and hear the news from both ends of the road. The cove has no monsters and wants none. Beyond it the road comes out onto the Long Sands, mile after mile of pale beach and dunes, where big grey tomcats hunt the tide line and do not care whether what they are hunting is a crab or a traveller's boot. At the western end of the Long Sands the cliffs rise again, and the road reaches the foot of the Gullwalk, the clifftop path that carries it the last way into Goa Harbour.

docs.title: The Old Cut
docs.text:
The Old Cut leaves the harbour's north quays and runs between stone banks and towpaths across the neck of the headland to the open sea. In the shipwrights' century it was the busiest water in the town, lined with timber ponds, lock basins and boathouses, but the great ships of today are too broad for its locks, and for a generation it has carried little more than barges and children's boats. A few winters ago a storm broke its sea gates, and since then the tide has run in and out of the Cut, and with it, from the deep water, has come the sea.

The Inner Cut is the harbour end, a long reach of locks, towpaths and quiet warehouses with their water doors shut. In recent years crabs have come up it from the shore and grown. The largest are big enough to take a boot off, and the dockworkers call them bootcrabs. Iron-backed crabs as wide as a cartwheel sit on the lock steps, glass jellies drift in the basins with stings no healer in the harbour can name, and pale-snouted snapjaws haul themselves out onto the towpaths. Where the Inner Cut ends lies the Pinch, the narrowest and deepest lock on the canal, whose gates rotted away long ago, so that it fills and empties with every tide.

The crab hunt. It begins with Bree of the Fish Market, who has found a crab in her rock pools that is not like any crab she has ever named. Keziah and Tristram, who cleared the rocks below the headland in Keziah's first week in the harbour, have found the bootcrabs back, and bigger, in the locks of the Inner Cut, and they want to know where they keep coming from. Clemence the healer wants the glass jellies brought to her, so that she can make a salve for stings she has so far only been able to write down. Then Kit, the shipwright's son, goes missing along the Cut, because he wanted to see one of the sailors' sea creatures for himself. He is found on a lock gate, cut off when the tide came in and filled the lock, surrounded by crabs, and once he is home he will talk about nothing but the enormous shell he saw moving in the Pinch.

The Bootbreaker. In the Pinch lives the crab the others come from: a Disturbance-touched shore crab the size of a fishing boat, its shell scarred and crusted with barnacles, which has been casting off its old shells in the lock and growing larger with each one. Keziah named it the Bootbreaker. Bree has her own name for it and will tell anyone who asks.

The Outer Cut runs on beyond the Pinch to the sea end, where the canal comes out at the foot of the headland, between the last boulders of the Clatterstones and the root of the Long Reef. Here the water is salt and deep, and a new kind of fish has come in from the deep water: the sawbill, long and narrow, with a flat bill edged on both sides with teeth like a saw. Sawbills hunt along the Cut in shoals, and they are bold enough now to haul themselves out onto the towpaths and the lock steps after anything that moves.

The torn nets. Twice this year Cobb's nets came up torn clean through in the deeper water just inside the headland, in long straight rents whose edges were pulled rather than cut. His mother Wenna kept a strip of the torn net, and the story begins when she lets someone carry it round the harbour. It matches the long straight tears that Tegan the sailmaker has been patching in sails that came back from deep water, and the grooved driftwood on Maren's shelf of beach finds. Cobb, who has not been past the middle of the bay since, goes out along the Outer Cut to see what tears his nets. Nerissa, whose reef lies just outside the sea gates, teaches the water of the Cut's sea end to anyone willing to learn it properly. On a night voyage of Seraphine's Bright Morrow, sawbills come leaping out of the dark across the deck, and that night it is plain how a sail gets a long straight tear in it. Finally Alwyn the shipwright wants a sawbill's bill and a scored plank laid on Dunstan's workbench, as proof the old man cannot argue with that the deep water calls for stronger hulls.

The Ripsaw. The shoal that works the Cut follows one fish: a deeply touched sawbill longer than a fishing boat, its saw scarred from end to end, which lies up in the Gullet, the narrow throat of the canal under the broken sea gates, where the tide runs hardest. When it moves, the whole shoal moves with it.

docs.title: The Holm Wood
docs.text:
From the Outer Cut's sea end the old timber path climbs onto the broad back of the headland, behind the lighthouse, where the Holm Wood grows: holm oaks and sea pines, dark and evergreen, where the shipwrights felled the timber they floated down the Cut. Nobody has felled it for a long time. Dusk wolves hunt in it now, and since the deep water turned strange, something stranger walks there after dark: tall shapes like hooded figures, which are not people at all, only shadow and salt mist with a pale light where a face should be. The harbour calls them lanternshades. Some carry long lashes of shadow, some hooked blades, and some a pale glim that draws the others to it, and they fade at dawn.

At the heart of the wood the roof of a great sea cave fell in long ago and left the Lantern Deep, a round, sheer-sided pool of sea water open to the sky, joined under the cliffs to the Drop itself. Its water rises and falls with the tide and never shows a bottom.

The lights in the deep water. Almost everyone in the harbour has seen one piece of this, and almost nobody has told anyone. The story begins with Halloran, the captain of the Watch, who has stood a watch on the outer pier every night since he found the Watch's launch hanging from a mooring line pulled straight down into the water, and long fresh grooves cut into the pilings below the waterline. Standing a night on the pier with him, and climbing down among the pilings at the lowest tide to look at them, shows the grooves for what they are: rows of round marks, each ringed with fine scratches. Halloran then does what he knows he should have done long ago, and brings together the people who have been writing down what the sea is doing: Brisa with her list, Delphine with her ledger of sailors' tales, Clemence with her casebook and its row of coin-sized round welts on a deckhand's forearm, and Ottilie with her tally of the small boats that no longer go out past the headland.

Ysolde, the Keeper of the Light, needs someone to climb the hundred and seventeen stairs and keep the lamp on a night her knees will not manage it. That is the night the pale lights come back, far out past the headland, and her grandson Ossie turns out to have logged the same lights in his blue logbook. Ysolde shows the private signs in the margin of the lighthouse log at last. With the Harbour Master's leave, Ambrose unlocks the chart he keeps in his drawer, with his son Jowan watching, and its marks are checked one by one from the cliffs at the Holm Wood's seaward edge, over the shelf where Annis's Saltlark felt something brush her keel and out over the Drop. The marks have been creeping towards the headland for years, and laid beside Ysolde's lights they show the same thing coming closer, until the newest lie under the headland itself. Nerissa, given back a pearl from the ledge she was reaching for, finally tells Tristram what she saw below the shelf, and Tristram takes his father's harpoon to the edge of the Lantern Deep at night, not to kill what is there but to see it clearly, once.

The Deep Lantern. What the harbour has been seeing in pieces is one creature and the shoals that hunt around it: a deeply touched squid as long as a ship, with eyes as large as cartwheels, arms whose rows of hooked suckers score wood like a chisel, and a body lit along its length with the same pale lights Ysolde has watched for three summers. It came up out of water too deep for anyone to know, and each summer it has followed its shoals a little closer to the coast, until it found the way in under the headland. Now it rises at night in the Lantern Deep, its light comes up through the trees, and the lanternshades walk wherever that light falls. The harbour, which named it after the lighthouse that saw it first, calls it the Deep Lantern.

docs.title: The Wreck of the Saltgrace
docs.text:
Under the harbour's south cliff, below the Waterfront, the sea has hollowed out a run of caves that boom like a bell at every high tide. Harbour children have always dared each other into the mouth of the Bellcaves, and salvagers have always known what lies further in: the wreck of the Saltgrace, a great trading ship of the harbour's early days, driven into the caves in a storm long ago and wedged there ever since, her hull broken open on the rocks and her decks tilted into the dark water.

For years old Kenwyn worked the wreck for iron and seasoned timber, going in at low tide by the salvagers' steps from the beach. This spring he found it full: crabs crusted with barnacles nesting in the holds, eels in the bilges, things moving behind the portholes. He stopped going in, and now he sits at the top of the steps telling anyone who will listen that he knows every plank of that ship and will draw them a map of her for nothing.

The Saltgrace has other ties to the harbour. Burned into her timbers is the same stamp that marks the four dark iron-bound crates at the back of Hobart's oldest warehouse, which nobody has opened in living memory. Somewhere in her purser's strongbox, wrapped in oilskin, is her bill of lading, still legible, listing four crates landed at Bain before she sailed her last. And carved into a beam of her forecastle by some long-dead sailor are the words of an old sea song, with a last verse that Wilmot the ropemaker would know at once.

The Holdfast. The Saltgrace's stern is broken open into the deepest cave, and her lowest hold is flooded with its water. In it, coiled through the broken decks and up under the floor of the captain's cabin, lives a Disturbance-touched conger eel so vast that its body runs through three decks at once. It strikes out of hatches, holes and stern windows all around anyone who comes into the cabin. Salvagers have long said there was something in the Saltgrace that did not like being disturbed, and Kenwyn calls it the Holdfast, because it has never once let go of the ship.

The creatures of the Bellcaves are strange even by the Disturbance's standards: however strong the adventurer who goes in, what waits in the wreck seems to have grown to match them.

docs.title: Leadership Today
docs.text: Quenna has been Harbour Master for eight years. She went to sea as a deck girl at twelve and was master of her own ship, the Kittiwake, by twenty-seven. The harbour council of captains, shipwrights and merchants chose her from among themselves, and most of them say it was the easiest choice they ever made and the noisiest they have lived with since. She chairs the council from the Harbour Hall and has skippered the town's race boat for fourteen summers.

docs.text:
Name Role Dunstan Master Shipwright, who builds the race boats Annis The oldest captain on the harbour council Halloran Captain of the Harbour Watch Ottilie Clerk of the Harbour Hall Ambrose Chartmaker, and Quenna's husband Ysolde Lighthouse keeper

People

Everyone who lives here in the first release: People of Bain Harbour.

Design notes

New with this page: the fishing cove origin, Old Bain, the harbour council, the summer race around Veligor, and sea creatures stirred up by the Disturbance. Bain Harbour is on the east coast, as the game's world map has it.

Bain Harbour's look is a sunlit merchant republic of the sea: canals and bridges cut in from the harbour, pale stone and terracotta, arcaded merchant streets, and the Harbour Hall as a council palace on its square. Fishing is the town's humble origin and trade its pride. Real-world inspirations: the maritime republics of Venice and Genoa, and MapleStory's San Commerci and the Commerci Republic. The canals and the Old Cut are new with this look, and so are the town's districts as described above; the people, their places and the history are unchanged.

New with "The Lands Around Bain Harbour": the Chalk Downs and Baysight Hill on the royal road from Selsior; the Dune Reach, Marram Cove and the Long Sands on the Southern Coastal Road; Shellbrook Mouth and the Strand, where the Verdant Coast Road comes in; the Clatterstones, the Long Reef, the shelf and the Drop as the sea around the headland; the Old Cut with the Inner Cut, the Pinch, the Outer Cut and the Gullet; the Holm Wood and the Lantern Deep; the Bellcaves and the Saltgrace, Kenwyn, the lanternshades, and four creatures: the Bootbreaker, the Ripsaw, the Deep Lantern and the Holdfast. The bootcrabs answer the crabs "big enough to take a boot"; the sawbills answer the long straight tears in nets, sails and driftwood; the Deep Lantern answers Ysolde's pale lights, Barnaby's eyes, the brushed keel, the grooves in the pilings, the welts in Clemence's casebook and the marks on Ambrose's chart. The lanternshades are creatures of shadow and mist thrown by the Deep Lantern's light, never people. What happened to last autumn's missing Kaldemor cart and its drivers is still open, and so is what is in Hobart's four crates. The Deep Lantern is a creature of the Disturbance, not a sign of the Balrog's intentions. Real-world inspirations: sawfish and swordfish for the sawbills, deep-sea squid (whose sucker rings carry small teeth) and bioluminescent shoals for the Deep Lantern, conger eels in wrecks for the Holdfast, ship canals across headlands and the collapsed sea caves of rocky Atlantic coasts for the Old Cut and the Lantern Deep. Inside the Bellcaves, the monsters' strength follows the player's own, which is why the wreck's creatures "grow to match" whoever goes in.

docs.title: Cavelor
docs.text:
The Underground City of Guardians

Cavelor is a small and very old city hidden deep beneath the World Tree. It was founded right after the first war against the Balrog, when some of the greatest warriors and guardians of that age chose to stay below and keep watch over the seal.

docs.title: The Oath Below
docs.text:
When the seal was finished and the four armies began to march home, a company of warriors stayed behind in the roots. They came from all four peoples: Savage warriors, Magicians who understood the seal, Commons who knew how to dig and build, and Aristocrat officers to lead them. They swore an oath, the Oath Below, to watch the Balrog's prison for as long as it held, and to send word to the surface if it ever began to fail.

Then they were nearly forgotten. The surface celebrated, the kingdom grew, and within a few generations, the guardians beneath the Tree had faded into legend. Kragvar songs in Midbarium still claimed that some of their warriors stayed below, but few took the songs as anything more than stories.

docs.title: A City in the Roots
docs.text:
Below, the guardians built a home. They carved halls out of the rock between the great roots, grew pale mushrooms and root-fruit in the dark, drew water from deep springs and lit their streets with lanterns fed by the faint glow of the Tree's magic. Their children were born below and learned the Oath before they learned to read. Over the centuries, the camp became Cavelor: small, orderly, and completely devoted to its task.

The guardians never stopped watching. Cavelor's Wardens of the Seal walk the deep passages around the prison in shifts, and have done so without a single gap for the whole of the kingdom's history. Its scholars keep careful records of every tremor and every change in the seal's glow, written in great ledgers that go back to the founding.

docs.title: Rediscovery
docs.text:
For generations, Cavelor had almost no contact with the rest of the kingdom. Then, fifty years ago, the Great World Tree Expedition reached its halls. The explorers were astonished to find the legend alive; the guardians were just as astonished to learn how completely the surface had forgotten them.

It was a joyful meeting, and a terrible one. Within days of that first contact, the expedition's explorers, pushing deeper than the guardians advised, opened the rift that damaged the seal. Cavelor's ledgers recorded the change at once. For fifty years since, the guardians have watched the seal grow weaker, and they have tried, with growing urgency, to make the surface understand what that means.

docs.title: The Swordmaster's Oath
docs.text: Since Queen Aveline's alliance with Cavelor fifteen years ago, the Royal Guard's Swordmasters come down the Upper Stair to swear their oath in the Oath Hall, before the Keeper of the Oath. They swear to stand with the guardians if the seal ever fails, and to carry Cavelor's warnings to the surface. For a city that was forgotten for generations, it is a promise that someone above is listening, and Cavelor takes it as seriously as its own Oath Below.

docs.title: Cultural Identity
docs.text:
Cavelor's people live by responsibility, vigilance, discipline and endurance. They keep the traditions of the first guardians and guard the records of the Balrog, the ancient battle and the magic that holds the prison shut. Every adult in Cavelor serves a turn as a Warden.

Their duty is a solemn one, but Cavelor is not a gloomy or oppressive place. Its people have built a real community with a life of its own: they are close-knit and fiercely loyal, quick to laugh among themselves, and deeply curious about the bright world above, which many of them have only recently seen for the first time.

Cavelor is still very much its own place, but since its rediscovery it has been part of the same united kingdom, and its people are as proud of Wonder Kingdom as anyone on the surface. They just know better than most what it might cost to keep it.

docs.title: Leadership Today
docs.text: Marrun has been Keeper of the Oath for twenty-two years, since old Keeper Ardith died, and leads Cavelor and the Wardens of the Seal from the Oath Hall. He has walked the Deep Watch for sixty-five years and was there the night the expedition came down. Fifteen years ago he swore Cavelor's alliance with Queen Aveline, and four years ago he climbed to the surface for the first and only time.

docs.title: Notable People
docs.text:
Name Role Brask Captain of the Deep Watch Oswin Master of the Ledgers, who wrote the entry recording the seal's change Ysra Healer of the Halls Annick Keeper of the Oath songs Doran A young Warden recently back from the surface

People

Everyone who lives here in the first release: People of Cavelor.

Design notes

New with this page: guardians from all four peoples, the Oath Below, the Wardens of the Seal and their ledgers, and the rift being opened days after the expedition reached Cavelor.

docs.title: Fairy Forest
docs.text:
The Magical Woodland

Fairy Forest is a settlement hidden among ancient trees, where enchanted plants grow, strange creatures wander and the air hums with magic. It is the historic home of the Magicians, one of the four founding peoples.

docs.title: The Listening Woods
docs.text:
The Magicians did not choose Fairy Forest so much as find it. Long before the Age of Division, the first of them came to these woods because magic gathered here more thickly than anywhere else on Veligor, like water collecting in a valley. They believed, and still believe, that the forest's roots reach all the way to the World Tree's, and that the Tree's magic flows outward through the soil and comes up again here.

They learned magic by listening: to the trees, to the wind, to the creatures that lived among them. Their first homes were built into living trunks and branches, shaped by coaxing the trees to grow rather than by cutting them, and the oldest of those homes are still lived in today.

docs.title: Keepers of the Tree
docs.text:
Through the Age of Division, the Magicians guarded the forest and, above all, the World Tree. Any attempt to cut, claim or exploit a place of power was met by Magician resistance, and that was the root of their long alliance with the Savages, who had no love for outside rulers either.

In the Balrog War, it was the Magicians of Fairy Forest who decided it could not be destroyed, and who designed the great seal that holds it beneath the World Tree. The knowledge of how that seal was made has been one of the forest's most closely guarded secrets ever since. Since the expedition damaged it, the forest's scholars have been studying old records day and night, trying to understand how it might be strengthened.

docs.title: The Children Arrive
docs.text:
Fifty years ago, the Great World Tree Expedition found a mysterious people of magical beings living high in the upper reaches of the World Tree. They came to be known as the Children of the Tree.

After that first meeting, the Children slowly came down from the Tree and settled in Fairy Forest, perhaps because its magic felt most like home. The forest welcomed them as family. They have since become part of its community and made friends across the kingdom, and their presence gives the forest much of its unique magic.

docs.title: Environment and Culture
docs.text:
The people of Fairy Forest live close to both magic and nature. Magical learning, care for the living forest and the study of supernatural wonders are at the heart of who they are. The settlement does not stand apart from the woods; its homes and gathering places are woven into the forest itself, linked by branch-bridges, lantern-lit paths and stairways that spiral around the trunks.

The forest's schools teach magic to anyone with the gift, from any town in the kingdom. Its people take only what the forest can spare, and they will gently but firmly stop any visitor who tries to take more.

The forest has its own friends in the wider kingdom, too. The Brenna of Midbarium have been welcome here since the days when the Savages and the Magicians were allies, and the friendship has outlasted the war that made it.

docs.title: The Lands Around Fairy Forest
docs.text: Inside the lantern light, Fairy Forest is as safe and bright as it has ever been. Beyond the last lantern the woods are wild, and in the Age of Disturbance they have grown wilder every year. Three roads lead in: the royal road from Selsior, the Eastern Forest Road from Kaldemor, and the Northern Woodland Trail, which comes in from the west out of Midbarium's highlands. A chain of ever deeper and darker places runs west from the forest toward the World Tree, whose crown stands far off above the canopy.

docs.title: The Eastern Forest Road
docs.text: The old woodland road runs north from Kaldemor's fields to the forest. At the Forest's Hem, where the last of the farmland gives way to birch and fern, carters stop at a stile to rest their horses before the trees close in. The road grows greener and older as it goes, until it becomes the Glimmer Path, a sun-dappled way under glowing moss and the first of the outer lanterns, which brings travellers in at the Forest Edge. Its creatures are small ones, bubbling things and slimes, mushrooms and walking stumps, but there are far more of them than there used to be, and the carters who bring Kaldemor's goods north now buy their travelling lights in the forest before they turn for home.

docs.title: The Royal Road to Selsior
docs.text: The royal road leaves the forest on its southwest side and runs through the Bloomwood, a wide flowering woodland of bluebell glades, wild roses and tall, light trees, before the land opens onto the central plain on its way to Selsior. It is one of the loveliest roads on Veligor, and lately one of the more troublesome: bright winged creatures the forest calls glimmerwings flit through the glades in swarms, and the largest of them, the crowned glimmerwings, will drive a traveller off the road. From the Bloomwood an old path turns west, toward the World Tree, and leads down to Shimmerwater.

docs.title: Shimmerwater and the Night Diggers
docs.text:
Shimmerwater is a quiet lake west of the Bloomwood that glows faintly at dusk, reached down three winding lakeside paths. Its slimes, sprites and wisps were once a pretty sight for courting couples. This summer the lake has soured.

It begins, as far as the forest knows, with Merrow's seedling beds in the Herb Gardens, dug up night after night by something nobody saw. A traveller who sits up with Ailo to watch finds the culprits: young slimes from the lake, seeping into the freshly watered beds and slipping away at the swing of a lantern. Hesper tastes the churned soil and finds it bitter. The lake's young are fleeing poison.

At the head of the lake, squatting over the spring that feeds it, sits the Blightstone: a Disturbance-touched hulk of mossy stone and rotten wood, from which a bitter sap seeps into the water. With it gone, Shimmerwater can begin to clear, and Merrow may at last walk out to the last lantern for the first time in years, carrying a basket of his wife's salves for the edge watch.

docs.title: The Hollow Oak and the Sharpened
docs.text:
Beyond the head of the lake, the shore climbs steeply into the High Shore, and above it stands the Hollow Oak, an immense, ancient hollow tree so tall that it is climbed in stages, from the wind-tossed lower boughs to where only birds go, and above them to the sky. A ravine runs below it, where the lake's outflow falls away.

This is the country Juniper and Kestrel know best, and it is where their worst fears show most clearly. The creatures here are sharpened: larger, bolder and angrier than in any old drawing, and kinds turn up on the oak that never lived there. Lizard-like eyes have multiplied in the wet ground at its foot, and the monkeys in its branches throw more than fruit. The edge watch's spears snap on hides like these, and Seren wants them refitted with ironbark from the oak's own fallen limbs, the only wood the forest will spare.

The cause sits in the crown. Old Grizzlemane, a vast, grizzled, Disturbance-touched ape, has made the top of the Hollow Oak its own, tearing the crown apart and driving everything beneath it down and out. In its nest lies Juniper's lost notebook, dropped the autumn before as she climbed out of the ravine with something large below her. Given that missing season, Hesper's list of what has attacked her patients, and Juniper's forty notebooks spread across his floor, Caelum builds his thirty-second theory. For the first time he does not file it as wrong. He starts a new drawer for it, labelled "not wrong yet", and will not say what it shows until he has checked it twice.

docs.title: The Gloaming and the Homes That Will Not Wake
docs.text:
West of the Hollow Oak lies the Gloaming, a deep, old wood where it is always dusk. In the Deepening, the forest's great roots break the surface, the roots that the Magicians have always believed run all the way to the World Tree's. Further on, the Twilit Wood is all brambles and glowing springs, where wisps drift, howlets watch from the branches and glimmerfoxes slip between the trees. The creatures of the Gloaming are the most strongly touched anywhere near the forest, and the worst of them are deeply touched.

The trouble shows first at home. A handful of the very oldest living homes around the Heart Tree, the ones the first Magicians shaped, woke late this spring, with thin sap and cold rooms. Oriel has kept it quiet. Soil and water from the great roots in the Deepening come back cold and thin. On the western side of the forest Sorrel's strange note in the wind is loudest, and there Ondine's outer lanterns keep dimming. If Ondine's book of nineteen years of lantern brightnesses ever reaches the top of the Heart Tree stair, the Grove Council, with Thessaly reading out the oldest unkept promise in her ledger, may at last give Seren the guards she has been asking for.

At the Hidden Spring, deep in the Twilit Wood, the oldest root rises through the water, and around it lies the Knotbriar: a vast, ancient, deeply touched bramble coiled round the root and slowly tightening, with a heart of dark thorn in its coils. Cut it away, and the sap rises again in the oldest homes, late but green, and Sorrel's note in the wind falls silent. Even then, Oriel says, the coldest room of the oldest home stays colder than he remembers, and he is not done listening.

docs.title: The Rootbound Wing
docs.text:
Behind the Grove School stands a bramble-grown door that students dare each other to touch. It leads to the Rootbound Wing, the oldest wing of the school, where the first Magicians taught, sealed so long ago that nobody's teacher's teacher remembers it open. Living trees have grown through and around it until wing and grove are one, and the old books inside have come alive in the Disturbance: they fly, snap and swarm through the Hushed Grove, the Stilled Grove and the Shadowed Grove to the Old Reading Room at the wing's roofless heart, where the great teaching-book of the wing, the Unbound, turns in a storm of its own pages.

The way in begins with Wynne. Copying an old seal record, she has found a gap in its numbering, leaves removed long ago by someone who knew how. A shelf list older than the one in use, which Ilwen can find by page and shelf without asking why, carries a note beside that record in a hand nobody knows: certain leaves "kept apart, in the old wing". Faelan makes the lantern to light the way, and Corisande, whose mother and grandmother kept the wing's key before her without anyone remembering why, opens the door for the first time in her life.

From the wing come fragments: scraps of old leaves, mostly faded or torn, a few with numbers that fall inside Wynne's gap. Whether the rest were torn up, taken elsewhere or never there, nobody can say. Wynne takes them to her grandmother, Isaura, who reads them in silence, says only "thank you", and carries them to the Eldest that night. What they say, she tells nobody else.

The wing never stays quiet for long. Corisande lets anyone with the nerve back in, and the books are always waiting.

docs.title: Leadership Today
docs.text: Calyra has been Eldest of the Grove for nine years and leads the Grove Council from the Heart Tree. She taught at the Grove School for forty years. When old Eldest Ferris died, the forest's teachers and elders gathered to choose one of their own, and Calyra was chosen over Thessaly by a handful of voices.
