docs.text:
Name Role Thessaly Grove Councillor Briony Grove Councillor Ilwen Steward of the Heart Tree Isaura Keeper of the Old Records, who studies the seal's history Seren Warden of the Forest Edge Sorrel Teacher of Listening

People

Everyone who lives here in the first release: People of Fairy Forest.

Design notes

The atmosphere is inspired by MapleStory's Ellinia. New with this page: magic gathering in the forest through the World Tree's roots, homes grown from living trees, and the Magicians designing the seal. The nature, appearance, abilities and origins of the Children of the Tree are still to be decided.

The lands around the forest draw on the woods, lakes and great trees around Ellinia and its neighbours. New with "The Lands Around Fairy Forest": the Eastern Forest Road's Forest's Hem and Glimmer Path, the Bloomwood on the royal road, Shimmerwater, the High Shore and the Hollow Oak, the Gloaming, and the Rootbound Wing; the Blightstone, Old Grizzlemane, the Knotbriar and the Unbound; and Corisande, keeper of the old wing's key. Still open: who removed the seal record's leaves, when and why, what the fragments say, where the rest went, and whether they bear on Isaura's belief that the most important parts of the seal's making were never written down; what Caelum's thirty-second theory shows; whether the oldest homes' lingering cold has another cause; and what Sorrel means when he says the woods are listening back. Nothing found in the lands around the forest says anything about the Children of the Tree.

docs.title: Goa Harbour
docs.text:
The Wilderness Harbour

Goa Harbour is a busy timber port on the west coast of Veligor, on the far side of the island from Bain Harbour. Its wooden quays are stacked with timber from the forests behind it and loud with ships coming and going through the gap. It feels like a little of Midbarium and a little of Fairy Forest, with highland ruggedness and woodland magic meeting the sea.

docs.title: Where the Mountains Meet the Sea
docs.text: The coast around Goa Harbour is wild: cliffs that drop straight into the water, forests that run down to the shore, and a single deep inlet cut between them. During the Age of Division, both Savages and Magicians came to that inlet. Savage hunters came down from the hills for the fishing, and Magicians came for the sea-herbs and the strange tides, which they believed were moved by the same magic that flowed through the forests. Being allies, they shared it, and a mixed camp grew up on the shore.

docs.title: The Sea Wardens
docs.text:
The camp gave the town its oldest tradition. The tides in the inlet are fast and treacherous, and the first families learned to read them the way Magicians read the forest. They called themselves wardens of the sea, and to this day, Goa Harbour's pilots guide every ship through the inlet, and no captain sails in without one.

The name Goa is said to come from an old Savage word for "the gap", the narrow gap between the cliffs where the inlet opens to the sea.

docs.title: After the Founding
docs.text: When the kingdom was founded, Goa Harbour opened to the whole island. Timber from its forests and furs and wool from the highlands went out by sea, and travellers began to come for the wild coast and the strange, half-magical town on it. It grew into a busy port, with timber ships loading at its quays on every tide, but it never grew as large as Bain Harbour, and its people prefer it that way.

docs.title: Environment and Identity
docs.text: Goa Harbour is rougher and wilder than Bain Harbour, shaped by the mountains, forests and rocky shores around it. It is a working port of timber and tar: its harbour front runs along the inner shore of the inlet, with wooded hills rising behind the roofs and the sea cliffs of the gap standing over its seaward end. Lanterns of the forest's making light its quays at night.

docs.title: The Town
docs.text:
• The Inlet Quay is the harbour front, where ships come and go all day: long wooden quays and piers on timber piles, stacks of sawn timber waiting for the holds, warehouses with wide doors onto the water, and ships riding at anchor out in the inlet while they wait for a pilot and a turn at the quay. The Wardens' House stands at its head, at the foot of the cliffs, looking out at the gap.
  • The Lantern Market is the busy heart of the town behind the quay, a market street of shops and stalls with the Gap Inn on it, where the houses are timber, steep-roofed and painted every colour their owners could find: red, blue, ochre and green.
  • The Fishers' Coves lie under the cliffs at the seaward end of the town, small coves full of boats drawn up on the shingle, net lofts, drying racks and smokehouses. The sea caves open in the rocks beyond them.
  • The Forest Shore is the town's other end, round the point, where the woods come down to the water. The timber crews roll their logs down to the raft landing there, and the rafts are towed round the point to the quay at slack tide.
  • The Cliff Stairs climb the cliff above the quay to the clifftop quarter, a row of timber houses along the top of the cliff, and to Gull Heath beyond it. The oldest is the Long Stair, from the quay to the clifftop, with houses on its landings; beside it the rope lift hauls goods and tired legs up the cliff; and rope bridges carry the paths above the harbour across the clefts in the cliff face. The stairs, the lift and the bridges are the town's way up, kept by the Master of the Stairs and his crew; its houses stand on the rock.

Its people keep proud seafaring traditions, along with the independent spirit of the highlands and a touch of the forests' magic. They are adventurous and welcoming, and the town is unlike any other on the island. It is also a natural home for adventurers: since the Age of Disturbance began, the wild coast and forests around it have filled with monsters, and Goa Harbour's people have never been the sort to wait for help.

docs.title: Independence
docs.text:
Goa Harbour is not Midbarium's port, nor Fairy Forest's. It has its own people, traditions and history, and its resemblance to those towns is cultural, not political. It is led by its First Warden, the most respected of its pilots, chosen by the others.

Bain Harbour and Goa Harbour are not rivals. Both are peaceful, prosperous parts of Wonder Kingdom, and every summer their sailors race each other all the way around Veligor.

docs.title: The Lands Around Goa Harbour
docs.text:
Goa Harbour sits where three wild things meet: the sea, the cliffs and the Saltwood, the old forest of pine and oak that runs down the west coast to the water's edge. Three roads reach the town from the rest of the kingdom, and all are fair going for anyone who can swing a sword. What lies off them is not. Since the Age of Disturbance began, the forest edge, the cliff faces and the outer rocks of the gap have each filled with their own trouble, and the people of Goa Harbour, who have never been the sort to wait for help, are glad of every hunter who comes.

Place Levels What is there The royal road from Selsior 14-18 The Gorse Downs and the Saltwood Road; hunting grounds The Western Merchant Road 16-20 The Seaward Woods and Dusk Ford; hunting grounds The Gullwalk 18-20 The clifftop path south of the town; hunting grounds The Strandwood 20-30 The forest edge and the wild coast; Old Brushtail The Saltface 30-50 The sea cliffs south of the town; the Gapclaw The Forest Jaw 50-70 The far cliff of the gap and the rocks beyond it; the Undertow The Sounding Caves 20-70 The sea caves under the town's cliffs, entered from the Fishers' Coves; the Inkmother

docs.title: The Roads
docs.text: The royal road and the Western Merchant Road both come out onto Gull Heath, the open clifftop above the town, where the grass is short and full of thrift and the wind smells of salt. Gull Heath is where Goa Harbour's own country begins: it ends at the head of the Long Stair, beside the windlass of the rope lift and the iron bar of the Cliff Watch. The hill road also starts from Gull Heath and climbs away into the highlands, where Goa Harbour's wool and pelts come from.

docs.title: The royal road from Selsior
docs.text:
The royal road crosses the capital's city bridge with the Urbanograd road, parts from it, and bears southwest toward the far coast, and for most of its length it climbs. It rises onto the Gorse Downs, a long, high country of yellow gorse, sheep-walk and wind, where the road runs between old waymarking stones and the sea first shows as a grey line on the horizon. Wild pigs root in the gorse, horned mushrooms crowd the hollows, and things with too many eyes watch the road from the ditches.

Beyond the downs the road drops into the edge of the Saltwood and becomes the Saltwood Road, a sunken track under tall pines, cool and resin-scented, with the sound of the sea somewhere off through the trees. Walking stumps, dark and rotten, and mushrooms of every colour live along it, and the timber carts of Goa Harbour pass in both directions. Halfway through the wood a narrow track turns off toward the sea: this is the way down to the Strandwood and the wild coast, and the town's hunters use it every day. The road comes out of the trees onto Gull Heath.

docs.title: The Western Merchant Road
docs.text: The Western Merchant Road is older than Urbanograd. It was the Aristocrats' road from their stronghold at Old Grad down to the sea, and the carters of Goa Harbour kept using it long after the stronghold stood empty; they still call it the merchant road, though the merchants on it now are mostly their own. From Gull Heath it runs inland through the Seaward Woods, the wind-bent northern reach of the Saltwood, oak and pine full of the smell of salt, where crabs scuttle far further inland than crabs should and noisy troops of tree-dwellers pelt travellers from the branches. Below the woods it crosses the river at Dusk Ford, where carters cross only in full daylight now, because something waits in the shallows at dusk, long and low and patient. Past the ford the road climbs toward Old Grad's walls and the Gate Meadows of Urbanograd.

docs.title: The Gullwalk and the south coast
docs.text: The Southern Coastal Road leaves the town to the south along the Gullwalk, a path along the clifftop with the sea breaking far below and the seabirds wheeling level with the walker's shoulder. Savage gulls and cliff crabs hold the turf, and the path is not as easy as it was. A little way along, a steep way leads down the cliff face itself to the Saltface. At the Gullwalk's foot the cliffs fall back onto the Long Sands, and the road runs on along the south shore to Bain Harbour.

docs.title: The Strandwood
docs.text:
The Strandwood is the strip of land where the Saltwood comes right down to the wild coast beyond the town's Forest Shore: pines bent by the wind, scrub and fallen trunks, and below them black rocks and weed that the tide uncovers twice a day. The timber crews cut along its edge, and Caddoc the trapper sets his traps across it at night. The track from the Saltwood Road comes down into it from the forest, and its far end, at the foot of the Forest Jaw, leads on to harder country.

The threat. The creatures of the Strandwood come out of the forest. Torva, who leads the hunters of the wild coast, has tracked them for years and is sure they come from deeper in the woods every season, as if something there were pushing them out. Boars with weed in their bristles root along the shore, stumps rotted to walking driftwood creep out of the scrub, and thin red-brown foxes hunt the rocks at dusk in packs, cleverer than any fox should be.

The story. It begins with Torva, who sends her hunters wherever Bethoc's sighting board at the Gap Inn says the trouble is worst, and lately that is always the Strandwood. Clearing the shore for the timber crews brings the player to Caddoc, whose biggest cage traps have been sprung all season without catching anything: bait gone, doors dropped, no hair, no blood, and the ground swept smooth. Sitting up with him through a night beside his biggest trap, the player sees what does it: a fox far bigger than the rest, grey at the muzzle, that lifts the door with its teeth, takes the bait without touching the wire, and sweeps its own tracks away with a great heavy tail.

Caddoc has spent his life believing that cleverness was the one thing the creatures did not have, and he takes it hard. He wants a trigger even the fox cannot learn, and building it takes the player across the Strandwood for what it needs. On the far rocks at low tide the player guards Brigid, Elspeth's herb gatherer, who now walks the wild coast alone to fill her basket, and Brigid, who notices everything, finds where the fox's swept trail leaves the rocks and goes up into the trees. Caddoc's new trap holds for the first time in a season, and catches only one of the old fox's cubs. The old one is still out there. Torva goes after it with the player, and with her young hunter Kenna, who wants something big enough to be talked about at the Gap Inn, into its earth under the roots of a fallen pine.

The boss: Old Brushtail. A huge grey-muzzled fox, touched by the Disturbance and grown sly with it. In its earth it fights with feints and false trails, vanishing into the dust it sweeps up with its tail and striking from where it was not, and when hard pressed it calls its cubs out of the dark. With Old Brushtail gone, Caddoc's traps hold again, and he complains about that too. Torva's question stays unanswered: the fox was only one of the things coming out of the forest, and it did not leave the deep woods by choice.

docs.title: The Saltface
docs.text:
The Saltface is the great sea cliff south of the town, reached by the steep way down from the Gullwalk: a sheer wall of dark rock streaked white by seabirds, with narrow ledges, crevices and the frayed stumps of old rope ways. At its foot lies the Undercliff, a beach of huge rounded boulders that the sea covers at high tide. Above it, just over the reach of the highest waves, run the Wrack Ledges, broad shelves of rock hung with dead weed.

The threat. Three winters ago the Cliff Watch saw the first creature climb the cliff face itself instead of coming down the forest paths. The climbers come out of the sea: long, grey, splay-footed sea newts, as big as a dog and bigger, which climb wet rock as easily as a fly climbs a wall. With them have come pale, flat, many-legged sea slaters, quicker than a cat on the rock, which chew anything with oil or tar in it, rope included. Crabs swarm the Undercliff, and gulls gone savage nest on the ledges. The low shelves where the newts used to lie out of the water are drowned now at the top of the spring tides, and the newts have been climbing higher every year, always on the stretches of cliff that no lantern reaches.

The story. Everyone who keeps the cliffs has seen part of it, and no one has seen all of it. Ruan, Captain of the Cliff Watch, has the player carry lanterns up to the high landings before dark, then sends them down the Saltface to thin the climbers. Moira of the watch has noticed that the climbers keep to the unlit stretches, and shows the player where they gather. Dougal, the old night watchman of the quay, sits up on the lowest quay steps with the player through a night to see what has been leaving wet, clawed tracks there, and they watch something long and grey come up out of the water, taste the air and slip back down. Following its wake along the cliff foot leads to the Undercliff, where the newts come ashore.

Gorm, the Master of the Stairs, has fallen behind on his new stair down to the far cove, because his crews will not work the lowest landings after dark. Guarding them below the cracked flight they call the Anvil, the player brings back a broken stone scored with deep scratches in sets of four, and old Ulric the stonecarver, judging it, says plainly what Gorm has not wanted to say: the scratches are claws, and they came from below.

The rope bridges have their own trouble. Kestra, who strings them, has found the ropes of the highest bridge chewed from below again and again, and never seen what does it. The player persuades Fionn, the stair runner, to tell her what he saw from that bridge one evening in spring, carries Tarran's new lantern up to her before he can change his mind about it, and sits out with her on the highest bridge after dark. The lantern lights the whole cliff face beneath, and the slaters are there in its light, dozens of them, pale and flat on the rock. The lantern does not drive them off; it only shows them. The player goes down into the crevices of the Saltface to clear them out.

With Dougal's measurements, Gorm's stone and Kestra's ropes, Ruan at last takes everything to Iska at the Wardens' House. The First Warden sends the player down to the Wrack Ledges to find what leads the climbers. Torva goes too, and she knows the creature as soon as she sees it.

The boss: the Gapclaw. The first climber, the one that reached the high landing three winters ago and scarred Torva's jaw before she and her hunters drove it back over the edge. It survived the fall and has grown huge, a deeply touched sea newt as long as a fishing boat, lairing in a black hollow behind the Wrack Ledges. It fights on wet, sloping rock, clinging to the walls and roof of its hollow and dropping from above, raking with its four-clawed forefeet, and calling the sea up its tunnel in surges that sweep the floor. When it falls, the climbers do not stop at once, but they come fewer and less boldly, and the Cliff Watch can hold the stairs again. Why the low shelves flooded in the first place is another question, and it belongs to the water.

docs.title: The Forest Jaw
docs.text:
The gap that gives Goa Harbour its name is the narrow mouth of the inlet between two cliffs. The town stands under one of them, with its clifftop quarter on top. The other, on the forest side, is the Forest Jaw: a tall headland of rock and stunted trees, out of reach from the town except by boat, or on foot the long way round through the Strandwood. Along the shore beyond it lies the Greystrand, where the spring tides now reach in among the trees and have left a band of grey, salt-killed pines standing in the weed. Out from the foot of the Jaw, uncovered only at low water, run the Skerries, a scatter of rocky islets, reefs and sea stacks reaching toward the open sea.

The threat. The things here come in from the deep water outside the gap. Great bull seals, savage and heavy, haul out on the Skerries and give way to no one. Hulking shapes of stone and weed lumber over the reefs at low tide. Salt-dead stumps walk on the Greystrand, and crabs as big as cartwheels hold the rocks under the Jaw. The water itself has grown strange: the strongest run through the gap presses harder against the forest-side cliff every year, and at slack water the sea under the Jaw turns in slow circles where no eddy used to be.

The story. This is the longest of Goa Harbour's stories, and it is told by the people who remember the water.

Brigid has watched the oldest herb beds on the Forest Shore wither since last autumn, the leaves pale, then soft and dark at the root, the beds shrinking from the bottom edge up, and she has noticed the wrack line sitting a little higher on those rocks. Walking the Greystrand with her, the player finds the same thing written across a whole shore of dead trees: the high water reaches further than it used to. With the player beside her, Brigid finally finds the courage to tell Elspeth, and the old healer is gentler about it than Brigid ever feared.

Agna, the net-mender of the coves, asks, gruffly, for someone to walk out to the notch she cut on the cove rocks as a girl of ten, at the highest spring tide anyone then remembered, and tell her where the water stands now. The player finds her granddaughter Eilidh already there, with the tide slate she keeps hidden in a crack in the rocks. The water has gone over Agna's notch twice this spring, and Eilidh has written it down and underlined it. Agna hears it in silence, and then tells Eilidh her slate is "not bad".

The slate, the notch and Brigid's dead trees go to Ailsa, Keeper of the Tide Book, who has watched the new pages drift from the old for years and has said only "Not yet." She wants tide marks from where the wardens' boats cannot go, and the player sets them for her on the Forest Jaw and out on the Skerries, fighting off what holds them. The marks agree with her pages: higher springs, a later slack, and the run drifting toward the forest cliff. Ailsa suspects the answer is already in the oldest pages of the Tide Book, in a Magician hand she can only half read.

The other half of the answer is in a song. Cormac, the old shanty singer at the Gap Inn, has never sung more than the first line of his verse about the gap, "the hour the water forgets", because he has never been sure of its ending. He is sure that Morven of the coves knew another version, and that her grandson Calder heard it. Coaxed by the player, Calder sings his grandmother's ending at last, quietly, over his nets. Cormac weeps, as he always does, and then he and the player carry the whole verse up to the Wardens' House.

It fits the oldest page. What the first camp's Savages kept as a song, its Magicians wrote in the Tide Book, and with the words of the one, Ailsa can finally read the other. Long ago, before the kingdom, the slack in the gap came late for a whole season and the run pressed against the forest cliff; the first wardens sounded the foot of the Jaw, found the rock there hollowed out, and found something great lying in the hollow. When it was driven back out to sea, the verse says, the water remembered its hour.

Old Varro, who has felt the eddies moving for years and never asked Ailsa about them, goes out with the player to the Forest Jaw at slack water and shows them where the eddy used to turn and where it turns now. Iska hears it all at the Wardens' table and gives the charge herself: at the lowest spring tide of the summer, go down under the Forest Jaw into the hollow the run has scoured there, and find what is lying in it.

The boss: the Undertow. In the Scour, a vast sea-hollow under the Forest Jaw that the water uncovers only at the lowest tides, lies a deeply touched deep-sea fish longer than any ship that comes through the gap, grey above and pale beneath, with a mouth full of curved teeth. Its bulk has bent the run of the water for years. It fights from the pools and channels across the floor of the Scour, dragging the water with it in rushes that pull at the player's feet, lunging from one pool and rising from another, and as the tide turns the water in the Scour rises and the fight grows harder.

When the Undertow is driven out, the next day's slack comes on its hour again, and Ailsa writes it in the Tide Book. The spring highs do not fall. They stay a hand's breadth above the old pages, and the first camp's page says nothing about that. Ailsa writes "Not all of it" in the margin and leaves it there. Brigid begins moving the healthiest of her herbs to new beds higher up the rocks, choosing each place the way her grandmother taught her, and Cormac sings the gap verse through, all of it, at the Gap Inn.

docs.title: The Sounding Caves
docs.text:
At the foot of the town's cliffs, between the Inlet Quay and the far cove, dark cave mouths open at low tide, and the water booms in and out of them. Nobody sensible goes in. Gwenna, the outfitter of the Lantern Market, was an adventurer until a bad fall in these caves, and she keeps a list of everyone who has gone in and not come back. Lachlan, who grew up in the coves, wants his name on the first true map of them, and he has started: a sheet of oilcloth marking every mouth, the tide each can be entered on, and how far in he has been, which is not very far. The caves are entered from the Fishers' Coves at low water, with Lachlan.

The Sounding Caves are a world of their own. Past the Mouths, the few dozen yards Lachlan has already mapped, a sheer fall that the cove people call Gwenna's Drop leads down into the dark. Beyond it the Long Echo runs on under the cliffs, where the sea surges through in rushes that a careful explorer learns to time, and at the end of the light lies the Still Pool, where the water should lie flat at slack tide, and does not. Cave crabs, blind bats, jellies that glow on the wet walls and small quick octopuses live in the caves, and the deeper in, the larger and stranger they grow. The caves are a match for whoever goes in: a young hunter and a seasoned one each find creatures worth their blade.

The story is Lachlan's. The first time, Ronan, the dreamy boy from the coves who thinks Lachlan the greatest hero in Goa Harbour, has gone down to a cave mouth with Lachlan's rope before anyone can stop him, and the player finds him there before Lachlan does. Further in, they find a tide mark scratched on the rock beside the letter A, where Lachlan's grandfather Alasdair stopped as a young man before he came out faster than he went in. Deep in, Lachlan admits what he has told no one: in the deepest cave he ever reached he heard the water moving where the tide should have been still, and turned back for the first time in his life. At the Still Pool they find out why.

The boss: the Inkmother. A vast, deeply touched octopus that has made the Still Pool its den, whose slow breathing, pushed through the narrow ways under the cliffs, is the water moving where it should be still. It fights from the pool with long arms that reach across the cavern, clouds of ink that put out the light, and broods of small octopuses that swarm the ledges. With it gone, Lachlan finishes the first true map of the Sounding Caves and writes the player's name on it beside his own. The caves stay dangerous, and new creatures always find their way back in, so hunters go down again and again.

docs.title: Leadership Today
docs.text: Iska has been First Warden for seven years. She learned the tides from Varro from the age of seven, and seven years ago the other wardens chose her to lead them and the town from the Wardens' House. Nessa was the other name spoken that night, and backed Iska herself in the end. Iska has skippered Goa Harbour's race boat for twelve summers.

docs.title: Notable People
docs.text:
Name Role Varro Eldest of the Sea Wardens, Iska's teacher Nessa Sea Warden Ailsa Keeper of the Tide Book Ruan Captain of the Cliff Watch Tamsin Boatwright of the race boat Torva Leader of the hunters

People

Everyone who lives here in the first release: People of Goa Harbour.

Design notes

New with this page: the shared Savage and Magician camp, the sea wardens and the First Warden, the meaning of the name "Goa", and the summer race with Bain Harbour. Goa Harbour is on the west coast, as the game's world map has it. New with "The Lands Around Goa Harbour": the Saltwood, Gull Heath, the stretches of the royal road (the Gorse Downs, the Saltwood Road) and of the Western Merchant Road (the Seaward Woods and Dusk Ford, as Urbanograd's page names them), the Gullwalk, the Strandwood, the Saltface, the Forest Jaw and the Sounding Caves, and their creatures and stories. The Forest Jaw story settles why the slack in the gap comes late and the run drifts, but not why the spring highs are higher: that, and what is pushing the creatures out of the deep Saltwood, stay open. What waits at Dusk Ford is left open. The verse ending and the first camp's page are paraphrased, not quoted, so their wording stays free. The town's look (a busy timber port: wooden quays and piers, warehouses and net lofts, ships at anchor in the inlet, colourful timber houses on the harbour front, and wooded hills behind) takes its inspiration from MapleStory's Lith Harbor; the cliff stairs, the rope lift and the rope bridges are the way up to the clifftop quarter and the paths above the harbour, not a town in the trees. New with that reshape: the clifftop quarter. Real-world inspirations: the sea lochs, skerries and saltings of rocky Atlantic coasts; the sea slater, a real shore creature; and the folk belief that a fox sweeps away its tracks with its tail.

docs.title: Kaldemor
docs.text:
The Town of Joyful Craftsmanship

Kaldemor is a cheerful pastoral town set among fertile fields, rolling hills and green countryside, "the greenest town this side of the old forest", as its mayor likes to say. Its heart is joyful craftsmanship: its people love making things with their own hands, growing their own food and living well together. Just under three hundred people live there, not counting the snails.

docs.title: One Seed
docs.text:
Every child in Kaldemor knows how the town began. Long ago, a traveller crossing the eastern meadows planted a single seed and slept beside it for the night. In the morning, the seed had become a tree taller than a tower.

People came from all over to see it, and some of them never left. They built their homes around the great tree, and then in it: the great treehouse behind the town square is the oldest building in Kaldemor. Nobody remembers the traveller's name, but the town still lives by the saying the story left behind: every great town starts with one seed.

Whether the seed came from the World Tree, as the Magicians of Fairy Forest suspect, nobody can say. But the soil around Kaldemor has been strangely generous ever since.

docs.title: Mushroom Houses and Windmills
docs.text:
That generous soil grows mushrooms big enough to live in, and Kaldemor's settlers did exactly that. The town's famous mushroom houses are real mushrooms, hollowed out, fitted with doors and windows, and painted in bright colors. They grow a little every spring, and their owners simply add another room.

The early settlers were mostly Commons: farmers, carpenters, potters and bakers. They planted the fields and orchards, raised a windmill farm in the park, and built workshops wherever there was room. When the Royal Road was laid from Selsior to the east, Kaldemor became the last stop before the eastern countryside, and its markets grew busy with travellers.

docs.title: The Clock Tower
docs.text:
The town's other landmark is the clock tower in the park. It was raised by the whole town together, a gift from every family and every workshop, and its bell has kept Kaldemor's time ever since. The terrace oven in the market was built the same year, by Rosa the baker's grandmother, and it has not gone cold since.

The clock stopped once, not long ago, when a Shroom from the woods carried off its great gear. The whole town held its breath until the gear came back and the bell rang again.

docs.title: The Town Today
docs.text:
Kaldemor is led by its mayor, chosen by the townspeople. Mayor Tobin has held the post for thirty years and knows every family by name. The town square sits in the middle, with the Market to the east for potions, weapons and bread, and the Park to the west with its clock tower and windmills.

Beyond the town lie the fields, hills and woods where young warriors learn their trade, and lately there has been plenty to learn on. Snails eat the gardens, Shrooms raid the woods, and something huge has settled in a hollow past the woods: a giant snail the townsfolk call the Snail King. The town's park ranger and drillmaster keep a close watch on the wilds, and they are always glad of help.

docs.title: Architecture and Environment
docs.text: Kaldemor is a town of colorful wooden houses and cozy cottages, mushroom houses and treehouses, workshops and gardens, barns and welcoming village greens. Beyond it stretch meadows, farmland, orchards, gentle hills and patches of woodland. It is a sunny, colorful place that seems to invite visitors in.

docs.title: Culture and Atmosphere
docs.text:
The people of Kaldemor value creativity, practical know-how, friendliness, cooperation and the quiet satisfaction of work done well. Traditional crafts are part of everyday life: woodworking, carpentry, pottery, baking and farming all shape who the town is.

Kaldemor is no poor backwater. It is a prosperous, happy town whose people love the life they have made. Where Selsior stands for the excitement and variety of the great city, Kaldemor stands for the joy of creating, growing and belonging to a close-knit community.

docs.title: The Lands Around Kaldemor
docs.text: Every young warrior in Kaldemor starts in the same two places: the meadow east of the square, thick with snails, and the hills to the west, where pigs root and orange mushrooms bounce along the slopes. From there three roads lead out into the world, and behind the woods past the hills lies a country that has grown far wilder this year than anyone in town likes to say aloud.

docs.title: The Royal Road
docs.text:
The Royal Road leaves Kaldemor by the west, over the hills and down into Kaldemor Woods, the old woods past the hills where Kaldemor's woodcutters worked for generations. The road runs between tall beeches here, and the woods are full of Shrooms and orange mushrooms that have lately stopped scattering when a traveller shouts. A path off the road leads to the hollow where Ranger Hale takes the bravest hunters to face the Snail King, and another, a farm track overgrown with hedges, turns south toward the last of the far farms.

Out of the woods the road climbs to the Crossing, a green hilltop with a gazebo where the lanes from the outlying farms meet the road, grazed by pigs and ribbon pigs and dotted with old stumps that walk when nobody is watching. Beyond it the road enters the Greenwood, a bright wood of tall trees and green mushrooms, and climbs out of it over the rise to the Selsior Approach and the capital's great gate.

It is a road travellers have always loved, and it has grown less kind this year. Pigs and stumps that once kept to the verges now come at carts. A pack of wild boars ran at the Guard's road patrol this spring, and something came out of the trees at Pell's cab at dusk last month and cracked two spokes. Carters now travel in company and keep their lanterns lit by day.

docs.title: The Verdant Coast Road
docs.text:
The Verdant Coast Road leaves the far side of the meadow and runs down through Kaldemor's farmland to the sea, green the whole way. First come the Cider Lanes, orchard lanes between hedges and apple trees, where snails creep out of the long grass and pigs gorge on the windfalls. Then the land flattens into the Greenmarsh, wide water meadows of reeds and slow channels, where marsh slimes wobble along the causeway, mud octopuses haul themselves out of the ditches and reed snakes strike from the edges. The road comes down through the dunes to Shellbrook Mouth, where a brook runs out across the sand and the Southern Coastal Road sets off along the south shore toward Goa Harbour, and follows the Strand, a long shingle beach full of scuttling crabs, east into Bain Harbour.

Every autumn Kaldemor's harvest carts go down this road with cider, flour, pottery and woodwork. Last autumn one of them never arrived. It lies tipped over in a reed bed in the Greenmarsh, its load spilled in the water. What turned it over, and what became of the people driving it, nobody has been able to say.

The Eastern Forest Road also leaves the meadow's far edge, running north through the woods to Fairy Forest.

docs.title: Beyond the Woods
docs.text:
The danger this year comes from the west, from the country behind Kaldemor Woods, and the people who keep watch over Kaldemor's fields have each seen a piece of it. The snails come at Wilbur's fields in lines. Elsie's cows will not graze the far pasture. Something gnaws the roots of Clem's youngest trees from below. Wilf's Shrooms carry shiny things away into the deep woods. From the lookout on Kaldemor Hills, Garrick has seen a line of broken treetops running toward the Snail King's hollow from somewhere much farther off. And Meg, who went farther than she has told anyone, felt the ground shudder under her feet on the far side of the woods, as if something far below had turned over in its sleep.

Followed back, these signs lead through three stretches of wild country, each deeper and more dangerous than the last.

docs.title: The Boarwood
docs.text:
The farm track from Kaldemor Woods ends at the Last Stile, where the hedges stop and the trees begin. Beyond it lies the Boarwood, the woods where Orin felled trees for forty winters, now churned to mud by wild boars. The boars came out of the deeper woods this spring, more of them and fiercer than any boar has a right to be, and they have been raiding the far farms ever since: the geese and hens and pumpkins missing from Mildred's ledger, the trampled trail across Wilbur's fields, the far pasture Elsie's cows refuse. Their tusks hook and wrench, and the curved gouges they leave are the marks Percy the wheelwright has been finding on broken wheels from the Royal Road.

At the heart of the Boarwood stands Stilebrook Farm, a farm empty since long before anyone now alive, and its old yard has become the herd's wallow. There lives Gnarltusk, the greatest of the boars, a deeply touched beast as tall as a cart, with tusks like ploughshares. It drives the herd before it, and where it charges, fences and young trees go down together.

Wilbur, who wants to know what crossed his fields, Mildred, who wants her losses counted, and Percy and Gareth, who have a wager on what made the gouges, all have a reason to send a hunter into the Boarwood. Orin has a reason of his own: forty years ago he cut his sign into the finest oak he left standing there, and he would like to know whether it still stands. Hale sends the hunters who come back to Stilebrook Farm.

docs.title: The Deepwood
docs.text:
On the far side of the Boarwood the trees close in and grow old. This is the Deepwood, the deepest part of the woods past the hills, where Wilf has gathered spores since he was a boy, and the boars ran from it for a reason. The Deepwood is full of mushrooms: horned mushrooms along the Humming Trail, where the wind sings through hollow trunks, mushrooms among the flowers of Windflower Glade, and great blue-capped mushrooms in the Bluecap Groves, where the light comes down blue through the caps. Shrooms swarm everywhere, bolder than ever, and the boldest carry off anything that shines.

The mushrooms have spread from a single place. In the Bluecap Hollow, at the woods' darkest point, grows the Bluecap Mother, a mushroom the size of a house, Disturbance-touched to the root, whose spores have filled the Deepwood with her brood. Her pale threads run under the woods for miles. They reach the edge of Clem's orchard and strip the roots of his youngest trees from below, and the mushroom houses of Kaldemor nearest the woods lean away from them, which is why Bertie, for the first time in fifty years, cannot hear what they want.

Wilf needs a hunter to walk with him through the Deepwood, and to find where the shiny things are going. Bess wants the cause of the bites from the woods that will not close. Winnie, quietly, wants to help Dottie find her lost lamb Button, and Molly wants to know why a pedlar who stops at the Sleepy Snail every summer is weeks late. In an old woodcutters' hut in Breezy Hollow, a quiet corner of the Deepwood, a hunter who looks hard enough will find all of them at once: Mott the pedlar, stranded there since the Shrooms stole his tinware, with a speckled lamb with a bent ear that wandered in out of the mist, and a fat, contented cat who answers to Mistress Whiskers.

The broken line Garrick saw begins at the Deepwood's southern edge. It was the Snail King's own road: the old giant snail Mano lived out its long life quietly in the far woods, until the boars came through and drove it ahead of them all the way to the hollow past Kaldemor Woods.

docs.title: Stonecap Keep
docs.text:
Where the trees thin out on the far side of the Deepwood, in the clearing where Meg felt the ground shake, stands Stonecap Keep. It was a fortress once, raised by the Aristocrats in the Age of Division to watch over the southeastern country, and it has stood empty since the founding of the kingdom. Kaldemor's generous soil has been at it ever since. Giant mushrooms have grown up through its courtyards, split its towers and capped its walls, until from a distance the keep looks less like a castle than a castle-shaped mushroom.

This spring the keep woke. Mushrooms now stand along its walls in rows, like sentries. Spores drift down its corridors in choking clouds, and on still evenings a grey spore cloud rises over it and hangs above the woods without moving, the same low cloud Nell has drawn three times in her book. Shrooms come to it from every part of the woods, each carrying something that shines: buttons, spoons, a pedlar's tin cups, once a clock tower's great gear. They carry them up the walls of the old keep road and the Battlements, through the Inner Ward, to the tower at the keep's crown.

There, grown up through the great hall and out over the top of the tower, sits the Cap King, a vast mushroom crowned with everything the Shrooms have ever stolen. It is deeply touched, and it is the oldest danger in the woods. When it rose, its roots heaved under the far country, shaking the ground under Meg's feet and sending the whole woods running. The Shrooms crowded to it, the Bluecap Mother's brood swelled behind them, the boars fled the Deepwood, and Mano fled the boars. Everything that troubled Kaldemor's fields this year ran from the same place.

Many of Kaldemor's people have a part in this last stretch. Hale wants Meg followed and brought home safe, and Meg wants company in the clearing, though she will put it as a dare. Nell has finally shown someone her page of grey cloud. Garrick wants to see the country from the top of the walls, Lottie wants copies of the old marks on the keep's gate for her notebook, Wilf wants to see where the shiny things went, and Mott wants his tinware back. Gareth would like some of the keep's old wall iron for his forge, and Bram has a draught in mind against the spores. In the end Hale wants to know what drove the Snail King out, and the answer is at the top of the tower.

docs.title: The Sleeping Stones
docs.text:
Not all of Kaldemor's troubles are out in the woods. Twice this spring Hob's windmill sails shuddered on windless mornings. One summer morning Mabel's jugs crept to the edge of her drying shelf, and one fell. Ewan, who listens to the clock tower the way other people listen to music, has heard it running a fraction fast, every day a little faster, as though something under the Park were pulling at it.

Something is. Under the clock tower, down a stair that Ewan and Alfie found when they lifted an old floor stone in its cellar, lie the Sleeping Stones: halls of carved stone, deep under the Park, older than Kaldemor itself. Nobody knows who built them. Their guardians are made of stone themselves, moss-grown figures that stood motionless in the dark for longer than anyone can reckon, and that the Disturbance has begun to wake. In the deepest hall, at the end of a long gallery, lies the Sleeper, a stone giant so large that its slow turning in its sleep shakes the windmills and pulls at the clock. Every time it stirs, the guardians stand up again.

Ewan keeps the stair. He lets down anyone he trusts who has the strength for it, and the guardians always seem to meet a hunter as an equal, however strong the hunter has grown. Hob would like his mornings still again, and Lottie would like copies of the carvings on the halls' walls. Ewan and Alfie would like one more thing, and they will ask it only of someone who can keep a secret: to compare a carving in the deepest hall with the one Alfie found on the old treehouse beam. What a hunter finds when they do, Ewan says, is to stay between the three of them.

docs.title: Leadership Today
docs.text: Mayor Tobin has led Kaldemor for thirty years. He was the town's cooper until, at forty-one, the townspeople chose him to follow old Mayor Hettie, mostly because he already knew everyone and nobody could imagine a town meeting without him talking at it. He is a widower; his wife Primrose, a potter, died twelve years ago. Every autumn he settles the price of Kaldemor's harvest with Bain Harbour's Harbour Master.

docs.title: Notable People
docs.text:
Name Role Mildred Town Clerk, keeper of the mayor's letters and ledgers Hale Park Ranger, who watches the fields and the hollow past the woods Quill Drillmaster, who runs the Kaldemor Gauntlet Ewan Clockkeeper for forty years Lia Town Guide Rosa Baker, keeper of the terrace oven

People

Everyone who lives here in the first release: People of Kaldemor.

In the game

Kaldemor is in the game today. See Kaldemor in the world guide for its maps, NPCs, quests and hunting grounds.

Design notes

The atmosphere is inspired by the bright, welcoming character of MapleStory's Henesys. The seed story, the treehouse, the mushroom houses, the clock tower, Mayor Tobin and the Snail King come from the game itself. New with this page: the guess that the seed came from the World Tree, and the clock tower being raised by the whole town.

The Lands Around Kaldemor (new): the Royal Road's Kaldemor stretch (Kaldemor Woods, the Crossing, the Greenwood), the Verdant Coast Road (agreed with Bain Harbour's page), and Kaldemor's three wild bands: the Boarwood with Gnarltusk (levels 20-30), the Deepwood with the Bluecap Mother (30-50) and Stonecap Keep with the Cap King (50-70), plus the theme dungeon, the Sleeping Stones under the Park, with the Sleeper. The chain of displacement (the Cap King's rising drives the Shrooms, the Deepwood's brood drives the boars, the boars drive Mano, Mano and the boars trouble the fields) answers Hale's question of what drove the Snail King out. Real-world touches: English hedgerow farms and stiles, boar wallows, mushroom rings and mycelium, and buried stone halls in the manner of barrows and stone circles.

Still open: who built the Sleeping Stones and why; what the carving in their deepest hall and the one on the treehouse beam show, who cut them and whether the likeness means anything (the one-seed traveller included); what overturned the harvest cart in the Greenmarsh and what became of its drivers; and why the Cap King rose this spring beyond "the Disturbance".

docs.title: Midbarium
docs.text:
The Highland Settlement

Midbarium is a rugged, rural mountain town and the ancestral home of the Savages' culture. It sits high in Veligor's dry uplands, among red-rock peaks, sheer cliffs, deep canyons and steep highland trails, and its people grew strong learning to live with them.

docs.title: The Land
docs.text:
The highlands around Midbarium are a hard, beautiful country. Rain is scarce, the sun is fierce, and the wind carries red dust down the canyons for days at a time. Above the town rise wind-carved mesas and bare stone spires; below it, dry riverbeds wind through rocky valleys dotted with caves, hardy scrub and the odd twisted tree. Nights are cold and clear, and the stars over the plateau are famous across the kingdom.

Life here follows the land. There are no grand fields like Kaldemor's. Instead, families farm small stone terraces on the slopes, watered by springs and carefully kept cisterns, and they drive herds of goats and other hardy beasts between the high pastures and the valley floors as the seasons turn. Many Midbarians live not in the town itself but in scattered homesteads and camps across the highlands, coming in to trade, to settle disputes and to celebrate.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Midbarium is built into the mountainside. Its houses are thick-walled and earthen-red, made of stone and sun-dried clay that keep out the heat of the day and hold warmth through the night. Heavy timber beams carry the roofs of the great halls, and terraces, carved stairways and swaying rope-and-plank bridges join the levels of the town across the cliffs.

Out in the highlands, herding families live in sturdy hide tents and stone shelters that can be moved or rebuilt with the seasons. Painted standards and carved totems mark the camps of each family.

docs.title: The Four Families
docs.text: Midbarium is not governed like Selsior. Its people belong to four great families, clans bound by blood, oath and shared history, and each family follows a chieftain.

docs.title: The Kragvar
docs.text: The stone-cutters. The Kragvar built Midbarium. Their ancestors cut the first terraces, raised the great hall and carved the stairways that climb the cliffs, and Kragvar masons still keep every wall and bridge in the town standing. In the Age of Division they were the hardest of the Savage warriors, and in the Balrog War they stood in the front line. Kragvar songs claim that some of their greatest fighters never came home from that war, but stayed beneath the World Tree to keep watch. The family keeps the council fire in the great hall burning, and counts that as its proudest duty.

docs.title: The Tolmach
docs.text: The herders. The Tolmach are the wanderers of the highlands. Most of the family still lives in hide tents and moves with its herds between the high pastures and the valley floors, as it has for longer than anyone remembers. They know every old path through the canyons and every spring that runs in a dry year, and that knowledge kept the Savages alive through the long wars. After the founding, it was Tolmach guides who first led traders from Kaldemor and Selsior up into the mountains, and they still bring most of the town's wool, hides and cheese down to market.

docs.title: The Uskari
docs.text: The hunters. The Uskari live along the canyon rims, and they are the best trackers, climbers and scouts in Veligor. They once hunted the great beasts of the plateau, and in the old wars they were the eyes of the Savage armies. Since the Age of Disturbance began, the Uskari have taken on a new duty: they patrol the highland trails, drive off the monsters that come up from the canyons, and see travelers safely from one camp to the next. Many young Uskari leave home to become adventurers.

docs.title: The Brenna
docs.text: The keepers. The Brenna are Midbarium's healers, storytellers and drummers. They know the highland herbs and how to set a broken bone, and they keep the memory of the families: the long songs that name every chieftain and every Old One back to the Age of Division, recited at every gathering. When the Savages and Magicians were allies, it was Brenna envoys who walked to the forests to talk with them, and the family still has old friends in Fairy Forest. The Brenna host every choosing, and their drums call the families together.

docs.title: The Chieftains and the Old One
docs.text:
A chieftain is not simply born to the role. When a chieftain dies, their family gathers around its fire and chooses a new one from among its own people, for strength, wisdom and fairness. A chieftain is expected to lead from the front: to walk the hardest trail first, to judge disputes fairly, to protect the herds and to look after the weakest members of the family.

Above the four chieftains stands one leader for all of Midbarium, whom everyone calls the Old One. The name is a title of respect, not a description: an Old One can be any age. The Old One is chosen the same way. When the Old One dies, the four families come together at the great hall, around the fire that is never allowed to go out, and choose the next. By custom, no family may hold the title twice in a row, so each Old One owes the role to all four families, not to their own.

The chieftains meet in council with the Old One to settle matters that touch the whole town. Debates are long and loud, but once the Old One closes the council, every family stands by its decision. Within Wonder Kingdom, the Old One speaks for Midbarium, and the families are as loyal to the kingdom as any lord in the capital.

docs.title: Culture and Atmosphere
docs.text:
Midbarium stands for strength, resilience, independence and respect for the ancestors. Its people admire anyone who overcomes hardship, and they guard the knowledge handed down by earlier generations: the old paths through the canyons, where water can be found in a dry year, and the stories of the four families.

Hospitality is sacred in the highlands, where a traveler turned away might not survive the night. Anyone who comes to a Midbarian fire in peace is given water, food and a place to sleep, no questions asked. Feasts, storytelling, contests of strength and long nights of drumming and song mark the families' gatherings.

For all its rugged looks, Midbarium is not hostile, primitive or grim, and it holds nothing against outsiders. Today it is a peaceful, welcoming town whose people are proud of both their ancestral traditions and their place in Wonder Kingdom.

docs.title: The Lands Around Midbarium
docs.text: The town itself is safe, as every town in the kingdom is. The highlands around it are not. Since the Age of Disturbance began, the red-rock country has grown harder to walk every year, and the Uskari Trail Watch, stretched thinner each season, holds the trails between the camps. Above the town lie the high ridges and the plateau; below it, the canyons. The Uskari like to say that every monster in the highlands comes up from the canyons sooner or later.

docs.title: The Royal Road
docs.text:
The royal road from Selsior climbs northwest off the central plain into the canyons. Its lower stretch, the Canyon Road, follows a dry riverbed between red walls, past Tolmach cairns and over a rope-and-plank bridge across a dry wash. Its upper stretch is the South Path, the old Tolmach caravan path that switchbacks up the last canyon to the town, along ledges a goat can stand on and a trader would rather not. Halfway up it, in a rock cleft, is the Greywater spring, which has run for as long as anyone remembers.

Dust boggles, quick little things that whirl up out of the dry ground, pester travelers on both stretches, and woken stumps have taken to the ledges near the top. Corwell of the Trading Post pays to have the road cleared for his caravans, and Ennek, the Tolmach guide, teaches the narrowest ledges of the South Path to anyone willing to walk them behind him.

docs.title: The Northern Woodland Trail
docs.text: The old trail to Fairy Forest leaves the town along the North Ridge, a high red ridge with an Uskari watch post and a view of the far-off woods. It drops down into the Edgewood, where the red rock gives way to the first trees, and on through the Young Woods to the forest's edge. The Brenna envoys walked it in the days when the Savages and the Magicians were allies, and the Brenna chieftain's spring letters to the forest still travel along it. Woken stumps hold the ridge, and the woods have creatures of their own.

docs.title: The High Ridges
docs.text:
From the North Ridge a path climbs onto the High Ridges: Windworn Hill, the Long Ridge and the Broken Ground, bare rock and wind, where old twisted trees cling to the ledges and the nearest Tolmach high pastures lie. The trees have woken. Stumps of dead wood and living trunk now walk the ridges, swing at anything that passes and root where they please, and they have driven the herds off the nearer pastures. The oldest of them, a great split tree called Old Gnarl, has rooted itself on Howling Peak.

This is where the Old One's quiet request begins: walk the patrols, and tell him the truth about them. Skarra, captain of the Trail Watch, has red marks on the ridges she wants checked; Sennu of the Tolmach wants a safe route back to a high pasture; Yarrek wants to know what his three goats met when they strayed down a ridge gully; and Tavi, chieftain of the Uskari, walks the worst stretch personally and will take company.

At the far end of the Broken Ground, the far canyon bridge swings across the Far Canyon to the far slopes. Vosk, the master of bridges, keeps it sound.

docs.title: The Far Slopes
docs.text:
Across the bridge lie the far slopes beyond the canyons, where rimwort grows and the Uskari once hunted the great horned beasts of the plateau. Old dry-season fires have scorched much of it. Past the Far Anchor, the ledge where the bridge's ropes are tied into the rock, the land runs out over the Scorched Slopes, the Boar Runs, the Ironback Flats and the Hot Rocks to the Ash Mesa.

The animals here have gone wild in the way an old Brenna verse describes: boars and flint-hided hogs that charge anyone on sight, and on the cliff below the Far Anchor, cliff gnawers, big sharp-toothed canyon rodents that climb sheer rock, nest in chewed rope and leave bites that fester. They are what has been gnawing the bridge's ropes by night. Above them all, a great horned plateau beast the Uskari call Grimhorn, huge, ash-coated and with one horn chipped, raids the Tolmach herds and returns to the Ash Mesa.

The story of the far slopes belongs to the town: two boys with a secret lookout and a notched stick, a bitten mason, a night watch on the bridge with Vosk and his apprentice Brakka, rimwort for Lessa the bonesetter, and Bekk, the young Trail Watch scout who wants to track the raider and has been forbidden to go alone. The great drum that calls the four families needs a new hide, and only a great horned beast's will do.

docs.title: The Withered Reach
docs.text:
Beyond the far slopes lies the Withered Reach, where the Disturbance lies thicker than anywhere else in the highlands. Dry storms break over it, bringing wind and lightning but never rain; the grass is dead and the trees are swollen and grey. Through the Dry Hills and the Weathered Rocks the way leads to the Old War Camp, the ruin of a Savage camp from the Age of Division that once held the highlands' western edge, where the Trail Watch now keeps a post. In the War Camp Ruins the camp's carved war masks have been stirred into moving, and hounds of bone and red dust prowl the broken walls. Beyond them, stone hulks, rock that walks, hold the Red Ravine.

The springs of the Reach are dying one by one, and the Greywater on the South Path, which ran through the driest year in living memory, has gone dry. In a hollow beneath the Red Ravine stands the reason: a vast dead tree, the Rootdrinker, which has driven its roots down through the rock into the deep water that feeds the highland springs and is drinking them dry.

Ennek, Sennu and old Mabbu of the Tolmach are at the heart of this story, with Brakka's eye for stone and Zirra's need for staves. So is Imre the stargazer, who has noticed that the stars low toward the island's heart sometimes shimmer as if seen through heat, and whose dates, set beside the red marks on Skarra's map, fall just before the worst stirrings of the year. Nobody can say why. The story ends in the great hall, at a gathering called by a drum with a new hide, where Ahvi the song-keeper sings an old verse about a season when the beasts grew wild before the Burning, and the four families say aloud in council what each of them has been too proud to say alone.

docs.title: The Dustfall Cave
docs.text:
Below the Uskari Rim, on the Trail Watch's canyon trail, a deep cave opens in the canyon wall. Ketta of the Uskari sheltered in it from a dust storm on her way home from adventuring, and the Uskari now call it the Dustfall Cave. It is reached from the rim by the Trail Watch's rope-way, and it goes down a very long way: through the Dustfall Mouth, down the Cliff Gallery, along the Cold Draught, where a wind blows up from below and never stops, and into the frost-rimed Chill Caves. Cave drakes have filled it and are breeding there.

At the bottom, in a lake in the dark called the Sunken Pool, lives the great drake Hollowmaw, grey-blue, frost-rimed and larger than any beast Ketta met in three years on the roads of Veligor. It is what she saw, and what saw her. Hunters of every strength go down into the cave again and again, because the drakes never stop coming up.

docs.title: Leadership Today
docs.text:
The Old One is Hask, born an Uskari. He led the Uskari as their chieftain for nine years, and six years ago, after Old One Varra of the Brenna died in her sleep, the four families gathered in the great hall and chose him through a long night of argument, drumming and song. He gave up his chieftainship that night, and the Uskari chose a new chieftain before dawn. Varra had been Old One for twenty-five years, and the Old One before her was a Tolmach, so no family has held the title twice in a row.

The four chieftains today are:

Family Chieftain Since Kragvar Dorrek 11 years, after his uncle Baruk died in a rockfall on the old north stair Tolmach Sennu 13 years, after old Bekku died Uskari Tavi 6 years, chosen the night Hask became Old One Brenna Odda 20 years

docs.title: Notable People
docs.text:
Name Role Ulm Keeper of the Council Fire Ahvi Song-Keeper, who remembers every chieftain and Old One Skarra Captain of the Trail Watch

People

Everyone who lives here in the first release: People of Midbarium.

Design notes

The geography and look are inspired by MapleStory's Perion. Midbarium is rural and mountainous, ruled by the chieftains of four families and the Old One, with a dry highland and desert feel. It should draw on highland, canyon and steppe cultures, not on Middle Eastern or Arabian desert cultures. Still open: how a family decides between rivals when it chooses a chieftain.

The lands around Midbarium draw on Perion's ridges, burnt lands, excavation ruins and drake caves. In the game, the roads hold levels 0 to 20; the High Ridges are the 20-30 band with Old Gnarl as its boss, the Far Slopes 30-50 with Grimhorn, and the Withered Reach 50-70 with the Rootdrinker; the Dustfall Cave is Midbarium's theme dungeon. Kept open on purpose: what makes Imre's stars shimmer; whether Grimhorn is the beast that killed Bekk's father; how Ketta got her scar; what Ahvi's verse means; and whether the bone hounds and moving masks of the war camp are anything more than the Disturbance working on what the old camp left behind.

docs.title: Selsior
docs.text:
The City of Everything

Selsior is the capital of Wonder Kingdom and by far the largest city on Veligor. It is a bustling fantasy metropolis: crowded, noisy, endlessly busy and remarkably diverse. People call it the City of Everything, and they mean it. Its residents trade, craft, teach, study, perform, govern and do a thousand other things besides, in marketplaces and workshops, schools and theatres, taverns and quiet residential lanes.

docs.title: The Treaty Field
docs.text:
Before there was a city, there was a field. When the Balrog had been sealed away, the leaders of the four peoples needed somewhere to meet that belonged to none of them. They chose a broad, empty meadow on the island's central plain, a day's ride from the World Tree, where the armies of all four peoples had camped together during the last months of the war. There, under open sky, they signed the founding treaty.

The field never emptied again. Envoys stayed to make the treaty work, traders came to sell to the envoys, craftsmen came to build for the traders, and within a generation the camp had become a town. The four peoples agreed to make it the seat of the new kingdom, precisely because it had never belonged to any of them.

docs.title: Growing Into a Capital
docs.text:
The Aristocrats brought the skills of building and government, and the early city looked much like their old fortress towns: thick walls, a stone keep and straight streets. But the Commons filled it with markets and workshops, Magicians founded its first schools, and Savage clans built halls for their envoys and their feasts. Over the centuries, Selsior outgrew every wall built around it, and the old quarters grew into the winding maze they are today.

The spot where the treaty was signed is now the central plaza. The Great Bell stands there on its dais, cast from metal given by all four peoples. It rings only when a new monarch is crowned, and the guards will tell anyone who asks that it rings for no one else.

docs.title: The Palace and the Crown
docs.text:
The kingdom's monarch rules from the palace at the head of the plaza, where the throne hall's red carpet runs up the palace steps. The crown's task, as Selsior's people like to say, is not to command the kingdom but to keep it together: to uphold the founding treaty, settle disputes between towns, keep the roads safe and speak for Wonder Kingdom as a whole. Each town keeps its own leaders and customs, from Kaldemor's mayor to Midbarium's Old One.

The Royal Vault beneath the palace keeps the kingdom's treasures and records, and its keepers will also guard the belongings of any citizen who asks.

docs.title: The Knights' Court and the Royal Guard
docs.text:
The Royal Guard keeps the peace in the capital and on the royal roads. Its home is the Knights' Court, where recruits drill from dawn and its captains train warriors in the way of the sword. The Guard is open to anyone from any town who can pass its trials, and since the Age of Disturbance began, it has had no shortage of work. Its ranks run from the Swordsman to the Swordmaster and the Grand Swordmaster, and old books name one more, the Sword Saint, earned by very few.

A warrior who passes the Swordmaster's trial is not a Swordmaster until they have sworn the Swordmaster's oath. They walk down the Upper Stair to Cavelor and swear it in the Oath Hall before the Keeper of the Oath, binding the Guard's blades to the founders' duty of keeping the Balrog imprisoned. The custom began with Queen Aveline's alliance with Cavelor fifteen years ago, when every serving Swordmaster and Grand Swordmaster went down to swear it, and every new Swordmaster has sworn it since.

docs.title: The Crown Market
docs.text: The Crown Market is the busiest place on Veligor. Here, Kaldemor's bread sits beside Midbarium's wool, Bain Harbour's fish beside Fairy Forest's herbs, and Urbanograd's strange inventions beside the finest blades in the kingdom. Its shopkeepers, apothecaries, weaponsmiths and armourers serve adventurers from every town.

docs.title: The Gate
docs.text: The city's great gate faces the Royal Road, which runs east past the Greenwood to Kaldemor. Gate guards greet every traveller, and taxis wait at the gate stand to carry visitors between the capital and the other towns.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Selsior is a classic medieval fantasy city. Timber-framed houses stand on stone foundations under brightly colored roofs, towers rise over the skyline, and cobblestone streets run between the neighborhoods.

At its heart lie broad avenues, great public squares, the palace and the city's most important civic spaces. Around them sprawl dense old quarters that grew without a plan: winding streets, narrow passages, hidden courtyards, crowded homes, little local markets, and skywalks that cross above the streets.

docs.title: Culture and Atmosphere
docs.text:
Selsior is cheerful, sociable and full of energy. Street performers draw crowds on every corner, dancers turn in the plaza, festivals fill the squares, and there always seems to be something to celebrate. The city is busy not only because people work there, but because its people love city life and throw themselves into it.

Folk from every corner of Wonder Kingdom live side by side in Selsior, and nobody thinks that strange. More than anywhere else, the capital shows what the founding of the kingdom achieved: prosperity, cooperation and a shared identity, with room for every kind of life and ambition.

docs.title: The Gates and the Roads
docs.text:
Selsior has three gates. The great gate faces east, the Tree Gate faces north toward the World Tree, and the Bridge Gate opens west onto the city bridge over the river, which runs down past the city's west side from the north. Every royal road begins at one of them:

  • The Royal Road to Kaldemor leaves by the great gate and runs east up the Selsior Approach, over the rise and on toward the Greenwood.
  • The road to Bain Harbour leaves by the great gate beside the Royal Road and soon parts from it, bearing east toward the coast.
  • The road to Fairy Forest leaves by the Tree Gate with the World Tree Road and bears away northeast once the hedges end.
  • The road to Midbarium leaves by the Bridge Gate, crosses the city bridge and climbs away northwest toward the highlands.
  • The road to Urbanograd leaves by the Bridge Gate over the city bridge and runs due west.
  • The road to Goa Harbour crosses the city bridge with the Urbanograd road and parts from it to bear southwest toward the far coast.

docs.title: The World Tree Road
docs.text:
The World Tree Road runs north from the Tree Gate to the foot of the World Tree, a day's ride across the plain. It is broad and well kept, marked every mile by tall old waystones, and busier than it used to be: royal couriers ride it with letters for the Tree, and every warrior who passes the Swordmaster's trial walks it on the way to the Upper Stair. The river is never far off to the west.

Outside the gate the road runs through the Hedge Lanes, farm lanes between tall hedgerows and orchards, where slimes and snails creep along the verges. Further on it crosses the Waystone Meadows, open grass where the great waystones stand and pigs and mushrooms have grown bold enough to block the road. Last come the Rootlands, where the plain rises and the Tree's outermost roots break the turf like low walls, and stumps that have learned to walk wander among them. The road ends at the Tree's foot.

The Road Patrol keeps the World Tree Road as it keeps the royal roads, and Lieutenant Edric posts bounties on all three stretches. Two ways lead off it into wilder country: east from the Hedge Lanes onto the downs, and west from the Waystone Meadows down to the river at the Quarry Landing.

docs.title: The Selsior Downs
docs.text:
East of the Hedge Lanes lie the Selsior Downs, the open downs beyond the capital: rolling chalk grassland, thyme and clover, sheepfolds, dew ponds and white chalk banks, where Selsior's shepherds have grazed their flocks for as long as there has been a city. Lately the shepherds have brought their flocks in.

The wild bees of the downs, which nest in the chalk, have turned mean, and boars have come up onto the grass from the woods to root up the folds. The danger grows the further one walks from the road: from Downs Edge, past the Thyme Banks where the boars wallow, to the Chalk Hives, where the bees have cut their nests deep into the banks. Beekeepers in the city say their own hives have been short-tempered since spring, and the palace gardener has been stung more this year than in all his life before.

Those who have gone to the bottom of it found the reason in the Hive Hollow, a hollow in the chalk walled with old comb, where Queen Amberwing rules the swarms: a Disturbance-touched bee queen grown larger than a calf.

docs.title: The Long Reach
docs.text:
From the Waystone Meadows a track runs west to the Quarry Landing, a stone wharf where the road from the quarries meets the river barges. Downstream of it lies the Long Reach, a deep, slow stretch of river between high banks, half a day upstream of the city, which the bargehands have learned to fear.

Since the roads grew dangerous the river has never been busier, and its creatures have never been bolder. Great lizards bask in the Reed Beds, crabs as big as cartwheels scuttle along the Long Reach Banks, and in the Undercut, where the river has eaten under the banks, larger lizards still lie in wait for anything that comes to the water's edge. Barges pass the Reach at speed now, if their masters are wise.

The worst of it is Longjaw, a deeply touched river beast as long as a barge, which hunts the whole river from the Long Reach down past the city. It flattens a cart-wide path through the reeds when it leaves the water, and lairs in the Heron Pool, the deepest pool of the Reach, where the herons used to stand before they left.

docs.title: The Upstream Quarries
docs.text:
Upstream of the Quarry Landing, on rising ground, are the Upstream Quarries, where the stone of Selsior has been cut since the first city was built. Terraced grey cuts climb the hillside among spoil heaps, cranes and sledge-ways, and a quarrymen's village stands among them, quieter than it was.

The stone has started to stand up. On the Spoil Heaps rubble gathers itself into small walking shapes; on the Terraced Cuts golems of solid rock step out of the faces the quarrymen were working; and in the Deep Cut, the oldest workings still in use, they are bigger, darker and harder to break. The quarrymen have stopped cutting the oldest faces. Nobody can say whether the golems slept in the stone all along or the Disturbance made them, and the scholars of the Academy, asked, say plainly that nobody knows. What is known, from the notebooks of an adventurer of the Crooked Lantern, is that they wake in waves.

At the top of the quarries is the First Cut, the ancient face that gave the first keep its stone. Out of it has risen Old Cairn, the Ancient of the Quarries, a golem as tall as a house.

docs.title: The Old Drains
docs.text:
Selsior's oldest danger is under its own streets. The Old Drains run beneath the old quarters, and below them lie the buried foundations of the first fortress-town that the Aristocrats built on the Treaty Field: its walls, its great cisterns, even whole streets that were walled over and built upon as the city grew.

For some months the night watch has heard something scratching under the gratings, slower and heavier than any rat. The rats themselves, grown as big as cats, have stopped running from lanterns and started moving up, out of the deep tunnels and into the cellars, and the mice under Theatre Row have fled to the rafters. When a grating in Steps Lane, a steep lane of the old quarters with steps instead of cobbles, was found pushed up from below, the Royal Guard set a watch on it.

Below Steps Lane the way runs down through the Old Drains themselves, into the pillared water halls of the Cisterns, along the Buried Street, a street of the first city with its doorways and lamp brackets still standing in the dark, and on to the Delver's Burrow. Fresh tunnels cut by great claws run through all of it, straight through walls the founders' masons laid. At the end of them waits the Delver, a deeply touched burrowing beast as big as a cart, blind and tireless, which has dug its way up from somewhere below. What drove it up, nobody knows.

docs.title: Leadership Today
docs.text:
Queen Aveline has ruled Wonder Kingdom from the palace for sixteen years. She was crowned under the Great Bell at twenty-eight, after the long reign of King Bertram, who sat on the throne for forty-two years and sent the Great World Tree Expedition. The Bell has not rung since her coronation. She is married to Leofric, once a road surveyor, and they have two children, Princess Elinor and Prince Alaric.

In the first year of her reign, Aveline became the first reigning monarch to walk down the Upper Stair to Cavelor, and she swore an alliance with its Keeper of the Oath: the crown answers every message from below. Eight years ago she made Rhys Captain of the Royal Guard.
